findings.requirement_type: Program Architecture — General Liability Policy Missing from Audit Scope
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance ... with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit. ... Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Comp/Op Aggregate: $2,000,000; Personal & Adv. Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000.
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.10, Page 6 of 41; Sacramento §III.A, Page 2 of 4
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No General Liability policy was provided for analysis. The two policies submitted (Gemini Tech E&O primary VIPL056495 and Convex Excess Tech E&O XPL000040-0425) are both Professional Liability coverage. The Gemini E&O expressly excludes 'Bodily Injury, Property Damage, ... emotional distress, mental anguish' (VP 00 06 10 17 §IV.C, Pg 8) — those exposures belong on a CGL form.
findings.gap_description: Both the Sacramento and Maricopa contracts require Commercial General Liability insurance with specific limits, blanket additional insured, primary & noncontributory, waiver of subrogation, severability, completed operations, blanket contractual, and (for Maricopa) no XCU exclusion and no action-over limitation. None of these requirements can be verified because no GL policy is in the audit scope. The E&O policy explicitly excludes BI/PD — a GL policy is therefore mandatory and almost certainly exists; it simply was not included in this audit batch.
findings.plain_english: We don't have your General Liability policy in this review — we only have your Professional Liability tower. GL is the foundation of every commercial program (third-party bodily injury, property damage, personal & advertising injury), and both your county contracts require it at $1M-$2M occurrence limits with specific endorsements (additional insured, primary & noncontributory, waiver of subrogation). Until we audit the GL policy itself, we cannot tell you whether you are compliant with either contract.
findings.recommendation: Provide the current Commercial General Liability policy (full forms list, dec page, all endorsements) so we can complete the audit. Until that's done, treat all Sacramento §III.A / §VII and Maricopa §8.2.10 GL-related compliance points as unverified.
discoveryQuestions: Can you send over the most recent GL policy and the full endorsement schedule? We want to confirm Sacramento and Maricopa's blanket AI, primary & noncontributory, and waiver of subrogation are actually endorsed — not just listed on the certificate.
Has anyone reviewed your GL endorsements line-by-line against the county contracts, or has the certificate been the extent of the verification?
When was the last time you had to produce actual endorsement copies (not a COI) to a county risk manager?

findings.requirement_type: Program Architecture — Commercial Auto Policy Missing from Audit Scope
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit ... not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles. ... Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit.
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.11, Page 6 of 41; Sacramento §III.B, Page 2 of 4
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy was provided for analysis.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test transports printed ballots and election mail across 31 states and DC — auto exposure is core to operations, not incidental. Both contracts require Commercial Auto with owned/hired/non-owned coverage; Maricopa requires $2M CSL and Sacramento $1M CSL. Without the auto policy, we cannot verify symbols 1/8/9, hired & non-owned auto, AI status, P&NC, waiver of subrogation, MCS-90 (if DOT-regulated), pollution endorsement CA 99 48, or fellow employee deletion.
findings.plain_english: Auto is a major exposure for you — you are physically moving ballots and election mail across the country. We don't have the auto policy in this audit, so we cannot confirm whether your fleet coverage meets Maricopa's $2M CSL or Sacramento's $1M CSL, whether the counties are properly endorsed as additional insureds on the auto, or whether hired and non-owned auto is included. This is a foundational gap that needs to be closed before either contract is performable.
findings.recommendation: Provide the Commercial Auto policy (dec, forms schedule, AI endorsement, WoS endorsement). If Run-Test is DOT-regulated for any election mail transport, also confirm MCS-90 status. Validate symbol selection (1 vs 7 vs 8/9) against actual operations.
discoveryQuestions: Walk us through how ballots and election mail physically move — owned trucks, leased vehicles, employee-driven personal cars, third-party logistics, USPS? Each of those triggers a different piece of the auto policy.
Are any of your routes DOT-regulated, or do you cross state lines with a vehicle weight that requires an MCS-90 endorsement?
When you bid into a county like Maricopa or Sacramento, who confirms that the county is named as an additional insured on the auto policy specifically (not just GL) before the certificate goes out?

findings.requirement_type: Program Architecture — Workers' Compensation Policy Missing from Audit Scope
findings.contract_quote: Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes ... Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit. ... WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California ... EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident.
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.12, Page 6 of 41; Sacramento §III.C–D, Pages 1–2 of 4
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No Workers' Compensation policy was provided for analysis.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is AZ-based with 50-200 employees and operates in 31 states + DC. Sacramento contract requires CALIFORNIA statutory WC — meaning either a CA monoline policy or 'Other States Coverage' on Item 3.C of an AZ-issued policy must include CA. WC waiver of subrogation is required by both contracts. Without the WC policy we cannot verify Item 3.A vs 3.C state schedule, EL limits, alternate employer endorsement (if staffing exposure), waiver of subrogation, classification codes, experience modification, or owners excluded status.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County is in California, which has statutory workers' comp requirements that are different from Arizona's. If you are AZ-based and dispatch any employee to perform work in California — even briefly to set up election equipment or train poll workers — you need California to be on either Item 3.A (specifically scheduled) of your WC policy, or in Item 3.C 'Other States Coverage' as a fallback. Both contracts also require waiver of subrogation. We can't audit any of that without the WC policy in front of us.
findings.recommendation: Provide the WC policy with Information Page (Items 3.A and 3.C), classification schedule, experience mod, and all endorsements (especially Waiver of Subrogation forms by state, Alternate Employer if staffing is used, and Other States Coverage). Confirm CA is on either 3.A or 3.C before any Sacramento performance.
discoveryQuestions: Do any of your employees ever travel into California — even briefly for a training, install, or election support — for the Sacramento contract? If yes, is California on Item 3.A or Item 3.C of your WC policy?

Do you use any staffing or temp labor, particularly during peak election cycles? If so, does the staffing firm carry the WC and is there an Alternate Employer endorsement on their policy in your favor?
When was the last time anyone walked the WC class codes against the actual operations — particularly the printing/mailing/equipment-handling split?

findings.requirement_type: Program Architecture — Cyber Liability Policy Missing from Audit Scope (CRITICAL)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for ... data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data, invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses ... network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber Liability policy was provided for analysis. The Gemini Tech E&O policy expressly EXCLUDES network security and privacy breach exposures: 'This policy does not apply to any Claim alleging, arising out of, or in any way related to ... actual or alleged ... network security failure, ... data breach, ... unauthorized access ... violation of GLBA, HIPAA, FTC §5(a), DPPA, CA SB 1386 ... Loss expressly excludes notification costs, credit monitoring, forensic, PR, fines, penalties.' (Endorsement #21, VP 09 97 06 22, Pg 44). It also excludes 'Extortion, blackmail or ransom' (End. #6, Pg 26) and 'Loss/transfer of funds, money, investments' (End. #6, Pg 26).
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County requires $5M cyber with a sweeping list of mandatory components — network breach, regulatory defense INCLUDING fines and penalties, cyber extortion, business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer, and third-party fidelity. The Gemini E&O endorsement #21 explicitly carves all of this out: data breach, GLBA, HIPAA, FTC §5(a), DPPA, CA SB 1386, biometric, notification costs, credit monitoring, forensic, PR, fines and penalties — all excluded. End. #6 separately excludes extortion/ransom and funds transfer. Run-Test handles voter data for 90+ million registered voters across 31 states; a breach could trigger 50-state breach notification statutes simultaneously. If no standalone Cyber policy exists, this is a catastrophic uninsured exposure AND a Maricopa contract breach.
findings.plain_english: This is the single biggest issue in this audit. Maricopa County requires you to carry $5M of dedicated cyber insurance with a very broad list of required coverages — including the regulatory FINES AND PENALTIES (not just defense), funds transfer fraud, third-party fidelity, business interruption, and ransomware. Your Tech E&O policy expressly excludes all of that. If you do not have a standalone Cyber policy in force right now: (1) you are in breach of the Maricopa contract, and (2) a single voter-data breach across the 31 states you operate in could be a business-ending event with zero insurance response. Notification statutes alone in a multi-state breach can cost $5-$25 per affected record before you even get to legal defense, regulatory fines, or credit monitoring.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — confirm whether a standalone Cyber/Privacy policy is in force. If yes, provide it for audit immediately. If no, secure $5M+ standalone Cyber coverage before any further Maricopa performance. Review the policy against Maricopa §8.2.13's enumerated requirements item-by-item: regulatory fines & penalties (not just defense), cyber extortion, computer fraud, funds transfer, third-party fidelity, business interruption, breach response (notification, credit monitoring, forensics, PR), biometric coverage if Run-Test handles biometric authentication. Limits should likely be substantially higher than $5M given the 90M-voter footprint.
discoveryQuestions: If a ransomware actor encrypted your ballot printing systems three weeks before a federal election, what's your plan — and which policy responds to the ransom payment, the lost election revenue, the forensics, and the extortion negotiator? The Tech E&O policy excludes every one of those.

You handle voter data for 90 million registered voters across 31 states. If a single laptop is stolen with that data, every state's breach notification statute is triggered simultaneously. Has anyone walked you through what that costs in notification and credit monitoring alone, before you get to litigation?
Does Maricopa know whether you have a $5M standalone Cyber policy in place today, or is the certificate hiding the fact that there isn't one?
Have you ever had a wire transfer fraud, vendor impersonation, or business email compromise incident? What happened and which policy paid?

findings.requirement_type: Program Architecture — Umbrella / Excess Liability Policy Missing from Audit Scope
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E, Page 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.9, Page 6 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Contract; Maricopa County Contract
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Umbrella / Excess Liability policy was provided for analysis. The Convex policy XPL000040-0425 is a single-line follow-form Excess Tech E&O — it expressly does NOT excess GL, Auto, or EL ('this policy does NOT excess GL, Auto, EL, or any other liability line — it ONLY sits over the Gemini primary Tech E&O').
findings.gap_description: If Run-Test is relying on an umbrella to bridge the gap between primary GL/Auto/EL limits and Maricopa's $2M CGL / $2M Auto CSL / $1M EL requirements, that umbrella is not in this audit. The Convex policy is NOT an umbrella — it is a dedicated Excess Tech E&O policy and does NOT provide coverage over GL, Auto, or EL. Without the umbrella in front of us, we cannot verify follow-form attachment, schedule of underlying, defense inside vs outside limits, drop-down provisions, maintenance of underlying clause, or punitive damages treatment.
findings.plain_english: If you have a standalone commercial umbrella sitting over your GL, Auto, and Workers' Comp policies, we don't have it in this review. The Convex policy people sometimes assume is the umbrella is actually a dedicated excess Professional Liability policy — it does not provide a single dollar of coverage over GL, Auto, or EL. Until we see the actual umbrella, we can't confirm that Maricopa's $2M GL and $2M Auto requirements are met, or that the umbrella properly follows form to your underlying policies.
findings.recommendation: Provide the Commercial Umbrella / Excess Liability policy (dec, schedule of underlying, all forms, all endorsements). Verify follow-form attachment to GL/Auto/EL and that primary underlying limits comply with the umbrella's required attachment points.
discoveryQuestions: Do you have a commercial umbrella sitting over GL, Auto, and Workers' Comp? If so, who is the carrier and what's the limit?
When you provide a certificate to Maricopa showing a $2M auto CSL, is that on the primary auto policy or are you stacking the umbrella to get there?

Have you ever had to confirm in writing to a county that your umbrella truly follows form — meaning every endorsement on the underlying flows up — rather than being a stand-alone excess form with its own carve-outs?

findings.requirement_type: Program Architecture — Course of Construction & Inland Marine Policies
findings.contract_quote: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR ... shall name COUNTY as loss payee ... Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation. Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: No Course of Construction or Inland Marine policy was provided for analysis.
findings.gap_description: COC is conditional and likely not relevant for an election-services manufacturer (no construction). Inland Marine, however, is highly likely for Run-Test given (a) high-value election technology equipment, (b) ballots and equipment in transit, and (c) the client-context flag of 'High-value equipment' as a special risk. If IM is in the program, it must include a waiver of subrogation in favor of Sacramento County. We cannot audit this without the IM policy.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County requires that if you carry Inland Marine — which is the policy that covers high-value equipment in transit and at temporary locations — it must waive subrogation against the County. Given that you handle expensive election technology and physically move ballots and equipment across multiple states, you almost certainly have IM. We need to see it to confirm the waiver is endorsed.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether an Inland Marine policy is in force. If yes, provide it for audit and confirm a Waiver of Subrogation endorsement in favor of Sacramento County (and any other county where required). COC is likely N/A absent physical construction work.
discoveryQuestions: What kind of equipment does Run-Test transport between facilities and county sites — ballot printers, mail sorters, scanning equipment? What's the replacement value of the most expensive piece in the field at any given time?
If a truck carrying $300K of election scanning equipment is in an accident, which policy pays for the equipment itself — Inland Marine, Property in transit, or are you self-insuring?
Have you ever had a county ask for proof of Inland Marine coverage with them named as loss payee or as a waiver of subrogation party?

findings.requirement_type: Program Architecture — D&O / Management Liability / EPLI / Crime Coverage Not in Audit Scope
findings.contract_quote: (Not contractually required by Sacramento or Maricopa, but operationally critical based on client profile.)
findings.policy_quote: No D&O, EPLI, Fiduciary, or Crime/Fidelity policies were provided for analysis. The Gemini Tech E&O contains broad exclusions for: Employment-Related Practices (VP 00 06 10 17 §IV.E, Pg 8), Third-Party Discrimination/Harassment (§IV.P, Pg 10), Loss/Transfer of Funds (End. #6 G., Pg 26), and ERISA/RICO/FLSA/WARN/COBRA (§IV.F, Pg 9).
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is PE-backed, has 50-200 employees, and operates in 31 states + DC — the EPL/D&O/Crime exposure profile is meaningful. The Tech E&O is a pure financial-loss policy; it expressly excludes wrongful termination, harassment, discrimination, retaliation (EPL); employee theft and funds transfer (Crime); and ERISA/Fiduciary. PE ownership heightens D&O exposure (regulatory scrutiny, governance disputes, transaction litigation). Without these policies in audit, we cannot confirm any of these exposures are addressed.
findings.plain_english: PE-backed companies your size typically need four other policies that aren't in this review: D&O (protects directors and officers personally from suits over governance, deal litigation, and regulatory matters), EPLI (wrongful termination, harassment, discrimination — your E&O excludes all of this), Crime (employee theft, computer fraud, wire transfer fraud — also excluded from E&O), and Fiduciary (ERISA exposure for the 401(k)). With 50-200 employees and PE backing, the absence of any of these would be a significant uninsured exposure. We need to know what you actually carry.
findings.recommendation: Provide D&O, EPLI, Crime, and Fiduciary policies if they exist. If any are absent, recommend them based on the PE ownership and 50-200 employee headcount. Crime is especially critical given the cyber-related funds transfer exclusion on the Tech E&O.
discoveryQuestions: Who's on your board, and how comfortable are they personally with the current D&O coverage given that PE-backed companies see roughly 30% higher D&O claim frequency?
If you fired a senior leader tomorrow and they sued for wrongful termination, age discrimination, and retaliation, which policy is paying defense costs from day one?
Have you tested your wire transfer controls against vendor impersonation? If your CFO authorized a $250K wire to a fake vendor, does any policy in your program respond to that loss today?
Does your 401(k) plan have a Fiduciary policy in place? PE ownership often triggers benefit plan design changes that can increase ERISA exposure.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Services Definition — Election Operations Coverage
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Professional Services means: 'Solely in the performance as an Election Services Firm including but not limited to: Election ballot services, printing ballot services, election printing, petition printing and services, election and petition design, ballot fulfillment, election hardware and software maintenance, support and technical services, outbound and inbound mail processing services, and election & petition products and services.'
findings.gap_description: The Professional Services definition has been bespoke-endorsed to align precisely with Run-Test's actual operations: ballot printing, election design, ballot fulfillment, election hardware/software maintenance, outbound and inbound mail processing, and election products. Endorsement #6 (VP 02 79 07 17 amendment) further extends coverage to Technology Services (data processing, software licensing, IT consulting, web hosting). The definition is industry-tailored and avoids the common gap of a generic 'consulting services' definition that fails to cover the actual work.
findings.plain_english: The carrier has tailored the Professional Services definition to specifically cover what you actually do — ballot printing, election mail, ballot design, election hardware/software support, technology services. This is an unusually well-aligned definition; many E&O policies for niche industries are written with a generic 'professional services' definition that leaves giant gaps when a claim hits. Yours doesn't.
findings.recommendation: No action needed — this is a well-constructed definition. Maintain at every renewal and confirm any new lines of business (e.g., voter registration data services, signature verification, biometric authentication) are added to the definition before they go live.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability Limits — Tower vs Contract Minimum
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Each Claim Limit: $5,000,000 / Aggregate Limit: $5,000,000 (Gemini primary VIPL056495). Excess: $5,000,000 xs $5,000,000 (Convex XPL000040-0425). Total Tech E&O tower: $10,000,000.
findings.policy_page: Gemini Dec page MPLDEC 07 19; Convex Dec page XPL-001 (01/24), Pg 6
findings.policy_file: Redacted2025 - 2026 Professional Liability Policy.pdf; RedactedConvex - 2025-2026 Excess Tech EO Policy.pdf
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §III.E requires $1M/$1M. The aggregate tower of $10M strongly exceeds the minimum. Maricopa §8.2 does not specify a Professional Liability minimum (only Cyber $5M is specified), but the $10M tower comfortably addresses any reasonable expectation. Note: see separate Split Limits finding — the full $10M tower is only available for Wrongful Acts committed on or after 04/01/2021.
findings.plain_english: Your $10M Professional Liability tower far exceeds Sacramento's $1M minimum and is appropriate for an election services firm operating across 31 states for 90M voters. Maricopa doesn't set a specific PL minimum, so $10M is more than enough there. The caveat — covered separately — is that the full $10M is only available for things that happened after April 2021.
findings.recommendation: No limit-shortfall action needed. See separate finding on Split Limits / tiered prior-acts protection.

findings.requirement_type: Split Limits of Liability — Tiered Prior-Acts Protection
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: Split Limits of Liability ... replaces the Limits of Liability section in its entirety with a tiered structure tied to when Wrongful Acts first commenced: (a) Acts on or after Retro Date 12/1/2007: $1M each claim / $1M aggregate; (b) Acts on or after 09/06/2019: additional $1M xs $1M each claim / $1M xs $1M aggregate; (c) Acts on or after 04/01/2021: additional $3M xs $2M each claim / $3M xs $2M aggregate. Effective full-tower $5M/$5M only available for Wrongful Acts first committed on or after 04/01/2021. Wrongful Acts committed between 12/1/2007 and 09/05/2019 are limited to $1M/$1M.
findings.gap_description: The Dec page shows $5M/$5M but Endorsement #4 silently replaces those limits with a tiered structure. A claim arising from a Wrongful Act committed before 09/06/2019 — for instance, a flawed ballot design or printing process used in a 2018 election that surfaces as a claim today — is capped at $1M, not $5M. Claims for acts between 09/06/2019 and 03/31/2021 are capped at $2M. This is uncommon and easy to miss because the Dec page is misleading.
findings.plain_english: Your $5M policy isn't actually $5M for everything. The fine print in Endorsement #4 says: if the underlying mistake happened before September 2019, you only have $1M. If it happened between Sep 2019 and March 2021, you only have $2M. You only get the full $5M for things that went wrong on or after April 1, 2021. For an election-services firm where a flawed system or print process can ship undetected for years and trigger a claim well after the fact, this is a meaningful narrowing — and it's not what the Dec page tells you.
findings.recommendation: (1) Push the carrier to remove the Split Limits endorsement at renewal and replace with a flat $5M/$5M from the policy retro date forward. If they won't move, (2) document the tiered structure explicitly in any internal limit summaries so the Dec page isn't misleading. (3) Identify any pre-2019 election cycles where Run-Test's work could still trigger a latent claim and assess whether $1M is adequate. (4) Consider whether the Convex excess applies to all tiers or only to claims that exceed the full $5M (likely the latter — confirm with carrier).
discoveryQuestions: Did you know that your $5M E&O policy actually only provides $1M for anything that went wrong before September 2019? When was the last time anyone showed you Endorsement #4 — most CFOs we audit have never been shown this language.
If a county sues you in 2027 over a ballot design used in the 2018 election, what's the limit available to defend and pay that claim? It's not $5M — it's $1M. Is that the answer you'd want?

Long-tail claims are particularly common in election services because election results can be challenged years after the fact. How comfortable are you with a $1M cap on anything from before 2019 — including Sacramento's prior business with you, if there was any?

findings.requirement_type: Mail Processing Services — Narrower Retro Date
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §V.A, Page 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.3, Page 5 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Contract; Maricopa County Contract
findings.policy_quote: Specific Professional Service Retroactive Date ... Retroactive Date of 04/01/2021 (instead of policy Retro 03/27/2017) applies specifically to 'outbound and inbound mail processing services.'
findings.gap_description: The policy retro is 03/27/2017, but Endorsement #1 carves out 'outbound and inbound mail processing services' with a much later 04/01/2021 retro. Mail processing is a CORE service for an election services firm — ballot mailing is the public-facing piece of every election cycle. Any claim arising from a mail-processing error before 04/01/2021 (e.g., misdelivered ballots in a 2018 or 2020 election) is excluded entirely.
findings.plain_english: The carrier carved out one of your core services — outbound and inbound mail processing — and gave it a later retro date than the rest of the policy. So if a county sues you over a mail processing mistake from a 2018 or 2020 election, your E&O won't respond at all. That's a four-year prior-acts gap on the most public-facing part of your operation.
findings.recommendation: Push at renewal to align the mail-processing retro to the master policy retro of 03/27/2017. If carrier resists, document the gap explicitly and consider whether older mail-processing exposures are still latent. If Sacramento or Maricopa contracts began after 04/01/2021, the contract requirement is technically met for those specific contracts — but ANY claim from older work is unrecoverable.
discoveryQuestions: Mail processing is half of what you do. Why would the carrier carve it out with a later retro date — what happened around 2021 that made them push that out?

If a 2020 election ballot mailing error surfaces in a lawsuit today, you have zero coverage for it. Are you aware of any pending complaints, county audits, or whisper of a claim that traces back to pre-April-2021 mail work?
When the policy renews next April, can we make the mail processing retro the same as the rest of the policy? It's worth asking — the carrier may have just done it as a default.

findings.requirement_type: Client Print Media Exclusion — Election Ballot Risk
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability or Errors and Omissions Liability: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: EXCLUDES Claims by clients of the Insured if Claim is a result of print media or Content furnished BY the client.
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #5 W. excludes any Claim by a client of the Insured if the Claim arises from print media or Content furnished BY the client. In election services, the COUNTY furnishes the ballot content (candidate names, ballot measures, voter rolls, addresses). If a county sues Run-Test alleging that the printed ballots were defective, miscoded, or mismailed — and the data underlying the print job came from the county — this exclusion arguably bars coverage entirely. This is the single most dangerous exclusion in the policy for an election services firm because it strikes directly at the core service-delivery model.
findings.plain_english: This is the most dangerous clause in your policy. The carrier has excluded claims from your customers when the print job is based on data the customer gave you. In your business, that's almost every job — the county sends you the ballot text, the candidate list, and the voter mailing addresses, and you print and mail. If a county sues you saying 'your ballot was wrong' or 'the wrong ballots went to the wrong voters,' the carrier can point at this exclusion and walk away. It's an enormous gap that's masquerading as standard print-media boilerplate.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — negotiate a carve-back at renewal that exempts election services from the Client Print Media exclusion, OR add language confirming that liability arising from the Insured's Wrongful Acts in handling, formatting, processing, or mailing client-furnished content remains covered. The current language is incompatible with the actual service model. Document the issue in writing with the carrier and broker. Consider whether to walk to a new market that won't apply this exclusion to election services.
discoveryQuestions: Walk through a typical Sacramento ballot job — where does the ballot content come from, where do the voter addresses come from, who controls the mail merge? Now: how much of that data flow is 'furnished by the client'?

Have you ever had a county dispute over a misprinted or mis-mailed ballot? What was the basis — your error, or theirs giving you bad data? Either way, your carrier is going to argue the data was 'furnished by the client.'
If a county sues you in November alleging your ballots disenfranchised voters — and the data came from their voter file — which policy responds? Right now the answer may be 'none of them.'
Has the carrier or broker ever flagged Endorsement #5 W. to you specifically? It's the single biggest gap in this policy and most clients have never seen it.

findings.requirement_type: Delay in Performance Exclusion — Time-Critical Election Work
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: [Excludes] delay in performance or delivery of Technology Products, services, or contractual obligations.
findings.policy_page: Endorsement #6 (Technology Services Extension), Section D, Pg 26
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #6 D. excludes claims arising from 'delay in performance or delivery' of Technology Products, services, or contractual obligations. Election work is uniquely time-critical: ballots must be printed, mailed, and counted by hard statutory deadlines. A delay claim — e.g., late ballot delivery causing voter disenfranchisement — is one of the most foreseeable claim patterns for this client and is excluded.
findings.plain_english: Election work has hard, statutory deadlines — ballots have to be in voters' hands by specific dates, period. Your E&O excludes any claim arising from being late. So if a press jam, a courier problem, or a software glitch delays a ballot mailing and a county sues you over it, the carrier won't pay. This is one of the most predictable claim patterns in your industry, and it's specifically excluded.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate a carve-back at renewal that confirms delay claims arising from a Wrongful Act of the Insured remain covered (the standard carve-back is 'except where caused by a negligent act, error or omission'). This is a common giveback in well-negotiated tech E&O forms.
discoveryQuestions: Election deadlines are statutory — ballots have to mail by a date specified in state law. What's your contingency if a press goes down 48 hours before mail-out, and what's the worst-case county claim if you miss?
How many of your county contracts have liquidated damages tied to delivery dates? When you signed those, did anyone mention that your E&O carrier excludes delay claims?
Has Run-Test ever paid liquidated damages or settled a complaint over late ballot delivery? Where did that money come from — operations, or insurance?

findings.requirement_type: Recall / Reprinting Exclusion — Defective Ballot Reprints
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes recall, withdrawal, remediation, replacement, or reprinting of print media alleged to cause Media Injury.
findings.gap_description: If a printed ballot is defective — wrong candidate, wrong ballot measure language, wrong voter precinct — and has to be reprinted and remailed, the cost of the reprint and re-mail is excluded. For an election services firm, this is the most common loss scenario and it's excluded.
findings.plain_english: If a ballot has to be reprinted because of a defect — wrong measure language, wrong candidate name, wrong precinct — the cost of doing it over isn't covered. That's the most common kind of loss in your business, and it's excluded. You'd still have defense for any third-party claim that resulted, but the actual reprint cost (which can be six or seven figures for a large county election) lands on your P&L.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate a Recall Expense buyback or sublimit at renewal. Some markets will offer a $100K-$500K Recall sublimit specifically for ballot reprinting. Alternatively, factor the uninsured reprint exposure into pricing on every county contract.
discoveryQuestions: How many ballot reprints does Run-Test handle in a typical election year, and what's the largest reprint cost you've absorbed in the last five cycles?
When a defect is caught at the press, does that cost go to the customer or to Run-Test? How do you reserve for it?
Would a $250K recall sublimit on the E&O materially change your year-end results in an election year?

findings.requirement_type: Hardware Malfunction & Internet Service Failure Exclusions
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: [Excludes] hardware malfunction (unless solely from Wrongful Act); electrical failure (unless solely from Wrongful Act); ... Internet failure/outage by ISP not owned by Insured.
findings.policy_page: Endorsement #6 (Technology Services Extension), Sections A, B, E & F, Pg 26
findings.gap_description: Hardware/electrical/ISP failures are excluded except when 'solely caused by Insured's Wrongful Act.' That carve-back is narrow: most hardware failures have multiple contributing causes and the 'solely' standard is hard to meet. For a tech-enabled election services firm running ballot printers, mail sorters, and election technology hosting, this is a non-trivial coverage limitation. The Internet/ISP exclusion is listed twice (likely a drafting error) — both paragraphs E and F say substantively the same thing.
findings.plain_english: If a printer fails, a server crashes, or an internet outage interrupts your ballot processing — and the carrier can argue that hardware or ISP failure (not just your error) was a contributing factor — they don't pay. The 'solely your fault' carve-back is too narrow to be useful in most claim scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate the carve-back from 'solely from Wrongful Act' to 'arising in part from Wrongful Act' or remove the exclusion entirely. Confirm that any Cyber policy in the program covers system failure / network business interruption to fill the gap. Flag the duplicate Internet exclusion (E & F) as a drafting defect to be cleaned up.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Standalone Cyber policy if in force — verify that 'system failure' and 'network business interruption' are included.
discoveryQuestions: If a ballot scanning system has both a hardware failure AND your team's setup was incorrect, your carrier can argue it wasn't 'solely' your fault. Have you tested that with the broker?
Where does Run-Test's election-day technology run — your servers, AWS, county hardware? Each of those creates a different argument the carrier can use to invoke this exclusion.
Is there a standalone cyber policy that picks up system failure and network business interruption? If not, this is a real gap.

findings.requirement_type: Network Security & Privacy Breach Exclusion — Confirms Need for Standalone Cyber
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes ... data breach, network security failure, mishandling of confidential/personal information, GLBA, HIPAA, FTC §5(a), DPPA, CA SB 1386 violations. ... Loss expressly excludes notification costs, credit monitoring, forensic, PR, fines, penalties.
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #21 carves out everything cyber-related from the E&O — network security, data breach, regulatory violations, notification, credit monitoring, forensic, fines & penalties. The endorsement notes 'Does NOT apply if a Cyber Coverage Endorsement is attached.' No such endorsement is on this policy. Coverage MUST exist on a standalone Cyber policy. This is partly an architectural finding and partly a confirmation of the criticality of finding-004 (missing cyber).
findings.plain_english: Your E&O policy has been deliberately stripped of all cyber-related coverage and all data breach response costs. The carrier is essentially saying 'go buy a separate Cyber policy.' If you don't have one, you have a massive uninsured exposure. If you do have one, this E&O endorsement is fine — it just confirms the cyber risk lives somewhere else.
findings.recommendation: Confirm that a standalone Cyber policy is in force (see finding-004). If yes, audit the Cyber policy against Maricopa's enumerated requirements (regulatory fines & penalties, cyber extortion, business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer, third-party fidelity). If no, this gap is catastrophic and Maricopa is in breach.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Standalone Cyber policy (NOT in audit scope)
discoveryQuestions: Do you have a standalone Cyber policy in force right now? Who is the carrier and what is the limit?

If yes — has anyone walked the Cyber policy line-by-line against Maricopa §8.2.13's required list (regulatory fines & penalties, cyber extortion, computer fraud, third-party fidelity, business interruption)?
If no — when was the last time anyone explained to you that the E&O explicitly excludes cyber, and that you are operating without coverage for the highest-impact loss scenario in your industry?

findings.requirement_type: Biometric Identifiers / Information Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes any Claim alleging violation of statutes governing collection/use/storage/destruction of biometric identifiers or information.
findings.gap_description: Absolute biometric exclusion (BIPA-style) — Illinois BIPA, Texas CUBI, Washington H.B. 1493, and similar statutes. If Run-Test handles signature verification (which is a form of biometric in many state laws), fingerprint authentication, voice authentication, or any biometric piece of voter identity verification, this exclusion will be invoked. BIPA statutory damages are $1K-$5K per violation per person — for an election services firm processing millions of voter records, the math is catastrophic.
findings.plain_english: Some states (Illinois most notably, but also Texas and Washington) have biometric privacy laws that allow $1K-$5K per affected person in statutory damages. If you process anything that could be characterized as biometric — signature verification, fingerprint, voice — and a class action hits, your E&O won't respond. Even if you don't currently do biometric, this is worth confirming because election authentication is moving in that direction.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Run-Test's signature verification process triggers any state biometric privacy statute. If yes, push for a biometric carve-back at renewal or seek a standalone biometric extension on the Cyber policy. If no, document the limitation and re-evaluate before any new biometric authentication line of business launches.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Standalone Cyber policy if biometric is endorsed in
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test's signature verification process count as 'biometric' under Illinois BIPA, Washington's biometric statute, or any state law where you operate? Has your privacy counsel weighed in?
Are there any pending product expansions into fingerprint, voice, or facial recognition for voter authentication? If yes, when does that launch and is the policy ready?
If a class action under Illinois BIPA hit you tomorrow alleging $1K per voter signature processed, which policy responds? Today the answer is none.

findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge — Officer-Limited Reporting
findings.contract_quote: (Not specifically required by contract, but standard broker best practice — General RMF #4)
findings.policy_quote: Notice trigger limited to awareness by CEO, CFO, General Counsel, or Risk Manager (rather than 'any Insured').
findings.gap_description: The default Notice & Knowledge trigger imputes any Insured's knowledge to the company. Endorsement #3 limits the trigger to four named senior officers (CEO, CFO, GC, Risk Manager). This is the broker best-practice construction and protects the policyholder from a low-level employee's failure to report internally voiding the entire policy.
findings.plain_english: If a junior employee gets a complaint and never escalates it, your old self wouldn't have been protected — the carrier could argue the company 'knew' and failed to report. This endorsement says coverage is only voided if your CEO, CFO, General Counsel, or Risk Manager actually had knowledge. That's the right way to do it.
findings.recommendation: No action — maintain at every renewal. Confirm the named roles still match the actual organization (e.g., if titles change after a PE transaction).

findings.requirement_type: Hammer Clause — 80/20 Consent to Settle
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: If Named Insured refuses Company's recommended settlement, carrier liability capped at recommended settlement amount + 80% of Claim Expenses and Loss in excess of recommended amount. Insured bears 20%.
findings.gap_description: Standard 80/20 hammer clause. If carrier recommends settling at $1M and Insured refuses, then case settles at $3M, the carrier pays $1M (recommended) + 80% of the $2M excess = $2.6M, leaving the Insured to pay $400K. This is moderate insured exposure relative to a 'soft' (no consent) or 'pure' (insured-controlled with no penalty) hammer.
findings.plain_english: If your carrier wants to settle a case and you say no, you'll pay 20% of whatever it costs from that point forward. So if the carrier wants to settle for $1M and you push for trial and lose at $3M, you write a $400K check. It's not the worst hammer clause out there — some are 100% insured-pays-all-excess — but it's not the best either. For high-stakes election cases where reputation matters, you may want a softer clause.
findings.recommendation: Push at renewal for a softer hammer (e.g., 50/50 or pure consent-to-settle for reputation-sensitive cases). At minimum, document the clause for senior leadership so refusal-to-settle decisions are made with the financial consequences understood.
discoveryQuestions: Election cases often have reputational consequences that go beyond the dollar amount of the settlement — are there scenarios where Run-Test would want to fight rather than settle? If so, the 20% you'd owe could be material.
Have you ever had a carrier push to settle a case you wanted to defend? How did that conversation go?
Would a 50/50 hammer clause be worth pursuing at renewal?

findings.requirement_type: Self-Insured Retention — $25K Self-Administered Defense
findings.contract_quote: Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §IV, Page 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.6, Page 5 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Contract; Maricopa County Contract
findings.policy_quote: Self-Insured Retention of $25,000 per claim. Insured must pay SIR for both Loss and Claim Expenses BEFORE carrier has any obligation. Carrier has no duty to defend until SIR exhausted ... Insured bears investigation/defense within SIR using Company panel counsel as Claim Service Provider. Cannot settle claims exceeding SIR without carrier consent.
findings.gap_description: $25K SIR is moderate, but the construction is operationally burdensome: Insured must self-administer defense within SIR using carrier-approved panel counsel, must report any claim where reasonable estimate exceeds 50% of SIR ($12.5K) or any class action, and Sacramento/Maricopa both require SIR disclosure and approval. Maricopa §8.2.6 may require Run-Test to post a bond or LOC as security for the SIR.
findings.plain_english: Your policy has a $25,000 self-insured retention — meaning Run-Test pays the first $25K of any claim's defense and settlement before the carrier picks up. You also have to administer that defense yourself using approved panel attorneys, report claims aggressively, and get carrier consent before settling. Both Sacramento and Maricopa require this SIR to be disclosed and approved, and Maricopa specifically reserves the right to require a bond or letter of credit as security. That's a real operational and capital burden the CFO should understand.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm SIR has been formally disclosed and approved by Sacramento and Maricopa risk managers. (2) Establish a panel-counsel relationship now, before a claim hits, so defense response is fast. (3) Build internal claim-reporting protocol that triggers at the 50%-of-SIR estimate and on any class-action or 3+-claimant matter. (4) Confirm Maricopa has not required a bond or LOC; if they have, structure it cost-effectively.
discoveryQuestions: Have Sacramento and Maricopa formally approved the $25K SIR in writing? If not, you're technically out of compliance with both contracts.
Has Maricopa required you to post a bond or letter of credit as security for the SIR? They have the right to under §8.2.6.
Who is your designated claim administrator and panel counsel today, and how fast can they spin up if you get a complaint on a Friday afternoon?

findings.requirement_type: Pending and Prior Litigation Date — 03/26/2017
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement.
findings.policy_quote: P&P Litigation Date: 3/26/2017. Excludes Loss/Claim Expenses arising out of pending or prior Claims, suits, or litigation existing prior to 3/26/2017, or future Claims related/associated with such matters.
findings.gap_description: P&P Litigation Date of 3/26/2017 is a long-standing date that should not affect any current Sacramento or Maricopa contract performance. Verify with Run-Test legal/risk that there are no known pre-2017 matters that could surface as related future claims.
findings.plain_english: The policy doesn't pay for anything tied to a lawsuit or complaint that was already on file before March 2017. That's almost a decade ago. Unless you have a known matter from before then that could resurface, this is fine.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Run-Test legal that no pre-3/26/2017 matters are known or pending. Maintain at renewal — don't let the carrier push the date forward (forward movement narrows protection).

findings.requirement_type: Communicable Disease Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Absolute exclusion for any Claim alleging/arising out of/attributable to any actual or alleged Communicable Disease — including supervisory/hiring/training acts, testing failures, prevention failures, reporting failures, and related communications.
findings.gap_description: Standard post-COVID communicable disease exclusion. For an election services firm with poll-worker training contracts and high-volume voter-facing operations during pandemic conditions, the exclusion is broad enough to capture training-related, supervisory, and reporting-related claims.
findings.plain_english: Any claim that touches on communicable disease — even indirectly through training, supervision, or reporting — is excluded. This is now standard across the market post-COVID. The likelihood is low for a printing and mail processing operation, but if you ever do on-site poll worker training during a pandemic and someone alleges your training caused exposure, no coverage.
findings.recommendation: Acknowledge as a standard market-wide exclusion. If communicable disease becomes a meaningful exposure (e.g., new pandemic, on-site county work), seek a separate communicable disease coverage extension.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test do any in-person poll worker training, on-site county work, or anything voter-facing that could create communicable-disease exposure?
Are there any state or county contracts that flow communicable-disease indemnity obligations to the contractor? If so, those obligations are uninsured.

findings.requirement_type: Loss/Transfer of Funds Exclusion — Confirms Crime Coverage Need
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes loss/transfer/attempted transfer of any funds, money, investments, or assets.
findings.policy_page: Endorsement #6 (Technology Services Extension), Section G, Pg 26
findings.gap_description: E&O explicitly excludes funds-transfer loss. This must be addressed by Crime/Cyber. Maricopa §8.2.13 requires 'computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity' — meaning these need to live on Crime or Cyber. Without those policies in scope, this is an uncovered exposure.
findings.plain_english: If a wire transfer fraud, vendor impersonation, or business email compromise hits Run-Test and money goes out the door, your E&O does not pay. This needs to live on a Crime policy or a Cyber policy that includes computer fraud and funds transfer fraud. Confirm at least one of those covers it.
findings.recommendation: Verify funds transfer / computer fraud is covered on Crime or Cyber. Confirm sublimit is sufficient (typical $250K-$1M). For a PE-backed company with multiple county relationships and recurring vendor wires, $250K is usually low.
findings.covered_by_other_policy: Should be — depends on Crime / Cyber
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Crime policy or Cyber policy (NOT in audit scope)
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test ever experienced a wire fraud, fake vendor, or BEC incident? Frequency and severity have exploded in 2024-2026.
Who has wire authority — and is there dual approval over a threshold? What's the threshold?
Do you have a Crime policy with computer fraud and funds transfer included? What's the sublimit?

findings.requirement_type: TCPA / Unsolicited Communications Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Unsolicited Faxes and Electronic Mail (TCPA) exclusion.
findings.gap_description: TCPA exclusion is standard but worth flagging because Run-Test handles outbound voter mail and may also handle voter outreach (text, email, phone). TCPA class actions have statutory damages of $500-$1500 per violation. If any voter outreach can be characterized as 'unsolicited,' the exposure can scale rapidly.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test sends voter outreach by text, email, or phone — even on behalf of a county — TCPA class action plaintiffs can argue those communications were 'unsolicited' and seek $500-$1500 per voter contacted. That's a class action waiting to happen and your E&O won't respond.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm scope of voter outreach activities — does Run-Test send anything beyond physical mail? (2) If yes, audit consent records and contract indemnity language to confirm TCPA risk is contractually transferred to the county. (3) Consider TCPA-specific buyback if outreach is meaningful. Cyber/Privacy policies often include narrow TCPA defense extensions.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Standalone Cyber policy if TCPA defense extension is endorsed
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test send any text messages, automated phone calls, or marketing emails to voters or constituents? Even on behalf of a county client?
If yes — what's the consent process and where's the documentation if a TCPA class action gets filed?
Do your county contracts indemnify you against TCPA claims for outreach that uses county-provided contact data?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice — Carrier-Side Provision
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa: 'Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. ... Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice ...' Sacramento: 'Contractor is required by this Agreement to immediately notify County if they receive a communication from their insurance carrier or agent that any required insurance is to be canceled.'
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.15, Page 7 of 41; Sacramento §VI.A.2, Page 3 of 4
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County Contract; Sacramento County Contract
findings.policy_quote: Cancellation: 60 days (other) / 10 days (nonpayment).
findings.gap_description: Sacramento places the notification obligation on the Contractor (not the carrier) — so a 30-day Designated Entity NOC endorsement is not strictly required there. Maricopa requires '30 days prior written notice TO Maricopa County' — this is best satisfied by a Designated Entity NOC endorsement, but the contract also accepts a 2-business-day pass-through from Contractor to County after receiving carrier notice. The Gemini 60-day standard cancellation provision is favorable. Convex follows form. Both meet Maricopa's 30-day floor and Sacramento's pass-through model.
findings.plain_english: Your E&O gives 60 days notice of cancellation, which is better than the 30 days Maricopa requires. Sacramento's contract just makes you (the contractor) responsible for telling them within their stated timeframe — no carrier endorsement needed. You're in compliance on cancellation notice for both contracts.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the 60-day cancellation provision at renewal. Build an internal protocol so that any cancellation notice from the carrier is forwarded to Maricopa within 2 business days as required.

findings.requirement_type: Carrier Rating — Surplus Lines / Non-Admitted Carriers
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.' Maricopa: 'Contractor ... shall purchase and maintain ... insurance from a company or companies duly licensed by the State of Arizona and possessing an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.'
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VI.A.1, Page 3 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.1, Page 5 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Contract; Maricopa County Contract
findings.policy_quote: Gemini Insurance Company (W.R. Berkley group; non-admitted in Arizona — surplus lines). Convex Insurance UK Limited (UK FCA/PRA regulated; surplus lines / non-admitted in AZ).
findings.policy_page: Gemini Dec; Convex Dec page (Pg 6) and CUS-003 Service of Suit (Pg 15)
findings.gap_description: Both PL carriers are surplus lines / non-admitted. Surplus lines placement is appropriate for niche election services tech E&O — admitted markets rarely write this risk. The questions are: (1) Does Gemini meet Sacramento's A-VII (A- and Size VII = $25M-$50M policyholder surplus)? Gemini is part of W.R. Berkley, which is rated A+ (Superior) by AM Best — Gemini itself typically inherits A or A+. Verify current rating. (2) Does Convex meet Sacramento's A-VII and Maricopa's B++? Convex Insurance UK Limited is part of Convex Group (Bermuda parent); AM Best rating must be confirmed. (3) Sacramento allows the Risk Manager to waive — confirm Sacramento has approved the surplus lines placement in writing.
findings.plain_english: Your two Professional Liability carriers are both 'surplus lines' — meaning they're not admitted in Arizona. That's normal and appropriate for niche election services E&O. But Sacramento County requires A.M. Best A-VII or better, and Maricopa requires B++. We need to verify current ratings on both Gemini and Convex against those minimums. If Gemini is A or A+ (likely, since it's part of W.R. Berkley), Sacramento is fine. Convex is the question mark — UK regulated, fairly new — confirm current AM Best rating.
findings.recommendation: (1) Pull current AM Best ratings for Gemini Insurance Company and Convex Insurance UK Limited. (2) If either fails Sacramento A-VII, obtain Risk Manager written waiver. (3) Document surplus lines placement on annual COI as required by AZ surplus lines disclosure rules. (4) Note guaranty fund non-applicability in writing for client.
discoveryQuestions: What's the current AM Best rating on Convex Insurance UK Limited? Do you have it in writing from the broker?
Has Sacramento County's risk manager formally waived the A-VII requirement, or signed off on the surplus lines placement?
Are you aware that if either Convex or Gemini becomes insolvent, the Arizona Property and Casualty Guaranty Fund does not protect you because they're non-admitted?

findings.requirement_type: Convex Excess — Conditional Follow Form Trap
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: If any Underlying Policy includes any more restrictive coverage, terms, definitions, exclusions, conditions, or limitations, then this policy will follow the more restrictive provisions of any Underlying Policy.
findings.gap_description: The Convex excess is conditional follow-form: it follows the more restrictive of itself or the underlying. So every restrictive endorsement on Gemini (Client Print Media exclusion, Delay in Performance exclusion, Recall/Reprinting exclusion, Network Security exclusion, Biometric exclusion, Communicable Disease exclusion, Hardware/ISP exclusions, Split Limits) flows up to and limits the Convex layer. There is no remediation possible at the excess layer alone — fixes have to happen on the primary.
findings.plain_english: Your $5M excess from Convex isn't a clean second $5M. It says 'whatever is more restrictive — me or the underlying — wins.' So every limitation we just walked through on the Gemini primary (Client Print Media, Delay, Recall, Cyber carve-out, Biometric, Split Limits, etc.) lives on the excess too. There's no fix at the excess layer; if you want broader coverage, you have to negotiate it on the primary.
findings.recommendation: Concentrate negotiation energy on the Gemini primary endorsements. Any improvement there flows to Convex automatically. Conversely, do not assume the excess provides any broadening above what's on the primary.
discoveryQuestions: Did anyone explain to you that the excess policy follows the more restrictive of itself or the primary? Most clients assume excess is 'cleaner' — it usually isn't.

When you renew the primary in April, do you want to bundle the negotiation of the Client Print Media exclusion, the Delay in Performance exclusion, and the Split Limits endorsement? All three would flow up to the excess automatically.

findings.requirement_type: Convex Excess — Sublimits Not Extended
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: If any Underlying Policy grants coverage subject to a sublimit of liability, this policy shall not afford such coverage, however this policy shall recognize any reduction or exhaustion of the Attachment Point by payments with respect to such coverage pursuant to that Underlying Policy.
findings.gap_description: Standard excess construction. Any sublimited coverage on Gemini (Disciplinary Proceedings $25K/$50K, Subpoena Response $2.5K/$5K, Supplementary Payments $250/day to $5K, etc.) is not extended above the underlying — but the dollars paid still erode the $5M attachment. Net effect: insured pays for the sublimited grants of coverage at the primary layer only, and any payment reduces the attachment.
findings.plain_english: Anything on the Gemini primary that's already capped at a sublimit (like the $50K disciplinary proceeding sublimit) doesn't get a second helping at the Convex excess layer. The sublimit is whatever Gemini gave you and that's the end of it. But those dollars still chip away at the $5M attachment point that has to be exhausted before Convex pays anything. Standard construction — just worth knowing.
findings.recommendation: No action needed beyond awareness. If any sublimit on the primary is meaningfully insufficient (e.g., a $5K subpoena response sublimit for an election firm with high subpoena exposure), address at the primary layer.
discoveryQuestions: How often does Run-Test get subpoenaed in election litigation (even when not a party)? The $5K aggregate subpoena response sublimit is going to feel small fast.
Has anyone walked you through how sublimited coverage on the primary still erodes your $5M attachment to the excess?

findings.requirement_type: Named Insured Mismatch — Inc. (Primary) vs LLC (Excess)
findings.contract_quote: (General RMF #3 — Named insureds list for each policy and flag any missing.)
findings.policy_quote: Gemini primary Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, Inc.' (with Runbeck Graphics Inc. added as Named Insured via Endorsement #13 VP 02 79 07 17). Convex excess Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC.'
findings.policy_page: Gemini Dec page; Endorsement #13 (Pg 36); Convex Dec (Pg 6)
findings.gap_description: The primary Tech E&O names 'Runbeck Election Services, Inc.' (corporation) and 'Runbeck Graphics Inc.' The excess names 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC.' These are different legal entities. Convex follows form on Insured definition (Section V.B: 'Insured means any person or organization that is an Insured pursuant to the Followed Policy'), which means in theory the LLC isn't a Named Insured on the excess at all — and the Inc. is, by virtue of being a Followed-Policy Insured. But the Convex Dec page lists the LLC, creating an internal inconsistency. If the LLC is the actual operating entity and the Inc. is a defunct or shell entity, this is a significant problem at the excess layer.
findings.plain_english: Your primary policy is in the name of Runbeck Election Services, INC. Your excess policy is in the name of Runbeck Election Services, LLC. These are different legal entities. If the LLC is the actual company doing the work today, the excess thinks it's covering one entity while the primary is covering a different one. If a claim hits, the carrier on the excess could argue the LLC isn't an Insured under the followed policy and decline coverage. This is the kind of thing that's invisible until a claim — and then it's catastrophic.
findings.recommendation: URGENT — confirm the correct legal entity name with Run-Test counsel. Issue immediate endorsements aligning the Named Insured on both the primary and excess. If both Inc. and LLC are legitimate operating entities, schedule both on both policies. Also confirm Runbeck Graphics Inc. is on the Convex excess (it currently appears not to be). This is a 30-minute fix that, left uncorrected, can blow up an entire claim.
discoveryQuestions: What's the actual operating entity right now — the Inc., the LLC, or both? When did the entity structure change, and was the insurance updated each time?
If a claim hit tomorrow against 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC,' which policy would respond and which would decline?
Is Runbeck Graphics Inc. a separate operating entity? It's on the primary but not on the excess — that's a real gap if it has revenue or operations of its own.
Has counsel reviewed the Named Insured schedules against the current corporate org chart? Most companies haven't done this in years.

findings.requirement_type: Convex Schedule — Policy Number Discrepancy
findings.contract_quote: (Administrative — endorsement integrity.)
findings.policy_quote: Dec page Item 5 shows Gemini policy VIPL056495; Schedule of Underlying Insurance (XPL-301, page 13) shows VIPL055885. Both Gemini, but the policy number doesn't match.
findings.policy_page: Convex Dec page Item 5; XPL-301 Schedule of Underlying, Pg 13
findings.gap_description: Two different Gemini policy numbers appear in the Convex policy. VIPL056495 is the actual primary number on the Gemini Dec; VIPL055885 is shown on the Convex Schedule. Likely a prior-term policy number that wasn't updated. Administrative defect, not coverage-threatening, but worth fixing.
findings.plain_english: The Convex excess names two different Gemini policy numbers in two different places. One of them (VIPL055885) is probably last year's policy. Get a corrected schedule endorsement before a claim hits and a coverage attorney spots it.
findings.recommendation: Request a Convex endorsement correcting the Schedule of Underlying to reflect the current Gemini policy number VIPL056495. Should be no-cost.
discoveryQuestions: Has the broker confirmed the Convex Schedule of Underlying matches the current Gemini primary policy number? It currently lists last year's number.
When the primary renews each April, does Convex automatically endorse the new policy number, or does someone have to chase it?

findings.requirement_type: Convex Excess — Maintenance of Underlying (Favorable Construction)
findings.contract_quote: (Umbrella RMF #6 — Maintenance of underlying.)
findings.policy_quote: If insured fails to maintain underlying or renews/replaces with lesser coverage, Convex is liable only as if the underlying had been fully maintained. Failure to maintain does NOT void the policy but the excess attaches as if the underlying limit were intact — the insured eats the gap.
findings.gap_description: This is the broker-preferred construction. Many umbrellas/excess policies say 'failure to maintain underlying voids this policy' — which is catastrophic. Convex says 'failure to maintain just means we attach as if it were maintained' — the insured bears the gap, not loses the entire policy. Material plus.
findings.plain_english: If for some reason the primary policy lapses or gets a smaller limit, the Convex excess doesn't disappear — it just attaches at the original $5M attachment as if the primary were still intact, and you eat the gap. That's much better than the alternative, which is policies that say 'lapse the underlying and you lose all the excess.' Good construction.
findings.recommendation: No action needed — this is the favorable construction. Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Convex Excess — Right and Duty to Defend on Drop-Down
findings.contract_quote: (Umbrella RMF #11 — Right and Duty when underlying exhausted.)
findings.policy_quote: We will have the right and duty to defend any claim made or suit brought or proceeding instituted against an Insured to which this policy applies if the applicable limits of Underlying Policies have been exhausted.
findings.gap_description: Strong drop-down provision. Once the $5M Gemini primary is exhausted, Convex assumes the right AND duty to defend. Some excess policies grant only the right to defend (no obligation), forcing the Insured to coordinate defense.
findings.plain_english: Once the primary is exhausted in a big claim, the Convex excess takes over the defense — right and duty. You don't have to argue with them about whether they'll defend. That's the broker-preferred construction.
findings.recommendation: No action needed. Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Convex Excess — Defense Inside vs Outside Limits
findings.contract_quote: (Umbrella RMF #5 — Defense inside vs outside limits.)
findings.policy_quote: Follows form to Followed Policy (Convex Section III.B). [Gemini primary defense treatment must be verified.]
findings.policy_page: Convex Section III.B; Gemini base form
findings.gap_description: The Convex excess follows form on defense treatment. The Gemini primary's defense-inside-vs-outside-limits treatment was not explicitly captured in the policy analysis JSON. Tech E&O is typically defense-inside-limits (PL standard) — meaning Claim Expenses erode Limits of Liability. The Supplementary Payments endorsement (Pg 40) confirms certain payments erode Limits, suggesting defense-inside-limits is in play. Worth confirming explicitly.
findings.plain_english: Most Professional Liability policies pay defense costs out of the policy limit — meaning if you have $5M and the carrier spends $1.5M defending you, you only have $3.5M left to settle or pay a judgment. That's standard for E&O but very different from GL where defense is typically outside the limit. Worth confirming whether your $10M tower is really $10M including defense or $10M minus defense.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with carrier whether Gemini Section III defense costs are within or outside Limits. Quote exact language. If defense-inside-limits (likely), document for client and consider higher limits if defense costs in election litigation are expected to be heavy.
discoveryQuestions: When you compare your $10M E&O tower to a comparable GL tower, did anyone explain that the E&O probably pays defense out of the limit, while GL pays defense in addition to the limit? Same dollar limit means very different actual protection.
Election litigation can run up million-dollar defense bills before trial. If a $5M claim takes $2M to defend, you only have $3M left to settle. Is $10M still the right number for this client?

findings.requirement_type: Convex Excess — Risk of Uncollectability Retained by Insured
findings.contract_quote: (Umbrella RMF — drop-down for uncollectability.)
findings.policy_quote: The risk of uncollectability with respect to any Underlying Policy or Underlying Insurers for any reason is expressly retained by the Insured and is not covered under this policy.
findings.gap_description: If Gemini becomes insolvent or refuses to pay for any reason, Convex does not drop down — Run-Test eats the $5M attachment. Gemini is part of W.R. Berkley (financially strong) and is non-admitted in AZ, so AZ Guaranty Fund does not protect. Low likelihood but high severity.
findings.plain_english: If Gemini goes insolvent or refuses to pay a claim, Convex doesn't drop down to fill the gap — you'd be on the hook for the entire $5M primary attachment yourself. Gemini is part of W.R. Berkley (financially strong), so this is unlikely, but worth knowing.
findings.recommendation: Monitor Gemini's AM Best rating annually. If it slips below A-, evaluate replacement. No structural fix available at the excess layer.
discoveryQuestions: If Gemini's AM Best rating slipped to B+ tomorrow, does the broker have a plan to move the primary? Convex won't drop down to cover the gap.
What's your visibility into the financial health of W.R. Berkley/Gemini? Has anyone monitored ratings since placement?

findings.requirement_type: Surplus Lines / Non-Admitted Carrier — AZ Guaranty Fund Disclosure
findings.contract_quote: (Informational — A.R.S. §20-401.01(B)(1) AZ surplus lines disclosure.)
findings.policy_quote: Both Gemini and Convex are surplus lines / non-admitted in Arizona.
findings.policy_page: Gemini End. #14 (VP 07 38 08 21) Pg 37; Convex Dec page Pg 6
findings.gap_description: Per the kb critical-thinking rules: surplus lines placement is informational, not Ugly or Bad, when admitted markets won't write the risk. Election services Tech E&O is one such risk. Disclosure should be made to client confirming AZ Guaranty Fund non-applicability per A.R.S. §20-401.01(B)(1). Sacramento allows Risk Manager waiver of A-VII; surplus lines is appropriate.
findings.plain_english: Both your E&O carriers are surplus lines — meaning not licensed in Arizona. That's normal and right for election services Tech E&O because admitted carriers don't write this risk. The trade-off is that if either carrier becomes insolvent, the Arizona Property and Casualty Guaranty Fund won't protect you. We just want to make sure you know.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm AZ surplus lines disclosure has been delivered to client (statutory requirement). (2) Document with Sacramento Risk Manager that the placement is approved despite non-admitted status. (3) Annual rating review for both Gemini and Convex.
discoveryQuestions: Did the broker provide the Arizona surplus lines disclosure form at the time of placement? It's a statutory requirement.
Are you comfortable with the trade-off — surplus lines breadth vs. no AZ Guaranty Fund safety net?

findings.requirement_type: Disciplinary Proceeding & Subpoena Response Sublimits
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Disciplinary Proceeding sublimit: $25,000 each / $50,000 aggregate. ... Subpoena Response sublimit per subpoena: $2,500; aggregate: $5,000.
findings.gap_description: $5,000 aggregate subpoena response is materially low for an election services firm. Election litigation is voluminous; Run-Test will be served subpoenas as a non-party in election challenges, recount disputes, and post-election litigation. Counsel time at $500-$700/hour exhausts $2,500 per subpoena before the first response. $50K aggregate disciplinary proceeding is reasonable.
findings.plain_english: Election companies get subpoenaed all the time — recount disputes, election challenges, ballot integrity audits — even when you're not a party. Your policy gives you $2,500 per subpoena and $5,000 total for the year. One serious election cycle eats that in week one. The disciplinary proceeding sublimit ($50K aggregate) is fine.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate higher subpoena response sublimits at renewal — $10K per / $50K aggregate is a reasonable target for an election services firm. Document any subpoenas received and response costs to make the case at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: How many subpoenas does Run-Test receive in a typical federal election year, and what does outside counsel charge to respond?
Have you ever exhausted the subpoena response sublimit on the E&O? If so, where did the rest of the response cost come from?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento PL — ERP Availability Verification (1-Year Minimum)
findings.contract_quote: If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed, and not replaced with another claims made policy form with a 'Retro Date' prior to the contract effective date, the CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion of the Agreement.
findings.policy_quote: [ERP availability terms not explicitly captured in policy analysis JSON.]
findings.policy_page: Gemini base form Section IX (cancellation); ERP terms typically in Section II
findings.gap_description: The policy analysis JSON does not capture ERP availability or cost. Standard Tech E&O forms typically offer 1, 3, 5-year ERP options with associated premiums. Confirm: (1) is ERP available on cancellation/non-renewal, (2) what is the cost (typically 100-300% of expiring annual premium), (3) does ERP last at least 1 year (Sacramento minimum)?
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires that if you cancel or don't renew the E&O without replacing it, you must buy a 1-year tail. We need to confirm that this policy actually offers a 1-year tail and what it costs. Most Tech E&O forms offer 1, 3, and 5-year options at 100-300% of annual premium, but it's not guaranteed.
findings.recommendation: Pull Section II of the Gemini base form and confirm ERP availability and cost. Document in renewal file. If less than 1 year is offered, escalate.
discoveryQuestions: If Run-Test had to non-renew this E&O tomorrow and replace with a different carrier with a fresh retro date, how much would a 1-year tail cost? Has the broker quoted that?
