Is the ERP buy-out provision unconditional, or can the carrier refuse if the policy was cancelled for cause?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa PL — ERP Availability Verification (2-Year Minimum)
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: [ERP availability terms not explicitly captured.]
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires 2-year ERP. Confirm Gemini base form offers at least a 2-year option. Tech E&O standard forms typically do (1/3/5 years), but verify. If only 1 year is available, this is a contract compliance issue.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires a 2-year tail if you ever cancel and don't replace this E&O. Most Tech E&O policies offer 1/3/5 year options; we need to confirm yours does. If it's only 1 year available, you can't comply with Maricopa.
findings.recommendation: Confirm 2-year ERP option exists on the Gemini base form. Document cost and terms. If unavailable, negotiate with carrier or replace at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Does the Gemini policy offer a 2-year ERP option? If only 1 year is available, you can't comply with Maricopa.
What's the cost of the 2-year tail? It's worth knowing in advance — these costs spike if the carrier pulls out of the market.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Indemnification — Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: (Contract-level acknowledgment — does not require a specific policy endorsement. The Blanket AI endorsement VP 07 83 07 17 (defense costs only) does not contradict §2782 carve-out.)
findings.gap_description: California public-policy limitation under Civil Code §2782(b) is a contract-level acknowledgment, not a policy endorsement requirement. The E&O Blanket AI endorsement is consistent with this carve-out (it's defense-costs-only and applies to AI claims arising from Named Insured's Wrongful Acts — not AI's own negligence).
findings.plain_english: California has a law (Civil Code §2782) that says you can't insure a county for the county's own active negligence. The Sacramento contract acknowledges this carve-out. Your E&O AI endorsement is consistent — it only covers claims arising from YOUR Wrongful Acts, not the county's own negligence. So you're aligned.
findings.recommendation: No action needed.

findings.requirement_type: AI Status — E&O Blanket Defense-Costs-Only & Excluded Lines
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.E does NOT require AI on E&O. Maricopa §8.2.7 expressly excludes E&O from the AI requirement: 'The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County ... as additional insureds.'
findings.policy_quote: Blanket Additional Insured: 'The Company will not pay any Loss on behalf of the additional Insured.' Coverage limited to defense costs (Claim Expenses) only, ongoing performance of Professional Services, ends at completion. (VP 07 83 07 17, Pg 20.) Benton County, WA scheduled as AI (End. #10, Pg 30).
findings.gap_description: Both contracts properly carve E&O out of the AI requirement, recognizing the conceptual mismatch (you can't 'name' a county as an additional insured on a Professional Services E&O the way you can on GL). The Blanket AI endorsement that IS on the policy is defense-costs-only — appropriate construction. Sacramento County and Maricopa County are not specifically scheduled, but they don't need to be because the contract excludes E&O from AI.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento and Maricopa both expressly EXCLUDE the E&O from the additional insured requirement. So we don't need to schedule the counties on this policy. The Blanket AI endorsement that's on it is defense-costs-only, which is the right construction for E&O. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: No action needed.

findings.requirement_type: Waiver of Subrogation — E&O Excluded from Requirement
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.8: 'The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County.' Sacramento §VIII addresses WC waiver only; §IX addresses Property/IM waiver. E&O is not listed as a WoS requirement.
findings.policy_quote: (No WoS endorsement on either E&O policy.)
findings.gap_description: Both contracts expressly exclude E&O from the waiver of subrogation requirement. No endorsement is needed. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: Both contracts say E&O doesn't need a waiver of subrogation, which makes sense for Professional Liability coverage. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: No action needed.

findings.requirement_type: Innocent Insured Carve-Back on Criminal/Dishonest Acts
findings.contract_quote: (General best practice — protects company from individual bad actor.)
findings.policy_quote: Innocent insured carve-out for natural persons (other than Named Insured) who did not participate in, ratify, or acquiesce. Defense provided until adjudication.
findings.gap_description: Strong innocent-insured carve-back. If a rogue employee commits a fraudulent or dishonest act, other innocent insureds (and the company in some readings) retain coverage and defense until final adjudication. This is a critical protection for an election services firm given the political sensitivity and bad-actor risk.
findings.plain_english: If one employee does something fraudulent or dishonest, the rest of the company is still protected — and defense continues until a court actually rules against the bad actor. That matters in election services where a single rogue employee could create headlines but shouldn't void the whole company's coverage.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm the carve-back protects the entity (not just other natural persons) — language varies by carrier.

findings.requirement_type: Media Extension — Copyright/Trademark Coverage Restored
findings.contract_quote: (General best practice for print media operators.)
findings.policy_quote: Replaces Intellectual Property exclusion (now only patent/trade secret excluded — copyright/trademark/trade dress now covered). Adds 'Media Injury' definition (privacy violations, libel/slander, copyright/trademark infringement, plagiarism, false light, etc.).
findings.gap_description: The base form excludes all IP. Endorsement #5 narrows the exclusion to only patent and trade secret, restoring copyright, trademark, trade dress, trade name, service mark, slogan, and Lanham Act claims to coverage. For a printing operation, this is the correct construction.
findings.plain_english: Most E&O forms exclude all intellectual property. Yours has been narrowed to only exclude patent and trade secret claims — meaning you do have coverage for copyright, trademark, and Lanham Act claims, which are the realistic IP risks for a printer. Good.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Right to Adjust Coverage — Sacramento §II.B
findings.contract_quote: COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions ... do not provide adequate protection ..., COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.
findings.policy_quote: (Contract-level — open-ended unilateral right.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento reserves the right to require ADDITIONAL coverage mid-term if the Risk Manager deems current insurance inadequate. Open-ended risk — limits and lines could grow during contract performance and create unbudgeted insurance costs.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has reserved the right to come back at any time and demand more insurance — higher limits, additional lines, whatever the Risk Manager wants. This is open-ended financial risk to budget for if Sacramento ever decides election services need stricter requirements.
findings.recommendation: Track Sacramento's stated insurance requirements at every renewal cycle. Build a 10-15% insurance cost buffer into Sacramento contract pricing for potential mid-term coverage increases. Maintain an ongoing relationship with Sacramento's Risk Manager.
discoveryQuestions: Has Sacramento ever exercised the right to require additional coverage mid-contract? Other counties on similar contracts?
Does Run-Test's pricing model on Sacramento work include a buffer for potential coverage upgrades, or is the insurance cost locked in?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Indemnity Uncapped by Policy Limits
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section. ... To the fullest extent permitted by law ... the contractor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the County (as Owner), its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees ...
findings.policy_quote: (Standard insurance non-limitation clause — uncovered exposure if claim exceeds tower.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's indemnity is uncapped — Run-Test's contractual obligation to defend and indemnify is independent of and not limited by insurance limits. Any claim above the program limits ($10M E&O / Cyber TBD / GL TBD / Auto TBD / Umbrella TBD) is paid out of balance sheet. For a PE-backed company touching 90M voter records, the worst-case scenario can exceed any reasonable tower.
findings.plain_english: Your contract with Maricopa doesn't cap your indemnity at your insurance limits. If a claim exceeds your insurance, the difference comes out of the company's pocket — and ultimately out of the PE sponsor's equity. For a company handling election data for 90M voters, the worst-case loss scenario can run higher than any commercially available tower. This is a balance-sheet exposure, not an insurance fix.
findings.recommendation: (1) Build the insurance program to a level that addresses likely worst-case (informed by industry loss data, not just contract minimums). (2) Discuss with PE sponsor and Run-Test board whether the tower is adequate. (3) Consider captive insurance, parametric coverage, or higher-limit options for cyber and E&O.
discoveryQuestions: Has the PE sponsor seen the indemnity-uncapped-by-limits clause? It's standard market language but it converts a bad day into an equity event.
What's your worst-case loss scenario in dollar terms — a multi-state voter data breach? A wrongful disenfranchisement class action? Has anyone modeled it?
Does the board have an opinion on the appropriate insurance tower height for an election services firm with this exposure profile?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Deductible/SIR — County May Require Bond or LOC
findings.contract_quote: Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.policy_quote: Self-Insured Retention $25,000 per claim.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa expressly waives the SIR/deductible against the County (i.e., contractor pays the SIR before County is exposed) and reserves the right to require a bond or LOC. The $25K SIR is small; if Maricopa demanded an LOC, the cost would be modest but nonzero. The bigger issue is whether Maricopa has been told about the SIR at all — see finding-020.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa has the right to demand that you back your $25K SIR with a surety bond or letter of credit. They probably won't for a $25K SIR, but they could. If your Cyber policy has a much larger SIR (say, $100K-$500K), Maricopa's right to demand collateral becomes more meaningful.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm SIR/deductible disclosure has been made to Maricopa Risk Management. (2) Establish whether they require LOC backing. (3) Apply same analysis to any Cyber, GL, Auto, or Umbrella deductibles/SIRs.
discoveryQuestions: Has the Gemini E&O $25K SIR been formally disclosed to Maricopa Risk Management?
What are the SIRs and deductibles across your other policies (Cyber, GL, Auto)? Maricopa's collateral right applies to all of them.

findings.requirement_type: Verification of Coverage — Endorsement Copies Required (Sacramento)
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall furnish the COUNTY with certificates evidencing coverage required below. Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences.
findings.policy_quote: (Procedural — relates to broker workflow.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires actual endorsement COPIES to accompany the COI before contract performance. This is procedural but often missed — most COIs are issued with checkbox references rather than attached endorsement copies. For E&O, this is moot because the contract excludes E&O from AI requirement, but the standard applies to all GL/Auto/WC/Umbrella endorsements once those policies are in scope.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires actual copies of additional insured endorsements (and other required endorsements) to be attached to the certificate of insurance. This is more than the standard COI — and many brokers default to checkbox-only certificates. We need to confirm this workflow is in place for the GL, Auto, and Umbrella endorsements once those policies are audited.
findings.recommendation: (1) Establish broker workflow that attaches actual endorsement copies (CG 20 10/CG 20 37 for GL, equivalent for Auto, follow-form Umbrella schedule) to every Sacramento COI. (2) Re-verify pre-performance approval was obtained for the existing Sacramento contract.
discoveryQuestions: When you issued the Sacramento certificate, did the broker attach actual endorsement copies (CG 20 10/CG 20 37) or just check the boxes?
Did Sacramento Risk Management formally approve the certificate before you started performance, in writing?

findings.requirement_type: Notification of Claim/Lawsuit — Contractual Notice to County
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: '... CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice ... within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.' Maricopa: 'Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice ...'
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §X, Page 4 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.15, Page 7 of 41
findings.policy_quote: (Operational — internal incident response protocol.)
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has independent contractual notice obligations to each county that are tighter than carrier notice obligations. Sacramento: 30 days from claim receipt, 10 days from service of process. Maricopa: 2 business days from any insurance-cancellation/material-change notice. These are easy to miss in a fast-moving litigation environment.
findings.plain_english: When you get sued or get a claim, you have to notify the county on a tight timeline — Sacramento is 30 days from claim receipt and 10 days from being served, Maricopa is 2 business days for any insurance change. These are independent of your insurance carrier notice obligations, and missing them is a contract breach in itself.
findings.recommendation: Build internal incident-response protocol with: (1) clear definition of 'claim' and 'lawsuit' triggers, (2) notification matrix per county contract, (3) designated person responsible, (4) calendar reminders. Confirm with each county the correct notice address and form.
discoveryQuestions: Who at Run-Test is responsible for notifying the counties when a claim or lawsuit hits? Is the timeline calendared and tracked?
Have you ever missed a contractual notice deadline? What were the consequences?
Do you have a written incident response protocol that addresses contract-by-contract notice obligations?

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through Insurance Requirements
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.' Maricopa: WC/EL waiver flows down to subcontractors and sub-subs.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VII.E, Page 4 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.12, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: (Subcontract management — independent of policy review.)
findings.gap_description: Both contracts contemplate subcontractor flow-down. Sacramento requires Run-Test to be responsible for sub acts/omissions and to ensure subs provide AI endorsements; Maricopa flows the WC waiver to subs and sub-subs. We need to know: (1) does Run-Test use subcontractors (printers, mail houses, IT, hardware vendors)? (2) are matching insurance reqs in those sub agreements? (3) does Run-Test get subs' COIs and endorsement copies?
findings.plain_english: Both counties expect you to flow your insurance requirements down to your subcontractors. So if you use a print partner, a mail house, an IT vendor, or a hardware partner — they need to carry GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, and (where applicable) E&O at matching limits, name you and the county as additional insureds, waive subrogation, and so on. We need to know what subs you use and whether your sub agreements actually require this.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory all subcontractors involved in Sacramento and Maricopa work. (2) Audit each subcontract for matching insurance reqs. (3) Maintain current COIs and endorsement copies from each sub. (4) Establish broker workflow to verify sub coverage annually.
discoveryQuestions: Who are Run-Test's key subcontractors on Sacramento and Maricopa work — print partners, mail houses, IT vendors, hardware vendors?
Do your sub agreements include the same insurance requirements your county contracts impose on you? Has anyone audited those agreements?
When was the last time you collected and reviewed COIs from each subcontractor?

findings.requirement_type: Unintentional Errors and Omissions — N/A on E&O Form
findings.contract_quote: (General RMF #2 — Unintentional Errors and Omissions giveback.)
findings.policy_quote: (N/A — the Unintentional E&O giveback is a GL endorsement; not applicable to a Professional Liability policy.)
findings.gap_description: The Unintentional E&O giveback (RMF Gen-2) is designed to protect against an inadvertent failure to report a location, vehicle, or operation on a property/casualty policy from voiding coverage. It is a GL/Property/Auto concept, not an E&O concept (the Professional Liability policy itself IS errors-and-omissions coverage). Confirmed N/A for the two policies in scope.
findings.plain_english: The 'Unintentional Errors and Omissions' giveback is a GL feature, not an E&O feature. Your E&O policy literally IS errors-and-omissions coverage, so this RMF item doesn't apply to the policies in this audit. We'll evaluate it on the GL once that policy is in scope.
findings.recommendation: No action on E&O. Apply the RMF item to GL, Property, and Auto when those policies are audited.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VII.A — Broad AI Class on Auto (E&O Not Implicated)
findings.contract_quote: The COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, and volunteers are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR; products and completed operations of the CONTRACTOR; premises owned, occupied or used by the CONTRACTOR; or automobiles owned, leased, hired or borrowed by the CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: (N/A on E&O — Sacramento expressly carves E&O out of AI scope. Applies to GL and Auto, both of which are not in audit scope.)
findings.gap_description: Broad AI class (officers, directors, officials, employees, volunteers) with 'arising out of' trigger covering ongoing AND completed operations, autos, and premises. Cannot be assessed without GL and Auto policies. Likely requires CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 (or equivalent broader-than-current edition) on GL, plus Auto AI form. No endorsed limitations on AI scope are permitted.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's additional insured language is broader than the typical contract — it includes officers, directors, officials, employees, AND volunteers, and covers both ongoing and completed operations. We can't audit this without the GL and Auto policies. Once we have them, we need to confirm no edition-date traps (e.g., a CG 20 10 04 13 with the 'caused by' trigger that arguably narrows the 'arising out of' broad reading), and no scope-limiting endorsements on the AI.
findings.recommendation: Defer until GL and Auto policies are in scope. Then audit AI endorsements for edition date, completed operations inclusion (CG 20 37), trigger language ('arising out of' vs 'caused by'), and any scope limitations.
discoveryQuestions: Once we audit the GL and Auto, the question becomes whether the AI endorsement is the broad CG 20 10 (1985 edition) 'arising out of' or the narrower 2004/2013 'caused by' edition. Has anyone confirmed which is on the policy?
Sacramento's AI list includes 'volunteers' — does the AI endorsement specifically pick up volunteers, or does it default to a narrower class?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Designated Entity NOC — 30-Day Notice Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt, if they receive notice of a policy that has been or will be suspended, canceled, materially changed.
findings.policy_quote: Gemini provides 60-day cancellation notice (other) / 10-day (nonpayment) — but is the notice TO Maricopa County, or only to the Insured? Standard ACORD COI cancellation language says notice will be given 'in accordance with policy provisions' which often means notice to the Insured, not third parties.
findings.policy_page: Pg 15 (Section IX.C); no Designated Entity NOC endorsement listed
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires 30-day prior written notice TO Maricopa County. The base policy 60-day cancellation provision is to the Insured, not third parties. The contract permits a 2-business-day Contractor pass-through — which makes a Designated Entity NOC endorsement technically not required, but it shifts the risk onto Run-Test to actually relay carrier notice within 2 business days. No carrier-issued Designated Entity NOC endorsement is on the policy. Verify whether one is needed for E&O specifically (note that for E&O, AI-style endorsements are typically not used; the contract pass-through should suffice).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 30 days notice before any cancellation — and they're flexible: either the carrier sends them notice directly (Designated Entity NOC endorsement), or YOU pass it through within 2 business days. Right now, neither carrier has a Designated Entity NOC endorsement to Maricopa, so the obligation lands entirely on you to relay any cancellation notice within 2 business days. Build a process for that.
findings.recommendation: (1) Establish internal protocol: any cancellation/material-change notice from any carrier triggers a 2-business-day notification to Maricopa Risk Management. (2) Consider requesting Designated Entity NOC endorsements (e.g., CG 20 12 equivalent on GL once that's in scope) to shift the notification obligation back to the carrier. For E&O, the contract pass-through model is acceptable.
discoveryQuestions: Is there a written internal process for the 2-business-day pass-through to Maricopa if a carrier issues a cancellation notice?
Would it be cleaner to put a Designated Entity NOC endorsement on the GL and Auto policies once they're in scope, so the carrier handles the notification directly?

findings.requirement_type: Insurance Survival / Maintenance — Material Breach Trigger
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'Failure to maintain required insurance in force shall be considered a material breach of the Agreement.' Maricopa: 'Failure to do so may, at the sole discretion of County, constitute a material breach of this contract.'
findings.policy_quote: (Operational compliance — applies to all policies in program.)
findings.gap_description: Both contracts treat insurance lapse as a material breach. The E&O policies are in force through 04/01/2026. As long as renewal is timely and continuous, this is compliant. Critical to flag because a missed renewal is more than an insurance gap — it's a contract default with potentially much broader consequences (termination for cause, damages, debarment).
findings.plain_english: Both contracts say if you let your insurance lapse, that's a material breach — meaning the county can terminate the contract and seek damages. Right now your E&O is in force through April 2026. The discipline this requires is timely renewal every cycle.
findings.recommendation: (1) Maintain renewal calendar with 90-day pre-expiry trigger for every policy. (2) Build broker workflow that issues renewal COIs to each county at least 15 days pre-expiry (Maricopa requirement) and 10 days pre-anniversary (Sacramento requirement). (3) Establish escalation protocol if any policy is at risk of non-renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VI.A.2 — 10-Day Pre-Anniversary Renewal Evidence
findings.contract_quote: The Contractor shall maintain all insurance coverages and limits in place at all times and provide the County with evidence of each policy's renewal ten (10) days in advance of its anniversary date.
findings.policy_quote: (Procedural — annual COI issuance workflow.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento wants renewal evidence 10 days before anniversary. The Gemini and Convex policies anniversary on 04/01 — confirm broker workflow has the renewal COI to Sacramento by 03/22 each year.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento wants proof of renewal 10 days before each policy renews. Your E&O renews April 1. Make sure the renewal certificate is on Sacramento's desk by March 22 every year.
findings.recommendation: Set broker calendar to issue renewal COIs to Sacramento by 03/22 annually. Confirm last cycle was met.
discoveryQuestions: Did Sacramento receive the 04/01/2025 renewal COI by 03/22/2025? Will they receive the 04/01/2026 renewal COI by 03/22/2026?
Is the 10-day pre-anniversary requirement built into the broker's renewal calendar?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Per-Project Aggregate — Likely N/A for Election Services
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 Amendment-Aggregate Limits of Insurance (Per Project).
findings.policy_quote: (GL endorsement requirement — no GL policy in audit scope to evaluate; conditional on construction work.)
findings.gap_description: Per-project aggregate (CG 25 03) is conditional on construction work. Run-Test is an election services manufacturer/printer/mailer — not a construction contractor. The requirement likely does not implicate Run-Test.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires per-project aggregate ONLY if you're a construction contractor. You're not — you're a manufacturer and election services firm — so this requirement doesn't apply to you.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Sacramento that Run-Test's scope of work does not constitute 'construction.' If any physical install/build work is performed (e.g., setting up election equipment at polling locations, building infrastructure), reconsider.

findings.requirement_type: Supplementary Payments — Erodes Limits
findings.contract_quote: Professional Liability appropriate to the Contractor's profession.
findings.policy_quote: Loss of wages reimbursement when attending proceedings at Company's request: $250/day per Insured, $5,000 max each Claim. Erodes Limits of Liability (part of, not in addition to).
findings.gap_description: Minor — supplementary payments erode the $5M limit rather than sit on top. Capped at $5K per claim, so financial impact is small. Worth flagging for awareness.
findings.plain_english: When your employees attend depositions or trials at the carrier's request, the carrier reimburses lost wages — but those payments come out of your $5M limit, not on top of it. The cap is $5K per claim so it's small money, but technically reduces your tower in any heavily-litigated case.
findings.recommendation: Note for record. No structural change recommended.
discoveryQuestions: In a heavily litigated election case, how many employee days could be spent in depositions and trial? The $5K cap is meaningful for moderate cases but trivial for major litigation.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — Limit Shortfall vs Maricopa $5M Requirement
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence.
findings.policy_quote: Aggregate Limit of Liability: $4,000,000 ... DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS.
findings.policy_page: Dec page Item 4, Page 2 of policy
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County requires Cyber of not less than $5,000,000 PER OCCURRENCE. The AmTrust policy carries $4,000,000 as a SHARED AGGREGATE across all 14 coverage lines, with defense costs eroding the limit. This is a triple-shortfall: (1) $4M is below $5M on its face; (2) the contract calls for per-occurrence and the policy provides annual aggregate; (3) defense within limits means the actual indemnity available on a single claim is materially less than the stated $4M aggregate (typically $800K–$1.6M after forensics, breach counsel, and regulatory defense). No excess Cyber tower exists in the program — the Hanover Umbrella does not follow form to Cyber.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa County requires you to carry $5 million of cyber coverage per claim. Your AmTrust cyber policy provides $4 million for the entire policy year, shared across every type of cyber loss, and your legal defense costs come out of that same bucket. On a real cyber claim — like a ransomware event — the lawyers, forensic firms, breach notification vendors, and regulatory defense often consume 60–80% of the limit before any actual loss is paid. That means on the day of a serious incident, you may have $1 million or less of actual money to pay the loss against a $5 million contract requirement. You are out of compliance with Maricopa County the moment the contract was signed, and a major cyber event would expose Runbeck's balance sheet for everything above the recoverable amount.
findings.recommendation: Bind a $5M (or higher, given enumerated coverage breadth) excess cyber tower above the AmTrust primary at next renewal — or replace AmTrust primary entirely with a $5M+ defense-outside-the-limits form. In the interim, send Maricopa County Risk Management a written disclosure of the $4M aggregate and shared-aggregate structure and request written acknowledgment, since unwritten 'they didn't notice' is not a defense to a material breach claim.
discoveryQuestions: When Maricopa County signed off on your insurance package, did anyone walk them through the fact that your $4M cyber limit is shared across 14 coverage lines and erodes with defense costs — or did they just see $4M on the COI and approve it?

Runbeck processes ballot data for over 90 million voters across 31 states — if a ransomware actor encrypted your printing systems three weeks before a federal election, what's your estimate of the all-in cost (forensics, breach counsel, business interruption, county notification, AG defense)? Does $4M, minus defense, cover that?

If Maricopa or another county invoked the material-breach clause because your cyber limit fell below the $5M requirement, what would happen to that contract and to your renewal posture with the other 30 jurisdictions?
Have you ever priced a $5M or $10M excess cyber tower? The premium delta is usually a fraction of what one breach notification campaign costs.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Deception / Social Engineering — Phantom Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance ... computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Cyber Deception (Social Engineering): Limit $250,000 / Retention $250,000.
findings.policy_page: Dec page Item 7 sublimit schedule, Page 3 of policy
findings.gap_description: The Cyber Deception (Social Engineering) sublimit and retention are both $250,000. Effective recoverable on any single loss is $0 until the loss exceeds $250K, and even then capped at $250K of indemnity. A $300K wire-fraud loss recovers $50K; a $500K loss recovers $250K (50%); a $1M loss recovers $250K (25%). For an election-services manufacturer that processes county invoices, vendor payables, and ballot-printing supply-chain wire transfers, social engineering is the #1 cyber loss vector by frequency in the SMB/middle-market segment. This is functionally phantom coverage.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy says it covers social engineering fraud — the scam where a bad actor impersonates a vendor or executive and tricks an employee into wiring money to the wrong account. But the fine print: the limit is $250,000 and the deductible is also $250,000. So if you lose exactly $250,000 to a fraudulent wire, the policy pays $0. If you lose $500,000, the policy pays $250,000 — half. The 'coverage' is essentially window dressing. Given Runbeck's volume of county invoicing, vendor payments, and supply-chain transactions, this is the most likely cyber claim you'd ever have, and the policy as structured won't meaningfully respond.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate at next renewal (or mid-term endorsement) to: (a) reduce the Cyber Deception retention to $25K–$50K, and (b) raise the sublimit to at least $500K — preferably $1M. If the incumbent carrier won't move, market the cyber program — this is a standard buy in the marketplace. Pair with internal controls: dual-approval on wire transfers above a threshold, callback verification on bank-detail changes, and quarterly phishing simulations.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your wire transfer process — who initiates, who approves, and what verification do you do when a vendor sends you new banking instructions by email?
If your AP team got an email tomorrow from someone claiming to be a county clerk asking to redirect a $400K invoice payment, would your team catch it? What would happen if they didn't?
Did anyone explain to you that your cyber policy's $250K social engineering sublimit has a $250K deductible — meaning it pays nothing on a $250K loss?
Have you done phishing simulation testing on your AP and finance staff in the last 12 months? What was the click-through rate?

findings.requirement_type: Defense Within Limits + Shared Aggregate Erosion
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to ... regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption ...
findings.policy_quote: DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS.
findings.gap_description: Defense Within Limits (DWL) combined with a shared $4M aggregate across 14 coverage parts (Ransom, Data Recovery, Bricking, BI, BI from Suppliers, Reputation Harm, Cyber Event, Cyber Deception, Proof of Loss, Cryptojacking, Privacy & Network Security, Regulatory Fines, Payment Card, Media) means a single claim can exhaust capacity for the entire policy year. On typical cyber claims, 60–80% of total spend is defense costs (forensics, breach counsel, regulatory representation, PR), leaving $800K–$1.6M of indemnity from a $4M stated aggregate. A $2M ransomware response leaves only $2M of program capacity for any other cyber event during the year.
findings.plain_english: Two structural problems compound each other. First, all your defense costs — lawyers, forensics, PR firms — are paid out of your policy limit, not on top of it. Every dollar your defense costs you is a dollar less for paying the actual loss. Second, all 14 different cyber coverages share the same single $4M bucket. If you have a ransomware attack and it eats $2M, you have $2M left for the rest of the policy year — that has to cover any future cyber event AND any regulatory action AND any payment card fines AND any business interruption. The policy looks like $4M of capacity but functions like $1M–$2M of usable capacity on any real-world claim. Standard-market cyber forms increasingly offer defense-outside-the-limit and split-aggregate structures — this is a market norm Runbeck is missing out on.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, market the cyber to carriers offering: (1) defense costs OUTSIDE the limit (or at minimum a separate sublimit for defense), and (2) per-coverage-part sublimits stacked over a single aggregate (so a ransom event doesn't eat the regulatory bucket). Coalition, Beazley, Chubb, AXIS, and Tokio Marine HCC all offer materially better structures in the $5M–$10M tower range for this size account. The premium delta is typically modest relative to the structural improvement.
discoveryQuestions: If you had a $2M ransomware event in May and a separate breach in October that triggered state AG investigations in three states, do you understand that the second event might find your cyber policy effectively empty?
Have you seen the sublimit schedule on your cyber dec page — do you know that all 14 coverage lines share the same $4M bucket?
What's the worst-case scenario you've ever modeled for a cyber event during election season? How does that number compare to $1M–$2M of effective indemnity?

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation Endorsement
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: Item 8 Endorsements list on Page 4 is blank in the extracted text — no Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement visible.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.15 requires 30-day prior written notice of cancellation, suspension, or material change to be sent directly to Maricopa County Risk Management on every required policy. The standard ACORD COI cancellation language (post-2010) explicitly disclaims any obligation by the carrier to notify the certificate holder. To meet the contract requirement, a carrier-issued Designated Entity NOC endorsement (e.g., IL 12 02 or AmTrust equivalent) must be added to the policy listing Maricopa County, c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003. No such endorsement is visible in the policy.
findings.plain_english: Your contract with Maricopa County requires the insurance carrier — not your broker, not your office — to mail Maricopa 30 days advance notice if your cyber policy is cancelled, suspended, or materially changed. That obligation only exists if your policy has been specifically endorsed to require it. The COI form most carriers issue today actually has language saying the opposite: 'the issuing insurer will endeavor to mail notice but failure to do so imposes no obligation.' Without the special endorsement on file, you are technically out of compliance with §8.2.15 from the day the contract was signed. If the cyber policy ever does get cancelled and Maricopa doesn't get carrier notice, that's a material breach exposure on top of any underlying coverage issue.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust issue a Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement naming Maricopa County, c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003 with 30-day notice (60-day for industry best practice). Repeat this exercise on every required policy in the program (GL, Auto, WC, Umbrella). Confirm the endorsement is in place via copy attached to the COI, not just a checkbox.
discoveryQuestions: Do you know what your COI actually says about cancellation notice — and whether Maricopa County is on a carrier-issued notice list, or just trusting the broker to call them?
If AmTrust non-renewed your cyber mid-term and Maricopa wasn't notified by the carrier, would that be your exposure or theirs?

findings.requirement_type: Additional Insured Status — Cyber Policy
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds.
findings.policy_quote: additional_insureds: [] (no AI endorsement visible)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.7 expressly carves out only WC and E&O from the AI requirement. Cyber is NOT carved out, meaning Cyber must name Maricopa County et al. as additional insureds. The AmTrust policy shows no AI endorsement and no scheduled additional insureds. Cyber policies historically do not accommodate AI status on the same terms as GL — this often requires a specific Vicarious Liability endorsement or third-party liability extension naming the entity. Verification with AmTrust required to determine whether they will issue any form of AI/vicarious extension on this form.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract requires Maricopa County to be added as an additional insured on most of your policies, including Cyber. The cyber policy as written has no additional insureds named at all. If a Maricopa employee sued Runbeck after a data breach involving voter information, Maricopa would not be able to tender to your cyber carrier as their own insured — they'd have to rely entirely on your indemnification obligation, which means slower response, contested coverage, and potentially uninsured defense. This is also a contract compliance issue independent of any actual claim.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust issue an AI / Vicarious Liability extension endorsement naming Maricopa County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees on the cyber policy. If AmTrust will not endorse AI status (common limitation on cyber forms), document that fact in writing and disclose to Maricopa Risk Management. Many cyber carriers in the standard market (Beazley, Chubb, Coalition) WILL accommodate AI status — consider this in any remarketing.
discoveryQuestions: Has Maricopa Risk Management ever asked to see your cyber endorsement schedule, or have they only ever asked for the COI?
If voter data was compromised and Maricopa was named in a class action alongside Runbeck, would you expect AmTrust to defend the County under your policy — and have you tested that assumption?

findings.requirement_type: Waiver of Subrogation — Cyber Policy
findings.contract_quote: The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.policy_quote: waiver_of_subrogation: false (no WoS endorsement visible)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.8 requires Waiver of Subrogation on all required policies except WC and E&O — Cyber is included. No WoS endorsement is visible on the AmTrust policy. Without it, AmTrust could pay a Runbeck cyber loss and then subrogate against Maricopa County (e.g., if a county system or county employee was the source vector for the breach), creating contract conflict and counterparty friction.
findings.plain_english: Your contract with Maricopa requires that if your cyber carrier pays out a claim, they cannot then turn around and try to recover that money from Maricopa County — even if Maricopa or one of their employees was somehow involved in the loss. Your cyber policy doesn't have that waiver in place. If a breach traced back to a vulnerability in a county-supplied system or a county employee's mistake, AmTrust could legally come after Maricopa, which would damage that relationship and breach your contract simultaneously.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust issue a Waiver of Subrogation endorsement on the cyber policy in favor of Maricopa County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees. Confirm endorsement copy is provided and attached to the COI — not just referenced.
discoveryQuestions: Has anyone explained to you what subrogation means and why your county contracts require you to waive it?
If Maricopa's IT system was the entry point for a breach into your network, would you want your insurer to be able to sue them — knowing it would end your relationship?

findings.requirement_type: Primary & Noncontributory — Cyber Policy
findings.contract_quote: Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it.
findings.policy_quote: primary_noncontributory: false (no endorsement visible)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.4 requires Contractor's insurance to be primary and noncontributory with respect to County. No P&NC endorsement visible on the cyber policy. P&NC on cyber is unusual and often requires specific carrier negotiation, but the contract requires it on all required policies (no carve-out). Practical claim impact is lower than on GL/Auto because Maricopa is unlikely to have its own cyber policy that would otherwise share — but the contract requires the endorsement regardless of practical impact.
findings.plain_english: If both you and Maricopa County had cyber insurance and the same loss triggered both, your contract requires that your policy pays first and Maricopa's policy doesn't have to chip in. Without the endorsement, the two policies would normally share the loss proportionally, which creates fights between carriers and slows claims response. On cyber specifically, this is more of a contract-compliance issue than a practical claim issue — Maricopa probably doesn't carry overlapping cyber that would trigger sharing — but the contract says you must have the endorsement.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust add a Primary & Noncontributory endorsement in favor of Maricopa County. If AmTrust will not endorse, document and disclose to Maricopa.
discoveryQuestions: Do you know whether Maricopa County carries its own cyber policy that could overlap with yours on a shared loss?
Has any county ever requested to see the actual endorsement copy proving Primary & Noncontributory, or do they typically just look at the COI box?

findings.requirement_type: Continuity / Retroactive Date Gap
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: Continuity Date: 4/1/2023
findings.policy_page: Dec page Item 5, Page 3 of policy
findings.gap_description: Continuity Date is 4/1/2023, only 2 years before current inception (4/1/2025). Runbeck has 50+ years of operating history. Any cyber incident with a wrongful act prior to 4/1/2023 — including persistent threat actor presence, a latent unauthorized-access event, or a long-undiscovered data exposure — would not be covered under this claims-made/discovery form. Maricopa §8.2.3 requires retroactive date to precede the contract effective date. Verification needed: confirm Maricopa contract effective date (referenced in finding-001 as 11/01/21 in the contract requirement notes), Sacramento County effective date, and Los Angeles County effective date are all on or after 4/1/2023, OR negotiate an earlier retro/continuity date.
findings.plain_english: Cyber policies cover wrongful acts that happened on or after a 'retro date' — anything before that date is excluded even if discovered today. Your cyber retro is 4/1/2023, but Runbeck has been processing election data for 50 years and your Maricopa County contract appears to have started 11/1/2021. If a forensic investigation discovers that an attacker was inside your network since, say, 2022, the policy would deny the claim because the wrongful act predates the retro date. And your Maricopa contract specifically requires the retro to precede the contract date — which it does NOT for the 2021 contract. This is both a real coverage gap and a contract compliance issue for any pre-April-2023 contracts.
findings.recommendation: (1) Verify all county contract effective dates against the 4/1/2023 continuity date. For any contract pre-dating 4/1/2023, request AmTrust extend the retroactive/continuity date back to the earliest contract effective date — this is often available for modest additional premium when there is a clean continuous-coverage history. (2) If AmTrust will not move the date, market the cyber to a carrier that will write to the earlier retro. (3) For any policy non-renewal/replacement, ensure either continuous-retro replacement OR purchase of the 1-year Extended Discovery Period (per Item 5 of Dec, available at 100% of annual premium).
discoveryQuestions: When was your Maricopa County contract first signed — and did anyone check whether your cyber retro date predates it?
What was the carrier on your cyber program before AmTrust, and did Runbeck have continuous cyber coverage going back at least to 2018–2019?
If a forensic investigation showed an attacker had been quietly in your environment since 2022, do you have any insurance that would respond?

findings.requirement_type: Proof of Loss Sublimit Adequacy
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to ... network business interruption ...
findings.policy_quote: Proof of Loss: Limit $250,000 / Retention $50,000.
findings.policy_page: Dec page Item 7 sublimit schedule, Page 3 of policy
findings.gap_description: Proof of Loss sublimit is $250K with a $50K retention — net usable for forensic accountants and BI quantification: $200K. For a $4M business interruption claim with multi-state, multi-county service interruption (Runbeck's 31-state footprint), $200K of forensic accounting and BI quantification expense is likely insufficient. Underestimating proof-of-loss expense is a common pathway to under-recovered BI claims because carriers will dispute calculations the insured cannot afford to fully document.
findings.plain_english: Proving up a business interruption claim — showing exactly how much money you lost and over what timeframe — requires forensic accountants and specialty consultants. The bills add up fast on a complex multi-state operation like yours. Your policy will only reimburse $200K of those costs (after the $50K deductible). On a $3–4M BI claim, $200K of accounting documentation often isn't enough to fight back when the carrier disputes your numbers. That can leave hundreds of thousands of dollars of legitimately incurred BI loss un-recovered simply because you couldn't afford to fully document it.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, negotiate Proof of Loss sublimit to at least $500K with retention reduced to $10K–$25K. This is a low-cost concession most carriers will make and pays for itself on the first BI quantification.
discoveryQuestions: If a ransomware event took your printing line down for 21 days during ballot season, who would you hire to calculate the BI loss — and have you ever priced what that engagement runs?
On any prior insurance claim, has a carrier ever pushed back on your loss calculation? How much did the dispute cost to resolve?

findings.requirement_type: Self-Insured Retention Disclosure & Approval
findings.contract_quote: Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY. ... The insurance policies may provide coverage that contains deductibles or self-insured retentions. Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §IV, Page 2 of 4 / Maricopa §8.2.6, Page 5 of 41
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Contract / Maricopa County Contract
findings.policy_quote: Retention: $50,000 (most coverage parts); $250,000 (Cyber Deception)
findings.policy_page: Dec page Item 7, Page 3 of policy
findings.gap_description: Both Sacramento §IV and Maricopa §8.2.6 require retentions/deductibles to be declared and approved by the county. The cyber policy carries a $50K retention on most coverage parts and $250K on Cyber Deception. No record provided of formal disclosure or approval letter from either county. Maricopa §8.2.6 additionally reserves the right to require a surety bond or LOC backing the SIR — a meaningful collateral demand that has not been pre-empted.
findings.plain_english: Your two main county contracts say you have to formally tell the county what your insurance deductibles are, and they have to approve them in writing. They can also demand you post a surety bond or letter of credit to guarantee you'll actually pay the deductible if a claim comes in. There's no evidence Runbeck has done either of these things for the $50K cyber retention (or the $250K Cyber Deception retention). It's a relatively low-likelihood enforcement issue, but it's a contract compliance gap that could become a leverage point in any dispute or contract renewal.
findings.recommendation: Send a formal disclosure letter to both Maricopa County Risk Management and Sacramento County Risk Management listing all retentions/deductibles across the program (cyber, GL, auto, WC, umbrella, E&O) and request written acknowledgment. If no objection within 30 days, retain the silence as constructive approval. Repeat at every renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever sent Maricopa or Sacramento a letter formally disclosing your deductibles, or does that just live on the COI?
If Maricopa invoked §8.2.6 and demanded a letter of credit backing your $50K retention, what would that do to your bank line availability?

findings.requirement_type: Surplus Lines / Non-Admitted Carrier Disclosure
findings.contract_quote: (No Maricopa or Sacramento provision strictly prohibits non-admitted placement; Maricopa §8.2.1 expressly contemplates 'Non-admitted carriers acceptable if approved by County.')

findings.gap_description: Cyber is placed with a non-admitted carrier in Arizona — standard for cyber, which is largely an E&S market. Per KB rule 15, surplus lines placement is not Critical/Ugly by itself: cyber is a market where E&S placement is normal and acceptable, and the carrier is financially strong (A- AM Best). Practical impacts: (1) no Arizona Insurance Guaranty Fund protection if AmTrust ever became insolvent; (2) Maricopa §8.2.1 permits non-admitted placement only if 'approved by County' — confirmation needed that this approval has been formally obtained.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy is placed with an insurance company that isn't formally licensed in Arizona — it's in the 'surplus lines' market, which is where carriers go to write coverage that admitted carriers can't or won't write. This is completely normal for cyber and isn't a problem on its own. Two practical points: First, if AmTrust ever went bankrupt, the Arizona state guaranty fund would NOT step in to pay your claims — that's a feature of every non-admitted placement. Second, your Maricopa contract says non-admitted is OK only if the County approves it — make sure that approval is documented on file.

findings.requirement_type: Unintentional Errors and Omissions Giveback — Verification Needed
findings.contract_quote: (General audit best practice — a giveback that prevents coverage denial when the insured inadvertently fails to report a location, vehicle, or operation.)
findings.policy_quote: Item 8 Endorsements list is blank in the extracted text. Cannot confirm presence of an Unintentional E&O giveback.
findings.gap_description: Cannot determine from the provided 4-page Dec excerpt whether an Unintentional E&O giveback (or equivalent 'Innocent Insured / Notice of Occurrence' protection) is endorsed or embedded in the AmTrust cyber base form. On cyber forms specifically, this concept maps to 'Innocent Coverage' — protection that one insured's misrepresentation/omission doesn't void coverage for other innocent insureds, and that an inadvertent failure to disclose doesn't void coverage for unrelated claims.
findings.plain_english: There's an industry-standard protection called 'Unintentional Errors and Omissions' that says: if you accidentally fail to report something to the carrier — like a new acquisition, a new system, or a network change — they can't deny an unrelated claim because of that mistake. We can't tell from the partial policy whether your cyber policy has this protection. It's worth confirming because election-services companies acquire technology and add systems frequently.
findings.recommendation: Request full policy and confirm presence of Unintentional E&O / Innocent Insured protection. If absent, request endorsement at next renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Notice and Knowledge — Officer-Limited Endorsement Verification
findings.contract_quote: (General audit best practice — endorsement so that a covered occurrence is only triggered when an officer, the person responsible for insurance, or the risk manager is notified — not when ANY employee's knowledge is imputed to the entity.)
findings.policy_quote: Item 8 Endorsements list is blank in the extracted text. Cannot confirm presence of an officer-limited 'Notice of Occurrence' endorsement.
findings.gap_description: Cannot determine whether an officer-limited Knowledge of Occurrence / Notice Manager endorsement is in place. On cyber, this is particularly important — a low-level IT staffer's discovery of an anomaly that goes unreported up the chain can later be argued to have triggered notice obligations. Without an officer-limited endorsement, a missed internal escalation can become a coverage denial argument.
findings.plain_english: Cyber claims often turn on the question of when 'the company' first 'knew' something was wrong. If an IT analyst noticed a strange log entry in March but didn't report it up, and a breach was discovered in July, the carrier might argue knowledge in March = late notice = no coverage. The fix is an endorsement that says only knowledge held by officers, the risk manager, or the IT director (etc.) counts as 'the company knowing.' We can't confirm from the partial policy whether this protection exists. Worth verifying on cyber especially.
findings.recommendation: Request full policy and confirm presence of an officer-limited Notice of Occurrence / Knowledge of Occurrence endorsement. If absent, request endorsement at renewal listing CIO, CFO, General Counsel, and Risk Manager as the only parties whose knowledge triggers notice obligations.

findings.requirement_type: Choice of Law — New York
findings.contract_quote: (Arizona-domiciled insured operating across 31+ states, with NY choice-of-law in cyber policy.)
findings.policy_quote: Choice of Law: New York
findings.policy_page: Dec page Item 5, Page 3 of policy

New York law affects litigation venue, recoverable damages categories, punitive damage availability, statute of limitations interpretation, and 'bad faith' standards — all of which differ materially from Arizona law. Not a coverage gap per se, but a material consideration in any future coverage dispute that should be understood by the insured.
findings.plain_english: If you ever had to sue your cyber carrier over a coverage dispute, the lawsuit would be governed by New York law — even though Runbeck is in Arizona and most of your contracts are with counties in California, Arizona, and elsewhere. New York is generally considered a more carrier-friendly venue than Arizona for things like bad-faith claims. This isn't a coverage gap, but it's a tilt of the table you should be aware of.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, ask whether AmTrust will accept Arizona choice-of-law endorsement (often available, sometimes for nominal premium). If not negotiable with this carrier, factor into renewal carrier selection.

findings.requirement_type: Indemnity Not Limited by Insurance Limits — Balance Sheet Exposure
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: (Not a policy provision — contractual obligation extends beyond policy limits.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.1.3 expressly states that insurance limits do not cap Runbeck's indemnification obligation. Combined with the cyber tower's effective $1M–$2M usable indemnity (per finding-001 and finding-003), this means liability for a major cyber event could pierce the insurance ceiling and become a direct balance-sheet exposure. PE-backed companies are particularly sensitive to this — uninsured liabilities directly reduce sponsor equity value.
findings.plain_english: Your contract with Maricopa says: 'just because your insurance limit is $5M doesn't mean we'll stop at $5M when you owe us money.' If a cyber event causes $20M of damage and your effective insurance recovery is $1.5M, Runbeck — and by extension your private equity sponsor — owes the rest out of pocket. This is a structural feature of every commercial contract; the answer is not to fight the contract, it's to make sure the insurance tower is tall enough that the gap to the indemnity ceiling is small. Right now it isn't.
findings.recommendation: Build a defensible cyber tower of at least $10M, ideally $15M, using a primary + excess structure. Pair with a robust incident response plan, dual-control wire transfer protocols, and a documented vendor security program — these reduce both frequency and severity of the underlying losses driving the indemnity exposure.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento County — Cyber Not Required (Policy Type Mismatch Notice)

findings.recommendation: Monitor Sacramento County contract amendments at each renewal cycle — counties are increasingly adding Cyber requirements as ransomware impacts municipal vendors more frequently. Anticipate that Sacramento may add a Cyber requirement in the next 12–24 months.

Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; Fire Damage: $100,000.' EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease.' Maricopa §8.2.12: 'Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes ... findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions — Sacramento $1M/$1M
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.D / §III.E: 'PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.' Sacramento §II.E: 'UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies ... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability).'

Sacramento expressly forbids the umbrella from satisfying the PL minimum — the underlying PL must independently meet $1M/$1M. The Hartford Management Liability D&O coverage does NOT serve as Professional Liability; in fact PP 00 H350 (Endt #19) on the D&O Coverage Part EXCLUDES claims for 'rendering or failure to render any services for fees.' For an election-services manufacturer whose entire revenue model is fee-for-service ballot printing, mailing, processing, and election technology, the absence of Professional Liability is a catastrophic uninsured exposure: the D&O won't respond, the GL excludes professional services, and there is no PL form in the program.
findings.plain_english: Your business is a service business — you process ballots, run mail-sorting for elections, and operate election technology for counties. If a county sues you for an election error, a missed ballot, a mail handling failure, or a software glitch on Election Day, that's a Professional Liability claim. The General Liability won't pay (services are excluded from GL), the D&O won't pay (the Hartford D&O has a manufacturing/services exclusion), and there is no E&O policy in the program. A single county lawsuit over a botched election is a business-ending event without PL.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Election Services / Technology E&O / Professional Liability policy IMMEDIATELY at minimum $1M/$1M (Sacramento floor). Given the 31-state, 90-million-voter scope and PE-backed risk profile, $5M–$10M is more appropriate. The 'Professional Services' definition must explicitly cover ballot printing, ballot mailing, election mail sorting, election technology / software, ballot processing, and emergency election support technology. Verify retro date predates the earliest county contract effective date so prior acts are covered. Coordinate with Cyber to ensure no retro/coverage gaps between PL and Cyber on data-related claims.
discoveryQuestions: If a county lost a primary because of a ballot you printed incorrectly or mailed late, what insurance policy do you believe would respond?
When was the last time you had counsel review the 'Professional Services' definition on any current Tech E&O or Media policy you carry?
How often do counties send you claim notices, complaint letters, or requests for credits or chargebacks for election performance issues — and how have you handled those historically?
Has anyone shown you the manufacturing/professional services exclusion sitting inside your Hartford Management Liability D&O? Most CFOs are surprised by what it carves out.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber / Network Security / Privacy Liability — Maricopa $5M
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.13: 'Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ..., crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.'
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber / Network Security / Privacy Liability policy provided for review.
findings.gap_description: No Cyber policy provided. Maricopa demands $5M with an unusually broad mandatory feature list including regulatory FINES AND PENALTIES (not just defense), third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer fraud, social engineering, network BI, electronic data restoration, cyber extortion, breach response, and 'no arrest and conviction requirement' on the crime-style components. Run-Test handles 90M voter records and runs election technology — election infrastructure is now classified critical infrastructure by CISA, and ransomware against an election services vendor is a top-tier nation-state-actor target. The Hartford Crime form's IA(V) excludes theft/disclosure of trade secrets, IP, and data — confirming that without standalone Cyber, voter PII exposure has zero coverage anywhere.
findings.plain_english: You hold voter information for 90 million Americans. You run election technology that has become a top target for foreign intelligence services and ransomware crews. Maricopa requires a $5 million Cyber policy with very specific features — regulatory fines, breach response, ransomware, business interruption, funds transfer fraud, and more. We see no Cyber policy at all. A single ransomware event in a primary-election week, or a single voter PII breach, could trigger millions in regulatory fines, multi-state breach notification costs, and class actions. Right now, there is no insurance behind any of that.
findings.recommendation: Bind standalone Cyber Liability immediately. Minimum $5M to satisfy Maricopa; given the threat profile and PE expectations, $10M–$25M is more defensible. Mandatory features per Maricopa: regulatory FINES & PENALTIES (insurable where law allows), third-party fidelity, social engineering / funds transfer fraud (uplift sublimits to $1M+ — the Hartford Crime form's $15K Deception Fraud is wholly inadequate), network BI, dependent BI, ransomware/extortion, breach response, and PCI-DSS coverage. Retro date must predate the earliest county contract. Separately, confirm with Coalition or the broker's preferred cyber market that election-vendor risks are written and not blanket-excluded.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your worst-case nightmare: a ransomware lockup in the 72 hours before a major election. Who pays for the recovery, the breach notification, the regulatory inquiries, and the lost county revenue?
How many voter records do you currently hold or process, and across how many states? Each state has its own breach notification law and its own dollar exposure.
Have you ever been the target of a phishing or social-engineering wire-transfer attempt? Your Hartford Crime form caps social engineering at $15,000 — most CFOs want $1M minimum.
Has CISA or any state Secretary of State ever asked you for evidence of cyber coverage as part of vendor onboarding? What did you provide?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability — Required by Both Contracts
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.E: 'UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability)...' Maricopa §8.2.9: 'If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.'
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E, Page 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.9, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella / Excess policy provided for review.
findings.gap_description: No Umbrella in the audit. Both Counties expressly contemplate umbrella stacking to reach minimum limits (Maricopa: $2M GL/$2M Auto/EL $1M); Sacramento expressly forbids the umbrella from being used to satisfy Professional Liability. For a $5M–$25M-revenue, PE-backed, 50–200 employee election-services manufacturer with 31-state operations and government counterparties, an umbrella is a baseline expectation regardless of contract language — most county contracts and a typical PE-sponsor expectation set umbrella at $5M–$25M. Without sight of the umbrella, follow-form, schedule of underlying, defense inside/outside limits, drop-down provisions, professional-services giveback, and punitive carve-out cannot be verified.
findings.plain_english: An umbrella is the catastrophic-claim layer above your GL, Auto, and Employer's Liability — the policy that pays when a single claim explodes past your primary limits. Both Counties anticipate you have one. We don't have it. For a PE-backed manufacturer your size in election services, you should be carrying $10M–$25M+ in umbrella limits. Without seeing it, we can't confirm it follows form, sits over the right policies, or doesn't have its own exclusions that defeat the underlying coverage.
findings.recommendation: Produce the umbrella policy. Verify (1) follow-form over GL, Auto, Employer's Liability at minimum; (2) schedule of underlying lists every primary; (3) defense costs OUTSIDE limits (typical of standard markets); (4) drop-down for exhausted aggregates; (5) punitive damages NOT excluded in jurisdictions where insurable; (6) NO non-follow-form exclusions broader than the underlying. Confirm umbrella limit is sized to PE-sponsor and largest-county expectations — a $10M minimum is the floor; $25M is a more defensible posture.
discoveryQuestions: What's the umbrella limit your PE sponsor expects you to carry, and is that documented anywhere in the LOI or post-close documentation?
When was the last time someone walked through every policy on your umbrella's schedule of underlying to make sure none of them have been replaced or moved carriers?
If a county sued you for $15M after an Election Day mishap, do you know which policies would respond and in what order?
Are punitive damages excluded on your current umbrella? In several states where you operate, punitives are insurable and a chunk of every catastrophic settlement.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine — Waiver of Subrogation (Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: 'Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.'
findings.policy_quote: No Inland Marine policy provided for review.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §IX requires Inland Marine WoS IF Inland Marine is maintained. Run-Test ships and transports election technology, ballot-printing presses, mail-sorting equipment, and high-value election equipment in transit — Inland Marine (Transit / Equipment Floater / Computers / Communications Equipment) is a near-mandatory line for this operation profile. Status of an IM policy unknown — if maintained, the CA WoS endorsement must be on it; if not maintained, equipment in transit and at off-premises sites is largely uninsured.
findings.plain_english: You move expensive equipment around the country. Insurance for property in transit or at off-site locations is called Inland Marine. We don't know whether you have an Inland Marine policy. Either you do — and Sacramento needs a waiver of subrogation endorsed onto it — or you don't, and your trucks and election technology are exposed every time they leave your warehouse.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether Inland Marine is in the program. If yes, produce policy and verify CA blanket WoS endorsement. If no, evaluate exposure (transit, off-premises equipment, ballot-printing presses, mail-sort equipment, computers, communication equipment) and recommend an IM placement.

findings.requirement_type: Course of Construction (Builders Risk) — Loss Payee + Waiver of Subrogation (Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: 'Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall contain the following provisions: 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.'
findings.policy_quote: Run-Test is an election services manufacturer (printing, mailing, processing, technology). Not a construction contractor; no physical construction implied by client profile.
findings.gap_description: N/A — Run-Test does not perform construction work for Sacramento County. The COC clause is conditional ('any COC policies maintained ... in performance of the Agreement'). Trigger does not fire.
findings.plain_english: Builders Risk (Course of Construction) coverage only applies if you're physically building something for the County. You aren't — you're an election services vendor. This requirement is dormant unless your scope of work changes.
findings.recommendation: Re-evaluate if scope of work expands to include physical construction (e.g., a new election operations center built for a county).

findings.requirement_type: Per-Project Aggregate (Sacramento) — Conditional
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.A: 'Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 Amendment-Aggregate Limits of Insurance (Per Project).'
findings.policy_quote: Run-Test is not a construction contractor — election services manufacturer per client profile.
findings.gap_description: N/A — Per-project aggregate trigger ('Contractors engaged in other projects of construction') does not fire for Run-Test's election services operations. CG 25 03 not required by this contract for Run-Test's scope.
findings.plain_english: Per-Project Aggregate is a construction-industry endorsement that protects your aggregate limit from being eaten up across multiple simultaneous projects. You're not a construction contractor, so this doesn't apply to you on the Sacramento contract.
findings.recommendation: If Run-Test expands into physical construction work for any county, revisit CG 25 03 Per Project Aggregate.

findings.requirement_type: D&O Manufacturing & Professional Services Exclusion — Operational Core Excluded
