findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk — not a specific contract requirement; flagged as the highest-impact policy defect against Run-Test's operational profile.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #19 (PP 00 H350 00 0616) — 'EXCLUSION FOR MANUFACTURING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICE ENDORSEMENT (D&O) ... bars D&O coverage for any Claim based upon, arising from, or in any way related to: (1) malfunction of any product or product failure due to deficiency/inadequacy/defect/dangerous condition in product or its design/manufacture; or (2) rendering or failure to render any services for fees (including services for customers/clients). Carve-backs: (i) civil proceedings brought by security holders without solicitation/assistance/active participation of Insured Entity or Manager; or (ii) Derivative Action or Derivative Demand. Section V Insuring Agreement (C) sub-paragraph (C) deleted.'
findings.gap_description: Hartford's PP 00 H350 endorsement bars D&O Entity Liability (Side C) for claims arising from product malfunction or rendering / failure to render services for fees. Run-Test is a manufacturer of election technology AND a fee-for-service provider of ballot printing, mailing, processing, and election support to counties. Both prongs of this exclusion target Run-Test's CORE BUSINESS. The likely D&O claim scenarios (county lawsuit alleging negligent service delivery, election errors, defective ballots, mail handling failures, election technology malfunction) are exactly what this exclusion eliminates. Side A (non-indemnifiable individual D&O Loss) remains, and the carve-back for security-holder civil proceedings preserves shareholder-style D&O — but the entity-level exposure that drives most operational D&O claims is gone. Compounded by absence of a separate Professional Liability / E&O policy in the audit, this is a complete uninsured operational exposure at the entity level.
findings.plain_english: The fine print on your D&O policy says Hartford won't pay any claim arising from a product defect or any service rendered for a fee. That's literally everything Run-Test does. The shareholder-style D&O claims (a derivative suit or a securityholder lawsuit) are still covered — but a county suing you for a botched election, a ballot misprint, or a mail-sort failure? That's specifically excluded. Combined with no separate Errors & Omissions policy in the program, your entity has no insurance behind its core operational risk at the management-liability level.
findings.recommendation: Two-track fix: (1) Bind a standalone Election Services / Technology E&O / Professional Liability policy to cover services-for-fees and product-malfunction claims (this is the right policy for those exposures, not D&O). (2) At next renewal, attempt to negotiate the exclusion off the D&O via a tailored carve-back, OR move the D&O to a carrier that doesn't apply this exclusion to election-services manufacturers. If Hartford insists on the exclusion, push for a 'failure to supervise' carve-back so individual director/officer Side A coverage isn't undermined when the underlying allegation is operational.
discoveryQuestions: If a county sued Runbeck and named your CEO and CFO personally for a missed election deadline, do you know whether Hartford would defend that claim?
Has your D&O underwriter ever explained the manufacturing/professional services exclusion to your board?
How many of your historical claims, complaints, or county notices have been about operational performance versus financial / shareholder issues? The first bucket is uninsured under your current D&O.
When your PE sponsor diligenced this policy, did anyone flag this exclusion to them — and did they accept it knowing the carve-out?

findings.requirement_type: D&O Prior Acts Exclusion — Short Look-Back Window
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk for PE-backed company.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #28 (PP 00 H033 00 0616) — 'Prior Acts Exclusion (Liability Coverage Parts) ... excludes Claims based upon/arising from/related to any Wrongful Act prior to 8/18/2023, or Interrelated Wrongful Acts thereto. Applies to D&O, EPLI AND Fiduciary.'
findings.gap_description: PP 00 H033 cuts off prior acts coverage at 8/18/2023. With a current policy effective 8/18/2024, this is a 1-year look-back. For a PE-backed company (typical PE hold periods 5–7 years), any pre-acquisition or pre-2023 wrongful act discovered now is uncovered across D&O, EPLI, and Fiduciary. CLAUDE.md flags this as a particular risk for PE-backed companies given heightened regulatory scrutiny.
findings.plain_english: Your policy will not pay for any wrongful act that happened before August 18, 2023. Most claims surface 1–4 years after the conduct, so this short look-back leaves you exposed for anything that happened earlier — pre-PE-acquisition employment claims, historical fiduciary issues, or older D&O matters that get discovered now. PE-backed companies are particular targets for these kinds of look-back claims.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push to extend prior acts to inception of operations (full prior acts) or at minimum to predate the PE investment date. If extension is uneconomic, document the cutoff with the board and PE sponsor so everyone understands the carve-out. Also ensure no individual director who joined before 8/18/2023 has an unprotected window — they may need separate Side A DIC.
discoveryQuestions: When did the PE sponsor close on Runbeck, and what does your prior-acts coverage look like before that closing date?
Has anyone done a pre-policy disclosure exercise listing every potential claim known to management before 8/18/2023?
Are any of your current officers or directors carrying personal exposure for pre-2023 conduct that this policy would not respond to?

findings.requirement_type: D&O Split Prior or Pending Date — Upper $1M Layer
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #34 (PP 00 H105 00 0616) — 'Amended Declarations — Split Prior or Pending Date ... 04/02/2024 applies ONLY to the additional/increased $1,000,000 layer in excess of the first $1,000,000.'
findings.gap_description: The upper $1M D&O / Entity Liability layer has a Prior or Pending Date of 4/2/2024. Any litigation, demand, or formal proceeding pending on or before 4/2/2024 is excluded from the upper $1M layer even if covered by the first $1M. Creates a 'donut' — first $1M responds, upper $1M does not, for claims pending between 8/18/2023 (lower P&P) and 4/2/2024.
findings.plain_english: The top half of your D&O limit (the second $1M layer) was added later and only protects against matters that emerged after April 2, 2024. If a lawsuit was already pending against you on April 1, 2024, you only have $1M of D&O for it — not $2M.
findings.recommendation: Make a written list of any claims, demands, governmental inquiries, or threatened litigation pending on or before 4/2/2024 so the carve-out is documented. At next renewal, attempt to align both layers to the original 8/18/2023 P&P date, or eliminate the split.
discoveryQuestions: What was happening at Runbeck between August 2023 and April 2024 that we should track for this prior-pending donut?
Were there any county complaints, regulatory inquiries, or threatened lawsuits during that window?
Why was the additional $1M added in April 2024 — was that a renewal increase, a PE-driven uplift, or something else?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Social Engineering / Deception Fraud Sublimit Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa §8.2.13 implies social engineering coverage as a mandatory cyber feature, but is silent on Crime sublimits — flagged as a standalone program issue.)
findings.policy_quote: Crime Coverage Part Declarations: 'Deception Fraud / Social Engineering: $15,000.' Endorsement form: PP 00 H600 (Crime Coverage Part).
findings.gap_description: Deception Fraud / Social Engineering sublimit is $15,000 — far below industry-standard $250K–$1M. Social engineering wire fraud is now the #1 financial-loss event for businesses Run-Test's size. A single CFO-impersonation email instructing AP to wire funds, or a vendor-impersonation invoice rerouting payment, regularly costs $200K–$2M+. The Hartford Crime form's cap of $15K means any meaningful social engineering loss is essentially uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Social engineering — where someone tricks one of your employees into wiring money to a fake bank account — is the most common financial fraud loss for companies your size right now. Your Hartford Crime policy caps that coverage at $15,000. Real losses average $200,000–$2,000,000. A single successful phishing email could cost you 10x to 100x what your insurance pays.
findings.recommendation: At next renewal, push Hartford to raise Deception Fraud sublimit to $250K minimum, ideally $1M. Many markets now offer $250K–$1M as standard pricing in this size band. If Hartford won't move, add a standalone Crime endorsement on the Cyber policy with a higher social engineering sublimit. Pair with annual employee training on wire-transfer verification protocols (call-back to known number) — most carriers credit premium for documented controls.
discoveryQuestions: What's your current wire-transfer verification protocol — call-back to a known number, dual approval, anything else? When was it last tested?
Have you had any near-misses — an email that almost got an AP person to wire funds before someone caught it?
If a $500,000 wire went out tomorrow to a fraudulent account because someone impersonated your CEO, do you know how much of that you'd recover from insurance?
Your finance team — are they trained on social engineering, and have they ever been red-teamed?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Voter PII / Data / IP Theft Excluded (Election Services Critical Gap)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk — Run-Test handles 90M voter records.)
findings.policy_quote: Crime Coverage Part §V(V) — 'No coverage for theft/disclosure of trade secrets, IP, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, etc. (unless covered under IA 8 Identity Recovery), or Data (unless covered under IA 7).'
findings.gap_description: Crime form excludes theft or disclosure of trade secrets, IP, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, and Data — except via IA 7 (Computer Systems Restoration: $25K sublimit) or IA 8 (Identity Recovery: $25K sublimit, personal identities only). For Run-Test handling 90M voter records, voter PII theft would not be a Crime claim. With NO Cyber policy in the audit, this leaves voter PII theft completely uninsured. Any voter-data exfiltration event would trigger 31 separate state breach notification statutes plus potential federal/state attorney general inquiries — and not a dollar of coverage anywhere in the current audited program.
findings.plain_english: If a hacker steals voter data — names, addresses, signatures, ballot images — your Crime policy does not cover it. Crime is for stolen money, not stolen data. There is no Cyber policy in the program either. So voter data theft is a 100% uninsured event. Given you handle 90 million voter records, this is an extinction-level exposure.
findings.recommendation: Bind standalone Cyber Liability immediately (see finding-006). Cyber, not Crime, is the right policy for voter PII exposure, breach notification, regulatory defense, and class-action defense. Confirm Cyber retro date predates first county engagement so historical exposures are picked up.
discoveryQuestions: How many voter records (PII / signatures / ballot images) does Runbeck currently hold across all 31 states?
Which states do you operate in that have private rights of action under their breach notification statutes? Those are the states where a class action follows automatically.
If your voter database was exfiltrated and posted publicly tomorrow, who would coordinate the breach response — and on whose dime?
Has any county audit or RFP ever asked for proof of cyber coverage with specific limits?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — LLC Member Theft Largely Excluded
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk — Runbeck Election Services, LLC is an LLC.)
findings.policy_quote: Crime §V(B) — 'Excludes loss from theft/deception fraud/forgery committed by partners or LLC members.' Limited carve-back for IA 1 (Employee Theft) and IA 2 (Forgery) subject to LLC-member-as-Employee paragraph (10) calculation.
findings.gap_description: Standard Crime exclusion for partner/LLC member dishonesty. Run-Test is an LLC, so the named members of Runbeck Election Services LLC fall under this exclusion. Carve-back exists for IA 1 (Employee Theft) and IA 2 (Forgery) only via the 'LLC member as Employee' paragraph. PE-backed structure typically has investor-affiliated members — this is a reminder that key person dishonesty at the LLC-member level is largely uncovered.
findings.plain_english: Standard policies exclude dishonesty by owners and LLC members on the theory that owners shouldn't be insuring against themselves. As an LLC, Runbeck has limited Crime coverage if a member of the LLC commits theft. Worth knowing — particularly relevant if the PE sponsor's representatives are formal LLC members.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with counsel and broker the list of formal LLC members. If any member is operationally close to financial controls, request the LLC-member-as-Employee carve-back be re-quoted to widen coverage, or rely on bond/insurance arrangements at the PE-fund level.
discoveryQuestions: Who are the formal members of Runbeck Election Services, LLC — beyond the operating company itself?
Do any PE sponsor representatives have signature authority or AP authority that would make a member-perpetrated theft scenario more than theoretical?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Wage & Hour Sublimit Inadequate for Workforce Size
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk — 50–200 employee workforce.)
findings.policy_quote: EPLI Wage & Hour Defense Sublimit: $100,000. EPLI form §IV exclusion: 'Excludes claims for unpaid wages/overtime ... plus violations of WARN, NLRA, OSHA, COBRA, ERISA, and Wage & Hour Violations. Carve-back: Defense Costs only for Wage & Hour, subject to a Sub-Limit per Item 5 Decs (sub-limit erodes the aggregate).'
findings.gap_description: Wage & Hour defense costs sublimited to $100,000 (and erodes the EPLI aggregate). Indemnity is excluded entirely. For an election-services workforce that includes hourly/temporary mail-handling and ballot-processing staff, especially during election cycles when long shifts and overtime are common, wage-and-hour exposure (misclassification, unpaid overtime, meal/rest break in CA if any operations there) is meaningful. CA in particular is the highest-frequency Wage & Hour state in the country. $100K of defense covers maybe 3–6 months of attorney work in a putative class case.
findings.plain_english: If a class action claims you misclassified workers or didn't pay overtime correctly, your insurance pays only $100,000 of defense costs and zero of any settlement or judgment. A real wage-and-hour class action runs $500K–$2M in defense alone. California — which you serve through Sacramento County — is the most aggressive wage-and-hour state in America.
findings.recommendation: Push to raise Wage & Hour defense sublimit to $250K–$500K at renewal. Ensure HR practices — exempt classification audits, meal/rest break compliance in CA, time-clock rounding policy — are reviewed annually. Consider a standalone Wage & Hour policy if any CA operations grow beyond incidental. Confirm retroactive coverage on any new W&H sublimit so historical practices aren't excluded.
discoveryQuestions: What's the breakdown of exempt vs non-exempt employees, and when was the last classification audit?
Do any Runbeck employees physically work in California, even occasionally? CA wage-and-hour rules are uniquely strict.
How do you handle overtime during election crunch — and is meal/rest break tracking automated?
Have you ever received a DOL or state labor inquiry, demand letter, or class-action complaint regarding wages or overtime?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Immigration Claim Defense Costs Erode Aggregate
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #22 (PP 00 H430 00 0616) — Immigration Claim Coverage Endorsement. '$100,000 (defense costs only — part of, not in addition to, EPLI aggregate). Retention $10,000. Prior/Pending 8/18/2023.'
findings.gap_description: Immigration claim defense is $100K, defense costs only (no indemnity), and erodes the EPLI aggregate. Useful but limited. Government election-services vendors increasingly face I-9 audits, E-Verify scrutiny, and immigration-status complaints. $100K covers initial defense; would not cover a full ICE administrative proceeding through trial.
findings.plain_english: Your policy gives you $100,000 toward defense if the federal government audits you for I-9 / E-Verify compliance or if an employee sues alleging immigration-status discrimination. That's a starter sum — a full ICE proceeding can chew through it in weeks. Indemnity (any fines or judgments) is not covered.
findings.recommendation: Confirm I-9 / E-Verify protocols are clean and audit-ready. At renewal, push for a standalone Immigration Claim sublimit (not erosive of EPLI aggregate) at $250K+ if available.
discoveryQuestions: When was the last time you ran an internal I-9 audit?
Do you use E-Verify for all new hires across all 31 states?
Have any election-services counterparties (counties or states) imposed immigration-related vendor compliance demands on you?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Workplace Violence Coverage Limited (Expense Only, No Third-Party Liability)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk — election services has elevated workplace-violence threat profile.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #31 (PP 00 H426 00 0616) — Workplace Violence Coverage Endorsement. '$100K sublimit per Dec ... Pays BI Expenses up to 90 days, Employee salary/wages up to 90 days, counseling, security guard up to 30 days, security consultant, PR firm. NO Retention. EXCLUDES war/insurrection/riot AND extortion-driven force AND legal costs/attorneys' fees/settlements/judgments — EXPENSE-only coverage, NOT third-party liability.'
findings.gap_description: Workplace Violence endorsement is $100K of EXPENSE coverage only — pays for security guards, counseling, lost wages, PR firm. Expressly excludes legal costs, attorneys' fees, settlements, or judgments. Third-party bodily-injury suits flowing from a workplace shooting incident are NOT covered here — they would flow to GL/Umbrella (BI) or possibly the EPLI third-party harassment insuring agreement if framed as discriminatory. Election services workers face elevated political-violence threat exposure.
findings.plain_english: If an active-shooter incident occurred at a Runbeck facility, this endorsement pays for security upgrades, counseling, and PR support — about $100,000 worth. It does NOT pay for the lawsuits that follow from the families of those harmed. Those lawsuits would have to be defended by your General Liability or Umbrella, which we don't have in this audit. Election workers and election infrastructure are an elevated political-violence target right now — this gap is increasingly material.
findings.recommendation: (1) Verify GL and Umbrella adequately cover third-party BI from workplace violence (no assault & battery exclusion). (2) Confirm physical security protocols at all Runbeck sites including badge access, panic buttons, and active-shooter training. (3) Consider raising the EPLI WPV sublimit if available, or adding a standalone Active Assailant policy ($1M–$5M aggregate, third-party liability included) — these have become common for high-profile vendors.
discoveryQuestions: What's your physical security posture at the AZ headquarters and any other Runbeck facilities — badge access, panic alarms, active-shooter drills?
Have you received any direct threats, suspicious mail, or harassment campaigns tied to election cycles?
Does your General Liability have an assault & battery exclusion? That's the policy that would face the wrongful-death suits if something happened on a Runbeck site.
Would you consider a standalone Active Assailant policy with third-party liability built in?

findings.requirement_type: D&O — PE Co-Defendant Coverage Endorsement (Lincoln Shields / Black Mountain)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program — appropriate for PE-backed company.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #33 (PP 00 H050 00 0616) — Co-Defendant(s) Extension Endorsement — Private Equity or Venture Capital Funds. 'Named Co-Defendants: Lincoln Shields, LLC and Black Mountain Investment Company, LLC. Defines Affiliated Entities (pooled investment vehicles, GP/managing entities, SPVs) and Co-Defendants. Coverage requires (i) actual/alleged Wrongful Act of an Insured, (ii) Claim first against Insured, (iii) Co-Defendants joined by reason of ownership/management control of Named Entity, (iv) same counsel. Coverage terminates if co-defendants dismissed/found not liable.'
findings.gap_description: PE-specific endorsement extending D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary defense coverage to Lincoln Shields, LLC and Black Mountain Investment Company, LLC (and defined affiliates) when joined as co-defendants in claims primarily against Run-Test arising from PE ownership/management control. Tightly conditioned (must be joined for that reason; dismissal terminates coverage; same counsel required) but provides meaningful protection for the PE sponsor entities — unusual and favorable for a PE-backed mid-market company.
findings.plain_english: When PE sponsors get sued alongside their portfolio companies, their D&O carrier typically pushes back. Hartford has expressly extended your D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary to defend Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain as co-defendants when they're sued because they own you. That's a real favorable feature and the kind of thing your PE sponsor cares about.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with PE sponsor that the named entities on the endorsement match the current ownership structure. If Lincoln Shields or Black Mountain has restructured, exited, or been replaced, request the endorsement be updated. Document this coverage in the PE sponsor's portfolio insurance file.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Personal Profit Final-Adjudication Endorsement (Favorable)
findings.contract_quote: N/A
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #14 (PP 00 H363 00 0718) — 'Amended Personal Profit Exclusion ... now triggered only by judgment or non-appealable final adjudication. Carve-back for Securities Act §§11, 12, 15 violations.'
findings.gap_description: Personal profit exclusion only fires after non-appealable final adjudication and carves back Securities Act §§11/12/15 violations. Insured-favorable — directors and officers retain defense and indemnity through the appeals process.
findings.plain_english: Your D&O won't drop a director or officer's coverage based on a personal-profit allegation until a court has finally and unappealably ruled they actually profited. They keep coverage through trial and appeals. That's a meaningfully better posture than a 'in fact' standard that would let the carrier walk earlier.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal — non-appealable final adjudication standard is the gold standard for conduct exclusions.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Books and Records / §220 Demand Coverage
findings.contract_quote: N/A
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #1 (PP 00 M138 00 0421) — Books and Records Request Endorsement. 'Adds D&O Insuring Agreement (D) Derivative Demands coverage for Books and Records Costs (e.g., Delaware Section 220 demand). $500,000 sublimit, part of (not in addition to) Investigation Costs sublimit.'
findings.gap_description: Books and Records / Section 220 demand coverage is included with $500K sublimit (within Investigation Costs limit). Useful for a PE-backed company facing minority-investor or class-action discovery exercises.
findings.plain_english: If a shareholder demands access to your books and records — often the first step before a derivative lawsuit — this policy will pay up to $500,000 of legal costs to respond. It's a relatively new D&O feature and worth having in the PE-backed context.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Investigation Costs Sublimit Modest for PE-Backed Profile
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk — PE-backed, government counterparties.)
findings.policy_quote: D&O limits per Dec: 'do_investigation_costs_sublimit: $500,000.' Books & Records (Endt #1) shares this sublimit.
findings.gap_description: Investigation Costs sublimit of $500K is modest for a PE-backed company in a regulated, election-services space where government investigations and Section 220 demands are foreseeable. The Books and Records endorsement is shared inside this sublimit, so a single Section 220 case can consume the entire investigation-costs limit.
findings.plain_english: Your D&O has $500,000 set aside for legal costs related to investigations and shareholder document demands. For a PE-backed election services vendor — which sees more government scrutiny than most — that's on the lighter side. A serious DOJ inquiry or a multi-front Section 220 from minority investors could chew through it.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push for $1M–$2M Investigation Costs sublimit, particularly with the elevated regulatory risk profile of election-services vendors.
discoveryQuestions: Have any state Secretaries of State, AGs, or federal agencies (CISA, EAC) ever asked Runbeck for documents or testimony?
How many active or threatened investigations does Runbeck face today?
What's your PE sponsor's expectation for investigation-costs limits — they often set a floor.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Cancellation/Material Change — Contractor-Side Notice Obligation
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.2: 'Contractor is required by this Agreement to immediately notify County if they receive a communication from their insurance carrier or agent that any required insurance is to be canceled, non-renewed, reduced in scope or limits or otherwise materially changed.'
findings.policy_quote: Notification obligation is on the CONTRACTOR (Runbeck), not the carrier. No Designated Entity NOC endorsement is required by Sacramento.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento expressly places the cancellation-notice burden on Runbeck, not the carrier. No Designated Entity NOC endorsement is required. As long as Runbeck has an internal process to flag any policy change to Sacramento, this requirement is administrative.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento doesn't ask your insurance carrier to send them a heads-up if your policy gets canceled — they ask YOU to send the heads-up. So this is an internal compliance task for Runbeck's risk management or finance team, not a policy endorsement issue.
findings.recommendation: Document an internal process: any cancellation, non-renewal, reduction, or material change notice from any carrier or agent triggers an immediate Sacramento Risk Management notification. Assign owner.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa 30-Day NOC vs ML Policy 10-Day AZ Cancellation Notice
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15: 'Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.'
findings.policy_quote: Endt #32 (HR 02 H003 01 0711) — Arizona Cancellation and Nonrenewal Endorsement. 'Insurer may ONLY cancel for nonpayment — 10 days written notice by certified mail. Nonrenewal: 45 days written notice by certified mail.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires 30 days' notice of cancellation/material change on every required policy. The Hartford ML policy's AZ amendatory caps cancellation notice at 10 days for non-payment. This is below Maricopa's threshold, AND below the broker-target 90-day NOC. Note Maricopa is technically asking for notice from CONTRACTOR (8.2.15 requires Contractor to relay carrier notices within 2 business days), but the practical effect is that Runbeck only has 8 business days from carrier notice to (a) relay to Maricopa and (b) Maricopa to react — extremely tight. (Note: Management Liability is not a contractually-required line under Maricopa, so this NOC mismatch is more about discipline across the program — but it foreshadows what every other policy will need.)
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 30 days' warning if any required insurance is cancelled or materially changed. Hartford's Arizona endorsement only gives you 10 days for non-payment cancellation. That's the AZ statutory minimum, not the broker target. Even though this Management Liability policy isn't directly a required Maricopa line, the same problem will repeat on every required line unless we explicitly add a Designated Entity NOC endorsement on each.
findings.recommendation: When the contractually-required policies (GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, Umbrella) are reviewed, request a 30-day Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement naming Maricopa County (and Sacramento County) on each. The broker target is 90 days where the carrier will give it. AZ statutory minimum only applies to the carrier-to-insured notice — a designated entity endorsement can be longer than the AZ statutory minimum because it's a separate contractual undertaking.
discoveryQuestions: Does any of your other policies (GL/Auto/WC/Cyber) currently carry a Designated Entity NOC endorsement naming any county or customer?
Has Maricopa or Sacramento ever pushed back on your COIs for cancellation language?
What's your internal process today if a carrier issues a cancellation notice — who at Runbeck gets the alert and within what timeframe?

findings.requirement_type: Carrier Rating — A.M. Best A-VII (Sacramento) / B++ (Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.1: 'Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.' Maricopa §8.2.1: 'AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.'
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VI.A.1, Page 3 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.1, Page 5 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Twin City Fire Insurance Company (Hartford). Hartford group is consistently rated A+ XV (Superior; largest size category) by A.M. Best.
findings.gap_description: Twin City Fire (Hartford) easily exceeds both A-VII (Sacramento) and B++ (Maricopa) thresholds at A+ XV. Compliant for the Management Liability line. (NOTE: same verification will be required on every other carrier in the program — GL, Auto, WC, PL, Cyber, Umbrella — when those policies are produced.)
findings.plain_english: Hartford / Twin City Fire is one of the strongest carriers in the country. Easily passes both Counties' financial-strength tests for this policy.
findings.recommendation: Verify A.M. Best ratings on every other carrier in the program at next audit cycle. Re-verify annually — ratings can move.

findings.requirement_type: General RMF — 90-Day Notice of Cancellation (Broker Target)
findings.contract_quote: (Broker benchmark — 90 days NOC across program.)
findings.policy_quote: Endt #32 (AZ Cancellation): 10 days nonpayment / 45 days nonrenewal. Endt #5 (PP 00 H107): 20 days nonpayment (overridden in AZ).
findings.gap_description: Broker target for cancellation notice across program is 90 days. ML policy provides 10 days (AZ-mandatory floor for non-payment). No designated-entity NOC endorsement is on this policy because no contracts directly require ML coverage — but worth flagging at next renewal as the program grows.
findings.plain_english: We benchmark all your policies against a 90-day cancellation notice standard. AZ law caps your ML notice at 10 days for non-payment. That's the statutory floor. We can't change AZ law, but at renewal we can ask for a longer notice on the carrier's side, and we can layer in designated entity notice endorsements where contracts demand it.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request the longest carrier-to-insured cancellation notice Hartford will offer. For required-coverage lines (GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, Umbrella) when produced, add Designated Entity NOC endorsements naming Sacramento, Maricopa, and any other key county counterparties at 30–90 days.
discoveryQuestions: Are there any other county or state counterparties (beyond Sacramento and Maricopa) who would also need designated-entity NOC endorsements on the required-line policies?
What's the largest county contract by revenue, and what's its insurance schedule's cancellation notice requirement?

findings.requirement_type: General RMF — Notice & Knowledge Endorsement (Officer-Limited)
findings.contract_quote: (Broker best practice — limit imputation of knowledge to senior officers.)
findings.policy_quote: Endt #10 (PP 00 H022 00 0616) — 'Amend Definition of Notice Manager - Listed. Notice Manager limited to CEO and CFO of Named Entity.' Endt #4 (PP 00 H052) further narrows imputation in the Application to CEO/CFO/signer.
findings.gap_description: Notice Manager limited to CEO/CFO of Named Entity (Endt #10). Imputation of knowledge in the Application limited to CEO/CFO/signer (Endt #4). This is the right posture — a low-level employee's unreported knowledge cannot void coverage on D&O/EPLI/Fiduciary.
findings.plain_english: If a junior employee knows about a brewing claim and doesn't tell anyone, your insurance does not get voided over it. Only the CEO and CFO's knowledge is imputed to the company. That's the right structure and exactly what we benchmark for.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Replicate this posture on the other lines once produced (GL, Auto, Cyber, Umbrella). Many carriers default to imputing all-employee knowledge — must be specifically endorsed.

findings.requirement_type: General RMF — Named Insured Schedule (Single LLC, No Affiliates Named)
findings.contract_quote: (Broker best practice — verify all entities are scheduled.)
findings.policy_quote: Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC' (LLC). Additional Named Insureds: none scheduled. Subsidiary definition (Endt #11, PP 00 H113) extends to controlled 501(c)(3)/foundations/PACs. Co-Defendant endorsement separately schedules Lincoln Shields, LLC and Black Mountain Investment Company, LLC.
findings.gap_description: Named Insured limited to Runbeck Election Services, LLC. No Broad Form Named Insured endorsement. Subsidiary coverage flows through the Common Terms Subsidiary definition with the §11 extension. Need to verify whether (a) any DBAs, real-estate holding LLCs, employee leasing entities, captive 401(k) plans, or PAC-style entities exist that should be scheduled; (b) Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain are correctly handled (they are Co-Defendants under Endt #33 — not Named Insureds, which is the right posture for portfolio-company-level D&O); (c) the LLC entity-type matches the entity-type the underwriter recognizes for automatic-subsidiary purposes.
findings.plain_english: Your policy lists 'Runbeck Election Services, LLC' as the only Named Insured. We don't know whether you have related entities — a real-estate LLC that owns the AZ facility, a benefits trust, a 401(k) committee — that should also be scheduled. PE-backed companies often have a holding-company / op-co stack. We need a current org chart to confirm everyone's covered.
findings.recommendation: Provide a current org chart showing all related Runbeck entities (op-co, holding co, real estate LLCs, benefit plans, charitable foundation if any, PACs). Verify each is either a Named Insured, an Additional Named Insured, or auto-covered as a Subsidiary under the policy definition. Add anything missing.

findings.requirement_type: General RMF — Waiver of Subrogation (Across Program)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VIII (WC), §IX (COC, IM); Maricopa §8.2.7–8.2.8 (broad WoS on GL/Auto/Cyber/Umbrella/WC, except E&O).
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VIII–IX, Page 4 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.7–8.2.8, Page 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Management Liability policy is not a line where WoS is typically required by either contract (E&O is expressly excluded from WoS under Maricopa §8.2.7; ML/D&O is not a contractually-required line). However, both Counties demand WoS on GL, Auto, WC, Cyber, Umbrella — none of which were provided for review.
findings.policy_page: N/A — verification deferred to other policies
findings.gap_description: Waiver of Subrogation is required across the underlying program (GL, Auto, Cyber, Umbrella, WC) by Maricopa, and on WC + COC + Inland Marine by Sacramento. None of those policies were provided for review. Cannot confirm WoS endorsement is in place on each. CA-WC requires the specific WC 04 03 06 form. Maricopa requires WoS expressly on WC (despite carve-out from the general WoS clause in §8.2.8).
findings.plain_english: Both contracts require Waiver of Subrogation endorsements on multiple lines we don't have in this audit. We'll flag this for the next round when those policies are produced — this is one of the items most often missed.
findings.recommendation: When GL/Auto/WC/Cyber/Umbrella are produced for review, verify each carries blanket WoS endorsement. For California WC, confirm WC 04 03 06 California Waiver of Our Right to Recover from Others endorsement is on the policy.

findings.requirement_type: General RMF — Unintentional Errors & Omissions (Not Applicable to ML)
findings.contract_quote: (Broker RMF item — typically a GL endorsement; sometimes embedded in package forms.)
findings.policy_quote: Unintentional E&O is a CGL concept — not applicable to Management Liability. The D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary forms have their own application-warranty and prior-acts mechanisms (Endts #4, #28).
findings.gap_description: N/A for ML policy. Will revisit when CGL is produced.
findings.plain_english: The unintentional-errors-and-omissions giveback is a General Liability concept (it protects you if you forget to report a vehicle, location, or operation). It doesn't apply to your Management Liability policy. We'll check this when the GL policy is reviewed.
findings.recommendation: Verify Unintentional E&O endorsement on the CGL policy when produced.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cyber Retro Date Requirement
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.3: 'In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.'
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber policy provided for review. Cyber is the most likely claims-made line in this program. (Hartford ML D&O/EPLI/Fiduciary are also claims-made — Endt #28 sets prior acts at 8/18/2023; Endt #25 provides ERP options up to 36 months at 200% premium — but ML is not a Maricopa-required policy.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa demands retro date predating contract effective date AND either continuous coverage OR a 2-year ERP. With no Cyber policy in the audit, retro date and ERP cannot be verified. Once Cyber is bound, retro must predate the earliest county engagement (likely well before any current contract date) — every prior year of operations needs to be picked up. Maricopa contract effective date 11/01/21 (per req-003 note) is the floor.
findings.plain_english: When you bind your Cyber policy, the 'retro date' (the earliest event date the policy will cover) must go back to before any of your county contracts started. Otherwise, an undiscovered breach from a prior year that surfaces later is uncovered. Maricopa explicitly requires this on any claims-made line.
findings.recommendation: When Cyber is bound, set retro date to inception of relevant operations (or at minimum predating 11/01/21 Maricopa contract effective date). On any non-renewal or carrier change, purchase 2-year ERP per Maricopa §8.2.3. Same retro-date discipline applies to PL/E&O.
discoveryQuestions: What was Runbeck's first engagement with Maricopa County, and is your historical loss runs clean back to that date?
Has Runbeck ever switched cyber carriers — and if so, was a tail purchased on the prior policy?
Are there any potential incidents (suspicious access, near-misses, employee-reported anomalies) from prior years that should be reported on application before binding new cyber coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Severability of Interest / Civil Code §2782 — Form-Level
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.D: 'SEVERABILITY OF INTEREST: The CONTRACTOR's insurance shall apply separately to each insured against whom claim is made or suit is brought, except with respect to the limits of the insurer's liability.' §VII.B Civil Code §2782 carve-out: 'Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured ...'
findings.policy_quote: Standard ISO CG 00 01 form includes Separation of Insureds. Civil Code §2782 carve-out is a contract acknowledgement, not an insurance endorsement.
findings.policy_page: N/A — applies to GL when produced
findings.gap_description: Both items are essentially form-level (CG 00 01 includes Separation of Insureds) or contract-level (§2782 is a public-policy acknowledgement, not an insurance endorsement). Once GL is produced and confirmed to be ISO CG 00 01, severability is satisfied automatically. §2782 is a contract acceptance — not a coverage modification.
findings.plain_english: Two of Sacramento's clauses — Severability of Interest and the California Civil Code §2782 carve-out — don't require any special endorsement. Severability comes built into the standard GL form. §2782 is just California public policy that says you can't be made to indemnify the County for the County's own active negligence. Both should be fine assuming your GL is on the standard form.
findings.recommendation: Confirm GL is on ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form (covered separately under finding-002). No additional action on §2782 at the policy level.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Indemnification Not Capped by Insurance Limits
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.1.3: 'The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.'
findings.policy_quote: Standard non-limitation clause — Run-Test's contractual indemnification of Maricopa County is not capped at policy limits. Any indemnity obligation exceeding insurance limits is a balance-sheet exposure.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa expressly preserves indemnity obligations beyond policy limits. With limited visibility into the program (no GL/Auto/WC/PL/Cyber/Umbrella in audit), Run-Test's actual exposure above-limits cannot be quantified. PE-backed companies are particularly sensitive to balance-sheet indemnity exposures because the PE sponsor typically has return-of-capital expectations that don't tolerate uninsured contingent liabilities.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract makes clear: the indemnity you owe them is whatever it is — your insurance limits don't cap it. So if a $10M Maricopa lawsuit exceeds your $2M GL and $10M umbrella, you owe the rest out of company assets. Until we see all your policies and confirm limits are sized appropriately, this is an open balance-sheet exposure.
findings.recommendation: (1) When all policies are produced, model worst-case indemnity scenarios against total available limits (primary + umbrella). (2) Confirm umbrella limit is sized to PE sponsor expectations and largest contract counterparty's expected damages. (3) Flag to PE sponsor that contractual indemnity is uncapped — appropriate for risk allocation conversations.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest single-contract revenue exposure in your county portfolio, and what's the worst-case damages estimate for a botched election in that contract?
Have you and your PE sponsor discussed the uninsured indemnity exposure baked into your county contracts?
How are your CGL and umbrella limits sized — by contract, by industry benchmark, by PE direction, or by premium budget?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa County Right to Require Bond/LOC for Deductibles & SIRs
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.6: 'Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County under such policies. Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.'
findings.policy_quote: Hartford ML retentions visible on declarations: D&O retention $10K, EPLI retention $10K, Fiduciary $0, Crime varies by IA. (No GL/Auto/WC/Cyber/Umbrella retention visible — those policies not in audit.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa reserves the right to demand a bond or LOC backing all deductibles and SIRs. ML retentions are modest ($10K D&O, $10K EPLI). Cyber and Umbrella SIRs (when produced) tend to be larger ($25K–$250K typical) and may attract Maricopa's bond/LOC right. Open-ended collateral risk.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa can demand you post a bond or letter of credit for any deductible or self-insured retention on your policies. They haven't yet, but they could. Your Management Liability retentions are small ($10,000); your Cyber and Umbrella retentions when those are bound will be bigger. If Maricopa pulls this lever, that's working capital tied up.
findings.recommendation: Track all deductibles and SIRs across the program in a single schedule. Pre-disclose to Maricopa per §8.2.6 to satisfy the disclosure-and-approval condition; reduce the chance Maricopa requires a bond or LOC. Maintain LOC capacity at the lender if needed.
discoveryQuestions: What's your total LOC capacity at your lender today, and how much is committed?
Has Maricopa ever invoked §8.2.6 against any other contractor you've worked alongside?
What's the largest SIR or deductible currently in your program?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VII.A Additional Insured — 'Arising Out Of' / Ongoing + Completed Ops / No Endorsed Limitations
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.A: 'The COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, and volunteers are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR; products and completed operations of the CONTRACTOR; premises owned, occupied or used by the CONTRACTOR; or automobiles owned, leased, hired or borrowed by the CONTRACTOR. The coverage shall contain no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection afforded to the COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, or volunteers.'
findings.policy_quote: No GL or Auto policy provided for review. AI scope (blanket vs scheduled, ongoing vs completed ops, current vs older edition) cannot be verified.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento demands: (1) broad AI class — officers, directors, officials, employees, volunteers; (2) 'arising out of' wording (broader than 'caused by'); (3) ongoing AND completed operations; (4) no endorsed limitations on scope. Standard CG 20 10 ongoing-ops endorsement satisfies ongoing only — needs CG 20 37 (or equivalent) for completed operations. Older edition CG 20 10 (2004 or earlier) used 'arising out of'; 2013+ editions narrowed to 'caused, in whole or in part, by' — Sacramento expressly demands 'arising out of,' so the older-edition or modified equivalent is required. Cannot verify until GL and Auto are produced. Same AI obligation flows to Auto policy for any County-related auto exposure.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento is unusually demanding on Additional Insured. They want: (1) the broadest possible class of named persons (including volunteers), (2) the broad 'arising out of' trigger language (most modern endorsements use a narrower 'caused by' standard), (3) coverage for both ongoing AND completed work, (4) no carve-outs of any kind. Many modern AI endorsements don't satisfy the 'arising out of' requirement. We can't verify yours until we see the policies.
findings.recommendation: When GL produced, verify CG 20 10 (older edition, 'arising out of') OR equivalent broader-than-current endorsement is in place AND CG 20 37 (or equivalent) provides completed-operations AI. Confirm no limiting endorsements (e.g., CG 21 39 'limitation of coverage to designated premises or project,' or CG 24 04 amend definitions, or AI-specific anti-broadening modifications). Same on Auto via CA 20 48 or blanket equivalent.
discoveryQuestions: When was the last time someone reviewed the form edition of your AI endorsements? The 2004-edition CG 20 10 vs the 2013-edition is a big deal here.
Do you have CG 20 37 separately for completed operations, or are you relying on a blanket form that you believe covers both?
Have any counties — Sacramento or others — pushed back on your AI form language?
Does your COI list specific AI endorsement form numbers, or just say 'as required by written contract'?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VII.C Primary & Noncontributory — Endorsement Required
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.C: 'For any claims related to this Agreement, the CONTRACTOR's insurance coverage shall be endorsed to be primary insurance as respects the COUNTY, its officers, officials, employees and volunteers. Any insurance or self-insurance maintained by the COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, or volunteers shall be excess of the CONTRACTOR's insurance and shall not contribute with it.'
findings.policy_quote: No GL or Auto policy provided for review. P&NC endorsement (CG 20 01 or equivalent) cannot be verified.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento expressly requires P&NC be ENDORSED, not merely stated on the COI. Maricopa §8.2.4 also requires P&NC across all required policies. Without GL and Auto in the audit, cannot verify CG 20 01 (or equivalent) is on the policy. P&NC is one of the most commonly-missed endorsements — many carriers default the AI as 'other insurance' / 'co-primary' which fails the contract requirement.
findings.plain_english: Both Counties want your insurance to pay first and not chase the County's insurance for contribution. This MUST be endorsed onto the policy — not just typed on the certificate. Many policies miss this. Without seeing your GL and Auto, we can't confirm it's there.
findings.recommendation: When GL/Auto produced, verify CG 20 01 (Primary & Noncontributory — Other Insurance Condition) or carrier-equivalent endorsement is in place. The endorsement should be blanket where required by written contract. Confirm same on Auto policy.
discoveryQuestions: When was the last time you compared your COI's stated P&NC language to the actual endorsements attached to your policy?
Has any County risk manager ever rejected your COI because P&NC wasn't shown by endorsement?
If a county-on-county claim arose, do you know whose insurance pays first today?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VII.E Subcontractor Pass-Through — Insurance Flow-Down
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.E: 'CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.'
findings.policy_quote: Subcontract insurance flow-down is a contract-management discipline, not an insurance endorsement. No subcontract template provided for review.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test must (1) be responsible for sub acts/omissions, and (2) ensure subs provide AI endorsements naming the County. Implicit: matching insurance reqs in sub agreements. Without sight of Run-Test's standard subcontract, cannot verify subs are required to (a) carry equivalent insurance, (b) name County as AI, (c) name Run-Test as AI, (d) provide WoS, (e) provide P&NC, (f) provide COIs and endorsement copies before performing.
findings.plain_english: When you sub work out — bulk mail handlers, courier services, IT vendors, third-party printers — your Sacramento contract says you own their mistakes AND you must collect AI endorsements from them naming the County. If your subs don't carry the right insurance or name the County properly, the County can come after you for the gap. We don't have your sub agreements to confirm the flow-down language is correct.
findings.recommendation: Audit Runbeck's standard subcontract template. Confirm it requires subs to: (1) carry minimum insurance matching or exceeding what the County requires of Runbeck; (2) name Runbeck AND the County as additional insureds; (3) provide WoS in favor of Runbeck and County; (4) be primary/noncontributory; (5) furnish COIs with endorsement copies BEFORE performance. Also collect and centralize sub COIs annually. Consider a vendor risk management software tool if not in place.
discoveryQuestions: What does your subcontract template require by way of insurance and AI status?
Who at Runbeck collects and reviews sub COIs — and how often?
Have you ever had a sub fail to deliver a required endorsement and you had to chase it?
Are there subs you're using right now where you don't have a current COI on file?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §X / Maricopa §8.2.14 Notice of Claim & Lawsuit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §X: '... CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.' Maricopa §8.2.14 references annual COIs for two years past completion on claims-made.
findings.policy_quote: Contract-side notice obligation; not a policy endorsement. Hartford ML notice obligations are governed by the policy's claim-reporting provisions (notice as soon as practicable; EPL notice extended to 365 days post-renewal under Endt #12).
findings.gap_description: Two parallel notice obligations: (1) notify the carrier under each policy's claim-reporting clause (typical 'as soon as practicable'), AND (2) notify the County within 30 days of receipt of claim / 10 days of service of process. Failure on either side has consequences — late carrier notice may void coverage, late County notice may breach the contract. Internal claim-management discipline must reflect both.
findings.plain_english: Two clocks start when a claim or lawsuit hits Runbeck: one for your insurance carrier, one for the County. The County wants to know within 30 days of any claim and 10 days of any lawsuit. Your insurance carriers want to know 'as soon as practicable.' Missing either is a problem.
findings.recommendation: Document a claim-intake protocol: any claim/demand/lawsuit/regulatory inquiry/complaint goes simultaneously to (a) general counsel, (b) the broker (for policy-level notice routing), and (c) Sacramento Risk Management within 30 days of claim / 10 days of service. Build a calendar trigger so deadlines aren't missed. Train front-line staff (sales, account managers, AP) on what constitutes a 'claim' that triggers reporting.
discoveryQuestions: What's your current process if a customer complaint letter arrives at AR or sales? Does it ever get to the broker or to the County?
Who decides when something rises to the level of a 'claim' worth reporting to insurance?
Have you ever had a late-reporting issue with any carrier?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §II.B / §VI.A.2 — County Right to Adjust Coverage Mid-Term
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.B (preamble): 'COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection ..., COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.'
findings.policy_quote: Contract-level — not a policy provision. Open-ended ability for Sacramento to demand higher limits or new lines mid-contract.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento reserves an open-ended right to require additional coverage if the Risk Manager deems current coverage inadequate. Practical consequence: budgeted insurance spend can grow mid-term without notice. PE-backed companies on multi-year contracts should price this in.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento reserves the right to demand more insurance from you at any time if their Risk Manager thinks your coverage is too thin. Practically, this is rare — but it's a contract right that means your insurance budget could grow mid-year if Sacramento changes posture or if there's a high-profile election incident in their county.
findings.recommendation: Build a contingency line into the insurance budget for mid-term limit increases. At each renewal, do a mock County risk-manager check-in to anticipate where they might push for more limit. Don't bind 5-year fixed pricing without escalators if Sacramento is a major counterparty.
discoveryQuestions: Has any county ever invoked a unilateral-modification clause and asked you to increase limits mid-contract?
Is the Sacramento contract multi-year, and do you have a budgeted reserve for insurance spend escalation?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa §8.2.14 Designated Entity / Certificate of Insurance Pre-Award
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.14: 'Prior to contract award, Contractor shall furnish the County with valid and complete Certificates of Insurance ... Certificates of Insurance shall identify Maricopa County as the certificate holder ... If a policy does expire during the life of the Contract, a renewal certificate must be sent to County 15 calendar days prior to the expiration date.'
findings.policy_quote: Administrative — broker-issued COI process. Not a policy endorsement.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires renewal COIs 15 days before expiration. Common operational gap if broker COI workflow isn't tightly calendared. Sacramento §VI.A.2 requires renewal evidence 10 days in advance, plus actual endorsement copies (not just COI references) per §I.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa needs a renewal certificate 15 days before each policy expires. Sacramento needs it 10 days before, AND needs actual copies of the endorsements attached. Both Counties want the County named correctly on the certificate. Calendar discipline on the broker side is the fix.
findings.recommendation: Confirm broker (Patriot GIS) calendar holds: (a) 15-day-prior renewal COI to Maricopa; (b) 10-day-prior renewal COI to Sacramento with endorsement copies attached; (c) any other county counterparties on similar timelines. Maintain a county-by-county COI requirements matrix.
discoveryQuestions: How many county COIs does Patriot issue for Runbeck each year, and how is the calendar managed?
Has any county ever flagged a late COI or improper certificate language in your file?
Are endorsement copies attached to your COIs as a matter of routine, or only when a specific county asks?

findings.requirement_type: Fiduciary — HIPAA / ERISA 502(c) Sublimits (Above-Average)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program — Run-Test sponsors employee benefit plans.)
findings.policy_quote: Fiduciary HIPAA sublimit: $500,000. Endt #17 (PP 00 H521) — ERISA §502(c) penalty sublimit: $250,000 (HIGHER than typical $100K). PPA / UK Pensions / ACA penalty sublimit: $250,000. Fiduciary aggregate $1M with $0 retention.
findings.gap_description: Fiduciary coverage is well-equipped: HIPAA $500K, ERISA §502(c) $250K (above-average), PPA/UK Pensions/ACA $250K, Order of Payments protects Side A first (Endt #26), $0 retention. COBRA $1M sublimit (Endt #18). Comprehensive build for a 50–200 employee benefit plan.
findings.plain_english: Your Fiduciary coverage is the strongest piece of the Management Liability policy — generous sublimits for HIPAA, ERISA penalties, COBRA, and PPA/ACA exposures, no retention to chew through, and individual fiduciaries are paid before the company. Solid.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm benefit plan structure hasn't changed (new plans added, plan sponsor entities added) since binding. Verify Subsidiary definition (Endt #11) covers any 401(k) committee or benefit plan trustee entity that's a separate legal organization.

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Broad Retaliation Definition (Whistleblower / SOX / FCA)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program — Run-Test is a federal/state government counterparty exposed to whistleblower / False Claims Act risk.)
findings.policy_quote: Endt #13 (PP 00 H433 00 0417) — Amended Definition of Retaliation (EPLI). 'Broadens Retaliation to expressly include workers' comp rights, FMLA, ERISA, ADA, refusing to violate law, cooperating with investigations, whistleblower claims (False Claims Act, SOX).'
findings.gap_description: Retaliation expressly broadened to cover whistleblower, False Claims Act, and SOX-style protected activity. Material upgrade for an election-services vendor working with government counterparties — FCA whistleblower risk is elevated when government contracts are involved. EPLI Third-Party Liability is also $1M (third-party harassment by non-employees) — important for customer-facing election workforce.
findings.plain_english: Your EPLI policy specifically covers whistleblower and False Claims Act retaliation claims — which is the highest-frequency retaliation exposure for any company with government contracts. That's the right posture for Runbeck.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Document an internal whistleblower policy with anonymous reporting and non-retaliation training to reduce frequency.

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Antitrust / Unfair Trade Sublimit (Carve-Back)
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program risk.)
findings.policy_quote: Endt #16 (PP 00 H377 00 0120) — 'Antitrust/Sherman/Clayton/FTC violations subject to sublimit of lesser of remaining limit or $1,000,000. Carve-back from total exclusion to sublimited coverage.'
findings.gap_description: Antitrust carve-back to $1M is a partial coverage rather than a full exclusion — better than nothing, but lower than the $2M D&O total. For an election-services market with limited competitors, antitrust risk (price-fixing allegations, bid-rigging, market-allocation suits) is non-zero, especially given recent DOJ scrutiny of government-vendor concentration.
findings.plain_english: Your D&O has a $1 million ceiling on antitrust claims, even though the rest of the D&O is $2 million. Election services is a relatively concentrated market — if a state or DOJ accuses you of bid-rigging or price-fixing with a competitor, defense alone could blow through this.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push to remove the antitrust sublimit OR raise it to match the D&O aggregate. If carrier won't, document the cap and ensure compliance training (DOJ vendor practices, fair-bidding) is current.
discoveryQuestions: How concentrated is the election-services vendor market — how many real competitors do you have?
Has Runbeck ever participated in any joint venture, teaming agreement, or industry trade-association pricing discussion?
How is your competitive bidding tracked across state and county RFPs?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Telephone & Toll Fraud Coverage / 30-Day Cap
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program — secondary coverage.)
findings.policy_quote: Endt #30 (PP 00 H672 00 0217) — Telephone System Access Fraud. 'Limit: lesser of $1,000,000 or Crime IA #1 limit. Loss capped to 30 consecutive days from discovery. Excludes losses from calling card / phone access card / phone credit card.'
findings.gap_description: Telephone toll fraud coverage exists but is capped to 30 consecutive days from discovery, with calling/credit/access cards carved out. Slow-rolling toll fraud beyond 30 days is uncovered. Lower-priority issue given declining frequency of toll fraud.
findings.plain_english: If hackers compromise your phone system and rack up international long-distance bills, this endorsement pays — but only for 30 days from when you discover it. After that, you're on your own. Worth knowing, lower priority than social-engineering and cyber concerns.
findings.recommendation: Confirm phone system has standard toll-fraud monitoring and international-call restrictions in place. Lower priority than other findings.
discoveryQuestions: Do you still operate a traditional PBX or have you moved to cloud telephony? Toll fraud is mostly an on-prem issue.

findings.requirement_type: ML Single-Retention When Multiple Coverage Parts Triggered
findings.contract_quote: (Internal program — favorable insured-side feature.)
findings.policy_quote: Endt #29 (PP 00 H109 00 0517) — 'Single Retention — Claims Covered Under Multiple Coverage Parts. When a Claim triggers multiple Coverage Parts, only the HIGHEST applicable Retention applies — no stacking.'
findings.gap_description: Single-retention rule: a single Claim that triggers D&O AND EPLI AND Fiduciary only attracts the highest applicable retention, not stacked retentions. Insured-favorable.
findings.plain_english: If one event triggers multiple parts of your Management Liability policy, you only pay the highest single retention — not all of them. That's how it should work and not all carriers structure it that way.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Extended Reporting Period — 90-Day Election + Tiered ERP Pricing
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa §8.2.3 ERP discipline applies to claims-made lines; Sacramento §V requires 1-year ERP minimum on claims-made PL.)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.3, Page 5 of 41; Sacramento §V, Pages 2–3 of 4
findings.policy_quote: Endt #20 (PP 00 H111) — 90-day ERP election period. Endt #25 (PP 00 H025) — tiered ERP: 12 mo @ 150%, 24 mo @ 175%, 36 mo @ 200%.
findings.gap_description: ML policy provides 90-day election window for ERP and three pricing tiers up to 36 months. Exceeds Sacramento's 1-year minimum and Maricopa's 2-year minimum (both apply to PL/Cyber, not directly ML). Discipline is right, will need to be replicated on PL and Cyber when produced.
findings.plain_english: If this Management Liability policy is ever cancelled or non-renewed, you have 90 days to elect a tail (extended reporting period) and three tiers of pricing. The tiers go up to 36 months at double premium. That's a normal, fair structure. We need the same on your Cyber and Professional Liability when those come in.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Verify same or longer ERP options on Cyber and PL when produced. Ensure broker has ERP-trigger calendar reminders for any non-renewal scenario.

findings.requirement_type: ML Policy Type vs Contract — Not a Required Line, But Operationally Critical
findings.contract_quote: (Neither Sacramento nor Maricopa requires Management Liability / D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary / Crime as a contractual minimum.)
findings.policy_quote: Hartford Twin City Private Choice Premier Management Liability — D&O, EPLI, Fiduciary, Crime. Not contractually required by either county.
findings.gap_description: Neither contract requires this line — but the coverage is operationally critical for a PE-backed mid-market company. Findings against this policy are program-discipline issues, not contract-compliance issues. The contract-compliance findings are concentrated on the missing GL/Auto/WC/PL/Cyber/Umbrella lines.
findings.plain_english: Neither county contract REQUIRES Management Liability — those contracts are about General Liability, Auto, Workers' Comp, Professional Liability, Cyber, and Umbrella. Management Liability is a different beast: it's about protecting your directors, your officers, your benefit plan, and against employee theft. You should keep it because your PE sponsor and your D&O exposure demand it — but the contract heat is all on the OTHER policies we don't have in this audit.
findings.recommendation: Maintain Management Liability at renewal regardless of contract requirements. Address the manufacturing/services exclusion (finding-011) and social engineering sublimit (finding-014) as the highest-priority improvements. Drive the rest of the audit toward producing the contractually-required policies.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation — California Statutory Coverage
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance.
findings.policy_quote: States Covered Part 3.A: AZ, AR, CA, CO, FL, GA, IL, IN, MN, NY, NC, OR, PA, SD
findings.gap_description: California is properly listed as a 3.A scheduled state with statutory WC coverage. Premium of $2,808 allocated to CA. California-specific Broad Form (WC 99 03 04) and CA Cancellation Endorsement (WC 04 06 01 B) are also in place.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County's contract requires you to carry California-statutory workers' comp before your people set foot in California. You do — California is a fully scheduled state on your Hanover policy, with state-specific endorsements correctly attached. This requirement is met.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Maintain CA on Item 3.A at every renewal so long as the Sacramento contract is active.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation — Arizona Statutory Coverage (Home State)
findings.contract_quote: Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes having jurisdiction of Contractor's employees engaged in the performance of the work or services under this contract.
findings.policy_quote: States Covered Part 3.A: AZ … (premium $23,179 — primary AZ WC base). Endorsement WC 02 06 01 C Arizona Cancellation and Nonrenewal Endorsement; WC 8424d Arizona Notice to Employees.
findings.gap_description: Arizona is the home state and primary scheduled state. Statutory AZ WC is in place with AZ amendatory and posting endorsements properly attached.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa County requires statutory workers' comp on any employee performing work in Arizona. You carry it as your home-state coverage, with all the Arizona-specific bells and whistles (cancellation amendatory, employee notice posting). Compliant.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: Employers' Liability Limits ($1M/$1M/$1M)
findings.contract_quote: EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease. (Sacramento) ... Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit. (Maricopa)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.D Pg. 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.12 Pg. 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Employers Liability — Bodily Injury by Accident $1,000,000 each accident; Bodily Injury by Disease $1,000,000 policy limit; Bodily Injury by Disease $1,000,000 each employee.
findings.gap_description: EL limits of $1M/$1M/$1M satisfy both Sacramento County and Maricopa County contract minimums. The $1M policy limits prevail over Oregon's $500K statutory floor (WC 36 03 06).
findings.plain_english: Both counties require a million dollars of employers' liability across the three standard buckets — accident, disease per employee, and disease policy limit. You carry exactly that. Compliant on both contracts.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Note: if any Umbrella adds attachment over EL, confirm umbrella schedule of underlying lists $1M/$1M/$1M EL.

findings.requirement_type: Waiver of Subrogation — Workers' Compensation
findings.contract_quote: The workers' compensation policy required hereunder shall be endorsed to state that the workers' compensation carrier waives its right of subrogation against the COUNTY... (Sacramento §VIII). The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver... §8.2.12 separately requires WC waiver. (Maricopa)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VIII Pg. 4 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.12 Pg. 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 03 13 Waiver of Our Right to Recover from Others Endorsement (Blanket): 'BLANKET WAIVER … for parties having a written contract with policyholder requiring waiver.' Schedule lists AZ, AR, CO, FL, IN, MN, NY, OR, PA. WC 04 03 06 California-specific blanket waiver (separate per CA rules).
findings.gap_description: Blanket Waiver of Subrogation is in place on a contractually-triggered basis (most favorable construction) and California is correctly handled under the state-mandated separate WC 04 03 06 form. Both Sacramento and Maricopa requirements are met without scheduled-customer maintenance.
findings.plain_english: Both counties require the WC carrier to waive its right to come after them if their negligence contributes to an employee injury. Hanover's policy carries a blanket waiver — meaning automatic for any party where a written contract requires it — plus the California-specific waiver form CA insurance regulators demand. You don't need to schedule Sacramento or Maricopa by name; they're already covered.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Confirm at audit that a CA-allocated payroll exists so the CA waiver charge (2% of CA WC premium) doesn't get inadvertently disputed.

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation — Maricopa County and Sacramento County NOT Listed
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa: Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. Contractor must provide to Maricopa County, within two business days of receipt... Sacramento: Contractor is required by this Agreement to immediately notify County if they receive a communication from their insurance carrier... that any required insurance is to be canceled, non-renewed, reduced in scope or limits or otherwise materially changed.
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.15 Pg. 7 of 41; Sacramento §VI.A.2 Pg. 3 of 4
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement 331-0342 (09 11) Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): Schedule lists El Paso County (CO), Coconino County (AZ), Amazon.com Services LLC. 30 days written notice for cancellation other than nonpayment.
findings.gap_description: The Designated Entity NOC endorsement is present and provides 30-day cancellation notice — this matches Maricopa's §8.2.15 carrier-side notice trigger. However, Maricopa County and Sacramento County are NOT listed on the schedule. Both contracts technically place the notice obligation on Contractor (not directly on the carrier), so this is partially mitigated, but adding both counties to the carrier-issued NOC schedule is the cleaner compliance posture and removes the risk of Contractor-side notice failure causing material breach.
findings.plain_english: Both counties want to know quickly if your WC policy is going to lapse. The contracts technically put that notice obligation on you (the Contractor), and Hanover's policy already has a designated-entity notice endorsement listing Coconino County and El Paso County — but neither Maricopa nor Sacramento is on that list today. If your team forgets to send the heads-up and the carrier-issued notice doesn't go out either, you could be in material breach. Cheapest fix: ask Hanover to add Sacramento County and Maricopa County to the Designated Entity NOC schedule so the carrier sends the notice automatically.
findings.recommendation: Endorse 331-0342 (or equivalent) to add Sacramento County (Risk Manager) and Maricopa County (c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003) to the Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation schedule. Keep on the schedule for the life of each contract.
discoveryQuestions: Who on the Runbeck team is responsible for sending the immediate carrier-cancellation notice to Sacramento County and the 2-business-day relay to Maricopa County if Hanover ever issued one?
Have you ever had a near-miss where a payroll or audit dispute almost triggered a cancellation notice — and would your contract-administration team have caught it in time?
How many county/state customer contracts is Runbeck currently performing under that have similar 'immediate notice' or 'designated entity NOC' provisions, and is there a single tracker?
Would you like us to ask Hanover to add every active government contract holder to the NOC schedule at no additional premium, so the notification burden shifts off your team and onto the carrier?

findings.requirement_type: Notice of Cancellation — 90-Day Broker Benchmark
findings.contract_quote: (Broker benchmark per Patriot/RMF General All Policies #1) — 90 days advance notice of cancellation is the broker target on every policy.
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 00 00 C Standard NCCI Form: 10 days advance written notice of cancellation. State amendatories override: AZ 30 days; CA 10/30; AR 10/30; FL 10/30/45; GA 10/75; IL 10/30/60; MN 30/60; NC 15/30; OR 10/45/90; SD 10/20.
findings.policy_page: Standard form Pg. 105; state amendatories Pg. 133–200
findings.gap_description: Standard 30-day notice (AZ amendatory) for non-payment-of-premium cancellation falls short of the Patriot/Hanover 90-day broker benchmark. Only Oregon (90 days for one specific category) and Georgia (75 days certified mail) approach the benchmark. The Designated Entity NOC endorsement (331-0342) provides 30 days — same as state law, no enhancement.
findings.plain_english: Best-in-class brokers push for 90 days of cancellation runway so their clients have time to find replacement coverage if a carrier walks. Your policy has the standard 30 days. It's not a compliance failure under either Sacramento or Maricopa (both are happy with 30 days), but it is below the Patriot benchmark and below what we'd typically negotiate at renewal.
findings.recommendation: At April 2026 renewal, ask Hanover to extend the Designated Entity NOC endorsement to 90 days for all scheduled customers (Sacramento, Maricopa, El Paso, Coconino, Amazon, etc.). Most carriers will agree at no additional premium for high-value accounts.
discoveryQuestions: If Hanover sent you a 30-day non-renewal notice in March, would your team realistically have time to remarket, bind replacement coverage, and get COIs out to all 31 states' worth of customers by April 1 — or would you be scrambling?
Have you ever experienced a non-renewal or mid-term cancellation, and how much lead time did you wish you'd had?

findings.requirement_type: Other States Coverage (3.C) — Multi-State Operations
findings.contract_quote: All States Endorsement on WC / Additionally are any states omitted from 3.A that were picked up under 3.C in the previous year? (RMF WC #3)
findings.policy_quote: Item 3.C Other States Insurance: 'All states except ND, OH, WA, WY (monopolistic) and the states named in 3.A.' Workers Compensation Broad Form Endorsement (990301B0316) extends 60 days for new state notification (vs standard 30) and adds Stop Gap Coverage for ND/OH/WA/WY.
findings.gap_description: Item 3.C covers all states except the four monopolistic states (which are themselves addressed via Stop Gap on the Broad Form). The 14 states scheduled in 3.A capture the bulk of operational footprint.
