The 60-day new-state notification window (broadened from 30) gives operational runway for incidental work in unscheduled states.
findings.plain_english: Runbeck serves customers in 31 states + DC. Your policy is properly built for that: 14 highest-exposure states are scheduled directly (3.A), every other non-monopolistic state is covered automatically (3.C), and the monopolistic states (ND/OH/WA/WY) get Stop Gap employers' liability via the Broad Form. You have a 60-day grace window — more generous than the standard 30 — to notify Hanover when you start work in a new state.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the 60-day new-state notification discipline. As ballot work expands to additional states, add high-payroll states to Item 3.A at renewal to lock in rates and avoid 3.C uncertainty.

findings.requirement_type: Indiana Voluntary Compensation / Other States Modification — Excluded
findings.contract_quote: (Internal review — IN-specific policy carve-out)
findings.policy_quote: WC 99 03 08 03 16 Indiana Exclusion - Other States Insurance & Voluntary Compensation: '...deletes the Broad Form's Other States Insurance modification, Transfer of Rights/Duties modification, and entire Voluntary Compensation/EL Coverage section for Indiana operations only.'
findings.gap_description: For Indiana operations only, the Broad Form Endorsement's enhancements are stripped — Indiana reverts to standard NCCI WC 00 00 00 with no Voluntary Compensation safety net and no broadened Other States provision. If a Runbeck Indiana employee performed work in a state not scheduled on Item 3.A, the Voluntary Compensation backstop that exists for non-IN employees would not exist for them.
findings.plain_english: Hanover's 'broad form' WC endorsement gives most of your employees a safety-net coverage called Voluntary Compensation — basically WC-equivalent benefits for employees who fall through the cracks (e.g., new state, unusual jurisdictional question). For Indiana employees only, that safety net has been deleted by carrier filing requirements. We need to confirm: (1) does Runbeck have any Indiana-resident employees, and (2) do they ever travel out-of-state for work? If yes to both, this gap is worth closing or at least monitoring.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Runbeck: do any IN-resident employees perform work outside the 14 scheduled states? If yes, request IN Voluntary Compensation reinstatement (Hanover may decline per state filing — alternative is scheduling all relevant work-states on Item 3.A in advance).

findings.requirement_type: Experience Modification — Favorable Trend
findings.contract_quote: Experience Modification - Is it being managed by the broker? (RMF WC #8)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 04 25 Experience Rating Modification Factor Revision: 0.690 in AZ/AR/CO/FL/GA/IL/IN/MN/NC/OR/SD; 0.970 in NY; 0.950 merit credit in PA. Schedule modifications: 0.75 AZ, 0.52 CA.
findings.policy_page: Pg. 132; CA schedule mod Pg. WCDEC
findings.gap_description: Experience modifier of 0.69 across the bulk of states (a 31% credit vs. industry baseline) plus a 0.52 California schedule modification (48% credit) and 0.75 Arizona schedule modification (25% credit) reflect strong loss history. NY at 0.97 and PA's merit credit of 0.95 are also favorable.
findings.plain_english: Your loss-history mod is excellent — at 0.69 in most states, you're paying about 31% less than an average risk in your class. The California and Arizona schedule modifications are even better (52% and 75% of standard). This is real money: Hanover is rewarding good claims management with substantial premium credits. Worth highlighting at renewal as leverage for continued favorable terms.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the safety/return-to-work programs that produced this mod. At renewal, document the loss-control narrative for use as leverage with carriers.

findings.requirement_type: Premium Credits Applied — RMF WC #11
findings.contract_quote: Does the comp policy contain all possible credits? (RMF WC #11)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 04 06 Premium Discount Endorsement scheduled in AZ, FL, IN, PA, IL, CA, CO, NY, AR, OR, GA, MN, NC. WC 37 04 05 PA Merit Rating (0.950 credit). Schedule modifications 0.75 AZ / 0.52 CA. CO premium credit available 0%–10% loss-history + 2.5% designated medical provider, capped 12.5%.
findings.gap_description: Multiple discount mechanisms are in place: standard premium discount, PA merit credit, AZ/CA schedule modifications, and a CO loss-history credit pathway. Combined with the 0.69 experience mod, the policy reflects a fully optimized credit posture.
findings.plain_english: We checked: every premium credit available to a risk profile like Runbeck's is on the policy. There's no free money on the table here.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, formally request a Hanover schedule-modification review to push the AZ schedule credit beyond 0.75 if loss experience continues favorable.

findings.requirement_type: Carrier A.M. Best Rating — Compliance with Sacramento A-VII Minimum
findings.contract_quote: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. (Sacramento §VI.A.1) Contractor … shall purchase and maintain … insurance from a company or companies … possessing an AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++. (Maricopa §8.2.1)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VI.A.1 Pg. 3 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.1 Pg. 5 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company (Hanover Insurance Group).
findings.gap_description: Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company (a Hanover subsidiary) historically carries an A (Excellent) Financial Strength Rating with a Financial Size Category in the IX–X range, which exceeds both the Sacramento A-VII minimum and the Maricopa B++ minimum. Verification against the current AM Best Rating (as-of audit date) is recommended to confirm no recent downgrade.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County wants your carrier rated A-VII or better; Maricopa County's bar is lower at B++. Hanover's Mass Bay Insurance Company is historically well above both — likely A IX or A X — but we should pull a current AM Best ratings printout for the audit file to lock this down formally.
findings.recommendation: Request current AM Best Rating Action printout for Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company (NAIC 22306) and file with the Runbeck audit binder. Repeat annually.

findings.requirement_type: Named Insured Cross-Program Consistency
findings.contract_quote: (RMF General All Policies #3) — For each policy, capture the full Named Insured + Additional Named Insured list. Compare across the program — if an entity appears on some policies but not others, flag the asymmetry.
findings.policy_quote: Named Insured: Runbeck Election Services Inc. Additional Named Insureds (per WCDECMISC): [redacted] Investments LLC, [redacted] Properties LLC, [redacted] Graphics Inc.
findings.gap_description: WC policy carries Runbeck Election Services Inc as Named Insured plus three Additional Named Insureds (a real-estate LLC, an investments LLC, and a graphics Inc subsidiary). Cross-program consistency check requires reviewing GL, Auto, Umbrella, Cyber, and PL named-insured schedules — none of which were submitted for this audit pass. The most common gap is entities scheduled on Auto/PL but missing from Umbrella.
findings.plain_english: Your WC policy correctly names the parent (Runbeck Election Services Inc) plus three sister entities — a holding LLC, a real-estate LLC, and a graphics Inc. The next audit step is verifying that those same four entities appear on every other policy in your program (GL, Auto, Umbrella, Cyber, E&O). The most common silent error is an entity that gets dropped off the Umbrella, leaving it without excess protection. We need to see those policies before we can sign off.
findings.recommendation: Request copies of all other policies (GL, Auto, Umbrella, Cyber, PL/E&O, Property, Inland Marine if applicable) and verify named-insured schedule consistency. Specifically check that the three Additional Named Insureds on the WC policy also appear on every other line — and that the Umbrella's Schedule of Underlying matches.

findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge of Claims (RMF General All Policies #4)
findings.contract_quote: Is the policy endorsed so that a covered 'occurrence' is only triggered when the company's officer, the person responsible for insurance, the risk manager, or equivalent is notified — rather than ANY employee's knowledge being imputed to the entity? (RMF General All Policies #4)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 00 00 C standard NCCI form. No Notice Manager / Knowledge of Occurrence / Imputation of Knowledge endorsement scheduled in the listed endorsements.
findings.gap_description: WC policies typically don't carry a separate Notice and Knowledge endorsement — Part Four (Your Duties If Injury Occurs) of the standard NCCI form already imposes a relatively narrow notice obligation on the insured. The RMF benchmark is more relevant to GL/Auto/Cyber/Property where line-employee knowledge can imputed to the entity. Documenting confirmation that this RMF item is best-practice met by the WC standard form is appropriate; the broader cross-program check still applies to GL, Auto, Cyber, E&O.
findings.plain_english: The 'notice and knowledge' protection — making sure only senior managers' knowledge of an incident counts as 'the company knew about it' — is mostly a GL/Auto/Cyber concern, not a WC concern. WC's standard form handles this differently and adequately. We'll close this RMF item on the WC policy but need to verify it's properly endorsed on the rest of the program (GL especially).
findings.recommendation: On the WC policy, no action. On GL, Auto, Cyber, and E&O — verify that Notice Manager / Knowledge of Occurrence / Imputation of Knowledge endorsements are in place, limiting notice triggers to officer / risk manager / insurance contact level.

findings.requirement_type: Unintentional Errors and Omissions (RMF General All Policies #2)
findings.contract_quote: Does the policy include an Unintentional Errors and Omissions giveback? Without it, an inadvertent failure to report a location, vehicle, or operation can result in coverage denial. (RMF General All Policies #2)
findings.policy_quote: No Unintentional E&O endorsement scheduled in the listed endorsements.
findings.gap_description: An Unintentional E&O giveback on a WC policy is uncommon — the standard form already requires the insured to report new states/operations/payroll within 30 days (extended to 60 by the Broad Form). The risk it addresses (failure-to-report a state or class) is real but is mitigated by the Broad Form's broader Other States provision. The bigger Unintentional E&O concern lives on GL (failure to report a new location/operation = coverage denial). Defer evaluation to GL when that policy is submitted.
findings.plain_english: On a WC policy, the question of 'what if we forgot to report a new state' is already softened by your Broad Form's 60-day grace window. Where Unintentional E&O really matters is the GL policy — that's where forgetting to schedule a new location can cause a claim denial. We'll review when the GL policy comes through.
findings.recommendation: On WC: confirm Broad Form's 60-day notification window is operationally tracked. On GL (when submitted): explicitly request Unintentional E&O endorsement.

findings.requirement_type: Alternate Employer Endorsement — Staffing/Leasing Exposure
findings.contract_quote: Alternate Employee Endorsement included on the leasing company's policy? (RMF WC #5)
findings.policy_quote: No Alternate Employer (WC 00 03 01 A) endorsement scheduled.
findings.gap_description: Whether Runbeck uses temporary staffing (PEO, election-day temp labor, scanner operators, mailroom temps for peak election cycles) is operationally important. Election services frequently scale up via seasonal/temp labor. If staffing firms are used, the Alternate Employer Endorsement should be on the staffing firm's WC policy (not Runbeck's), and Runbeck's CGL definition of 'employee' must exclude leased workers.
findings.plain_english: Do you bring on temp labor during the election peak? If yes, two things need to happen: (1) the staffing firm's WC policy should name Runbeck as 'alternate employer' so injured temp claims don't bounce; (2) your CGL needs to treat those temps as covered persons but not 'employees' (otherwise the employee exclusion bars coverage if a temp gets hurt). We need to verify your staffing model before scoring this.
findings.recommendation: Producer to confirm with Runbeck operations: (1) is temp/leased labor used during election cycles? (2) which staffing firm? (3) request copy of staffing firm's COI showing Runbeck as alternate employer.

findings.requirement_type: Owners Excluded from WC Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Owners Excluded (RMF WC #12)
findings.policy_quote: (No specific owner-exclusion endorsement identified in the policy analysis.)
findings.gap_description: PE-backed companies typically have working executives who serve as employees as well as owners. Whether any such individuals are excluded from WC coverage (state-by-state) is undetermined from the data provided. Owner-exclusion elections vary by state and can be a significant uninsured personal exposure for the excluded individual.
findings.plain_english: Some states let owners opt out of WC for themselves to save premium. If that happened, the excluded owner is personally on the hook for any work injury — and PE-backed companies sometimes do this without realizing the personal-liability tail. We need to confirm with Runbeck leadership whether anyone has elected out.
findings.recommendation: Ask Runbeck CFO/HR: are any executives or owners excluded from WC coverage in any state? If yes, confirm they have personal accident/disability coverage to fill the gap.

findings.requirement_type: Classification Codes — Verify Match to Operations
findings.contract_quote: Are the classification codes correct? (RMF WC #15)
findings.policy_quote: (Schedule of Operations classification detail not enumerated in policy analysis.)
findings.gap_description: Runbeck's operations span ballot printing (likely 4299 or 4304 — printing classes), ballot mail processing (potentially 8810 clerical / 8742 outside sales / 7382 trucking auxiliary), election technology hardware (scanner setup — may be 5191 office machine installation or 5192 electronics installation), and warehouse/distribution (8018 mercantile / 8292 storage). The Schedule of Operations should be reviewed line-by-line against actual operations. NCCI Class Code 9014-style phraseology questions should be flagged Informational rather than Bad/Ugly per Critical Thinking Rule 14.
findings.plain_english: Election services is a multi-class operation: printing, mailing, equipment installation, and warehousing. The right WC classification depends on what each employee actually does, not what their title says. We need to walk the Schedule of Operations against payroll and roles before signing off — but a code mismatch is almost always corrected at audit (premium adjustment, not coverage denial).
findings.recommendation: Producer to request full WC Schedule of Operations and walk class codes against Runbeck job descriptions. Common codes for review: 4304 (printing), 8810 (clerical/admin), 5192 (electronic equipment installation), 8018/8292 (warehousing/distribution), 7382 (trucking auxiliary).

findings.requirement_type: Small Indemnity & Medical Claims Management — RMF WC #1, #2
findings.contract_quote: # & amount of small indemnity claims in experience period — Can these be treated, in the future, with the utilization of a 'back to work' program, as medical only claims … resulting in a 70% reduction for mod calculation purposes? (RMF WC #1, #2)
findings.policy_quote: Experience modifier 0.69 (broadly favorable). Loss runs not provided.
findings.gap_description: Mod of 0.69 is favorable but indicates room for sub-1.0 floor pursuit via small-claim management. Loss runs needed to identify indemnity claims under the threshold where back-to-work conversion to medical-only would yield a 70% ELR reduction.
findings.plain_english: Your 0.69 mod is good. With loss-run analysis, we may be able to push it lower — small indemnity claims (the kind where someone misses a few days) often convert to 'medical only' under a structured back-to-work program. NCCI counts only 30% of medical-only claims toward your mod, so this can be 70% off-the-books premium savings.
findings.recommendation: Request 5-year loss runs from Hanover. Identify indemnity claims convertible to medical-only via a back-to-work program. Coordinate with Runbeck HR on accommodation/light-duty protocols.

findings.requirement_type: Federal Acts Coverage (USL&H, Jones Act, FELA, DBA, MEL)
findings.contract_quote: Is the Maritime coverage endorsement included? (RMF WC #9) USH&L on an 'if any' basis? (RMF WC #14) Is Defense Base Act (DBA) included? (RMF WC #13)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 00 00 C Part Two §C.8-10: 'Excludes work subject to USL&H, Nonappropriated Fund, OCSLA, Defense Base Act, FELA, and crew of any vessel.'
findings.gap_description: USL&H, Jones Act, FELA, DBA, OCSLA, and MEL exclusions are present but N/A — Runbeck is a landlocked Arizona-based election services manufacturer with no maritime, harbor, or US-government-overseas operations.
findings.plain_english: These specialty federal-act extensions (longshoreman, maritime crew, defense base act, etc.) don't apply to a ballot printing and election services operation in Arizona. Properly omitted.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Reassess only if Runbeck takes on overseas US government election work or maritime contracts.

findings.requirement_type: Foreign Voluntary Compensation / Endemic Disease / Repatriation
findings.contract_quote: Endemic Disease, Foreign Voluntary and Repatriation costs. (RMF WC #7)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 00 00 C Part Two §C.6: 'Excludes BI occurring outside US/territories/possessions/Canada, except for US/Canadian citizens temporarily abroad.'
findings.gap_description: Foreign Voluntary / Endemic Disease / Repatriation N/A — Runbeck operates exclusively in 31 US states + DC. No overseas business travel exposure suggesting a need for these covers.
findings.plain_english: Foreign business travel coverage isn't needed here — Runbeck's people don't work outside the US.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Reassess if Runbeck adds international operations.

findings.requirement_type: Personnel Practices Exclusion — EPLI Required to Fill
findings.contract_quote: (Coverage gap — RMF General All Policies / cross-program review)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 00 00 C Part Two §C.7: 'Excludes damages from coercion, criticism, demotion, evaluation, reassignment, discipline, defamation, harassment, humiliation, discrimination, termination, or any personnel practices/policies/acts/omissions.'
findings.gap_description: Standard EL exclusion — personnel practices and discrimination claims are not covered under the WC policy. This is universal across NCCI WC forms; the gap must be filled by an Employment Practices Liability (EPLI) policy. Runbeck has 50–200 employees and is PE-backed (heightened scrutiny). Whether an EPLI policy is in the program is unknown — not provided for this audit. Failure to carry EPLI for an organization of this size is a meaningful exposure.
findings.plain_english: Your WC policy explicitly does not cover the entire universe of HR-driven lawsuits — discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination, retaliation. That's normal; WC doesn't cover those. The fix is a separate Employment Practices Liability Insurance (EPLI) policy. We need to confirm whether Runbeck carries one. For a 50–200 employee, PE-backed company, EPLI is a must-have — class certification, plaintiff's-bar attention, and ADA suits are real risks.
findings.recommendation: If EPLI is not already in the program, recommend $2M–$5M EPLI policy with third-party coverage (harassment by non-employees), wage-and-hour defense sublimit, and broad 'employee' definition including temps.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: EPLI policy — not submitted for audit; verify in program
discoveryQuestions: Does Runbeck currently carry a standalone Employment Practices Liability policy, or is EPLI bundled into a Management Liability package?
With 50–200 employees and PE ownership, you're in the prime EPLI risk zone — have you ever had a discrimination, harassment, or wrongful termination claim, and what was the cost?
Do you use temporary or seasonal labor for election peak periods, and does your EPLI definition of 'employee' extend to those workers?
Has your PE sponsor's Reps & Warranties insurance audit ever flagged your EPLI coverage as inadequate?

findings.requirement_type: TRIPRA / Terrorism Coverage Disclosure
findings.contract_quote: (General audit hygiene — TRIPRA disclosure)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 04 22 C Terrorism Risk Insurance Program Reauthorization Act Disclosure: 80% federal reimbursement above insurer deductible; $100B annual cap. Premium charged $1,463. Catastrophe (Other Than Certified Acts of Terrorism) Premium charged $1,265.
findings.gap_description: TRIPRA disclosure properly attached. Both certified-act terrorism and non-certified catastrophe premiums charged. Election infrastructure is a politically-targeted asset class — TRIPRA participation is appropriate.
findings.plain_english: Election services are a politically-charged target — election infrastructure attacks are a real-world threat, and federal terrorism backstop coverage is correctly elected on your WC policy. ($1,463 for terrorism, $1,265 for non-terrorism catastrophe — money well spent.)
findings.recommendation: Maintain TRIPRA election. Verify that Property and Cyber policies also have TRIA elections affirmatively.

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice State Variability — Florida & Georgia Shorter Periods
findings.contract_quote: (General audit hygiene — state-by-state cancellation review)
findings.policy_quote: FL: 10 days nonpayment / 30 days if ≤60 days / 45 days if 61+ days (WC 09 06 09 A). GA: 10 days if <60 days or nonpayment / 75 days certified mail if 60+ days (WC 10 06 01 C). IL: 10/30/60 days. CA: 10 days nonpayment / 10 days for grounds (a)-(f) / 30 days for (g)-(k).
findings.gap_description: State amendatories properly attached for each scheduled state. Notice periods reflect statutory minimums and Hanover's filed forms.
findings.plain_english: Each scheduled state's cancellation rules are correctly built into the policy. No surprises here.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: Audit Noncompliance Charge — Up to 2X (3X in California, 10X in Florida for Concealed Payroll)
findings.contract_quote: (General audit hygiene)
findings.policy_quote: WC 00 04 24 Audit Noncompliance Charge — up to 2X estimated annual premium. WC 04 04 21 California Optional Premium Increase — 3X if audit access not provided within 90 days. WC 09 04 07 A Florida Non-Cooperation — up to 3X EAP, $500 cost-defrayment, 10X penalty + attorney fees for understated/concealed payroll.
findings.gap_description: Audit noncompliance charges are standard but worth flagging operationally. Florida's 10X concealed-payroll penalty is severe — Runbeck's quarterly earnings reports (UCT-6) must be sworn-officer attested.
findings.plain_english: If you don't cooperate with a Hanover premium audit, the carrier can charge you up to double the estimated premium (triple in California, with a Florida penalty of 10X for hidden payroll). Make sure your finance team treats premium audits like an actual audit — cooperate fully, document everything, and never under-report payroll.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Runbeck CFO has a documented premium audit cooperation protocol. Florida quarterly earnings reports require sworn officer attestation — assign one specific officer responsibility.

findings.requirement_type: California — Punitive Damages, §2810.3 Labor Contracting, Flying Crew Exclusions
findings.contract_quote: (California-specific exclusions review)
findings.policy_quote: WC 04 03 01 D / WC 04 03 60 B: CA punitive/exemplary damages uninsurable; minors illegally employed not insured; flying crew of any aircraft excluded; failure to secure WC obligations excluded; Labor Code §2810.3 labor contracting liability excluded.
findings.gap_description: Standard California EL amendatories. None create unexpected gaps for a ballot manufacturer. §2810.3 labor contracting exclusion is relevant only if Runbeck contracts via labor brokers in California for ballot operations.
findings.plain_english: California has its own quirky WC rules — punitive damages can't be insured, illegally-employed minors aren't covered, and Labor Code §2810.3 labor contracting liability (the rule that holds you co-liable for staffing-firm payroll violations) is excluded. None of these create an unusual problem for Runbeck unless you use a CA labor broker for ballot work — in which case, that broker's WC policy needs to name you as alternate employer.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Runbeck does not use California labor brokers for ballot operations. If so, update finding-015 (Alternate Employer) accordingly.

findings.requirement_type: General Liability Policy — Not Submitted for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.A: Building Trades General Aggregate $2M; Products $2M; Personal & Adv. Injury $1M; Each Occurrence $1M; Fire Damage $100K. Maricopa §8.2.10: $2M each occurrence, $4M Products, $4M GA. ISO CG 0001 occurrence form. Blanket contractual, XCU not excluded, no third-party action-over limit.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.A Pg. 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.10 Pg. 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: (General Liability policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: No General Liability policy was provided for cross-reference. The contracts impose substantial GL requirements (Sacramento $1M/$2M minimum on ISO CG 0001 occurrence; Maricopa $2M/$4M/$4M with XCU non-exclusion, blanket contractual, and prohibition on third-party action-over limits). Several requirements (Additional Insured CG 20 10 + CG 20 37, Primary & Noncontributory CG 20 01, Severability of Interest, California Civ. Code §2782 carve-out, Mental Anguish in BI, Care Custody & Control, Fellow Employee, Notice & Knowledge, Damage to Premises sublimit, Per-Project Aggregate, Duty to Defend, Total Pollution review, Unintentional E&O, TRIA) cannot be evaluated without the policy.
findings.plain_english: Your contracts demand a sophisticated General Liability program — particular limits, particular endorsements, the ISO occurrence form, no exotic exclusions, and a Sacramento Civil Code §2782(b) carve-out. We don't have your GL policy in front of us, so we can't tell whether you're compliant. This is the single biggest gap in the audit binder right now.
findings.recommendation: Submit current General Liability policy (full PDF including all endorsements) for cross-reference audit. Priority verifications: (1) ISO CG 0001 occurrence form, (2) limits meet $2M/$4M/$4M Maricopa, (3) AI endorsements CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 with 'arising out of' language, (4) CG 20 01 P&NC, (5) CG 25 03 Per-Project Aggregate (Sacramento conditional), (6) no XCU exclusion, (7) Mental Anguish in BI, (8) Fellow Employee deletion, (9) Notice & Knowledge endorsement, (10) Unintentional E&O giveback, (11) TRIA election.

findings.requirement_type: Commercial Auto Policy — Not Submitted for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.B: $1M CSL including non-owned and hired. Maricopa §8.2.11: $2M CSL each occurrence — owned, hired, non-owned vehicles.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §III.B Pg. 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.11 Pg. 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: (Commercial Auto policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: No Commercial Auto policy was provided. Maricopa requires $2M CSL — a meaningful step up from typical $1M starter Auto policies. RMF Auto items not evaluated: AI status (automatic + WoS + P&NC), Mental Anguish in BI, Broad Named Insured, Lease Gap, Drive Other Car, CA 9933/CA 2054 employee endorsements, environmental endorsement (CA 99 48), Fellow Employee deletion, HNOA, Mobile Equipment, Notice & Knowledge, Symbols 1/2 vs 7, Temp/Leased Worker definition, UM/UIM. Run-Test/Runbeck likely operates a fleet for ballot transport and election support — Auto is a non-trivial line.
findings.plain_english: Election ballot transport, mailing logistics, equipment delivery, and field-tech vehicles all flow through your Auto policy. We don't have it in hand — and Maricopa's $2M CSL is above the typical $1M starter limit, so this is one we need to look at quickly.
findings.recommendation: Submit current Commercial Auto policy. Priority verifications: (1) $2M CSL meets Maricopa, (2) Symbol 1 (Any Auto) coverage, (3) HNOA included, (4) AI endorsement CA 20 48 or equivalent with WoS + P&NC, (5) CA 99 48 limited pollution, (6) Mental Anguish in BI, (7) Fellow Employee deletion, (8) Notice & Knowledge, (9) UM/UIM at full policy limits, (10) MCS-90 if any DOT-regulated transport.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability — Not Submitted for Audit
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.E: Umbrella may stack on GL/Auto/EL but CANNOT satisfy Professional Liability minimum. Must be follow-form. Maricopa §8.2.9: program-level umbrella permission; COI must indicate which lines umbrella covers.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §II.E Pg. 2 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.9 Pg. 6 of 41
findings.policy_quote: (Umbrella/Excess policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: No Umbrella policy submitted. RMF Umbrella items not evaluated: follow-form vs stand-alone, AI follow-form vs conditional exceptions, named insured matching, defense inside/outside limits, maintenance of underlying provisions, notice & knowledge, per-project/per-location follow-form aggregate, professional liability extension/giveback, punitive damages, right and duty when underlying exhausted, total pollution exclusion, schedule of underlying completeness, horizontal exhaustion / P&NC for AIs. Maricopa Auto §8.2.11 has umbrella-attachment ambiguity (does program-level §8.2.9 umbrella permission apply to Auto's $2M CSL even though §8.2.11 doesn't inline-mention umbrella?) — this needs human resolution before signing off.
findings.plain_english: Excess limits sit on top of your GL/Auto/EL — and Sacramento explicitly bars umbrella from satisfying Professional Liability. Maricopa's clauses are ambiguous on whether the program-level umbrella permission stacks on Auto. We need to see the umbrella to evaluate (1) follow-form integrity, (2) defense inside/outside limits, (3) horizontal exhaustion, and (4) punitive damages. Also: there's a real interpretive question whether Runbeck's $1M Auto + Umbrella satisfies Maricopa's $2M Auto requirement, or whether the Auto must independently hit $2M.
findings.recommendation: Submit current Umbrella/Excess policy and full Schedule of Underlying. Priority verifications: (1) follow-form on AI/Named Insured/WoS/P&NC, (2) defense outside limits, (3) all required underlying lines listed (GL/Auto/EL), (4) per-project follow-form aggregate, (5) punitive damages NOT excluded where state allows, (6) right and duty to defend when underlying exhausted, (7) named insureds match other policies. Separately: confirm with Maricopa County Risk Manager whether umbrella stacking satisfies the §8.2.11 Auto $2M CSL requirement, or whether underlying Auto must independently meet $2M.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / E&O — Not Submitted; Critical for Election Services
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.D, §III.E: Professional Liability or E&O $1M per claim and aggregate. Umbrella expressly cannot be used to satisfy this minimum. If claims-made: Retro Date on or before contract effective date; ERP/tail at least 1 year post-completion.
findings.policy_quote: (Professional Liability / E&O policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: No Professional Liability/E&O policy submitted. For an election services manufacturer, this is mission-critical: the definition of 'Professional Services' must squarely cover ballot printing, election mail processing, scanner operations, voter file handling, and emergency support technology. Bodily injury and property damage are GL territory — but a misprinted ballot, a mis-routed mail file, a scanner calibration error, or a voter eligibility data breach are pure E&O exposures. Retro date must be on or before contract effective date. Umbrella cannot stack on PL.
findings.plain_english: This is the keystone policy for an election services company. If a county sues Runbeck because a ballot was misprinted, voters were misclassified, mail-in ballots were misrouted, or election technology malfunctioned — that's a Professional Liability / E&O claim. GL won't respond (no bodily injury, no property damage). Sacramento requires $1M independently — umbrella cannot stack. We need this policy in front of us immediately to verify (1) the definition of 'Professional Services' actually covers election operations, (2) the Retro Date predates each contract, (3) cyber/data exposure isn't carved out, (4) subcontractor work is included. This is the audit's most urgent open item.
findings.recommendation: Submit current Professional Liability / E&O policy with all endorsements. CRITICAL verifications: (1) 'Professional Services' definition covers ballot printing, election mail processing, election technology services, voter data handling, scanner/tabulator operations, emergency support; (2) Retro Date predates oldest active county contract (likely 2019–2021 era for long-tenured customers); (3) limits ≥$1M per claim and aggregate independently of any umbrella; (4) duty to defend (not right to defend); (5) hammer clause not punitive; (6) subcontractor work included; (7) ERP/tail availability for 1 year+ post-completion (Sacramento) and 2 years (Maricopa-style claims-made). If any county contract is pre-2020, verify Retro Date predates it.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber / Network Security & Privacy Liability — Not Submitted; Maricopa Demands $5M
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.13: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. … coverage for network risks, data breaches, invasion of privacy, crisis management, identity theft response, breach notification, credit remediation/monitoring, regulatory defense costs PLUS fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration, network business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: (Cyber Liability policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: No Cyber policy submitted. Maricopa's $5M cyber requirement with prescriptive coverage components (regulatory defense PLUS fines and penalties, third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer, business interruption, no-arrest-and-conviction social engineering) is unusually specific and demanding. For a $5M–$25M revenue contractor handling 90M+ voters' data across 31 states + DC, $5M is on the right order of magnitude but well below catastrophic-breach loss tables. Election-infrastructure cyber events have material political and reputational tail.
findings.plain_english: Runbeck handles personal voter data for over 90 million Americans. A breach, a ransomware event, or a social-engineering wire fraud could be a business-ending event — and Maricopa County contractually demands $5 million of very specific cyber coverage including some unusual asks (third-party fidelity, regulatory fines AND penalties, no arrest-conviction requirement). We need to see your cyber policy ASAP. If you don't have one, this is the most urgent gap in the program.
findings.recommendation: Submit current Cyber policy with all endorsements. CRITICAL verifications: (1) per-occurrence limit ≥$5M (Maricopa); (2) regulatory defense AND fines/penalties (many forms exclude or sublimit fines — push for affirmative coverage); (3) third-party fidelity / social engineering ≥$1M, no arrest-conviction precondition; (4) computer fraud and funds transfer fraud each ≥$1M; (5) business interruption and dependent BI (counties depend on Runbeck — third-party DI is meaningful); (6) cyber extortion / ransomware ≥$1M; (7) breach notification and credit monitoring ≥1M records; (8) Retro Date precedes oldest active contract; (9) PCI-DSS coverage if any payment data; (10) regulatory exposure includes state election integrity laws, not just HIPAA/CCPA. If no cyber policy exists, recommend $10M tower (primary $5M + excess $5M) given voter data scope.

findings.requirement_type: Crime / Fidelity — Embedded Within Maricopa's Cyber Spec (Third-Party Fidelity)
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.13 cyber spec mandates: '...third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.'
findings.policy_quote: (Crime / Fidelity policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's cyber clause includes 'third-party fidelity' — a coverage typically found in Crime/Fidelity policies (ISO Discovery Form) rather than Cyber forms. Whether Runbeck's program addresses this through (a) a standalone Crime/Fidelity policy with third-party coverage, or (b) a Cyber policy with embedded third-party fidelity, or (c) a Management Liability / Crime tower — needs verification. Election services involve high-volume payment processing, vendor accounts, and county-funded contracts — employee theft and social engineering are material exposures.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants protection if a Runbeck employee defrauds the County (third-party fidelity) — that's not a normal cyber coverage; it usually lives on a Crime policy. Either Runbeck's cyber form has it embedded, or there's a separate Crime/Fidelity policy doing the work. We need to see whichever policy handles this so we can confirm Maricopa's spec is met.
findings.recommendation: Submit current Crime / Fidelity policy (or confirm Cyber form embeds third-party fidelity). Priority verifications: (1) employee theft ≥$1M including third-party (client property) coverage, (2) social engineering / impersonation fraud ≥$500K with no arrest-and-conviction requirement, (3) computer fraud and funds transfer fraud, (4) loss outside premises of the named insured, (5) coverage for Runbeck-led wire transfers using county funds.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine / High-Value Equipment — Sacramento Conditional WoS
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: (Inland Marine policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: Client profile flags 'High-value equipment' as a special risk. Election scanners, ballot tabulators, mail processing equipment, and computers in transit between Runbeck facilities and county election offices are classic Inland Marine exposures. If Runbeck carries IM coverage, Sacramento §IX requires a Waiver of Subrogation endorsement on it.
findings.plain_english: Election technology hardware — scanners, tabulators, sorter machines — is high-value, mobile, and travels between your facility and county election offices. That's textbook Inland Marine territory. If you carry IM, Sacramento County wants a waiver of subrogation on it. If you don't carry IM, you may have an uninsured property-in-transit exposure that hasn't been priced.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Runbeck operations: (1) is there an Inland Marine policy in the program? (2) does it cover equipment in transit, equipment on county premises, and equipment at Runbeck facilities? If yes, request WoS endorsement naming Sacramento. If no, recommend pricing IM at minimum $1M–$5M depending on equipment value at risk.

findings.requirement_type: D&O / Management Liability — PE-Backed Exposure
findings.contract_quote: (Cross-program review — PE-backed entity exposure)
findings.policy_quote: (D&O / Management Liability policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: Runbeck is PE-backed, in a politically sensitive industry (election services), and faces heightened regulatory and reputational scrutiny. D&O / Management Liability is essential for protecting individual directors/officers personally and the entity from regulatory investigation costs, derivative actions, and Insured-vs-Insured (IvI) carve-outs. Lessons-learned note (2026-03-24): for PE-backed companies, prior acts dates and investigation cost sublimits warrant special attention.
findings.plain_english: PE ownership + election industry = heightened regulatory and shareholder scrutiny. If Runbeck doesn't carry D&O, the directors and officers (including PE sponsor representatives) are personally exposed to regulatory investigations, securities-style claims, and derivative actions. Whether D&O is in the program is unverified.
findings.recommendation: Submit current Management Liability / D&O policy. CRITICAL verifications: (1) entity coverage (Side C), not just Sides A and B; (2) Insured-vs-Insured carve-back for whistleblower and derivative actions; (3) prior acts date predates PE acquisition and oldest county contract; (4) bump-up exclusion not present; (5) regulatory investigation coverage with adequate sublimits (≥$1M for election regulatory investigations); (6) broad definition of 'Claim'; (7) Hartford Private Choice Premier or similar package — check for manufacturing/professional services exclusion that could bar entity coverage for core operations.

findings.requirement_type: Property — Course of Construction (Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall contain the following provisions: (1) The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. (2) The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: (Conditional — only triggers if Runbeck maintains a COC/Builders Risk policy.)
findings.gap_description: Course of Construction / Builders Risk N/A — Runbeck is an election services manufacturer, not a construction contractor. The condition only triggers if Runbeck performs physical construction work for Sacramento County, which is not part of the disclosed scope.
findings.plain_english: Builders Risk / Course of Construction insurance is for actual construction projects. Runbeck doesn't build buildings for the County — you process ballots and operate election technology. This requirement is properly N/A.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Reassess only if Runbeck takes on physical construction scope.

findings.requirement_type: Per-Project Aggregate (Sacramento §III.A — Construction Conditional)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.A: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503.
findings.policy_quote: (Per-project aggregate condition triggers only for construction. Runbeck is an election services manufacturer.)
findings.gap_description: CG 25 03 Per-Project Aggregate is a construction-specific endorsement. Runbeck is not a construction contractor — the condition does not trigger. Note: if Runbeck-as-Manufacturer ever takes on physical-installation scope (e.g., installing voting infrastructure inside polling places), this condition reactivates.
findings.plain_english: This requirement only kicks in if you're building something for the County, which you're not. Properly N/A.
findings.recommendation: Reaffirm scope of work with Sacramento County to confirm no construction component. If election technology installation includes any construction-trigger activity (electrical, structural, HVAC integration), revisit and add CG 25 03 to the GL.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cyber $5M Requirement — Likely Coverage Shortfall Risk
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence.
findings.policy_quote: (Cyber policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: For a $5M–$25M revenue election services manufacturer, $5M cyber is a high-end ask — not unusual for the lower middle market. The likelihood that Runbeck carries less than $5M (or doesn't carry a separate cyber tower at all) is meaningful, particularly if cyber is bundled into a Tech E&O package with shared limits. This finding flags the requirement as Bad pending confirmation; if Runbeck carries ≥$5M with affirmative regulatory fines/penalties and third-party fidelity, this auto-converts to Good.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa County's $5M cyber demand is steep for a company your size — many companies in the $5M–$25M revenue bracket carry $1M to $3M of cyber. If Runbeck is below $5M, you're contractually short on Maricopa, and a real cyber event (especially a voter-data breach) could blow through whatever you do carry quickly. Plus: Maricopa wants regulatory fines AND penalties (most policies sublimit fines) and third-party fidelity (usually a Crime coverage). Without seeing your cyber form, the odds of a clean compliance pass are not high.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Runbeck cyber limit immediately. If <$5M, build a tower: $5M primary cyber + $5M excess cyber for a $10M Maricopa-compliant program. Push primary form to affirmatively cover regulatory fines and penalties (not just defense), embedded third-party fidelity ≥$500K, no arrest-conviction precondition for social engineering, business interruption + dependent BI ≥$2M.
discoveryQuestions: What's your current cyber limit, and is it dedicated cyber or part of a shared Tech E&O tower?
When was the last time your cyber broker stress-tested the policy against a Maricopa-style spec — regulatory fines, third-party fidelity, no arrest-and-conviction social engineering?
If a county filed a regulatory complaint after a voter-data exposure, does your current cyber pay BOTH the defense costs AND any GLBA/state-AG fines and penalties — or just the defense?
How many of Runbeck's 31 state customer contracts have similar $5M-or-higher cyber requirements you may not currently be meeting?

findings.requirement_type: Auto $2M CSL Likely Shortfall (Maricopa) — Pending Auto Policy Submission
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services or use or maintenance of the premises under this contract.
findings.policy_quote: (Auto policy not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: Most middle-market manufacturing fleets carry $1M CSL on Auto, with umbrella stacking. Maricopa §8.2.11 demands $2M CSL — and §8.2.11 does NOT inline-mention umbrella stacking, even though the program-level §8.2.9 umbrella provision exists. Strict reading: $1M Auto + $10M Umbrella does not satisfy $2M Auto minimum. Permissive reading: program-level umbrella stacks. This is an ambiguous-umbrella-attachment scenario per the audit instructions.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2 million on your Auto policy. The typical mid-market fleet carries $1 million underlying with umbrella on top — and we don't yet know which side of that line Runbeck sits on. There's also a contract-interpretation question: Maricopa's Auto clause doesn't mention umbrella stacking even though the rest of the contract permits it generally. Strict reading of §8.2.11 alone says you need $2M underlying. Permissive reading combining §8.2.9 + §8.2.11 says umbrella works. We recommend confirming with Maricopa's Risk Manager which interpretation they apply.
findings.recommendation: (1) Submit Auto policy to confirm CSL limit. (2) If <$2M, raise to $2M underlying or formally confirm with Maricopa Risk Manager that umbrella stacking is acceptable for §8.2.11. (3) In parallel, file a Needs Review finding (separate, finding-038) for the umbrella-attachment ambiguity.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Umbrella — depends on contract interpretation; see finding-038
discoveryQuestions: What's your current Auto CSL — $1M or $2M? And does your umbrella schedule explicitly list Auto as an underlying line?
Has Maricopa County's Risk Manager ever pushed back on a $1M Auto + Umbrella stack for any prior contract, or accepted it as compliant?
How many of your other 30 state/county customers have $2M Auto requirements you're meeting via underlying vs. umbrella?
If you raised Auto to $2M underlying at next renewal, what's the premium delta, and would the umbrella attach $2M lower (saving offset on the umbrella side)?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Auto $2M — Umbrella Attachment Ambiguous (Needs Review)
findings.contract_quote: §8.2.9: 'If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.' §8.2.11 (Auto): no inline umbrella mention.
findings.policy_quote: (Awaiting Auto and Umbrella policy submission.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.9 contains a program-level umbrella permission stating umbrellas may stack 'to meet the minimum limit requirements.' But §8.2.11 (Auto) and §8.2.13 (Cyber) do NOT inline-mention umbrella attachment, while §8.2.10 (CGL) explicitly does inline-mention umbrella. This drafting asymmetry creates ambiguity: does §8.2.9's general permission apply to lines that don't internally repeat it, or does the absence of inline mention signal an intent to require underlying-only? Strict reading: $1M Auto alone fails $2M. Permissive reading: umbrella stacks per §8.2.9.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract is internally inconsistent: §8.2.9 says umbrellas can stack to hit minimum limits in general, but the Auto clause and Cyber clause don't repeat that language while the CGL clause does. A strict reader would say: 'where umbrella stacking is intended, it's spelled out — and Auto doesn't spell it out, so it's underlying-only.' A permissive reader would say: 'the program-level §8.2.9 covers everything not affirmatively excluded.' We can't resolve this by reading the contract alone — Maricopa's Risk Manager has to tell us how they actually enforce it.
findings.recommendation: Producer to send Maricopa County Risk Manager (301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003) a written interpretation request: 'For §8.2.11 Auto $2M CSL and §8.2.13 Cyber $5M, does the County accept umbrella stacking under §8.2.9, or are these underlying-only limits?' File written response in the audit binder. Until then, do NOT treat any Auto or Cyber compliance as final.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VII.A — Broad Additional Insured Class with No Endorsement Limitations
findings.contract_quote: The COUNTY, its officers, directors, officials, employees, and volunteers are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR; products and completed operations of the CONTRACTOR; premises owned, occupied or used by the CONTRACTOR; or automobiles owned, leased, hired or borrowed by the CONTRACTOR. The coverage shall contain no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection afforded to the COUNTY...
findings.policy_quote: (GL and Auto policies not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's AI clause is broad: covers the County itself plus officers, directors, officials, employees, AND volunteers. Triggered by 'arising out of' (broad scope, much more favorable to AI than 'caused by'). Both ongoing AND completed operations. No endorsed limitations permitted. The current ISO standard CG 20 10 12 04 covers ongoing only via 'caused by' — the older 1985/1993/2001 editions used 'arising out of' (broader). To meet Sacramento's spec without limitation, the GL likely needs CG 20 10 (ongoing) + CG 20 37 (completed ops) on a current edition AND a manuscript or carrier-specific blanket AI form using 'arising out of' language — or an older edition CG 20 10 11 85.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's additional insured clause is one of the broadest in the public-sector contracting world: it pulls in volunteers (poll workers!) and explicitly forbids any endorsement that narrows the protection. The standard ISO endorsement most carriers use today is technically narrower than what Sacramento demands (modern CG 20 10 says 'caused by,' Sacramento's contract says 'arising out of'). We can't tell whether your GL/Auto are wired for this without seeing the policies — but expect to need a manuscript blanket AI form or an older-edition ISO endorsement.
findings.recommendation: Once GL and Auto policies are submitted: (1) confirm AI endorsement edition and language ('arising out of' required, not just 'caused by'); (2) confirm CG 20 37 or equivalent for completed operations; (3) confirm AI extends to officers, directors, officials, employees, volunteers (broader than typical 'County and its directors and officers'); (4) confirm no AI exclusion endorsements (e.g., professional services exclusions, work-from-home exclusions); (5) verify Auto AI extends to owned, leased, hired, AND borrowed vehicles.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VII.B — California Civil Code §2782(b) Active Negligence Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: (California public policy carve-out — does not require a special endorsement.)
findings.gap_description: California Civil Code §2782(b) is statutory — a contract cannot require a contractor to indemnify a public entity for that entity's own active negligence. Sacramento's clause is a contract-level acknowledgement aligning AI coverage with this public policy limit. No specific policy endorsement is required; the carve-out operates at the contract/statutory level.
findings.plain_english: California state law forbids public agencies from making contractors indemnify them for their own active negligence. Sacramento's contract acknowledges this — meaning your insurance doesn't have to (and legally can't) cover the County for the County's own bad acts. This is a statutory protection, not a policy gap.
findings.recommendation: No action required. The carve-out is a public-policy limit, not a coverage gap.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa §8.2.6 — Deductible/SIR Bond or LOC Demand Right
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies may provide coverage that contains deductibles or self-insured retentions. … Contractor shall be solely responsible for the deductible and/or self-insured retention and County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.policy_quote: (All policies — deductibles/SIRs not enumerated for this audit.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa reserves a unilateral right to demand a surety bond or irrevocable LOC backing any deductible or SIR on any required policy. Cyber and E&O often carry SIRs of $25K–$250K, sometimes higher. If Maricopa exercises this right mid-contract, Runbeck would face a meaningful collateral demand affecting working capital.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa County has the right to demand you post a surety bond or letter of credit equal to your deductibles/SIRs. They probably won't exercise it — but they can, at any time during the contract. If Runbeck has a $250K cyber SIR and $50K E&O retention, a demand letter from Maricopa could mean $300K of pledged collateral. Worth knowing before it happens.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory all deductibles/SIRs across the program. (2) Disclose all SIRs proactively to Maricopa per §8.2.6 / §IV (Sacramento parallel) — pre-emptive disclosure may reduce the risk of a mid-term demand. (3) Pre-negotiate with carriers a deductible buy-down option as a contingency.
discoveryQuestions: What are the SIRs and deductibles on your cyber, professional liability, and umbrella policies right now?
Has any government customer ever demanded you post a bond or LOC for your deductibles, and how did Runbeck handle it?
If Maricopa called tomorrow demanding $250K of LOC backing for your cyber SIR, how would your CFO respond — and could it disrupt working capital?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa §8.2.14.4 — Renewal COI 15 Days in Advance
findings.contract_quote: If a policy does expire during the life of the Contract, a renewal certificate must be sent to County 15 calendar days prior to the expiration date.
findings.policy_quote: (Operational COI process — not policy-specific.)
findings.gap_description: Operational obligation: renewal COIs must be in Maricopa's hands 15 calendar days before expiration. Most brokers issue renewal COIs at or after binding — which can be days, not 15 days, before expiration. Process discipline check.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants your renewed COI 15 days before the old one expires. That means by mid-March each year for an April 1 WC renewal. Make sure your broker has this on the COI auto-issuance calendar — getting it right prevents a paperwork lapse triggering a 'material breach' under §8.2.2.
findings.recommendation: Patriot/Hanover to set up automated COI re-issue 15 days before each policy expiration with Maricopa as required-distribution recipient. Same protocol for Sacramento (10 days under §VI.A.2).

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through (Sacramento §VII.E)
findings.contract_quote: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: (Operational — subcontractor risk transfer process.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento (and similar in Maricopa indemnity §8.1) imposes vicarious liability for sub acts/omissions and an obligation to flow down AI requirements to subcontractors. Whether Runbeck has a documented subcontractor risk transfer process — vendor onboarding COI requirements, AI endorsement verification, audit cadence — needs review.
findings.plain_english: When you hire a subcontractor (a print vendor, a logistics partner, a tech contractor), Sacramento County is treating you as if their bad acts are yours. You need to be making them carry their own insurance, name you and the County as additional insureds on it, and verify it. If you're not actively running a subcontractor compliance program, you've got a sleeping exposure.
findings.recommendation: Producer to walk Runbeck operations through subcontractor inventory: (1) who do you sub work to? (2) do they carry GL/Auto/WC at limits matching Runbeck's contract reqs? (3) do their COIs name Runbeck AND the customer counties as AI? (4) is there a documented onboarding/audit cycle? Recommend annual COI refresh discipline.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §X — Contractor's Direct 30/10-Day Notice of Claim/Lawsuit
findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR... CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.
findings.policy_quote: (Operational — Contractor's direct notice obligation, not a policy term.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento imposes a contractual notice duty independent of any carrier obligation: 30 days from claim receipt, 10 days from lawsuit service. Runbeck's claims-handling protocols must distinguish between claim receipt (broad) and lawsuit service (narrow), and route notices to Sacramento Risk Management as well as to the carrier within these windows.
findings.plain_english: Beyond what your insurance carrier requires, Sacramento County wants a direct heads-up: 30 days from when you receive a claim, 10 days from when a lawsuit is served. This is on YOU (the company), not on the carrier. Failure here could be argued as a breach of contract independent of any insurance issue.
findings.recommendation: Build a claim/lawsuit notice protocol into Runbeck's general counsel / risk function: any claim or suit related to a Sacramento contract triggers a parallel notice to Sacramento Risk Management within 30/10 days. Document the protocol in writing. Same approach for Maricopa per §8.2.15 (2 business days for cancellation pass-through).

findings.requirement_type: Indemnity Uncapped by Insurance Limits (Maricopa §8.1.3)
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: (Indemnity exposure exceeds insurance — uninsured balance-sheet exposure.)
findings.gap_description: Standard non-limitation clause. Runbeck's contractual indemnity to Maricopa is not capped at the $2M GL / $5M Cyber / $10M Umbrella aggregate. Catastrophic losses (mass voter-data breach, election-day technology failure causing widespread reputational and political damage) could exceed insurance limits, leaving Runbeck's balance sheet exposed.
findings.plain_english: If the worst happens — say, a massive data breach exposing voter records across multiple counties — your contractual indemnity to Maricopa County isn't capped at your insurance limits. The first $X million is paid by your carriers; everything above that is on Runbeck's balance sheet. For a $5M–$25M revenue company in a politically sensitive industry, that's the line between recoverable disruption and existential threat. The ONLY mitigation is buying enough coverage to make the gap implausibly small — typically a $25M–$50M umbrella tower for a company with this profile.
findings.recommendation: (1) Stress-test current total tower against catastrophic-event scenarios: voter-data mass breach (~$10M–$50M), election-day technology failure causing reputational and political damage (~$10M–$30M), employee fraud (~$5M–$10M). (2) If current umbrella is <$25M, evaluate building toward a $25M–$50M tower. (3) Discuss with Runbeck CFO and PE sponsor — this is a board-level capital allocation conversation.
discoveryQuestions: What's Runbeck's largest current contract exposure — and if a catastrophic claim hit that contract tomorrow, how would your $X million tower hold up?
Has your PE sponsor done a catastrophic-scenario analysis on Runbeck's insurance program — what do they consider the right tower height for an election services platform?

If a multi-county voter data breach exposed 90 million records, what would the regulatory fine, notification, and credit-monitoring tab realistically look like, and does your current cyber tower carry it?
What level of total CGL + Umbrella tower would you need to feel personally comfortable as CFO that an existential event is insured rather than balance-sheet?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §VI.A.2 — Maintenance of Insurance / Material Breach Trigger
findings.contract_quote: Failure to maintain required insurance in force shall be considered a material breach of the Agreement.
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §VI.A.2 Pg. 3 of 4 (Maricopa parallel §8.2.2 Pg. 5 of 41)
findings.policy_quote: WC policy is in force 4/1/25–4/1/26 with all state amendatories properly attached. Cancellation requires 30-day notice in most states.
findings.gap_description: WC policy is currently in force. Renewal cycle (April 1 each year) means a 30-day notice in mid-March would create exposure if renewal is contested. The 60-day Broad Form new-state grace and 30-day cancellation notice provide reasonable runway. Premium audit non-cooperation provisions (2X-3X-10X penalties) reinforce the importance of audit cooperation as a renewal-stability lever.
findings.plain_english: Both contracts treat any insurance lapse as a material breach — a contract-killer trigger. Right now your WC is in force and properly maintained. The discipline to keep it that way is operational: pay premium on time, cooperate with audits, and don't let renewals slide.
findings.recommendation: Maintain renewal cycle discipline. Premium audit cooperation is non-negotiable per §8.2.2 / §VI.A.2 risk.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §II.B — County Right to Unilaterally Adjust Coverage
findings.contract_quote: COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection for COUNTY and for members of the public, COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.
findings.policy_quote: (Open-ended contractual right held by County — affects all policies.)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento reserves an unconditional right to require Runbeck to obtain MORE coverage mid-term if the Risk Manager subjectively decides current coverage is inadequate. This is open-ended — limits could be raised, lines added, or specific endorsements demanded. Difficult to budget for, particularly across multiple county contracts (if Runbeck has 30+ similar contracts, similar clauses likely cascade).
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County has reserved the right to walk in mid-contract and tell you 'you need more insurance.' Maybe they ask for higher cyber after a national election cyber-incident, or higher GL after a different vendor's claim. You're contractually obligated to comply. Worth budgeting in mind that your insurance program is not strictly fixed for the life of these contracts.
findings.recommendation: (1) Build buffer into renewal budgeting for mid-term increases. (2) Consider proactive over-buying on cyber and umbrella to reduce the likelihood Sacramento (or any county) finds your tower inadequate. (3) Track which counties have similar unilateral-adjustment clauses — likely most of them.
discoveryQuestions: Has any of your 31 state customers ever exercised a unilateral coverage-increase right mid-contract?
What's the budgetary buffer you keep for unexpected mid-term insurance changes, and is the PE sponsor aware of this exposure?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa §8.2.5 — Claims-Made Retro Date & 2-Year ERP
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: (Cyber and Professional Liability policies not submitted with this audit pass.)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's claims-made requirement: Retro Date must precede 11/01/21 contract effective date AND either continuous coverage OR 2-year ERP/tail. Cyber and Professional Liability are typically claims-made. Without those policies, retro-date compliance cannot be verified. Sacramento §V parallels this with a 1-year ERP (less stringent than Maricopa's 2-year).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires that any claims-made policy (cyber, E&O) have a Retro Date predating November 2021 — and if you ever drop the policy, you have to buy a 2-year tail. Sacramento parallel is 1 year. We need to confirm Retro Dates against your contract effective dates once the cyber and E&O policies are submitted.
findings.recommendation: When cyber and E&O policies are submitted: (1) verify Retro Date predates Maricopa contract effective date; (2) verify Retro Date predates Sacramento contract effective date; (3) confirm 2-year ERP availability quoted in the policy (Maricopa); (4) maintain continuous claims-made coverage to avoid ERP trigger.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation Policy — MISSING FROM PROGRAM
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance. ... EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease. ... Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes ... Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit.
findings.policy_quote: No Workers' Compensation policy was provided in the program submitted for audit. Only the Hanover Commercial Package (Property + GL + Business Income + Equipment Breakdown + Data Breach) was made available.
findings.gap_description: Both Sacramento and Maricopa contracts mandate statutory WC + EL $1M/$1M/$1M. No WC policy exists in the program. Run-Test has 50–200 employees in AZ — workers' comp is a state statutory requirement regardless of contract. Absence is both a regulatory exposure (AZ A.R.S. §23-961 mandates coverage; criminal penalties + uninsured employer fund liability) and a contractual material breach.
findings.plain_english: There is no workers' comp policy in the file. That's a problem on three fronts at once: (1) Arizona law requires it for any company with employees — operating without it is a criminal violation and exposes the owners personally; (2) every county contract demands proof of it before performance, so contracts are technically in breach right now; (3) if an employee is injured tomorrow, the company pays the medical and lost-wage claim out of its own checkbook with no carrier defense and no statutory cap. For a 100-ish employee manufacturer running ballot-printing equipment, a single back injury or hand-in-press claim can run $250k–$1M+. This is the single biggest exposure in the program.
findings.recommendation: Bind a WC policy immediately. Required: (a) AZ statutory primary state with all states endorsement listing CA, NY, and any other state where work is performed (Run-Test serves 31 states); (b) EL limits $1M/$1M/$1M minimum; (c) Blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (WC 00 03 13); (d) CA-specific Waiver of Our Right to Recover (WC 04 03 06) for Sacramento; (e) Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation listing Maricopa, Sacramento, and other contractually-required counties; (f) verify Other States 3.C is NOT being used to substitute for primary coverage in any state where regular operations exist. Also confirm whether owners are excluded.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through how WC is currently being handled — is there a separate carrier we haven't received documents from, or has Run-Test been operating without a policy in force?
When was the last time someone audited whether the WC policy lists every state where Run-Test performs election services? With 31 states served, even a missed state can leave an employee uninsured.

Has anyone walked you through what happens to the owners personally if AZ industrial commission discovers there's no WC in force — penalties, personal liability, and how it interacts with PE-investor liability waivers in your operating agreement?
If a press operator's hand is caught in a sorter today, who do you call — and have you stress-tested that answer with your CFO?

findings.requirement_type: Commercial Auto Policy — MISSING FROM PROGRAM
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit. Maricopa: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit ... not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles.
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy was provided in the program. Hanover GL package does not include Hired & Non-Owned Auto coverage.
findings.gap_description: Both counties require Commercial Auto liability covering owned + hired + non-owned vehicles. None exists. Run-Test transports printed ballots, mail trays, and high-value election equipment by truck. Maricopa requires $2M CSL; Sacramento requires $1M CSL. Even if Run-Test claims no owned fleet, every employee using a personal vehicle for any company errand (post office runs, supply pickups, county drop-offs) generates non-owned auto exposure that is uncovered.
findings.plain_english: There is no auto policy and no hired/non-owned auto coverage anywhere in the program. The day a salaried employee runs a courier errand to a county election office and rear-ends another vehicle, the personal auto policy will tap out at its limit and the company gets sued for the rest — directly, with no defense. For a company that physically moves ballots between facilities and counties, this is a multi-million-dollar uninsured exposure. Both Sacramento and Maricopa contracts are in technical breach without it.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Commercial Auto policy with $1M CSL minimum (Maricopa requires $2M — bind to the higher floor). Required components: (a) Symbol 1 (any auto) for liability; (b) Hired & Non-Owned Auto liability; (c) Auto Symbol 8 & 9 if no owned vehicles; (d) Blanket Additional Insured by written contract endorsement; (e) Blanket Waiver of Subrogation; (f) Primary & Non-Contributory; (g) UM/UIM at policy limits; (h) Mental anguish included in BI definition; (i) Drive Other Car for executive officers; (j) Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation. If Run-Test has no owned vehicles, at minimum bind a Business Auto policy with HNOA + Symbol 8 & 9.
discoveryQuestions: Does Run-Test own any trucks, vans, or vehicles outright — or are all transport runs done by leased vehicles, courier services, or employees in their own cars?

When an employee drives to a county election office to deliver a ballot proof or pick up materials, whose insurance pays if they cause a serious accident? Have you ever asked your personal auto agent about that scenario?
Maricopa's contract requires $2M of auto coverage; Sacramento requires $1M. How would Run-Test produce a current auto certificate today if either county asked?
Have you priced what a basic business auto policy with hired/non-owned coverage would cost? It's typically in the $2k–$5k range — orders of magnitude less than a single uninsured accident.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / E&O Policy — MISSING FROM PROGRAM
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... Umbrella expressly cannot be used to satisfy this minimum (Section II.E).
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability / E&O policy was provided. The Hanover GL is endorsed with multiple cyber/data privacy exclusions and a professional services AI carve-out (421-2915 §1.c.(5)). EBL endorsement (CG 04 35) is administrative-employee-benefits-only and is NOT professional liability.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is an election technology company performing ballot printing, mail sorting, election processing, and emergency support technology — these are professional services (the contracted work product itself, not a tangible product). Sacramento explicitly requires $1M E&O and explicitly prohibits umbrella from satisfying it. The CGL excludes professional services from AI status (421-2915 §1.c.(5)) and broadly excludes data privacy / cyber claims (CG 00 69, CG 21 06, 421-5286). A claim arising from a printing error that causes ballots to be misread, a mail sort error that delivers ballots to wrong voters, or a data feed error has zero coverage anywhere in the program.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test sells expertise — accuracy, integrity, and security in election services. If a ballot is misprinted, a mail file is mis-sorted, or election data is mishandled, the harm is purely economic (election delays, revote orders, regulatory action, reputational damage) — not bodily injury or property damage. General liability does NOT cover that. Neither does any other policy in the file. For a company whose entire value proposition is professional accuracy on a 90-million-voter scale, going without E&O is the equivalent of a brain surgeon practicing without malpractice. One contested election cycle and the company is uninsured against the lawsuit. Sacramento's contract explicitly forbids the umbrella from filling this gap — so a richer umbrella would not help.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Miscellaneous / Technology Professional Liability or election services E&O policy IMMEDIATELY. Required: (a) $1M minimum (Sacramento contract); recommend $5M–$10M given 90M voter records; (b) definition of 'Professional Services' must explicitly include ballot printing, mail processing, election services, ballot scanning/sorting, and election technology operations; (c) retroactive date on or before the earliest active county contract effective date; (d) tail/ERP option of at least 2 years to satisfy Sacramento §V.C; (e) coverage for subcontractor's professional acts; (f) regulatory defense for state/federal election authority investigations. Markets to consider: Beazley election/tech, Coalition, Tokio Marine HCC, AXIS, Hiscox.
discoveryQuestions: If a county claimed your printing error caused 12,000 ballots to be unreadable and demanded reimbursement plus reprint costs plus reputational damages, who pays — and on what policy?
When you talk to your PE sponsor about this business's largest insurable exposures, where does professional liability rank? Should it rank higher than property?
Sacramento's contract explicitly says the umbrella cannot stand in for E&O — were you aware of that, and how would you produce a $1M E&O certificate to them today?
What's the worst-case scenario your engineering team has war-gamed for an election cycle going wrong? Has that scenario ever been modeled against actual policy coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber / Network Security & Privacy Liability — INSUFFICIENT (Token $10K Data Breach Only)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence.
