The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses, network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Data Breach Coverage Form 411-0669 01 15: '$10,000 aggregate / $10,000 sublimit for breach expenses / $1,000 deductible / 24-hour cyber BI waiting period.' Excludes 'any fees, costs, settlements, judgments, or liability of any kind arising in the course of, or as a result of a claim for damages, lawsuit, administrative proceedings' (§B.1.d) and 'fines, penalties, fees or assessments' (§B.1.c) and 'legal obligations arising by reason of assumption of liability in a contract or agreement' (§B.1.g).
findings.gap_description: Maricopa contract requires $5,000,000 per-occurrence Cyber with broad enumerated coverages including third-party liability, regulatory fines and penalties, cyber extortion, BI, third-party fidelity, computer fraud, and funds transfer. The Hanover Data Breach form provides $10,000 aggregate of FIRST-PARTY-ONLY coverage, expressly excludes third-party liability (§B.1.d), expressly excludes regulatory fines (§B.1.c), and expressly excludes contractual indemnity obligations (§B.1.g). The shortfall is 99.8% of the required limit and most enumerated components are entirely absent. The GL is then layered with three overlapping cyber exclusions (CG 00 69, CG 21 06 12 23, 421-5286 01 25) and a data privacy law exclusion. Net coverage for an actual cyber event involving 90M voter records is effectively zero against the contractual standard.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test handles voter data for 90 million Americans and processes ballots for 31 states — this is the highest-target election services workload in the country and a known nation-state cyber target. The only 'cyber' coverage in the file is a $10,000 token endorsement, of which $0 covers third-party lawsuits, $0 covers regulatory fines (Maricopa explicitly demands fines coverage), and $0 covers contract indemnification to counties. A single ransomware event would consume the entire $10,000 in the first hour of a forensic engagement, and then the company is on its own — paying $250k+ in IR costs out of pocket, owing breach-notice costs to potentially millions of voters, defending regulatory inquiries from 31 state AGs, and indemnifying every county under the contract while uninsured. Maricopa contract is in flat material breach. This is a five-alarm fire.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone $5M+ Cyber & Privacy Liability policy IMMEDIATELY (Maricopa floor; recommend $10M given 90M voter data and PE-backed status). Mandatory components per Maricopa §8.2.13: (a) third-party privacy/network security liability; (b) regulatory defense + fines & penalties (not just defense); (c) cyber extortion / ransomware incl. ransom + restoration; (d) network business interruption + dependent BI; (e) computer fraud + funds transfer; (f) social engineering / fraudulent instruction (separate sublimit acceptable but at meaningful level — $1M+); (g) third-party fidelity; (h) data restoration; (i) breach notification + credit monitoring + PR. Specialty election-cyber markets: Beazley, Coalition, Resilience, Tokio Marine HCC, AXIS, At-Bay. Carve-out the 'war/cyber-war' exclusion to the maximum extent available given nation-state targeting risk.
discoveryQuestions: If Run-Test was hit with ransomware tonight that encrypted ballot files mid-cycle, walk me through the first 48 hours — who pays the forensic firm, who pays the ransom decision, and how do counties learn about it?
Maricopa's contract requires $5M of cyber including regulatory fines coverage. Did anyone tell you the current 'data breach' coverage is only $10,000 — and that fines are excluded?

Election infrastructure is a designated DHS critical-infrastructure sector. Has your security team modeled what a state-sponsored attack would cost in legal exposure across 31 states and DC, and how that maps against your current insurance?

Your PE sponsor likely has portfolio-wide cyber benchmarks — what does the comparable Beazley or Coalition limit look like for other portfolio companies of similar size and risk profile? How does $10K compare?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability — MISSING FROM PROGRAM
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted ... If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella / Excess Liability policy was provided in the program submitted for audit.
findings.gap_description: No umbrella exists. Maricopa's $2M CSL Auto, $2M GL each occurrence, and $1M EL minimums all exceed what a typical primary CGL/Auto carries — umbrella stacking is the standard mechanism. Without an umbrella: (1) Maricopa GL aggregate $4M is structurally not met (Hanover capped at $2M policy aggregate per 421-3635); (2) Maricopa Auto $2M is not met without auto policy + umbrella; (3) any catastrophic loss above $1M underlying eats directly into balance sheet with no excess defense. For a $5M–$25M revenue PE-backed manufacturer with election-cycle event risk, having no umbrella is unusual and a major program defect.
findings.plain_english: There is no umbrella policy. For a PE-backed company on government contracts with 90M voter records, this is structural under-insurance. Beyond just satisfying contract limits, an umbrella is what protects the company from the catastrophic single-event claim — the multi-vehicle accident, the products-liability class action over a defective ballot, the slip-and-fall at a facility tour. The company is currently exposed dollar-for-dollar above the $1M GL each-occurrence limit. A $3M judgment becomes a $2M out-of-pocket loss. PE sponsors typically require $10M–$25M umbrella minimums for portfolio companies of this size — the absence of any umbrella is likely a covenant or sponsor-policy issue too.
findings.recommendation: Bind a $10M–$25M Commercial Umbrella IMMEDIATELY. Required structure: (a) follow-form over GL, Auto (once bound), EL; (b) drop-down for exhausted aggregates; (c) Defense costs OUTSIDE limits; (d) Right and Duty to defend when underlying exhausts; (e) blanket AI follow-form; (f) blanket WoS follow-form; (g) per-project / per-location aggregate follow-form; (h) Punitive damages where insurable by law; (i) Schedule of Underlying must list all primary policies; (j) maintenance of underlying language reviewed — penalty for non-maintenance limited to gap, not policy invalidation; (k) Designated Entity NOC. NOTE: Sacramento expressly forbids umbrella from satisfying Professional Liability — so umbrella does NOT solve the missing E&O finding.
discoveryQuestions: What does your PE sponsor require as a minimum umbrella limit across portfolio companies — and how does the current $0 umbrella square with that requirement?

If a press operator caused a fatality in a delivery vehicle accident tomorrow, the family's wrongful death suit will exceed the GL $1M limit — does the company have $5M cash to settle that case out of pocket?
How are you currently demonstrating to Maricopa County that Run-Test meets the $4M aggregate requirement with a $2M-capped GL?
Have you ever had a prior carrier or broker explain how the per-project aggregate cap on the Hanover GL works in practice — and what it actually leaves you with?

findings.requirement_type: GL Limits — Maricopa $2M Occurrence / $4M Aggregate Shortfall
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products/Completed Operations Aggregate: 'Included in General Aggregate (NOT a separate limit).' Per-project/location aggregate (form 421-3635 07 16) further provides: 'capped at $2,000,000 Policy Aggregate.'
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M each occurrence, $4M PCO aggregate (separate), and $4M general aggregate. Hanover provides $1M occ / $2M GA / PCO included in GA (not separate) / capped at $2M policy aggregate even with per-project endorsement. Three failures: (1) occurrence $1M short by half; (2) general aggregate $2M short by half; (3) PCO is not a separate limit at all — it shares the $2M GA, meaning a series of products claims could exhaust the entire policy. Without an umbrella in the program, none of these are cured.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract demands $2M per occurrence and $4M of overall coverage with a separate $4M bucket for product claims. The actual policy delivers half of each, and there is no separate product bucket — a string of ballot-defect claims could blow through the entire policy in a single year. With no umbrella behind it, the company is in flat material breach of Maricopa's insurance terms today and is also under-protected against any claim approaching $1M.
findings.recommendation: Two-step: (1) increase Hanover GL to $2M each occurrence / $4M GA / $4M separate PCO at renewal — this is a standard increase and pricing is typically modest; OR (2) bind an umbrella of $5M+ that drops down for limit shortfalls AND the per-project cap. Verify with carrier whether the 421-3635 $2M cap can be removed or raised to $4M to align with Maricopa. Until cured, Run-Test is in technical breach of Maricopa §8.2.10.
discoveryQuestions: When did anyone last walk Maricopa County's risk manager through the actual GL aggregate numbers on the certificate vs. the $4M they're requiring?

How many active county/state contracts are running concurrently? With the $2M policy aggregate cap, a single bad year could wipe out coverage for every other contract simultaneously — has that scenario been modeled?

Run-Test produces millions of ballots per cycle. If a printing defect triggered claims from three different counties in one year, the policy could exhaust — does your CFO know the products bucket isn't separate?
Would your PE sponsor accept being named as Additional Insured under a policy with a $2M aggregate cap, or do their portfolio insurance covenants require separate products limits?

findings.requirement_type: Per-Project / Per-Location Aggregate — Capped at $2M (Effectively Neutralized for Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.10 requires $4M General Aggregate; Sacramento §III.A separately requires per-project aggregate (CG 25 03) for construction projects.
findings.policy_quote: 421-3635 07 16 Aggregate Limits of Insurance Per Project and Per Location With Cap: Per-project and per-location aggregate applies, but capped at $2,000,000 Policy Aggregate. Does NOT apply to products-completed operations hazard.
findings.gap_description: The endorsement nominally provides per-project / per-location aggregate, but the $2M policy aggregate cap means that no matter how many projects/locations are concurrently active, total non-products GL recovery is hard-capped at $2M for the year. This functionally negates the per-project benefit — the very purpose of the endorsement is to reset the aggregate per project.
findings.plain_english: On paper the policy has a 'per-project aggregate' which sounds good, but the fine print caps total payouts at $2M no matter how many projects are running. So if you have ten active county contracts and one of them triggers a $2M loss, the other nine have no aggregate left for the year. The endorsement is nominally there to give you a fresh limit per project — the cap takes that benefit away.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request removal of the $2M cap on form 421-3635 (or migration to ISO CG 25 03 / CG 25 04 unrestricted). If carrier won't remove the cap, secure an umbrella that responds with its own per-project aggregate follow-form to provide effective per-project relief. Until then, treat the GL as a single-aggregate policy when communicating with counties.
discoveryQuestions: When you bid on a new county contract, does anyone factor in that a major loss on contract A could leave contracts B through J without aggregate for the rest of the year?
Is the carrier willing to remove the $2M cap on the per-project endorsement at renewal, or is this a market-wide restriction?
How do you currently allocate aggregate exposure across your active contracts — and would the carrier even know if you were running 12 simultaneous projects vs. 3?

findings.requirement_type: Additional Insured — Completed Operations on GL
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento: 'The COUNTY ... are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR; products and completed operations of the CONTRACTOR ...' Maricopa: 'The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County ... as additional insureds.' (scope ongoing/completed not specified — interpreted broadly).
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15 §1: Additional Insured – By Contract, Agreement Or Permit covers ongoing operations only. The endorsement provides AI status 'with respect to liability for bodily injury, property damage or personal and advertising injury caused, in whole or in part, by your acts or omissions or the acts or omissions of those acting on your behalf in the performance of your ongoing operations for the additional insured.' Completed operations AI is NOT included.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento expressly requires AI status for 'products and completed operations' as well as ongoing. Hanover blanket AI form 421-2915 covers ongoing operations only. There is no CG 20 37 or equivalent completed-operations AI endorsement in the policy. Once a county contract concludes, county loses AI status for any completed-operations claim arising thereafter (e.g., a printing defect discovered after election cycle ends).
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires the County to be an additional insured on both ongoing AND completed-operations claims. The current policy only extends AI status during active work. If a printing defect or sorting error is discovered after Sacramento's contract ends — which is typical, since election issues often surface during post-election audits — the County is no longer an AI and the policy will not respond to defend or indemnify them. This creates a contract breach AND a coverage cliff right at the moment claims are most likely to occur.
findings.recommendation: Add ISO CG 20 37 (10 01 or later edition) — Additional Insured – Owners, Lessees Or Contractors – Completed Operations — on a blanket basis where required by written contract. This is the missing companion to CG 20 10 / 421-2915 ongoing-ops form. Most carriers will add at low or no cost. Verify endorsement applies to all named insureds and uses 'arising out of' rather than 'caused by' language to align with broader AI scope counties typically require.
discoveryQuestions: If a Sacramento County election goes bad and an issue surfaces three months after the contract ends, who do you think their county counsel calls — your carrier, or you personally?
Have you ever been asked by a county to provide proof of completed-operations AI coverage and discovered there wasn't a CG 20 37 on the policy?
Election-defect claims often emerge months after the cycle — has anyone walked through what happens to coverage on the day the contract ends and the policy reverts to ongoing-ops-only AI?

findings.requirement_type: AI Endorsement — Professional Services Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.A: 'The coverage shall contain no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection afforded to the COUNTY ...'
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 §1.c.(5): 'This insurance does not apply to ... bodily injury, property damage or personal and advertising injury arising out of the rendering of, or failure to render, any professional services by you or on your behalf.'
findings.gap_description: The blanket AI endorsement carves out professional services. Run-Test's core operations — ballot printing, mail processing, election technology — are arguably professional services. A claim that includes any professional-services nexus (e.g., 'your election services caused our county harm') could trigger this carve-out and strip AI status precisely when the County most needs it. Sacramento further forbids any endorsed limitation on AI scope, which 421-2915 §1.c.(5) violates as a contract matter.
findings.plain_english: The fine print on the additional-insured endorsement says it doesn't apply when the claim involves professional services. Since the company's job IS professional services — election technology, ballot work, processing — almost any meaningful claim a county brings will involve them. The endorsement says 'we'll defend the county, except when the actual work matters.' Sacramento's contract specifically prohibits this kind of carve-out. The contract is in technical breach and, more importantly, the coverage is illusory for the most likely claim scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Address with two layers: (1) bind a true Professional Liability / E&O policy that covers professional services exposure directly (see finding-003); (2) request a manuscript AI endorsement that removes the professional services carve-back, OR a stand-alone scheduled AI form (CG 20 10 / CG 20 26) without the 421-2915 carve-out for tier-one county contracts (Maricopa, Sacramento). Some carriers will issue a manuscript AI without the professional services exclusion for additional premium.
discoveryQuestions: When Sacramento says 'no endorsed limitations on AI scope,' how would Run-Test respond if their risk manager asked specifically about a professional-services exclusion in the AI endorsement?
Have you ever had a claim where the carrier denied AI defense to a county on the grounds that the underlying work was 'professional services'?
Where in the program is professional services liability actually being addressed — and how does that interact with the AI carve-out on the GL?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber / Data Privacy Exclusions on GL — Triple-Layered
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.13 mandates broad cyber liability; Sacramento and Maricopa both require AI status without endorsed limitations on coverage scope.
findings.policy_quote: (1) 421-5286 01 25 Cyber Incident – Cyber Content: 'caused by, arising out of or as a consequence of' a cyber incident — absolute exclusion. (2) CG 00 69 12 23 Violation Of Law Addressing Data Privacy: excludes BIPA, CCPA, GDPR, and similar laws. (3) CG 21 06 12 23 Access Or Disclosure Of Confidential Or Personal Material Or Information: excludes any access/disclosure of confidential information including notification, credit monitoring, forensic, PR, data restoration costs.
findings.gap_description: GL is layered with THREE overlapping cyber/data privacy exclusions, each absolute. Combined effect: any claim with a cyber, data privacy, BIPA, CCPA, or unauthorized-access nexus has zero GL coverage. For an election services company processing 90M voter records, this eliminates the GL as a backstop for the very exposures most likely to materialize. The exclusions go further than typical — CG 21 06 12 23 (the 12/23 edition) is the broadest version industry-wide and even sweeps in notification costs and forensic expenses.
findings.plain_english: The general liability policy has been stacked with three different exclusions that, taken together, eliminate any cyber or data privacy claim from coverage. Voter data, ballot data, election records — every one of those is the kind of confidential information now excluded. There is no Cyber policy in the program to fill this gap (see finding-004). For a company sitting on 90 million voter records, the cyber exposure is now functionally uninsured under the GL and inadequately addressed by a $10K Data Breach token. This is the single most material coverage failure in the program for this client's risk profile.
findings.recommendation: These exclusions are now industry-standard on GL forms — they cannot be 'fixed' on the GL itself. The proper response is a robust standalone Cyber policy (see finding-004 recommendation) that affirmatively covers what the GL excludes. Match coverage scope to the GL exclusion language: data privacy law liability (BIPA/CCPA/state election-data statutes), unauthorized access, malicious code, notification, forensic, PR, regulatory defense + fines, BI, cyber extortion. Confirm the Cyber policy has NO 'follow form' to GL exclusions.
discoveryQuestions: Did the prior broker walk you through these three GL exclusions and how they interact with the absence of a real cyber policy?
Run-Test holds voter data subject to dozens of state privacy regimes. Has your legal team mapped which state statutes apply, and how the CCPA/BIPA exclusion affects coverage in each?
If a CCPA class action is filed against Run-Test for handling California voter data, where exactly would the defense come from in the current insurance file?
What's your security team's current threat assessment for the next election cycle, and how does that match against the actual coverage available?

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity NOC — County Schedule Incomplete
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15: 'Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.' Sacramento §VI.A.2 requires immediate cancellation notice to County.
findings.policy_quote: 401-1235 Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): scheduled entities are: 'The New York State Office Of General Services; Procurement Services (Albany, NY); Amazon.com Services LLC (Seattle, WA); ARC Airport 2800, LLC (Scottsdale, AZ - Landlord); Banterra Bank (Marion, IL - 2nd Mortgagee).' 30-day NOC to designated entities.
findings.gap_description: The Designated Entity NOC schedule lists NY State, Amazon, the landlord, and a mortgagee — but does NOT list Maricopa County, Sacramento County, Los Angeles County, Contra Costa County, or any other county on the active contract list. Maricopa requires direct 30-day notice and Sacramento requires immediate notice on cancellation. ACORD COI cancellation language alone does not satisfy these requirements — a true endorsement-driven NOC is needed.
findings.plain_english: The policy does have a cancellation-notice endorsement that lists specific entities to notify if the policy lapses or changes — but the counties Run-Test contracts with aren't on the list. So if the policy is non-renewed or canceled mid-cycle, NY State and Amazon get a heads-up; Maricopa and Sacramento don't. Maricopa's contract specifically requires 30-day direct notice. The current schedule is incomplete and the contracts are technically out of compliance with notice obligations.
findings.recommendation: At next renewal (or via mid-term endorsement), expand 401-1235 schedule to include every contractually-required entity. At minimum: Maricopa County c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003; Sacramento County Risk Manager; Los Angeles County (if active); Contra Costa County (already on Property loss-payee — add to NOC). Maintain a master schedule of all required notice recipients tied to active contracts.
discoveryQuestions: How does the current process work for adding new counties to the cancellation-notice schedule when a new contract is signed — is there a workflow?
If the carrier non-renewed the policy tomorrow, who from your team would notify each county within their contractual notice window — and do you have addresses on file for all of them?
Have you ever had a county audit your COI and ask specifically whether they were on the policy's NOC schedule, not just listed as certificate holder?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice — 90-Day Broker Best-Practice Benchmark
findings.contract_quote: Patriot best-practices: 90-day notice of cancellation is the broker target. Maricopa §8.2.15 requires 30-day; Sacramento §VI.A.2 requires immediate notice from contractor.
findings.policy_quote: IL 02 58 04 21 Arizona Changes - Cancellation And Nonrenewal: 'AZ amendatory: 10 days nonpayment / 45 days other reasons / 45 days nonrenewal.' 401-1235 Designated Entity NOC: 30 days.
findings.gap_description: Standard cancellation notice for the policyholder is 45 days (AZ amendatory). Designated-entity notice is 30 days. Both fall short of the broker best-practice 90-day benchmark for sophisticated insureds. This is not a contract violation (Maricopa requires only 30 days) but it is below where a $5M–$25M PE-backed company should be sitting.
findings.plain_english: Industry best-practice for a company of this size and complexity is a 90-day heads-up before any cancellation or non-renewal. The current policy gives the company 45 days for most cancellations and 30 days to notify counties. That's adequate for the contract but tight for orderly replacement of coverage if the carrier walks away mid-cycle.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request endorsement extending insured-side cancellation notice to 90 days for cause and 45 days for non-payment. Carriers often resist non-payment extensions but will agree to longer for-cause notice. Worth having on file as a negotiation item.
discoveryQuestions: If the carrier non-renewed mid-election cycle, how long do you realistically need to find replacement coverage given your specialty risk profile — 45 days, or longer?
Has your PE sponsor expressed any preference on cancellation-notice terms in their portfolio insurance covenants?

findings.requirement_type: Carrier A.M. Best Rating — Verify Citizens Insurance Company A-VII Compliance
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.1: 'Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.' Maricopa §8.2.1: 'AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.'
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: Citizens Insurance Company of America (The Hanover Insurance Group). A.M. Best rating not stated in policy analysis JSON.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires A-VII minimum; Maricopa requires B++. Citizens Insurance Company of America (Hanover subsidiary) typically holds 'A' rating with a financial size category of XV — well above both thresholds — but the rating must be confirmed at COI issuance time and re-verified at each renewal.
findings.plain_english: Counties want carriers above a minimum financial-strength threshold. Sacramento's bar (A-VII) is meaningfully higher than Maricopa's (B++). The current carrier almost certainly clears both, but it should be confirmed in writing at every COI issuance and at renewal in case of any rating downgrade.
findings.recommendation: Confirm current Citizens Insurance Company of America A.M. Best rating (expected: A or A+, FSC XV). Document on each COI. Set a calendar reminder to recheck at every renewal and any time A.M. Best publishes a rating action.

findings.requirement_type: Stop Gap / Employer's Liability — No WC = No Stop Gap Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.12: 'Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit.'
findings.policy_quote: Hanover GL does not include Stop Gap or Employer's Liability coverage. No WC policy exists in the program (see finding-001).
findings.gap_description: Stop Gap / EL is required by both contracts at $1M minimums. Without a WC policy in the program, there is no EL Part 2 in force. If an employee in a non-monopolistic state sues outside the WC system (third-party-over claim, dual capacity, intentional tort exception), there is zero coverage. Even within the WC system, EL Part 2 typically pays for serious injury claims that escape the WC exclusive remedy (e.g., consortium claims by spouse).
findings.plain_english: Beyond the basic workers' comp problem (finding-001), there's a separate gap for the Employer's Liability piece — the part that pays for lawsuits employees can sometimes bring outside the comp system, or claims their families bring. Without a WC policy, there is no EL coverage either. This is a multi-million-dollar uninsured layer.
findings.recommendation: Cured by binding WC with EL $1M/$1M/$1M — see finding-001 recommendation. Verify EL limits are adequate to support the umbrella attachment point once umbrella is bound (most umbrellas require $1M EL underlying minimum).
discoveryQuestions: If an employee's spouse sued the company directly for loss-of-consortium after a workplace injury, do you know which policy in your file responds?
Are there any operations in monopolistic states (ND, OH, WA, WY) where Stop Gap on the GL would normally be the substitute for EL — and how is that handled today?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — MISSING FROM PROGRAM
findings.contract_quote: RMF requires EPLI evaluation. CGL CG 21 47 explicitly excludes employment-related practices from GL.
findings.policy_quote: CG 21 47 12 07 Employment-Related Practices Exclusion: 'Excludes BI and Personal & Advertising Injury arising out of refusal to employ, termination, or employment-related practices (coercion, demotion, evaluation, reassignment, discipline, defamation, harassment, humiliation, discrimination, malicious prosecution).' No EPLI policy provided in program.
findings.gap_description: GL excludes employment-related claims (standard) and there is no EPLI in the program. For a 50–200 employee PE-backed manufacturer in AZ (with operations potentially in CA — most plaintiff-friendly employment jurisdiction in the country), absence of EPLI is a meaningful uninsured exposure. PE-backed companies often face concentrated EPLI exposure during reorganizations, RIFs, or post-acquisition integration.
findings.plain_english: There's no Employment Practices Liability policy. That means harassment, discrimination, wrongful termination, and wage-and-hour defense claims have no coverage. For a 100-ish employee company that may have CA workers and is owned by a PE sponsor (organizational changes more likely), this is a real gap. EPLI claims in CA routinely hit $100k–$500k in defense alone before any settlement.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone EPLI policy with $1M–$3M limits depending on employee count and CA exposure. Required components: (a) third-party liability (harassment by non-employees — important for client-facing operations); (b) wage-and-hour defense sublimit (CA exposure); (c) broad 'Employee' definition including temps, contractors, leased workers; (d) prior acts coverage; (e) CA-specific endorsement if any CA employees. Often packaged with D&O / Management Liability for cost efficiency.
discoveryQuestions: When was the last RIF or organizational change at Run-Test, and how would an aggrieved employee's claim be handled today insurance-wise?
Does Run-Test employ any CA-based workers or contractors? CA wage-and-hour and PAGA exposure can dwarf base employment claims.
If a former employee filed an EEOC charge alleging discrimination tomorrow, who pays for defense counsel?

findings.requirement_type: D&O / Management Liability — MISSING FROM PROGRAM
findings.contract_quote: Special Risk: PE-backed / Private Equity. Government contracts. Election services regulatory exposure.
findings.policy_quote: No D&O / Management Liability policy provided in program.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is PE-backed, in a politically-charged regulated industry (elections), with government contracts and 90M voter records. D&O exposure is acute: (1) PE sponsor reps on the board face derivative-suit and regulatory-action exposure; (2) election services subjects directors and officers to state AG investigations, federal scrutiny (DOJ, EAC), and political litigation; (3) PE-backed companies face heightened post-acquisition class-action risk on disclosure issues. No coverage anywhere in the program for any of this.
findings.plain_english: There's no D&O policy. For a PE-backed election services company, this is a serious gap. Directors and officers face personal liability exposure from regulators, state AGs, the EAC, contested-election litigation, and PE-style disclosure suits. Without D&O, those individuals — including PE-firm appointees — have no defense funding when (not if) an election cycle goes contentious. PE sponsors typically require D&O as a condition of investment; verify whether this is a covenant compliance issue too.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Management Liability / D&O package with: (a) $5M–$10M limits; (b) Side A coverage for individual directors/officers; (c) Side B reimbursement to entity for indemnification; (d) Side C entity coverage if SEC-reportable; (e) regulatory investigation coverage; (f) broad 'Claim' definition including subpoenas; (g) prior acts coverage; (h) PE-specific exposure (often via a Private Company D&O form). Typically issued as a Management Liability package combining D&O + EPLI + Fiduciary + Crime — coordinate with finding-015 (EPLI) and finding-017 (Crime).
discoveryQuestions: Does your PE sponsor's investment agreement require maintenance of D&O at a specific limit — and is that requirement currently being met?
If a state AG opened an investigation into Run-Test's handling of voter data tomorrow, who pays for the directors' personal defense counsel?

After a contested election cycle, has Run-Test ever received a subpoena or document preservation notice from a state legislature, election commission, or federal agency? How was it handled insurance-wise?
Has any board member ever asked specifically about Side A coverage to protect them personally?

findings.requirement_type: Crime / Fidelity — Token Sublimits Only
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.13 cyber spec includes 'computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity.'
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Property Broadening Endorsement 411-0793 02 23 sublimits: Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud $50,000; Employee Theft $250,000; Forgery/Alteration $100,000; Money & Securities $50,000; social engineering coverage 'NARROW — only the §2 fraudulent instruction received from a computer software contractor carve-back.'
findings.gap_description: Crime exposures are addressed only via property-form sublimits, not a standalone Crime policy. Limits are inadequate for a $5M–$25M revenue manufacturer: Employee Theft $250k is below industry benchmark for this size; Computer Fraud $50k is token; Social Engineering coverage is extremely narrow (only fraudulent instruction from a 'computer software contractor' — does not cover the typical CEO-impersonation wire-fraud scenario). No third-party fidelity (required by Maricopa cyber spec).
findings.plain_english: There is no real Crime policy — just small sublimits buried in the Property package. Employee theft is capped at $250k, which is light for a 100-employee manufacturer with bookkeeping and AP staff. Computer fraud is $50k, which would be exhausted by a single wire-transfer scam. Social engineering — the 'CEO email' scam where someone impersonates a senior executive and tricks AP into sending a wire — is essentially uncovered. For a PE-backed company with separated finance functions, this is below where it should be.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Crime policy with: (a) Employee Theft $1M; (b) Computer Fraud $1M; (c) Funds Transfer Fraud $1M; (d) Social Engineering / Fraudulent Instruction $250k–$1M (separate coverage grant, not narrow carve-back); (e) Forgery/Alteration $1M; (f) Client / Third-Party coverage (for handling counties' funds/property — Maricopa's 'third-party fidelity' requirement); (g) Money Orders / Counterfeit Currency. Often issued via Management Liability package alongside D&O / EPLI for efficiency.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your AP wire-transfer authorization process — is there any scenario where a single employee can authorize a wire over $50,000 unilaterally?
Has Run-Test ever received a phishing or CEO-impersonation email asking for an urgent wire? What happened?
If an AP clerk embezzled $750,000 over two years, the policy stops paying at $250,000 — is that the loss exposure you're comfortable with?
Maricopa's contract specifically requires 'third-party fidelity' coverage. Have you confirmed whether that's available under the current Property-form sublimits?

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine — Ballot/Equipment Transit Exposure (Verify Coverage)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: 'Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR ... shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.'
findings.policy_quote: Property package includes BPP In Transit $100,000 (411-0793) and BPP Off Premises $250,000. No standalone Inland Marine policy provided. Property base form excludes mobile equipment categories.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's operations involve transit of ballots, mail, and high-value election technology equipment (sorters, scanners, printers) between facilities, post offices, and counties. BPP In Transit limit of $100,000 is likely inadequate for an active election cycle where multiple high-value pieces are concurrently in transit. A standalone Inland Marine policy would typically be expected at this scale. If IM is not currently in the program, that's a gap; if it exists separately, Sacramento WoS endorsement must be confirmed.
findings.plain_english: The company physically moves ballots, mail trays, and expensive sorting/scanning machines around. The Property policy gives only $100,000 of in-transit coverage — a single sorter or batch of ballots in transit can exceed that. There may or may not be a separate Inland Marine policy that nobody has produced for audit. Need to confirm: (a) is there one, (b) does it have adequate limits per item / per occurrence, (c) does it have blanket waiver of subrogation as Sacramento requires.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with insured: (1) is a standalone Inland Marine / Equipment Floater policy in force? If yes, obtain it and audit; if no, evaluate need based on transit values and equipment schedule; (2) limits should reflect concurrent in-transit values during peak election cycle; (3) blanket WoS endorsement required for Sacramento; (4) consider mysterious-disappearance and theft coverage at full equipment values; (5) consider Equipment Floater for owned election technology hardware on owned premises (separate from BPP if EB sublimits are inadequate).

findings.requirement_type: Course of Construction (COC) Builders Risk — N/A
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IX: 'Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall contain the following provisions: 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.'
findings.policy_quote: Conditional requirement — only triggers if Contractor maintains a COC/Builders Risk policy.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is an election services manufacturer/printer, not a construction contractor. COC requirement does not apply absent a construction-related scope of work.
findings.plain_english: N/A — Run-Test does not perform construction work that would require Builders Risk coverage. This contract clause is dormant for this client.
findings.recommendation: No action required unless scope of work expands to include physical construction. If that occurs (e.g., facility build-out for a county), bind Builders Risk with County as loss payee and blanket WoS at that time.

findings.requirement_type: GL Per-Project Aggregate (Construction-Specific) — N/A
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §III.A: 'Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project.'
findings.policy_quote: Hanover policy includes 421-3635 Aggregate Limits Per Project / Per Location (with $2M cap — see finding-007).
findings.gap_description: Conditional requirement only applicable to construction projects. Run-Test does not perform construction. The endorsement is in place anyway (with cap defect noted in finding-007), so the requirement is satisfied to the extent applicable.
findings.plain_english: The construction-specific per-project aggregate clause does not apply to Run-Test's election services operations. The endorsement is in place anyway for any project-based work.
findings.recommendation: No action required for this construction-specific clause. See finding-007 for the broader per-project cap defect.

findings.requirement_type: Severability of Interest (CG 00 01)
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.D: 'The CONTRACTOR's insurance shall apply separately to each insured against whom claim is made or suit is brought, except with respect to the limits of the insurer's liability.'
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §IV.7 Separation of Insureds: standard ISO occurrence form clause included.
findings.gap_description: ISO CG 00 01 standard severability/separation of insureds is in place. Sacramento requirement satisfied structurally by the form.
findings.plain_english: The standard GL form already has the 'separation of insureds' clause Sacramento requires. Each insured is treated independently for purposes of determining coverage. No action required.
findings.recommendation: No action — structurally satisfied by ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form.

findings.requirement_type: California Civil Code §2782 Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.B: 'Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.'
findings.policy_quote: Statutory CA public policy carve-out. Does not require a special endorsement; this is a contract-level acknowledgement.
findings.gap_description: California Civil Code §2782(b) operates by force of law — AI coverage is automatically carved back to exclude indemnification of the County for the County's own active negligence. No policy endorsement required.
findings.plain_english: California law automatically prevents indemnifying a public entity for their own active negligence. This is a statutory clause — no endorsement is needed and no action is required. The contract is just acknowledging the law.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: Blanket Additional Insured (Ongoing Operations) — GL
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.A; Maricopa §8.2.7.
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15 §1: blanket AI by written contract for ongoing operations — covers 'your work for the additional insured', premises owned/rented/leased/occupied, equipment leased to you. 421-2916 06 15 includes Broad Form Vendors AI.
findings.gap_description: Blanket AI for ongoing operations and broad-form vendors is in place. Satisfies the AI requirement at the ongoing-ops layer for both counties — but see finding-008 (no completed-ops AI) and finding-009 (professional-services carve-out) for the related defects.
findings.plain_english: The policy does provide automatic additional-insured status for counties on ongoing work, plus a broad-form vendors AI. That's the right structural starting point. The two defects on top of it (no completed-ops, and the professional-services carve-out) are addressed in separate findings.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Address related defects in findings 008 and 009.

findings.requirement_type: Primary & Non-Contributory — GL
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.C; Maricopa §8.2.4.
findings.policy_quote: 421-0452 12 14 Additional Insured – Primary and Non-Contributory: 'Provides primary & non-contributory only when required by written contract/agreement/permit.' Also embedded in 421-2915.
findings.gap_description: P&NC endorsement is in place via two channels (standalone 421-0452 and embedded in 421-2915 broadening) when required by written contract. Satisfies both county requirements at the GL.
findings.plain_english: The policy correctly makes itself primary (and non-contributory to) the County's own insurance when a contract requires it. This is in place. No action required at the GL.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Same endorsement must be confirmed once Auto and Umbrella are bound (findings 002 and 005).

findings.requirement_type: Blanket Waiver of Subrogation — GL
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VIII; Maricopa §8.2.8.
findings.policy_quote: CG 24 04 05 09 Waiver Of Transfer Of Rights Of Recovery Against Others: 'Blanket where required by written contract.' Applies to CGL and Products/Completed Operations Liability, ongoing and 'your work' under products-completed operations hazard.
findings.gap_description: Blanket WoS by written contract is in place across CGL — satisfies both counties' requirements at the GL layer. Note: Sacramento separately requires WC WoS (finding-026) and conditionally Inland Marine WoS (finding-018), neither of which is cured by this GL endorsement.
findings.plain_english: The GL policy waives the carrier's right to come after the County for reimbursement after paying a claim — standard requirement, properly endorsed on a blanket basis. Good. This does NOT cover the WC waiver (no WC policy at all) or the Inland Marine waiver.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm WoS endorsement is also in place once Auto, WC, and Inland Marine policies are bound.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation Waiver of Subrogation — Cannot Satisfy Without WC Policy
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VIII: 'The workers' compensation policy required hereunder shall be endorsed to state that the workers' compensation carrier waives its right of subrogation against the COUNTY.' Maricopa §8.2.12: 'Contractor, its subcontractors, and sub-subcontractors waive all rights against this contract and its agents, officers, directors, and employees for recovery of damages to the extent these damages are covered by the workers' compensation and Employer's Liability or Commercial Umbrella Liability insurance.'
findings.policy_quote: No WC policy in program (see finding-001). No WoS endorsement possible.
findings.gap_description: WC WoS is required by both counties. Cannot be satisfied because no WC policy exists. This is a derivative finding to finding-001 but has its own contract-compliance dimension and Sacramento requires the CA-specific form WC 04 03 06.
findings.plain_english: Both counties require the workers' comp carrier to waive its right to come after them after paying a claim. Since there's no WC carrier at all, there is no waiver to be issued. Cannot fix without first binding WC.
findings.recommendation: Once WC is bound (finding-001), endorse with: (1) Blanket Waiver of Subrogation WC 00 03 13 for general purposes; (2) CA-specific Waiver of Our Right to Recover WC 04 03 06 for any Sacramento operations. Each waiver typically carries a 2–5% surcharge on the underlying premium for the relevant state.
discoveryQuestions: When WC is bound, are you OK with the per-state waiver surcharge that comes with both general WoS and the CA-specific endorsement?
Does the company self-administer or use a carrier for WC — and if self-insured, are you willing to provide a contractual waiver in lieu of a policy endorsement (Sacramento allows this)?

findings.requirement_type: Auto AI / WoS / P&NC — Cannot Satisfy Without Auto Policy
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.A: AI as respects 'automobiles owned, leased, hired or borrowed by the CONTRACTOR.' Maricopa §8.2.7 (AI), §8.2.8 (WoS), §8.2.4 (P&NC) extend to Auto.
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy in program (see finding-002). No AI / WoS / P&NC endorsements possible.
findings.gap_description: Counties require AI, blanket WoS, and Primary & Non-Contributory on Auto. None can be provided because no Auto policy exists. Even if a personal auto or unscheduled auto is used for any business purpose, no commercial endorsements can attach.
findings.plain_english: Counties want to be additional insureds on the auto policy and want the same blanket waiver and primary/non-contributory protection that's on the GL — but there's no auto policy at all. Cannot satisfy until one is bound. See finding-002.
findings.recommendation: Cured when Auto is bound (finding-002). At binding, ensure: (a) Blanket AI when required by written contract (CA 20 48); (b) Blanket Waiver of Subrogation; (c) Primary & Non-Contributory.
discoveryQuestions: When auto is bound, will the carrier issue blanket AI / WoS / P&NC by endorsement, or will each county need to be scheduled?

findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge of Occurrence — GL
findings.contract_quote: RMF General item 4 / CGL item 25: 'Is the policy wording endorsed so notice of an occurrence is only considered when an officer, the person responsible for insurance, and/or the risk manager is notified?'
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15 §6 Knowledge of Occurrence: 'Knowledge of an occurrence is when knowledge is held by an officer of the Named Insured, manager of an LLC named insured, or person designated to give or receive notice of an occurrence.' Plus §13 Unintentional Failure to Notify.
findings.gap_description: Knowledge-of-occurrence endorsement is in place. Limits imputation of knowledge to officer / LLC manager / designated person — preventing low-level employee unreported incident from voiding coverage. Also has unintentional failure to notify giveback. Strong RMF item.
findings.plain_english: The policy properly limits 'knowledge' to officers and the designated risk manager — so a junior employee not reporting an incident won't void coverage. This is a meaningful protection that's correctly in place.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm same endorsement is added to Auto and Umbrella when bound.

findings.requirement_type: Unintentional Errors & Omissions Giveback — GL
findings.contract_quote: RMF General item 2.
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15 §12 Unintentional Failure to Disclose Hazards and §13 Unintentional Failure to Notify embedded in CGL Broadening.
findings.gap_description: Both unintentional E&O givebacks (failure to disclose hazards and failure to notify) are embedded in the CGL broadening endorsement. Standard best-practice, properly in place.
findings.plain_english: If the company inadvertently fails to disclose a location, operation, or notify the carrier of something, coverage is preserved. Properly endorsed.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Add equivalent to Auto, WC, and Umbrella when bound.

findings.requirement_type: Mental Anguish in BI Definition — GL
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 23.
findings.policy_quote: 421-2915 06 15 §4: BI definition modified to include 'mental anguish, mental injury.'
findings.gap_description: Bodily Injury definition properly extended to include mental anguish/injury — including stand-alone mental anguish, not requiring a connection to physical bodily injury. Strong RMF item.
findings.plain_english: The policy treats mental anguish as a covered injury — and even stand-alone mental anguish without an underlying physical injury. This is the broader form of the endorsement and is what you want.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Verify same scope is provided on Auto BI definition once bound.

findings.requirement_type: Damage to Premises Rented to You — $1M Limit
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 10/11.
findings.policy_quote: Damage To Premises Rented To You: $1,000,000 each occurrence; via 421-2916 §10 Property Damage Legal Liability Broad Form.
findings.gap_description: $1M sublimit for damage to premises rented to insured, broadened by 421-2916 to include perils beyond fire (Broad Form Property Damage Legal Liability). Adequate for typical leased-facility exposure.
findings.plain_english: If the company damages a rented building (fire, water, mechanical), the policy covers up to $1M with broad-form perils. That's significantly above the standard $300K and matches a real-property exposure.
findings.recommendation: Validate against actual lease values at largest facility — if lease replacement cost exceeds $1M, request increase at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Duty to Defend — GL
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 13.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 standard duty-to-defend language in Coverage A and Coverage B Insuring Agreements.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO occurrence form duty to defend — carrier has the right and duty to defend any suit seeking damages. Defense costs are outside policy limits (Supplementary Payments). Standard and adequate.
findings.plain_english: The carrier must defend any covered lawsuit and the cost of defense doesn't reduce the limit available for settlement/judgment. Standard for ISO CG 00 01.
findings.recommendation: No action required.

findings.requirement_type: Contractual Liability — Insured Contract Definition Unmodified
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 6.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 unmodified Insured Contract definition; standard contractual liability included. Maricopa §8.2.10: 'blanket contractual coverage' — present.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO Insured Contract definition is intact (no amendment endorsement narrowing scope). Provides contractual liability for liability assumed in covered contracts. Maricopa's 'blanket contractual' requirement is met.
findings.plain_english: The contractual indemnity protections in the contract with counties are properly backed by the GL — the policy covers liability assumed under those contracts. No restrictive amendment to the standard definition.
findings.recommendation: Maintain unmodified. Watch for any future amendment-of-insured-contract-definition endorsements at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Contractual Liability for Personal & Advertising Injury — Standard Exclusion Not Endorsed Back
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 7.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Coverage B Section I.B.2.e: 'This insurance does not apply to ... Personal and advertising injury for which the insured has assumed liability in a contract or agreement.' No endorsement reinstating contractual liability for PI&AI was identified.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO Coverage B excludes contractual liability for personal & advertising injury. No giveback endorsement is on the policy. For an election services contractor with broad indemnification obligations to counties, any P&AI exposure assumed under contract is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: The policy will defend personal/advertising injury claims (defamation, libel, copyright in advertising, etc.) brought directly against the company, but not those assumed contractually for the County. Some counties demand broad indemnity that includes P&AI — those obligations would be on the company's own dime.
findings.recommendation: Request a Contractual Liability for Personal & Advertising Injury endorsement at renewal. Most carriers will provide for additional premium. Particularly relevant given election services involve heavy public communications.
discoveryQuestions: Have any of the county contracts you're signing required indemnification for defamation, libel, or invasion of privacy claims?
When Run-Test publishes voter outreach communications or sample ballots, has anyone reviewed those for libel/false-light exposure?

findings.requirement_type: Coverage Territory — Standard ISO US/PR/Canada
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 8.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 standard coverage territory includes US, its territories and possessions, Puerto Rico, Canada plus international waters/airspace and worldwide for products with suit brought in the US.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO territory adequate for Run-Test's US-based election services operations.
findings.plain_english: Coverage applies in the US and Puerto Rico — adequate for an election services company serving 31 states.
findings.recommendation: No action required unless international expansion contemplated.

findings.requirement_type: TRIA / Terrorism Coverage — Accepted (with Conflicting Exclusion to Verify)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 32; election infrastructure is a designated DHS critical infrastructure sector.
findings.policy_quote: 401-1374 TRIA Disclosure: 'TRIA disclosure — terrorism coverage accepted, $468 premium charged.' BUT also CG 21 73 01 15 Exclusion Of Certified Acts Of Terrorism is attached (page 246). Per analysis: 'TRIA acceptance overrides this; verify.'
findings.gap_description: TRIA coverage is reportedly accepted with $468 premium, but a separate certified-acts-of-terrorism exclusion (CG 21 73) is also attached. Standard practice when TRIA is accepted is for the exclusion to be removed or rendered inoperative — having both creates ambiguity. Election infrastructure is a high-profile terrorism target.
findings.plain_english: Terrorism coverage is paid for, but there's also a terrorism exclusion in the same policy. These shouldn't both be in force simultaneously. Need the carrier to clarify in writing which one controls. For an election services company — election infrastructure is officially listed as critical infrastructure that's a known target — getting this right matters.
findings.recommendation: Get a written clarification from the carrier: confirm that with TRIA acceptance, CG 21 73 is inoperative or removed. Recommend removal of CG 21 73 from the schedule of forms to eliminate ambiguity. Separately, evaluate stand-alone Terrorism coverage given election infrastructure target status — TRIA only responds for 'certified' acts of terrorism (Treasury certification), and many domestic actor scenarios don't qualify.

findings.requirement_type: Pollution Exclusion — Conflicting Forms (CG 21 49 vs CG 21 55)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 31.
findings.policy_quote: CG 21 49 09 99 Total Pollution Exclusion (no hostile fire exception) AND CG 21 55 09 99 Total Pollution Exclusion With Hostile Fire Exception are BOTH attached. Per analysis: 'CONFLICTS with CG 21 49 09 99 — typically the broader exclusion controls.'
findings.gap_description: Two pollution exclusion forms with different scopes are both attached. Industry practice: the broader one (CG 21 49 absolute) typically controls. The conflict creates documentation uncertainty and an unfavorable read in litigation.
findings.plain_english: Two different pollution exclusions are stapled to the policy at the same time. They don't agree with each other. The stricter one almost certainly wins — but having both creates avoidable ambiguity. Should ask the carrier to remove the unintended one and confirm the other.
findings.recommendation: Request carrier confirmation of which form actually controls. Recommend removing CG 21 49 (absolute exclusion) and retaining CG 21 55 (with hostile fire exception), as the latter is the more insured-favorable. Either way, clean up the schedule of forms to eliminate ambiguity at renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Pollution Exclusion + No Contractors Pollution Liability (CPL)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 17 / 31.
findings.policy_quote: Total Pollution Exclusion in place (whichever form controls). No CPL or Environmental Liability policy in program.
findings.gap_description: GL has total pollution exclusion. Run-Test operates printing/mailing operations with chemical exposure: inks, toners, solvents, cleaning agents. Phthalates and PFAS exclusions also apply (findings-040 and 041). No CPL/Environmental policy exists to backstop these gaps. A pollution event from on-site or in-transit operations is uninsured.
findings.plain_english: The GL excludes pollution. Run-Test's printing, mailing, and processing operations use inks, toners, solvents, and cleaning chemicals — all classic pollution sources. Plus phthalates and PFAS specifically excluded. Without a contractors pollution / environmental policy, a chemical spill, ink fire releasing toxic smoke, or a long-tail employee/neighbor claim related to chemical exposure would be uninsured.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate Contractors Pollution Liability or Environmental Site Liability policy. Recommended specifications: (a) $1M–$2M limits; (b) on-site, off-site, and transit-related pollution; (c) emergency response coverage; (d) third-party BI/PD; (e) cleanup costs; (f) bring-back coverage for phthalates/PFAS where market allows. Markets: Beazley environmental, Liberty IronshoreEnvironmental, AIG environmental, Berkley Environmental.
discoveryQuestions: What chemicals are used in the printing, sorting, and cleaning operations — and are SDS sheets on file for each?
If an ink truck overturned in transit and contaminated a roadway, who would handle and pay for the cleanup?
Have any past or current employees raised long-tail health concerns related to chemical exposure (asthma, respiratory issues, dermatitis)?

findings.requirement_type: Care, Custody, and Control — Default ISO Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 2.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Coverage A exclusions j.(4) and j.(5): 'Personal property in the care, custody or control of the insured' and 'That particular part of real property on which you or any contractors or subcontractors working directly or indirectly on your behalf are performing operations, if the property damage arises out of those operations.' No CCC giveback endorsement identified.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO CCC exclusion intact. Run-Test's operations involve handling counties' property — voter registration data files, county-supplied paper stock, county-owned ballot designs, and potentially county-owned equipment. While much of this is electronic data (separately excluded), tangible property in the company's possession (county-supplied stock, returned ballot envelopes pre-counting) could trigger this exclusion.
findings.plain_english: If the company damages property belonging to a county that's currently in the company's possession or being worked on, the GL doesn't cover it. For an election services contractor that handles county-supplied paper stock, ballot designs, and (sometimes) county-owned equipment, this is worth understanding. Most claims here would be small (ruined paper batches), but a fire destroying a county's blank ballot inventory while in custody could be material.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate need for CCC bailee/customers' goods endorsement or Inland Marine bailee coverage if county-supplied tangible property is regularly held in custody. Quantify exposure: typical value of county property in custody at any time, longest custody period, peak-cycle concentrations. If material, add a Bailee's Customers Goods endorsement or stand-alone Inland Marine bailee floater.

findings.requirement_type: Phthalates Exclusion — Manufacturing Risk
findings.contract_quote: Election services manufacturing — printing inks, vinyl ballot envelopes, plastic mailing components historically may contain phthalates.
findings.policy_quote: 421-5203 07 23 Exclusion — Phthalates: 'Absolute exclusion for BI/PD/PI&AI arising from exposure to or presence of phthalates (DBP, DIBP, BBP, DEHP, DnOP, DINP, DIDP, DEP, MEHP, etc.) — applies to CGL and Products/Completed Operations Liability Coverage Parts.'
findings.gap_description: Absolute phthalate exclusion applies to both CGL and Products/Completed Ops. Phthalates are common in printing inks, vinyl, plastic mailing components, and adhesive systems. A long-tail toxic-tort claim arising from ballot supplies, mailing materials, or printing operations would have zero coverage. This is a tightening industry-wide exclusion, but for a print/mail operation it has acute relevance.
findings.plain_english: The policy excludes any claim arising from phthalates — chemicals historically used in printing inks, vinyl ballot envelopes, plastic, and adhesives. If a class of voters or workers later sued over phthalate exposure from ballot supplies, there's no coverage. The exclusion is industry-wide hardening, but for a manufacturer like Run-Test it's a real toxic-tort gap.
findings.recommendation: Verify with operations whether phthalate-containing materials are still used in printing, mailing, or packaging components. If yes: (a) initiate substitution program where commercially viable; (b) document material composition for liability purposes; (c) explore CPL/Environmental policies that may carry-back phthalate exposure; (d) on Products Liability, evaluate stand-alone Products Liability with phthalate buyback. Document supplier SDS records.
discoveryQuestions: Do current ink and material suppliers certify phthalate-free formulations? If not, what's in use?
Has anyone modeled the products-liability exposure if a class action emerged in 5–10 years over phthalate-leaching from mailing components?

findings.requirement_type: PFAS Exclusion — Forever Chemicals Risk
findings.contract_quote: Election services manufacturing — paper coatings, printing inks may historically contain PFAS.
findings.policy_quote: CG 40 32 05 23 Exclusion — Perfluoroalkyl And Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS): 'Absolute PFAS exclusion — excludes BI/PD/PAI arising from any inhalation, ingestion, absorption, contact with, or presence of perfluoroalkyl/polyfluoroalkyl substances. ... Election services use printing inks, toners, paper coatings — some printing chemistry historically contained PFAS.'
findings.gap_description: Absolute PFAS exclusion. Industry-wide hardening exclusion with particular relevance for printing/paper-coating operations where fluorinated chemistry has historically been used in ink fixatives, paper coatings, and water/grease repellents. Long-tail PFAS litigation is the next mass-tort wave.
findings.plain_english: PFAS — 'forever chemicals' — are now absolutely excluded. Some historical printing and paper chemistry has contained them. PFAS lawsuits are the next major mass-tort wave; for a printing/mailing operation, this exclusion has long-tail teeth.
findings.recommendation: Same approach as phthalates: (a) verify supplier formulations PFAS-free; (b) substitute where possible; (c) document material chemistry; (d) on the environmental side, evaluate stand-alone PFAS coverage if available (very limited market currently). Document a PFAS-free position with paper and ink suppliers prospectively.
discoveryQuestions: Have your paper and ink suppliers certified PFAS-free formulations? When was the last time you asked?
Has anyone audited historical inventory or finished-goods archives for PFAS-containing materials in the supply chain?

findings.requirement_type: Property Valuable Papers / Electronic Data — Severely Inadequate Sublimits
findings.contract_quote: Run-Test handles ballot data, voter rolls, election records, election technology IP.
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 10 10 12: 'Cost to replace/restore information on valuable papers and records ... excluded from Covered Property. Limited Coverage Extension provides only $2,500 per premises unless higher limit shown.' Electronic Data limited to $2,500/year Additional Coverage. Equipment Breakdown Data Restoration $100,000.
findings.gap_description: Property valuable-papers limit is $2,500 per premises. Electronic data is $2,500. Even Equipment Breakdown data restoration at $100,000 is light for an election technology firm. For a company that maintains voter registration data, ballot records, election archive files, and proprietary election software, these sublimits are token. Cyber/Tech E&O policies are the proper home for the data values, but no Cyber exists either (finding-004).
findings.plain_english: The Property policy provides $2,500 of coverage for damaged business records and another $2,500 for damaged electronic data. For a company sitting on voter data for 90M Americans plus its own proprietary election technology software and historical archives, these limits are essentially zero. The proper place for this exposure is Cyber/Tech E&O — and there isn't one. Property is not designed to be the answer here, but the limits as they stand are token.
findings.recommendation: Two-track: (1) on Property, increase Valuable Papers and Electronic Data sublimits to meaningful levels ($250K–$1M each) at renewal; (2) more importantly, bind a Cyber policy with Data Restoration coverage at $5M+ (see finding-004). Evaluate whether owned proprietary election software needs to be inventoried as 'Stock' for Property purposes (some carriers will treat developed software as covered Stock).
discoveryQuestions: What is the total replacement cost of voter data files and proprietary election software currently in custody — and where is it stored physically and in cloud?
If the data center burned tonight, what's the cost to reconstruct the data from backups, including labor and recertification?

findings.requirement_type: Equipment Breakdown — Adequate Limit, Inadequate Sublimits for Election Tech
findings.contract_quote: RMF Property/EB review.
findings.policy_quote: EB Limit $49,040,381; BI $11,500,000; Data Restoration $100,000; Expediting Expenses $100,000. Excludes 'defect, programming error, programming limitation, computer virus, malicious code, loss of data, loss of access, loss of use, loss of functionality.' Direct deductible $100,000.
findings.gap_description: EB primary limit is appropriate ($49M, matching equipment values). However: (a) Data Restoration sublimit $100K is very low for an election technology firm dependent on data; (b) the carve-out for programming error / virus / malicious code / loss of data eliminates the most likely modern-equipment failure scenarios — software-driven shutdowns, firmware bugs, and update incompatibilities — which is exactly how election scanners and sorters fail in real life. (c) $100K direct deductible is high.
findings.plain_english: The base equipment breakdown coverage is fine for a fire-or-mechanical-failure event. But the policy carves out the failure modes that are most likely on modern election scanners and sorters — software bugs, firmware updates, virus/malware, loss of data. Those are 80% of how this equipment actually breaks. Plus a $100K deductible eats into smaller claims.
findings.recommendation: (1) Increase Data Restoration sublimit at renewal — $1M+; (2) negotiate carve-back for non-malicious programming error if available; (3) confirm whether $100K deductible can be reduced; (4) the software/virus/malicious-code failure mode is best addressed via Cyber policy (Network BI, Tech E&O). When Cyber is bound (finding-004), confirm Network BI and dependent BI cover ballot-scanner / sorter outages.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Should be addressed via Cyber Network BI when bound — see finding-004.
discoveryQuestions: When a ballot scanner has gone down in the past, what was the typical root cause — mechanical, electrical, software, firmware update, or virus?
What's the average and peak replacement cost of a single sorter or scanner, and what's the lead time to replace one mid-cycle?

findings.requirement_type: Protective Safeguards Warranty — Sprinkler System
findings.contract_quote: RMF Property item.
findings.policy_quote: CP 04 11 09 17: 'Premises 1, Building 1, Symbol P-1 (Automatic Sprinkler System). Insured must maintain sprinkler system in working order and notify carrier of any suspension/impairment (>48 hours). Failure to comply triggers fire exclusion.'
findings.gap_description: Protective Safeguards endorsement creates a warranty: if the automatic sprinkler is impaired for more than 48 hours and the carrier is not notified, fire coverage is barred. For a printing/manufacturing facility (paper, inks, electrical equipment, high fire load), a fire claim during an unreported sprinkler outage means total uninsured loss.
findings.plain_english: If the sprinkler system goes offline for more than 48 hours and you don't tell the carrier, and a fire happens during that window, the policy will deny the entire claim. For a paper/printing operation — high fire load — this is a real operational risk. Maintenance crews need to know.
findings.recommendation: Operational hardening: (1) document a written procedure that any sprinkler impairment triggers immediate carrier notification and alternative protection (fire watch); (2) confirm with facility operations the procedure is in maintenance personnel's handbook; (3) consider increasing impairment notice window with carrier if 48 hours is operationally tight (some carriers will agree to 7 days with fire watch); (4) ensure facility manager has direct contact info for carrier reporting.
discoveryQuestions: Who at the facility is responsible for carrier notification if the sprinkler is impaired for any reason — maintenance, facility manager, or risk function?
When was the last sprinkler inspection / test, and was the carrier notified during the test?
Is there a fire-watch procedure in place if the system goes down during a maintenance window?

findings.requirement_type: Property Earth Movement / Flood / Utility Services — Standard Exclusions
findings.contract_quote: RMF Property review.
findings.policy_quote: CP 10 30 09 17: standard Earth Movement, Water/Flood, Utility Services failure exclusions in place.
findings.gap_description: Standard exclusions for earthquake, flood, surface water, sewer backup, utility service failure. AZ premises have moderate earthquake exposure; flood depends on facility-specific flood zone. Utility service failure is meaningful for an election technology operation dependent on power and connectivity.
findings.plain_english: Standard property doesn't cover earthquakes, flood, sewer backup, or utility service failures. AZ has some earthquake exposure (low frequency, moderate severity); the flood and utility risks depend on the specific facility. Worth confirming if there's a stand-alone flood policy or DIC/earthquake coverage.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with insured: (1) Flood zone of each facility; (2) presence of any DIC/earthquake/flood policy; (3) need for Utility Services BI/EE endorsement (typically modest cost; would cover BI losses from off-premises power/communication outages — relevant for an election cycle dependent on uptime). Recommend Utility Services BI endorsement and evaluation of Earthquake DIC if facility values warrant.

findings.requirement_type: Broad Form Named Insured — LLC/Partnership/JV Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: RMF General item 3 / CGL item 24.
findings.policy_quote: 421-2916 06 15 §4.b: 'b. That is not a partnership, joint venture or limited liability company.' Coverage only extends to organizations >50% owned that are NOT LLCs/partnerships/JVs.
findings.gap_description: The Broad Form Named Insured extension expressly excludes LLCs, partnerships, and joint ventures from automatic coverage. Runbeck Investments LLC is on the Dec page so it's covered by direct schedule. But any other affiliated LLC (real estate holding LLC, JV with a county, partnership entity) is NOT automatically a Named Insured. For a PE-backed corporate structure, affiliated LLCs are common.
findings.plain_english: The 'broad form named insured' language sounds protective but quietly excludes LLCs, partnerships, and joint ventures. So if Run-Test has any related real-estate holding LLCs, election technology JVs with counties, or PE-backed partnership structures, those entities are NOT automatically covered just because Run-Test is the named insured. Each one must be added by name.
findings.recommendation: (1) Obtain a current organizational chart from the insured and identify all affiliated LLCs, partnerships, and JVs; (2) for each, confirm whether it's already on the Dec page or scheduled separately; (3) for those not scheduled, decide whether to add by endorsement (each is a separately named insured) or accept the gap; (4) at renewal, request 421-2916 §4.b carve-back to include LLCs/partnerships/JVs (some carriers will negotiate this).
discoveryQuestions: Can you provide a current organizational chart showing all entities — including real estate LLCs, JV entities, and PE-fund affiliated structures?
Has the PE sponsor created any holding-company structures (typically LLCs) that are part of the Run-Test investment? Are those on the policy?
If Run-Test enters a JV with a county or another contractor, will the JV entity be covered under this policy as currently endorsed?

findings.requirement_type: Fellow Employee Coverage — GL
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 20.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §II Who Is An Insured, paragraph 2.a.(1): 'Your employees, other than either your executive officers ... or your managers ... but only for acts within the scope of their employment by you or while performing duties related to the conduct of your business. However, none of these employees ... is an insured for: (a) Bodily injury or personal and advertising injury: (i) To you, to your partners or members ..., to any of your other employees ...' (Standard fellow-employee exclusion.)
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO fellow-employee exclusion intact — employee-on-employee BI claims not covered under the GL (typically belongs in WC/EL anyway). No CG 22 80 / CG 22 86 fellow-employee giveback identified. For most clients this is appropriate; for high-risk employee interaction environments, a giveback can be valuable.
findings.plain_english: Right now, if one employee causes BI to another while on the job, the GL does not respond — that's a WC claim. That's normally fine. The decision to add a fellow-employee giveback comes up if there are scenarios where employees might be sued by other employees outside the workers' comp system.
findings.recommendation: Default position: leave standard exclusion in place; rely on WC/EL for employee-on-employee injury. If any specific exposure exists (e.g., employees as drivers in personal vehicles, dual-capacity employees), evaluate fellow-employee giveback at renewal.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: WC/EL handles employee-on-employee BI under exclusive remedy doctrine.

findings.requirement_type: Hired & Non-Owned Auto on GL — NOT Endorsed (Critical Given No Auto Policy)
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 21: 'Hired and Non-owned Coverage - is this included on the CGL as needed, when the insured does not have an auto policy.'
findings.policy_quote: No CG 04 22 (Hired Auto / Non-Owned Auto Liability) endorsement identified on the GL package. Standard ISO Coverage A exclusion 2.g excludes 'Aircraft, Auto Or Watercraft.'
findings.gap_description: Standard GL excludes auto liability. No HNOA endorsement on the GL. No standalone Auto policy in the program (finding-002). The combined effect is that any vehicle-related liability — owned, hired, non-owned, employee personal vehicle on company errand — is uninsured.
