Even if the company claims to have no owned vehicles, employee personal-vehicle use for any business purpose is uncovered.
findings.plain_english: There is no auto coverage anywhere — neither a separate auto policy nor an HNOA endorsement on the GL. The day an employee runs a courier errand to a county election office in their own car and causes an accident, the personal auto policy will respond and tap out, then the company gets sued directly with no carrier defense. This is finding-002 from a different angle and equally ugly.
findings.recommendation: Cure by binding a real Commercial Auto policy with HNOA (see finding-002 — preferred). As an interim or fallback for very small employers with truly no driving exposure, request CG 04 22 (Hired Auto / Non-Owned Auto Liability) endorsement on the GL — but this is a stop-gap, not a substitute. Strongly recommend the standalone Auto.
discoveryQuestions: Do any employees drive their personal vehicles for company purposes — even occasional errands like supply runs, post office, or county drop-offs?
Has anyone documented a 'no driving for company' policy? In court, that's the only thing that limits the exposure if there's no insurance — and it's hard to enforce.

findings.requirement_type: Leased / Temporary Workers — Definition Review
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 22.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 standard 'Employee' definition includes leased workers but not temporary workers (separately defined). No specific endorsement modifying definition identified.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO definition. For an election services operation that may use temp staffing during peak election cycles (mailing, sorting, ballot inserting), need to verify: (1) whether temp/leased workers are used; (2) whether the staffing agency provides Alternate Employer endorsement on its WC; (3) whether temp/leased workers should be excluded from this policy's 'Employee' definition to avoid coverage overlap and EL gaps.
findings.plain_english: Election cycles typically require seasonal/temp labor for sorting, inserting, and processing. Need to confirm: do you use a staffing agency? Does that agency's workers' comp cover the temp workers and name Run-Test as an Alternate Employer? If yes, you may want the standard 'employee' definition modified to exclude leased workers so coverage isn't duplicated and the staffing agency's policy responds first.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with insured: (a) staffing/temp arrangements during peak cycles; (b) whether staffing agency provides Alternate Employer endorsement (WC 00 03 01) naming Run-Test; (c) whether to modify CGL 'Employee' definition to exclude leased workers. Coordinate when WC is bound (finding-001).

findings.requirement_type: Employee Benefits Liability (EBL) — In Place
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 14.
findings.policy_quote: CG 04 35 12 07 Employee Benefits Liability Coverage (Claims-Made): $1M each employee / $1M aggregate. Deductible $1,000. Retroactive Date: 04/08/2017. Premium $275.
findings.gap_description: EBL is in place at adequate $1M/$1M with retro date 04/08/2017 — long retro is favorable. Note: EBL is administrative-error E&O for benefits enrollment errors only; it does NOT replace ERISA Fiduciary Liability or D&O. Verify retro date covers full administrative history.
findings.plain_english: There is EBL coverage in place — handles administrative errors in benefits enrollment, eligibility, etc. with a $1M limit and a long retro date going back to 2017. Good. This is NOT the same as ERISA fiduciary liability (which protects plan fiduciaries against breach claims) — that's a separate gap.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Confirm retro date 04/08/2017 is appropriate (i.e., covers full administrative history). Note that ERISA Fiduciary Liability is a separate gap (see finding-051).

findings.requirement_type: ERISA Fiduciary Liability — MISSING (CG 04 35 EBL Does Not Cover)
findings.contract_quote: Special Risk: PE-backed; 50–200 employees suggests qualified retirement plan and health plan in force.
findings.policy_quote: CG 04 35 EBL excludes ERISA fiduciary liability per analysis: 'EBL does NOT cover wrongful termination/discrimination (need EPLI), ERISA fiduciary liability (need stand-alone Fiduciary), or investment performance failures.'
findings.gap_description: No standalone Fiduciary Liability policy in program. EBL covers administrative errors only — not ERISA fiduciary breach claims. PE-backed companies typically have 401(k) and health plans where plan fiduciaries (often the same individuals as company officers) face personal liability for prohibited transactions, breach of duty, and excessive fee claims. Recent ERISA litigation trend has expanded class actions against mid-size plans.
findings.plain_english: There's no Fiduciary Liability policy. The 401(k) and health plan fiduciaries — typically the CFO and HR director — face personal lawsuits if a plan participant alleges breach of fiduciary duty, prohibited transactions, or excessive fees. Recent ERISA class actions have hit mid-sized plans hard. The current EBL policy doesn't cover this.
findings.recommendation: Bind standalone Fiduciary Liability $1M–$3M, often as part of a Management Liability package alongside D&O / EPLI / Crime (see findings 015–017). Specs: (a) ERISA fiduciary coverage; (b) prohibited transaction excise tax; (c) plan administrator E&O; (d) HIPAA defense; (e) prior acts coverage.
discoveryQuestions: Who serves as named fiduciary on the 401(k) plan, and have they been told they have personal liability without a Fiduciary policy?
When was the last 401(k) fee benchmarking review? Excessive fee class actions are the dominant theory for mid-size plan litigation.

findings.requirement_type: Product Recall — Token Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 28.
findings.policy_quote: 421-2916 §9 Product Recall Expense: $25,000 each occurrence / $50,000 aggregate / $500 deductible.
findings.gap_description: Product Recall sublimit is $25K/$50K — token. For an election services manufacturer, a recall of misprinted ballots, mis-targeted mail, or defective sample ballots could cost hundreds of thousands or low millions. The sublimit covers a token amount.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test had to recall a defective batch of ballots, mail pieces, or election supplies, the policy provides only $25,000 to do it — a fraction of what a real recall would cost in transportation, reprinting, expedited delivery, and customer notification. Worth either increasing the sublimit or binding a stand-alone recall policy.
findings.recommendation: (1) Increase Product Recall sublimit at renewal — $250K–$1M typical for a print/manufacturing operation; (2) consider stand-alone Product Recall policy if recall exposure is material (election cycles create natural recall scenarios when defects discovered mid-cycle). Coordinate with Products Liability (currently embedded in CGL) where defect-driven exposure is concentrated.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest production run for a single county or single election? If an entire batch were defective, what would full recall and reprint cost?
Has Run-Test ever had to do a partial or full recall? What did it cost?

findings.requirement_type: TCPA / CAN-SPAM / FCRA Exclusion — Mail-Distribution Risk
findings.contract_quote: Run-Test specializes in 'election mail sorting' and 'mailing services.'
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 Coverage A para 2.q and Coverage B para 2.p: 'Recording And Distribution Of Material Or Information In Violation Of Law' — absolute exclusion for BI/PD and Personal & Advertising Injury arising out of violations of TCPA, CAN-SPAM, FCRA/FACTA.
findings.gap_description: Standard CG 00 01 exclusion bars coverage for any claim alleging violation of telecommunications/communications statutes. Run-Test's mail distribution and voter outreach communications are exactly the activities subject to TCPA and CAN-SPAM class actions. Without a Cyber/Privacy or specialty Media policy carving back this exposure, distribution-related class actions are uninsured.
findings.plain_english: The GL excludes any claim that you violated TCPA (telemarketing/text-message rules), CAN-SPAM (commercial email rules), or FCRA (credit-reporting/identity rules). Run-Test does mass mail distribution for elections — exactly the kind of activity that gets class-action attention. There's no Cyber/Privacy policy to backstop this either. A single class action on disputed voter outreach could cost mid-six-figures in defense alone.
findings.recommendation: Cured primarily via Cyber & Privacy policy (see finding-004) — most modern Cyber forms include a TCPA/CAN-SPAM/FCRA defense sublimit (typically $250K–$1M). When binding Cyber, confirm specifically that the form includes statutory communications-law defense. If not, evaluate a Media Liability policy.
discoveryQuestions: What kinds of voter outreach communications does Run-Test send — direct mail, email, text, automated calls?
Has Run-Test or any contracted county ever received a TCPA or CAN-SPAM complaint or pre-litigation demand?
Are voter contact lists used by Run-Test scrubbed against do-not-contact registries before each campaign?

findings.requirement_type: Asbestos / Silica / Fungi-Bacteria Exclusions — Standard, Low Concern
findings.contract_quote: RMF review.
findings.policy_quote: 421-0022 Asbestos Liability Exclusion (absolute); CG 21 96 03 05 Silica Exclusion; CG 21 67 12 04 Fungi/Bacteria Exclusion.
findings.gap_description: Standard industry-wide exclusions. Low concern for an election services manufacturer — none of these are core operational exposures. Documented as Good for completeness.
findings.plain_english: These are standard industry-wide exclusions and don't materially impact election services operations. Documented for the record.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.requirement_type: Deductibles / SIR Disclosure to County
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §IV: 'Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY.' Maricopa §8.2.6: deductibles 'shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County'; County may require bond/LOC.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover deductibles: Property $100K direct EB / $1K Data Breach. Other deductibles per schedule. No central declaration of all SIRs/deductibles.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento and Maricopa both have deductible/SIR disclosure obligations. Maricopa goes further — deductibles are not applicable to County's recovery (i.e., Run-Test pays the deductible, not County), and County may demand bond/LOC backing. Need to (a) compile a master deductible/SIR schedule across all bound policies; (b) declare to each county per their procedure; (c) be prepared to respond to bond/LOC demand.
findings.plain_english: Both counties want full disclosure of every deductible and self-insured retention in the program — and Maricopa reserves the right to demand the company post a bond or letter of credit to back up those deductibles. This is administrative compliance work that needs to happen before performance, not after.
findings.recommendation: (1) Build a master deductible/SIR schedule covering all current and future policies (Property, GL, Auto when bound, Cyber when bound, etc.); (2) submit to each county risk manager per contract requirements; (3) prepare for potential bond/LOC demand from Maricopa — confirm with insured's banking partner whether LOC capacity exists; (4) track any approval/conditions imposed by counties.

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Insurance Pass-Through — Procedure Required
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VII.E: 'CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.'
findings.policy_quote: Administrative — not policy-driven.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento (and standard practice) requires Run-Test to flow down equivalent insurance and AI requirements to its subcontractors. This is an administrative/contracting process, not a policy gap. Need to confirm: (a) does Run-Test have a written subcontractor insurance compliance procedure; (b) are sub COIs collected and reviewed; (c) are subs naming both Run-Test and the County as AI; (d) are sub limits adequate.
findings.plain_english: When Run-Test uses subcontractors (printers, mailing services, IT vendors, transportation), the County wants those subs to carry equivalent insurance and to name both Run-Test AND the County as additional insureds. This is a contracting and procurement workflow, not a policy fix. Worth confirming the process exists.
findings.recommendation: Build/confirm a subcontractor insurance compliance procedure: (a) standard insurance language in subcontract template that mirrors county requirements; (b) annual COI collection and review; (c) AI verification (Run-Test AND county); (d) tracking system for renewal dates; (e) escalation for non-compliant subs. Many brokers offer COI tracking platforms (myCOI, CertFocus, Tractic) at low cost.

findings.requirement_type: 30-Day Claim / 10-Day Lawsuit Notice Procedure
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §X: 'Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.' Maricopa §8.2.15: 2-business-day cancellation notice relay.
findings.policy_quote: Administrative — Contractor's contractual notice duty to County, independent of carrier notice obligations.
findings.gap_description: Three independent notice obligations: (1) carrier notice on occurrences (handled by Knowledge of Occurrence endorsement, finding-028); (2) county notice within 30 days of any claim received and 10 days of lawsuit service; (3) county notice within 2 business days if carrier notifies of cancellation. Need a documented internal procedure to ensure compliance.
findings.plain_english: Beyond carrier reporting, the contracts impose direct notice obligations TO THE COUNTY. Within 30 days of getting a claim, within 10 days of being served a lawsuit, and within 2 business days of being told a policy is canceling. These are easy to miss in practice. Worth a documented procedure.
findings.recommendation: Build a written incident-and-claim notice protocol: (a) any claim or correspondence alleging Run-Test caused harm to a county-related party triggers a 30-day notice clock to that county; (b) any lawsuit served on Run-Test relating to a county contract triggers a 10-day notice clock; (c) any insurance change/cancellation notice triggers a 2-business-day relay; (d) name a single accountable person (CFO or General Counsel); (e) standard notice template letter on file.

findings.requirement_type: COI + Endorsement Copies Pre-Performance
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §I: 'Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences.' Maricopa §8.2.14.
findings.policy_quote: Administrative — broker COI and endorsement-copy delivery process.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento explicitly requires actual endorsement copies (not just COI references) attached to the COI before performance commences. Maricopa requires COI prior to contract award. Both reserve the right to require certified policy copies. This is broker administrative work that must be done correctly and in time — particularly the endorsement-copy delivery, which many brokers default to skipping.
findings.plain_english: Counties want both the certificate AND copies of the actual endorsements (CG 20 10, CG 20 37, CG 24 04, etc.) — not just a COI listing them. This is a deliverable that has to happen before performance, and the broker has to be staying on top of it.
findings.recommendation: Build a county-by-county COI pack template containing: (a) Acord 25 with all required AI/WoS/P&NC bullets; (b) actual PDF copies of the AI endorsements (CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 once added), WoS endorsement (CG 24 04), P&NC endorsement (421-0452 or equivalent); (c) carrier A.M. Best confirmation; (d) cover letter referencing contract effective date and certificate holder address. Deliver pack at contract execution and on each renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Right to Adjust Coverage — Open-Ended County Discretion
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §II.B: 'COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions ... do not provide adequate protection ... COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.'
findings.policy_quote: N/A — contract clause, not policy.
findings.gap_description: County reserves unilateral right to require additional/expanded coverage mid-term if Risk Manager deems current insurance inadequate. Open-ended cost-creep risk: limits and lines could grow without renegotiation. No real defense against this — it's a standard public-entity clause.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento can unilaterally tell Run-Test to buy more or different insurance mid-contract if their risk manager doesn't like the current setup. There's no negotiating the clause out — public entities almost always insist on it. The protection is to start with strong, well-documented coverage so the risk manager has nothing to point at.
findings.recommendation: Defensive posture: maintain best-in-class program documentation so any review by County Risk Manager is met with a clean program. Document in client file that this clause exists so any adjustment demand is anticipated. No policy fix.
discoveryQuestions: Has any county Risk Manager ever exercised this right and required additional coverage mid-term? What did they require?
Is there any contract negotiation leverage to narrow this clause to material changes — or is it truly take-it-or-leave-it?

findings.requirement_type: Indemnity Not Limited by Insurance Limits — Balance-Sheet Exposure
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.1.3: 'The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.'
findings.policy_quote: Standard Maricopa indemnity clause; not addressable by policy.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's contractual indemnification obligation is not capped at insurance limits. Liability above the GL/Auto/Cyber limits flows to the company's balance sheet directly. With current limit shortfalls (findings 006, 002, 004), the gap between insurance available and indemnification owed is material — and uninsured.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa says the indemnification obligation is uncapped — even if your insurance runs out at $1M, you still owe them whatever the actual loss is. Combined with the limit shortfalls already identified, this means the company's balance sheet is the backstop for any catastrophic claim. Cure: bind a real umbrella, real cyber, and address each limit gap.
findings.recommendation: Cure operationally by closing the underlying limit shortfalls in findings 002, 004, 005, 006. Cannot be cured by contract — public entities won't cap. Once GL is at $2M/$4M, Auto at $2M, Cyber at $5M, plus a $10M+ Umbrella, the practical balance-sheet exposure narrows substantially.
discoveryQuestions: Have you stress-tested a worst-case scenario — say, a $25M election-cycle judgment — against the actual balance sheet impact given current insurance?
Does the PE sponsor have any guidance or covenant on minimum insurance-to-revenue ratios for portfolio companies?

findings.requirement_type: Owners Excluded — WC (Verify When Bound)
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC item 12: 'Owners Excluded.'
findings.policy_quote: No WC policy in program. Verification deferred until WC is bound.
findings.gap_description: When WC is bound (finding-001), confirm whether owners/officers are included or excluded from coverage. PE-backed structures often have working executives whose status (W-2 employee vs. partner/member) affects WC inclusion.
findings.plain_english: When the workers' comp policy gets bound, need to confirm whether the operating executives are included or excluded. Some owners/officers can lawfully exclude themselves to save premium — but if they're injured on the job, they have no coverage. PE-sponsor reps on the board generally aren't AZ employees and are properly excluded.
findings.recommendation: Address at WC binding (finding-001). Recommend including all working executives unless they have private health/disability that fully covers occupational injury — most carriers will require explicit AZ Form WC-902 to exclude.

findings.requirement_type: Composite Rating / Premium Audit Strategy
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 4.
findings.policy_quote: Standard receipts/payroll-based GL rating.
findings.gap_description: Election services revenue is highly cyclical — heavy in even election years (Presidential, midterm), lighter in odd years. A composite rate based on average revenue could smooth premium fluctuation across the cycle vs. straight payroll/receipts rating that swings widely. Worth exploring with carriers at renewal.
findings.plain_english: Election cycles are volatile — big revenue every two years, slow in between. Some carriers will offer a 'composite rate' that averages the cycle and gives a more stable premium. Worth asking at renewal as a competitive lever and budgeting tool.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request composite rating proposal from incumbent and competing markets. Election cyclicality is a recognized rating discussion in the specialty market.

findings.requirement_type: Contract Review Procedure
findings.contract_quote: RMF CGL item 5.
findings.policy_quote: Administrative — not policy-driven.
findings.gap_description: 31-state operation with multiple county contracts implies high contract volume. A consistent contract-review procedure ensures insurance terms are flagged at signing rather than discovered later. Worth confirming whether legal/risk function reviews insurance provisions on every county RFP/contract.
findings.plain_english: With contracts in 31 states and DC, having a consistent process for reviewing the insurance section of every new contract is the difference between proactively managing risk and discovering problems after signing. Worth confirming the company has one.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with insured: (1) is there a standard contract-review procedure that includes insurance-terms review; (2) who reviews — General Counsel, CFO, broker; (3) standard 'insurance schedule' language Run-Test can propose to standardize across counties. Offer broker-side contract review as a service.

findings.requirement_type: Claims-Made / Retro Date — Applies When Cyber and E&O Are Bound
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §V (claims-made retro on/before contract; 1-year ERP). Maricopa §8.2.3 (retro precede contract; 2-year ERP).
findings.policy_quote: Hanover GL is occurrence form (not claims-made). EBL CG 04 35 is claims-made with retro date 04/08/2017 — predates current contracts. No Cyber or E&O policy currently in program.
findings.gap_description: Claims-made/retro requirements apply when claims-made coverage is bound. Current claims-made coverage in program is only EBL (retro 04/08/2017 — adequate). When E&O and Cyber are bound (findings 003 and 004), retro dates must be set on or before the earliest active county contract effective date and ERP/tail of 1 year (Sacramento) or 2 years (Maricopa) must be available.
findings.plain_english: Both counties have detailed rules about how claims-made policies (Cyber and E&O typically) must be structured: retroactive date has to predate the contract effective date, and a 'tail' coverage of 1–2 years has to be available if the policy is canceled. Currently no relevant claims-made coverage exists; this is a placeholder that needs to be operationalized when E&O and Cyber are bound.
findings.recommendation: When binding E&O (finding-003) and Cyber (finding-004): (a) retroactive date on or before the earliest active county contract effective date — gather list of all active contract effective dates and use the earliest; (b) confirm ERP/tail option available for at least 2 years (Maricopa floor); (c) document retro and ERP terms on COI for each county.

findings.requirement_type: Auto-Specific RMF Items — DEFERRED Until Auto Bound
findings.contract_quote: RMF Auto items 1–18.
findings.policy_quote: No Commercial Auto policy in program (see finding-002).
findings.gap_description: All Commercial Auto RMF items (Additional Insured automatic + WoS + P&NC, BI Mental Anguish, Broad Named Insured, Lease Gap, Drive Other Car, Employee as Insured CA 9933 / Hired Autos CA 2054, Endorsements review, Environmental CA 99 48, Fellow Employee Exclusion deletion, HNOA, No-fault state ops, Mobile Equipment, Notice & Knowledge, Ownership of Vehicles, Parked Vehicles, Symbols 1/2/7, Temp/Leased Workers, UM/UIM) are pending Auto binding. Each becomes a live RMF item once Auto is in force.
findings.plain_english: Every Auto-specific RMF item is dormant until an actual Auto policy is bound. When that happens (finding-002), the binding broker should walk through this full list to ensure the new auto policy is properly structured. For now, each is a deferred Needs Review.
findings.recommendation: On Auto binding, conduct full Commercial Auto RMF walk and confirm: (1) Symbol 1 liability + 8/9 if no owned vehicles; (2) Blanket AI + Blanket WoS + P&NC; (3) BI definition includes mental anguish; (4) Broad Named Insured + all entities listed; (5) HNOA; (6) Mental Anguish in BI; (7) Notice & Knowledge officer-limited endorsement; (8) Fellow Employee Exclusion deletion if needed; (9) Environmental CA 99 48 limited pollution endorsement; (10) UM/UIM at policy limits with insured education. CA-specific items (Lease Gap, Drive Other Car, no-fault) are 'N/A — verify on binding.'

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella-Specific RMF Items — DEFERRED Until Umbrella Bound
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella items 1–14.
findings.policy_quote: No Umbrella policy in program (see finding-005).
findings.gap_description: All Umbrella RMF items (Endorsements review, Non-follow-form exclusions, Horizontal Limit Exhaustion / P&NC, Insureds follow-form, Defense inside vs outside limits, Maintenance of underlying, Notice & Knowledge, Per Project / Per Location aggregate, Professional Liability follow form, Punitive damages, Right and Duty when underlying exhausted, Total Pollution Exclusion, Underlying Policies schedule, Specific follow-form concerns) are deferred until Umbrella is bound (finding-005).
findings.plain_english: All Umbrella-specific items are dormant until Umbrella is bound. When that happens, full RMF review must be conducted at binding. Critical items: defense outside limits, drop-down for exhausted aggregates, follow-form scope, schedule of underlying must list everything.
findings.recommendation: On Umbrella binding (finding-005), conduct full Umbrella RMF walk. Critical specs: (a) follow-form over GL, Auto, EL; (b) defense costs OUTSIDE limits; (c) Right and Duty when underlying exhausted; (d) drop-down for exhausted aggregates; (e) per-project and per-location aggregate follow-form; (f) blanket AI follow-form; (g) blanket WoS follow-form; (h) punitive damages where insurable by law; (i) maintenance of underlying — penalty limited to gap, not policy invalidation; (j) full schedule of underlying including foreign liability if any; (k) Notice & Knowledge officer-limited.

findings.requirement_type: WC-Specific RMF Items — DEFERRED Until WC Bound
findings.contract_quote: RMF WC items 1–16.
findings.policy_quote: No WC policy in program (see finding-001).
findings.gap_description: All WC RMF items (Small indemnity claims & back-to-work program, Small medical claims management, All States Endorsement 3.A vs 3.C, Alternate Employer Endorsement on staffing co policy, EL Limits adequate to support Umbrella, Endemic Disease/Foreign Voluntary/Repatriation, Experience Modification trend, Maritime endorsement, Large claims management, All possible credits applied, Owners Excluded, DBA, USL&H/MEL, Classification codes, WoS) are deferred until WC is bound (finding-001).
findings.plain_english: Every WC-specific RMF item is dormant until WC is bound. Critical items at binding: All States Endorsement 3.A list of states; experience modification; classification codes; back-to-work program; WoS endorsements (general WC 00 03 13 + CA-specific WC 04 03 06); EL limits adequate for Umbrella attachment.
findings.recommendation: On WC binding (finding-001), conduct full WC RMF walk. Critical specs: (1) All States Endorsement 3.A listing every state with operations (31 states served); (2) Alternate Employer Endorsement on any staffing/leasing co's WC; (3) EL $1M/$1M/$1M (umbrella attachment requirement); (4) Experience modification reviewed and trended; (5) classification codes audited against actual operations (printing/manufacturing/clerical/transit); (6) Owners exclusion documented; (7) Blanket WoS WC 00 03 13 + CA WC 04 03 06; (8) Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation listing counties. Foreign voluntary, DBA, MEL — N/A unless international or maritime exposure surfaces.

findings.requirement_type: Property — Pollutant Cleanup Sublimit & Ordinance/Law Sublimit Inadequate
findings.contract_quote: Standard property best practice for printing/manufacturing operations.
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 10: 'Pollutant clean-up at premises capped at $10,000 per 12-month period ... reported within 180 days.' 'Increased Cost of Construction $10,000 or 5% of building Limit, whichever less.' Gold Property Broadening 411-0793: Pollutant Cleanup increased to $100,000; Ordinance or Law B&C $500,000.
findings.gap_description: Even with Gold Broadening: Pollutant Cleanup $100K and Ordinance or Law $500K are below typical recommended levels for a $21M building / $16M BPP manufacturing facility. A meaningful chemical spill cleanup at the printing facility could exceed $100K; code-driven rebuild costs after a substantial loss to a printing facility commonly exceed $500K.
findings.plain_english: After a fire or other major loss, current building codes will often require upgrades that aren't covered by basic replacement cost — sprinkler upgrades, ADA compliance, electrical to current code. The policy provides $500K for that, which is light for a $21M facility. Pollutant cleanup is similarly capped at $100K, light for a printing operation with chemical inventory.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request Ordinance or Law Coverage A/B/C with limits at 25% of building values minimum (i.e., $5M+) and Pollutant Cleanup increase to $250K-$500K. Both are typically modest premium adjustments at this property scale.
discoveryQuestions: When was the Phoenix facility built and last upgraded? Older buildings have larger ordinance/law gaps after a substantial loss.
What's the largest single chemical inventory on-site at any time, and what would a release-and-cleanup event realistically cost?

findings.requirement_type: Property Vacancy Provision — 60-Day Cliff
findings.contract_quote: Standard property best practice.
findings.policy_quote: CP 00 10: 'If building vacant >60 consecutive days, NO coverage for vandalism, sprinkler leakage, glass breakage, water damage, theft. Other Covered Causes reduced by 15%.'
findings.gap_description: Standard 60-day vacancy clause. For an election services operation with cyclical use of facilities (heavy peak election cycles, lighter off-cycle), vacancy could become an issue if any space is dormant between cycles. Need to verify all insured locations are continuously occupied at the 31% occupancy threshold the standard uses.
findings.plain_english: If any building is empty for more than 60 consecutive days, several big perils stop being covered (vandalism, water damage, theft) and the rest gets a 15% haircut. If you have any leased or owned space that goes quiet between election cycles, that's a real problem. Worth confirming all locations are continuously used.
findings.recommendation: Confirm all insured premises are continuously occupied. If any space is seasonally vacant: (a) request vacancy permit endorsement; (b) consider security/monitoring upgrades to prevent vandalism/theft losses; (c) document use patterns.

findings.requirement_type: Maintenance of Insurance — 10-Day Renewal Evidence
findings.contract_quote: Sacramento §VI.A.2: 'provide the County with evidence of each policy's renewal ten (10) days in advance of its anniversary date.'
findings.policy_quote: Administrative — broker COI delivery procedure.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires renewal COI 10 days in advance of policy anniversary. Maricopa requires 15 days (§8.2.14.4). Tight windows — broker must front-load renewal certificates. Failure to deliver = material breach trigger.
findings.plain_english: Both counties want renewal certificates ahead of expiration — Sacramento says 10 days, Maricopa says 15 days. Broker workflow has to be set up to deliver these proactively, not on the day-of. Missing the window = material breach.
findings.recommendation: Build a renewal COI calendar tied to each policy's anniversary, set 30-day pre-expiration alerts, and front-load county COI delivery to meet 15-day Maricopa floor. Track delivery confirmations in client file.

findings.requirement_type: Stand-Alone Terrorism Coverage — Election Infrastructure Target
findings.contract_quote: Election infrastructure is a designated DHS critical infrastructure subsector (since 2017).
findings.policy_quote: TRIA accepted via 401-1374 ($468 premium); CG 21 73 conflicting exclusion (see finding-036). TRIA only responds for Treasury-certified acts.
findings.gap_description: TRIA only responds when Treasury formally certifies an act of terrorism — historically rare. Many domestic-actor scenarios, partial-attack scenarios, and below-threshold incidents do not certify. For an election services contractor — a designated critical infrastructure target — stand-alone terrorism coverage covers the broader 'act of political violence' scope and does not depend on Treasury certification.
findings.plain_english: The TRIA terrorism coverage in the policy only kicks in when the U.S. Treasury formally declares an event a 'certified act of terrorism' — which has happened almost never. A domestic-actor attack, a smaller-scale incident, or politically-motivated violence often doesn't qualify. Election infrastructure is on DHS's critical-infrastructure target list. A standalone Terrorism / Political Violence policy fills the gap.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate stand-alone Terrorism & Political Violence (T&PV) policy. Markets: Hiscox, Beazley, Liberty Mutual T&PV, Pool Re facilities. Specs: (a) coverage for property + BI from acts of terrorism, sabotage, riots, civil commotion; (b) no Treasury-certification trigger; (c) malicious-damage carve-back; (d) cyber-terrorism coordination with Cyber policy (when bound).
discoveryQuestions: Election infrastructure is officially DHS-designated critical infrastructure. Has Run-Test ever received a security briefing or threat assessment from CISA or local FBI field office?
Has your security team modeled a scenario where a non-certified terrorism event (domestic actor, below threshold) damages the facility — and how that interacts with TRIA-only coverage?

findings.requirement_type: Named Insured List — Inc vs LLC Mixed Entities
findings.contract_quote: RMF General item 3.
findings.policy_quote: Named Insured: Runbeck Election Services Inc. Additional Named Insureds: Runbeck Graphics Inc, Runbeck Investments LLC — all listed on Common Declarations.
findings.gap_description: All known affiliated entities (Inc and LLC) are listed by name on the Dec page — bypassing the 421-2916 §4.b LLC exclusion (finding-046). For the entities currently disclosed, this is correctly handled. Risk remains for any undisclosed affiliated LLC/JV/partnership.
findings.plain_english: The known related entities are properly listed on the policy. The risk is that any unlisted affiliated LLCs or JVs aren't automatically picked up — see finding-046. For the entities we know about, this is good.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Coordinate with finding-046 — confirm complete organizational chart and add any missing entities by endorsement.

findings.requirement_type: Mortgagee/Loss Payee Schedule on Property — Documented
findings.contract_quote: Standard property practice.
findings.policy_quote: CP 12 18 10 12 Loss Payable Provisions: ARC Airport 2800 LLC (1st Mortgagee), Banterra Bank (2nd Mortgagee), Wells Fargo Equipment Finance, Cisco Systems Capital, MailFinance, Canon Financial Services, Western Alliance Bank, Hewlett Packard Financial Services, Sunflower Bank, Black Mountain Investment Co LLC, Peoples Capital and Leasing, Contra Costa County, Runbeck Properties LLC, Lincoln Shields LLC.
findings.gap_description: Property loss payees properly scheduled. Lender-required loss payee status appears comprehensive — covers facility mortgagees and equipment financiers. Note that property loss payees are NOT GL Additional Insureds (different rights and forms).
findings.plain_english: All the lenders, equipment financiers, and landlords with security interests are properly listed as loss payees on the Property side. This is a standard requirement of those financing relationships and is correctly handled.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. At any new equipment financing or facility mortgage, add new loss payee promptly. Note: Contra Costa County is on the Property loss-payee schedule — confirm with insured why (suggests an active CA contract not in the contract requirements list).

findings.requirement_type: Policy Term Status — Verify Current/Renewed
findings.contract_quote: All county contracts require continuous in-force coverage during performance.
findings.policy_quote: Policy effective dates: 04/01/2025 – 04/01/2026. Audit date: 2026-05-01.
findings.gap_description: Policy submitted for audit shows term ending 04/01/2026 — one month BEFORE the audit date of 2026-05-01. Either: (a) the policy was renewed and the renewal version is materially identical (most likely); (b) the policy lapsed and there is currently no in-force coverage (catastrophic). Audit conclusions assume the renewal is in force on substantively identical terms.
findings.plain_english: The policy on file shows it expired April 1, 2026, but today is May 1, 2026. Either it was renewed (and we need the current declarations page) or it has lapsed (which would be a catastrophic gap, since every county contract requires in-force coverage). Assume renewed — but get the current dec page.
findings.recommendation: Immediately confirm: (1) current renewal effective dates 04/01/2026 – 04/01/2027; (2) obtain current dec page and any material endorsement changes; (3) re-validate every finding against the renewed terms; (4) if not renewed, this is a five-alarm fire — bind immediately.

findings.requirement_type: Punitive Damages Treatment — Most-Favored-Jurisdiction Wording
findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella item 10.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 does not separately exclude punitive damages, but punitive insurability is a state-law issue. AZ does not categorically prohibit insuring punitive damages; CA generally prohibits insuring intentional-conduct punitive damages.
findings.gap_description: Punitive damages are not specifically excluded on the GL. Default ISO form treats them as included to the extent insurable by law. Cross-state operations (31 states) means various state public-policy rules apply. When Umbrella is bound (finding-005), insist on most-favored-jurisdiction (MFJ) wording so coverage attaches in the most favorable state of any state with arguable connection to the claim.
findings.plain_english: Punitive damages are partially insurable depending on state. Across 31 states, the rules vary. When the umbrella is bound, the umbrella should have 'most-favored-jurisdiction' language — meaning if any state with a connection to the claim allows insuring punitive damages, the policy will pay. This is a standard ask in specialty markets.
findings.recommendation: On Umbrella binding (finding-005), specify: (a) punitive damages covered to fullest extent permissible by law; (b) most-favored-jurisdiction wording; (c) coordination with GL. Verify GL does not have a punitive-damages exclusion endorsement at next renewal review.

findings.requirement_type: Cross-Policy Notice & Knowledge Consistency
findings.contract_quote: RMF General item 4.
findings.policy_quote: GL: 421-2915 §6 Knowledge of Occurrence in place (good — see finding-028). Property: standard ISO conditions, no officer-limited Knowledge endorsement identified.
findings.gap_description: Knowledge-of-occurrence endorsement is on the GL but does not extend to Property, Equipment Breakdown, Data Breach, or Crime sublimits within the package. When WC, Auto, Cyber, E&O, Umbrella, D&O, EPLI are bound, each should have an equivalent officer-limited Knowledge/Notice endorsement.
findings.plain_english: The notice-and-knowledge protection is great on the GL — but it's only on the GL. Each other policy needs the same protection so a low-level employee's unreported incident on the Property side, Cyber side, or any other line doesn't void coverage there.
findings.recommendation: Confirm or request officer-limited Knowledge/Notice endorsements on every policy as bound: GL (in place), Property (request at renewal), Crime, Cyber, E&O, D&O, EPLI, Auto, WC, Umbrella. Standardize the trigger language across the program.

findings.requirement_type: Cross-Policy Waiver of Subrogation Consistency
findings.contract_quote: RMF General item 5.
findings.policy_quote: GL: CG 24 04 blanket WoS (good — finding-025). Property: CP 00 90 §I 'subrogation — waiver permitted in writing prior to loss' (waiver permitted but no blanket endorsement). EB, Crime sublimits, Data Breach: no blanket WoS identified.
findings.gap_description: Blanket WoS is in place on GL but Property only allows waiver if executed in writing prior to loss — not blanket. For counties requiring WoS on Property (lease premises requirements, COC requirements where they apply), this is a procedural step Run-Test must take before each loss occurrence. When Auto, WC, Cyber, Inland Marine are bound, blanket WoS should be standardized.
findings.plain_english: Waiver of Subrogation is blanket on the GL but only permitted on Property if you sign a written waiver before the loss happens. For each new contract requiring property WoS, that needs to happen proactively. Across the program, WoS handling should be standardized.
findings.recommendation: (1) On Property, request blanket WoS by written contract endorsement at renewal — most carriers will provide; (2) On every other policy as bound, ensure blanket WoS is present (Auto, WC including CA-specific, Inland Marine if used, Cyber); (3) Standard exception: typically not on Professional Liability/E&O.

findings.requirement_type: Material-Change Notice Endorsement (Maricopa Specific)
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.15: 'Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.'
findings.policy_quote: 401-1235 provides 30-day NOC for cancellation/non-renewal but does not address 'material change.' Standard ACORD COI cancellation language does not include material change.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires notice not just for cancellation but for any 'material change' to coverage. The current 401-1235 endorsement covers cancellation/non-payment/non-renewal but does not appear to cover material change. Few carriers will agree to material-change notice on the policy itself; the contract effectively shifts the burden to Run-Test (2-business-day pass-through if Contractor receives notice from carrier).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 30 days' notice if the policy is materially changed — which is a broader trigger than just cancellation. The current notice endorsement doesn't quite cover that. Practically, this puts the burden on Run-Test to monitor any material change communications from the carrier and pass them to Maricopa within 2 business days.
findings.recommendation: (1) Request material-change addition to 401-1235 schedule for Maricopa at renewal — some carriers will accept; (2) Build internal procedure: any carrier communication regarding the policy is reviewed within 2 business days for material-change implications and passed to Maricopa Risk Management; (3) Document the procedure in contract compliance file.
discoveryQuestions: Who currently receives carrier communications at Run-Test, and is there a procedure for reviewing them within 2 business days against contract notice obligations?
Has the carrier indicated whether they would amend 401-1235 to include 'material change' as a trigger?

findings.requirement_type: Indemnification Clause Backed by Insurance — Maricopa AZ Comparative Negligence
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.1.1–8.1.4: 'To the fullest extent permitted by law ... the contractor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the County ... but only to the extent caused by the negligent acts or omissions of the contractor.'
findings.policy_quote: GL Insured Contract definition (CG 00 01 standard) backs contractual indemnity within policy scope. Carve-out for County's sole negligence is consistent with AZ comparative-negligence principles.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's indemnification is appropriately limited to Run-Test's negligence (not broad-form 'arising out of'). GL contractual liability properly backs this within policy limits. But limit shortfalls (finding-006) and absence of Cyber/E&O/Auto/Umbrella (findings 002–005) mean the indemnity exceeds available insurance. See finding-060 (uncapped indemnity).
findings.plain_english: The indemnification clause itself is fair — it tracks the company's actual fault (AZ comparative negligence). The GL properly covers contractual indemnification within policy limits. The problem is the limits are short and several required policies don't exist. Once those are fixed, the indemnification flows back to a properly insured backstop.
findings.recommendation: Cure underlying limit shortfalls (findings 002, 004, 005, 006). The indemnification clause itself is well-drafted and appropriately limited; insurance is the lever, not the contract.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Auto Umbrella Attachment — Ambiguous Reading
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.9 (program-level umbrella permission): 'the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.' §8.2.11 (Auto): does not inline-mention umbrella.
findings.policy_quote: No Auto policy in program (finding-002). No Umbrella in program (finding-005).
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.9 has program-level umbrella permission to stack on Auto $2M; §8.2.11 Auto clause does not inline-mention umbrella. Strict reading: $1M Auto + $X Umbrella does not satisfy $2M Auto minimum because the Auto clause itself doesn't reference umbrella. Permissive reading: program-level §8.2.9 allows stacking. Today both readings yield non-compliance because there's no Auto policy at all and no Umbrella.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract has an ambiguity: the general clause allows umbrella to stack to meet limits, but the specific auto-clause doesn't say so explicitly. When auto and umbrella are bound, this becomes a live question — strict readers say umbrella doesn't count for Auto; permissive readers say it does. Better to bind the Auto at $2M outright and remove the question.
findings.recommendation: Practical recommendation: bind Commercial Auto at $2M CSL primary (not $1M with reliance on umbrella stacking). This eliminates the interpretive ambiguity entirely and matches Maricopa's strictest reading. Cost differential between $1M and $2M primary auto is typically modest. Confirm interpretation with Maricopa Risk Management at first contact if going with $1M + umbrella stacking.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cyber Umbrella Attachment — Ambiguous Reading
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.9 (program-level umbrella permission). §8.2.13 (Cyber): does not inline-mention umbrella.
findings.policy_quote: No Cyber policy in program at the required scale (finding-004). No Umbrella in program (finding-005). Most umbrellas do not follow form to Cyber.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.9 program-level umbrella permission could theoretically apply to Cyber $5M; §8.2.13 Cyber clause is silent on umbrella. Standard market practice: umbrellas do NOT follow form to Cyber unless specifically endorsed (Cyber attachments are typically separate excess Cyber towers, not commercial umbrella). Strict reading wins by industry custom.
findings.plain_english: On paper, Maricopa's general clause says umbrella can stack to meet limits. But standard umbrellas don't extend to cyber liability — that's a specialty excess tower question. So the practical answer is: bind primary Cyber at $5M, don't rely on umbrella stacking for cyber. Industry custom and most carriers will not entertain cyber stacking under a standard commercial umbrella.
findings.recommendation: Bind primary Cyber at $5M (Maricopa minimum) — see finding-004. Consider a separate excess Cyber tower at $5M+ above primary if higher limits warranted by exposure profile (90M voter records justifies $10M+). Do not rely on commercial umbrella to satisfy Cyber requirement.

findings.requirement_type: CGL Scope — Classification Limitation Excludes Election Services Operations
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance ... The policy shall include coverage for premises liability, bodily injury, broad form property damage, personal injury, products and completed operations and blanket contractual coverage, and shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims.
findings.contract_page: §8.2.10, Page 6 of 41 (Maricopa); also Sacramento §II.A, Page 1 of 4
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County contract; Sacramento County Appendix G
findings.policy_quote: This insurance applies only to the insured's operations for which a classification is listed on the declaration page of this policy. If any classification is not shown, the corresponding insured's operations is not insured hereunder. Classifications: Code 91127 — Alarms and Alarm Systems Installation (IF ANY); Code 91636 — Detective or Investigative Agencies-Pvt (IF ANY); Code 98751 — Security and Patrol Agencies.
findings.policy_page: Pages 38–39 (Form 00 GL0713 00 08 11 — Classification Limitation; Form FAIC-SKLBUS-SCGL Schedule)
findings.gap_description: The only General Liability policy in the program is a monoline form purpose-built for SECURITY GUARD OPERATIONS — Named Insured business description is 'Security Operations,' the only premium-bearing class is 98751 Security and Patrol Agencies ($190,000 payroll, $9,416 premium), and Form 00 GL0713 strictly limits coverage to operations under the listed classifications. Run-Test's actual business — election technology manufacturing, ballot printing, election mail processing, ballot fulfillment, and SaaS election technology — is NOT a listed classification and is therefore NOT INSURED under this CGL. Both Sacramento County (§II.A) and Maricopa County (§8.2.10) require a CGL responsive to the Contractor's actual operations, and Sacramento explicitly requires ISO CG 0001 'without additional exclusions or limitations.' The Classification Limitation is a fundamental additional limitation that strips coverage from the very operations the County contracts contemplate.
findings.plain_english: This is the single most important finding in the audit. The 'General Liability' policy on file does not actually cover the company's main business. It only covers security guard work. If a printed ballot causes a fire at a customer site, if an election worker is hurt at the Phoenix facility, if a ballot envelope contains a defect — none of that is covered under this policy because it falls outside the security-guard classifications. Both county contracts require GL coverage for the actual contracted operations. As written, Run-Test is performing $5M+ revenue election services with no GL backstop for that work. A single bodily injury or property damage claim out of election operations would land directly on the balance sheet.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: Bind a primary CGL policy covering election services / commercial printing / mailing-services operations (likely classifications 47053 Stationery/Paper Goods Manufacturing, 50071 Printing/Mailing, or similar) at $2M/$4M/$4M to satisfy Maricopa §8.2.10 and Sacramento §II.A. The current Arch security-guard CGL should remain in place for the security operation only — but a parallel operations CGL is mandatory before performing under either county contract. Confirm whether Patriot Growth Insurance Services placed a separate operations CGL that was not provided in this audit packet.
discoveryQuestions: When you signed the Maricopa and Sacramento County contracts, did you understand that the GL policy on file only covers your security guard operation — not your ballot printing, mailing, or election technology work?
If a stack of ballots caused a fire at a county facility tomorrow, who do you think would defend you and pay the claim — and have you ever asked your carrier to confirm that in writing?

Is there a separate General Liability policy covering Run-Test's election services manufacturing operations that wasn't provided for this audit, or is the security guard policy genuinely the only GL on the program?

What's the annual revenue split between your security operations and your election services work? Because the GL premium ($9,416) suggests the carrier underwrote a tiny security guard piece, not a $5M–$25M election services manufacturer.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation — Policy Missing from Program
findings.contract_quote: Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes having jurisdiction of Contractor's employees engaged in the performance of the work or services under this contract; and Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit. (Maricopa) ... WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance ... EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease. (Sacramento)
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.12, Page 6 of 41; Sacramento §II.C / §III.C–D, Page 1–2 of 4
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County contract; Sacramento County Appendix G
findings.policy_quote: [NO WORKERS' COMPENSATION POLICY PROVIDED IN AUDIT PACKET]
findings.gap_description: No Workers' Compensation policy was provided for review. Both county contracts require statutory WC plus $1M/$1M/$1M Employers' Liability, with Sacramento requiring California-statutory WC if any work is performed in California. Run-Test has 50–200 employees and is AZ-based with operations potentially in CA — this is a mandatory line and a foundational program element. Cannot evaluate Other States Coverage (3.A vs 3.C), classification codes, experience modification, Alternate Employer endorsement, Waiver of Subrogation (Maricopa §8.2.12, Sacramento §VIII), Voluntary Compensation, USL&H, DBA, or any other RMF item.
findings.plain_english: There is no Workers' Comp policy in the file we audited. With 50–200 employees, Workers' Comp isn't optional in any state — it's the law. Both county contracts also require a WC waiver of subrogation and at least $1M Employers' Liability. Until we see the actual WC policy, we cannot confirm a single item of WC compliance, and we cannot tell the County the program meets contract minimums. If WC truly isn't in force, every employee injury becomes a direct lawsuit against the company with no insurance defense and no statutory benefits buffer.
findings.recommendation: IMMEDIATELY produce the active Workers' Compensation policy for full audit. Verify (1) Item 3.A includes Arizona and California (or that an All-States 3.C is in place for CA work); (2) Employers' Liability is at least $1M/$1M/$1M to support umbrella attachment and meet Maricopa/Sacramento minimums; (3) Blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (CA: WC 04 03 06 with separate premium); (4) Alternate Employer endorsement if any leased/temp workers are used; (5) Foreign Voluntary if any out-of-country employee travel occurs; (6) Classification codes match actual operations (ballot printing, election mail, security guards likely span 4 or more class codes).
discoveryQuestions: Where is your active Workers' Comp policy — is it placed by Patriot, or by another broker we should pull into this review?
If you send employees to support a Sacramento County election event, does your WC policy specifically list California in Item 3.A, or are you relying on Other States coverage?
Have you received a current Experience Mod from NCCI or your carrier — and if so, is your broker actively managing it, or does it just show up at renewal?
Do you use any temporary or staffed workers during peak election cycles, and if so, has the staffing company added you as Alternate Employer on their WC policy?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — $5M Required by Maricopa, No Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy ... crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: [NO CYBER POLICY PROVIDED IN AUDIT PACKET] ... CGL: 'This insurance does not apply to bodily injury, property damage, or personal and advertising injury arising out of any cyber incident.' (Form CG 40 35 12 23, Pg 68) ... CGL: 'This insurance does not apply to bodily injury, property damage, or personal and advertising injury arising out of any access to or disclosure of any person's or organization's confidential or personal information.' (Form CG 21 06 12 23, Pg 64) ... CGL: 'Exclusion — Violation Of Law Addressing Data Privacy ... including BIPA, CCPA, and GDPR.' (Form CG 00 69 12 23, Pg 56)
findings.policy_page: GL Pgs 56, 64, 68 — multiple absolute cyber/privacy exclusions
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County mandates $5M Cyber/Privacy/Network Security with an extensive feature checklist (regulatory fines AND penalties, third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, business interruption, cyber extortion). No Cyber policy was provided. The CGL contains THREE overlapping absolute exclusions (CG 40 35 cyber incident, CG 21 06 access/disclosure, CG 00 69 data privacy law) that strip any cyber/privacy coverage from the GL — including specific naming of BIPA, CCPA, and GDPR. Run-Test's core business is election technology, voter data processing, ballot printing, and SaaS — this is one of the most sensitive PII/election-integrity exposures in the U.S. economy. There is no fallback within the program for a data breach, ransomware event, social engineering wire fraud, or state regulatory privacy investigation.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test handles voter registration data and ballots for over 90 million registered voters. A cyber breach is not a hypothetical here — election companies are nation-state-level targets. The Maricopa contract requires $5M of Cyber. There is no Cyber policy on the program. The GL has three layered exclusions explicitly stripping out all cyber/privacy coverage — including BIPA, CCPA, and GDPR claims by name. If a ransomware attack hits before the next election, or if voter data leaks, the company's response costs (notification, forensics, regulators, lawsuits, business interruption, ransom) come directly out of the bank account — and the company is also in material breach of the Maricopa contract.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: Bind a $5M standalone Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability policy with a specialty cyber market (Coalition, At-Bay, Beazley, Chubb Cyber, AIG Cyber-Edge). Required components per Maricopa §8.2.13: regulatory defense + fines/penalties (verify carrier covers PCI, HIPAA, and election-specific regulators), third-party fidelity / social engineering / funds transfer fraud (often sublimited — push for $5M concurrent limit), business interruption + dependent BI (election cycle peaks), cyber extortion / ransomware, breach response (notification/credit monitoring/forensics/PR), data restoration, no arrest/conviction requirement on crime triggers. Retro date must precede 11/01/21 contract effective date per Maricopa §8.2.3. Given election-industry threat profile, push for $10M with sublimit-free cyber crime if budget permits.
discoveryQuestions: Run-Test handles voter data for over 90 million registered voters — what's your current incident response plan if your ballot fulfillment system is hit with ransomware 30 days before an election?
Have you ever had your IT vendor or counsel walk you through what California's CCPA or your state's election-data laws would require you to do, and pay, after a breach?
Does your CFO or CEO know that Maricopa County is contractually requiring $5M of Cyber and that there is currently no Cyber policy on the program?
If a wire-transfer fraud (someone impersonates a vendor and gets your AP team to wire $400k) happened tomorrow, who would pay for that loss — and have you tested whether any policy you have responds?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / E&O — $1M Required by Sacramento, No Standalone Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability) designated under the Minimum Scope of Insurance.
findings.policy_quote: [NO STANDALONE PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY / E&O POLICY PROVIDED] ... CGL Coverage D — E&O Liability: 'Coverage D adds limited E&O for negligent acts/errors/omissions in declared services, BUT shares the General Aggregate and Each Occurrence limits with A/B/C. Excludes intentional acts, statutory violations, contractual liability (except insured contracts), fraud, intra-insured claims, employment law, electronic data damage. Punitive/multiplied damages and fines also excluded.' Subject to General Aggregate AND Each Occurrence limits — shared with A/B/C, NOT a separate aggregate.
findings.policy_page: GL Pgs 23–26 (Form 00 GL1049 — Errors & Omissions Coverage Extension)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento County requires standalone $1M/$1M Professional Liability / E&O AND expressly forbids using Umbrella to satisfy that minimum. The only 'E&O' in the program is Coverage D bolted onto the security-guard CGL — which (1) is restricted to declared classifications (security/patrol/alarms/detective), so it does NOT respond to election services E&O exposure, (2) shares aggregate and per-occurrence limits with the GL Coverage A/B/C, so a single GL claim could exhaust the E&O limit before any election-services error or omission is even reported, and (3) excludes electronic data damage, statutory violations, fraud, and contractual liability beyond insured contracts. Run-Test's election services exposure (ballot design errors, mail-sort errors causing voter disenfranchisement, processing errors, software/SaaS bugs, vendor specification deviations) is the textbook professional liability exposure for this industry — and it is uncovered.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test's core service is providing accuracy. Election-mail sorting errors, ballot printing defects, voter file processing mistakes, software bugs in election technology — these are professional services failures, not bodily injury. A standard GL doesn't pay for those. Sacramento County requires a real, standalone E&O policy at $1M and explicitly says you cannot fill that requirement with an umbrella. The only 'E&O' on the program is a small extension hanging off a security-guard policy that doesn't even apply to election operations. If a ballot printing error causes 50,000 voters to receive defective ballots in a contested election, the resulting class-action lawsuit, ACLU claims, and re-election costs are uninsured.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Tech / Media / Miscellaneous E&O policy specifically rated for election technology and election mail services. Minimum $1M/$1M to satisfy Sacramento §II.D — but given PE-backed status, government-contract exposure, SaaS/technology risk, and election-industry visibility, recommend $5M with first-dollar defense and a bumped retention only on regulatory/government claims. Carrier targets: Beazley TMB, Tokio Marine HCC, Coalition, Travelers Tech E&O, AIG. Retro date must be on or before the earlier of (a) 11/01/21 (Maricopa contract effective date) or (b) any earlier Sacramento contract effective date. ERP/tail of at least 1 year (Sacramento §V.C) plus 2 years (Maricopa §8.2.3) — bind 3-year ERP option.
discoveryQuestions: If a ballot misprint causes 50,000 voters in Maricopa County to receive defective ballots in a contested election, what's your plan for paying defense costs and ACLU-led class actions — and which policy do you think would respond?
Have you ever had Sacramento or Maricopa formally accept the GL policy as 'professional liability' — or has your COI been issued without a separate E&O line?
What's the largest single contract value Run-Test has lost or been threatened with cancellation over due to an alleged service failure, and how did you handle it without an E&O policy in place?
Does your team know that Sacramento explicitly forbids using your umbrella to cover the E&O requirement — meaning you need a standalone policy, not just a higher umbrella?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella / Excess Liability — Required, No Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: UMBRELLA or Excess Liability policies are acceptable where the need for higher liability limits is noted in the Minimum Limits of Insurance and shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements where necessary for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage. ... Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Appendix G; Maricopa County contract
findings.policy_quote: [NO UMBRELLA / EXCESS POLICY PROVIDED IN AUDIT PACKET]
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M/$4M/$4M GL — current Arch CGL provides $1M/$3M/$3M. Maricopa requires $2M Auto CSL — current Hanover Auto provides $1M CSL. Maricopa requires $1M Employers' Liability (assumed compliant when WC is produced). Without an umbrella policy, the GL and Auto BOTH fall short of Maricopa's primary minimums on their face. Sacramento's $1M/$2M GL minimum is met by primary GL (when responsive), but its $1M Auto CSL is met. The contract permits umbrella stacking on GL, Auto, and EL — but no umbrella is in the program, so the gaps cannot be closed by excess. PE-backed manufacturer with government contracts, $5M–$25M revenue, high-value election technology, public-interest exposure, and 50–200 employees absolutely should carry $5M–$25M of umbrella as standard practice.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test has $1M of GL and $1M of Auto. Maricopa County wants $2M on each. There is no umbrella policy to bridge that gap, which means the program is below the contract minimum on its face. Beyond the contract issue: a single auto accident with multiple injuries, a single bodily injury claim at a customer site, a slip-and-fall at the Phoenix facility — any of those can blow through $1M in a heartbeat. PE-backed companies in regulated industries with government contracts simply do not operate at $1M primary limits. This is industry-standard insurance hygiene that's missing.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Commercial Umbrella / Excess Liability policy at $10M minimum (target $25M given PE ownership and election-industry visibility). Must follow form over GL, Auto, and Employers' Liability. Schedule of Underlying must list ALL underlying policies — including any new election-services CGL once placed. Confirm: (1) defense costs OUTSIDE limits; (2) carrier has Right and Duty to defend when underlying exhausted (typically standard market — be cautious of E&S forms with this gap per RMF UMB-11); (3) drop-down for exhausted aggregates; (4) NO follow-form exclusion narrower than underlying; (5) maintenance-of-underlying language not draconian; (6) blanket AI / WoS / P&NC follow form to underlying. Carrier rating must meet A.M. Best A-VII (Sacramento §VI.A.1) and B++ (Maricopa §8.2.1) — Sacramento threshold is the binding constraint.
discoveryQuestions: What's your current PE sponsor's expectation for umbrella limits — do they have a portfolio insurance schedule that mandates a minimum, and does Run-Test currently meet it?
If a Run-Test van rear-ends a school bus on the way to an election event, do you understand that $1M of Auto liability would be exhausted by the time the ambulances reach the hospital?
Have you ever had a county or state contract require a higher GL or Auto limit and discovered mid-bid that your program couldn't satisfy it?
When was the last time your broker walked you through a 'limits adequacy' analysis benchmarked against your peers in the election services and commercial printing space?

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine — Likely Exposure, No Policy Provided
findings.contract_quote: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: [NO INLAND MARINE POLICY PROVIDED IN AUDIT PACKET]
findings.gap_description: Client profile lists 'High-value equipment' as a special risk. Run-Test transports ballots, ballot printers, mail-sort equipment, and election technology between facilities, customers, and county sites. Property in transit, mobile/transitory equipment, and contractors' equipment are typically scheduled on Inland Marine. The Auto policy excludes property in care/custody/control and cargo — Auto Liability does not cover Run-Test's election equipment in transit. Sacramento §IX requires WoS endorsement on any IM policy maintained, but only triggers IF an IM policy exists. Could not assess: scheduled limits, transit limits, EDP/computer equipment coverage, customer's property coverage, or WoS compliance.
findings.plain_english: Run-Test moves expensive election equipment around — ballot printers, mail sorters, scanners, computers, and customer ballots. None of that is covered by the Commercial Auto policy if it's damaged in transit. Inland Marine is the right policy for that exposure, but no Inland Marine policy was provided. Either it's missing from the program or it wasn't included in this audit packet.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether an Inland Marine policy exists. If not, scope an IM placement covering: (1) scheduled Equipment / EDP / Computer Equipment for ballot-printing and mail-sort gear; (2) Property In Transit / Cargo coverage for ballot and equipment movement; (3) Customer's Property / Bailee's Coverage for any third-party property held at Phoenix facility or in transit. If IM is in force, add WoS endorsement to comply with Sacramento §IX. Verify if any equipment is leased — confirm Loss Payee / Lender's Loss Payable endorsement.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Minimum CGL Limits — $1M/$2M Required vs $1M/$3M Carried (limits OK, scope NOT)
findings.contract_quote: Building Trades General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Comp/Op Aggregate: $2,000,000; Personal & Adv. Injury: $1,000,000; Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; Fire Damage: $100,000.
findings.policy_quote: Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; General Aggregate: $3,000,000; Products/Completed Ops Aggregate: $3,000,000; Personal & Advertising Injury: $1,000,000; Damage to Premises Rented: $1,000,000.
findings.gap_description: On a numerical basis, the Arch CGL limits ($1M/$3M/$3M) exceed Sacramento's minimums ($1M/$2M/$2M). HOWEVER, this is the security-guard CGL, and the Classification Limitation (00 GL0713) means the policy will NOT respond to Run-Test's election services operations under the Sacramento contract — making the limits compliance moot for the actual contracted work (see finding-001). Sacramento also requires ISO CG 0001 occurrence — that base form IS present (CG 00 01 04 13, Pg 40). Damage to Premises sublimit is $1M which exceeds the $100,000 Fire Damage minimum. Nominal compliance, fundamental scope failure.
findings.plain_english: On paper, the limits look fine. In reality, the policy doesn't apply to the work Sacramento is paying you to do. So the limits compliance is a mirage — the right answer is to bind an operations-CGL that actually covers ballot printing and election services.
findings.recommendation: Once an election-services CGL is bound (per finding-001), confirm primary occurrence-form ISO CG 0001 at minimum $1M/$2M/$2M, with no additional exclusions or limitations beyond ISO base form, per Sacramento §II.A. Push for $2M/$4M/$4M to satisfy Maricopa simultaneously.
discoveryQuestions: Has Sacramento County's Risk Manager ever reviewed your COI and accepted the Arch security-guard CGL as the policy responsive to election services work, or are you sending COIs without anyone confirming scope?
What does your renewal application disclose about Run-Test's actual operations — security guards, election services, or both? The premium ($9,416) suggests only security was rated.
If you needed to expand limits for a new state contract bid, would you go to your current carrier first or shop the broader operations to a different market entirely?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Minimum CGL Limits — $2M/$4M/$4M Required vs $1M/$3M/$3M Carried
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; General Aggregate: $3,000,000; Products/Completed Ops Aggregate: $3,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa minimums are $2M/$4M/$4M with explicit umbrella stacking permitted. Current Arch CGL provides $1M/$3M/$3M — short on Each Occurrence ($1M shortfall) AND short on both Aggregates ($1M shortfall each). Maricopa §8.2.9 permits umbrella stacking on GL — so a $1M umbrella over the GL would technically satisfy the per-occurrence minimum. However, no umbrella is in the program (see finding-005). Independent of the Classification Limitation issue (finding-001), the limits themselves are short on this policy.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M-each / $4M-aggregate. The current GL gives you $1M-each / $3M-aggregate. You're short, and there's no umbrella to bridge the gap. Even setting aside the bigger problem that this GL doesn't cover election services — the limits don't even add up.
findings.recommendation: Bind operations CGL at $2M/$4M/$4M minimum (per finding-001) AND/OR bind a $5M+ umbrella that follows form to GL. Confirm CGL has 'no third party action over' limitation, blanket contractual, and no XCU exclusion (Maricopa §8.2.10 explicitly forbids those).
discoveryQuestions: When the Maricopa County contract was signed in 2021, did anyone verify that the GL limits met the $2M/$4M/$4M requirement, or did the COI just go through?
Are you concerned about the optics if Maricopa Risk Management does a mid-term audit and finds the program below the contract minimum?
Have other county contracts started asking for $2M/$4M minimums — and is your renewal cycle the right moment to step up before more contracts demand it?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Minimum Auto Limits — $2M CSL Required vs $1M CSL Carried
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles.
findings.policy_quote: Liability Combined Single Limit: $1,000,000.
findings.policy_page: Auto Pg 26 (Item Three Schedule of Covered Autos)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.11 requires $2M CSL on owned, hired, and non-owned. Current Hanover Auto provides $1M CSL — $1M shortfall. Maricopa §8.2.11 does not inline-mention umbrella attachment — only the program-level §8.2.9 provides general umbrella permission. Strict reading of §8.2.11 alone may NOT permit umbrella attachment to satisfy the Auto minimum (see finding-010 — umbrella ambiguity). Underlying gap is real on either reading.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M per accident on the auto policy. You have $1M. That's a hard shortfall.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) increase Auto CSL to $2M at next renewal (cost likely modest given small fleet — 2 owned vehicles + 55 employees H&NO basis), or (b) confirm an umbrella stacking on Auto satisfies Maricopa with a separate Risk Manager confirmation in writing.
discoveryQuestions: How many miles do your two scheduled vehicles run per year, and where do your employees drive on company business — particularly to/from county election sites?
If your driver caused a multi-injury accident on I-10, do you understand $1M would likely be exhausted before settlement?
What's the realistic cost increase to take Auto from $1M to $2M CSL on a fleet this size — has your broker quoted it recently?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Auto $2M Minimum — Umbrella Attachment Ambiguous
