findings.requirement_type: Named Insured Asymmetry Across Program
findings.contract_quote: [RMF General §3 — Named insureds: list for each policy and flag any missing.]
findings.policy_quote: GL Named Insured: 'Runbeck Election Services LLC' (only). Auto Named Insureds (Form 461-0174): 'Runbeck Election Services Inc' + Runbeck Investments LLC + Runbeck Properties LLC + Runbeck Graphics Inc + Runbeck Companies 401(k) Profit Sharing Plan + Lincoln Shields LLC + Black Mountain Investment Co. LLC.
findings.policy_page: GL Pg 7 (Common Policy Dec); Auto Pg 28 (Form 461-0174)
findings.gap_description: Significant Named Insured asymmetry. Auto policy lists a 7-entity family — Inc parent, multiple LLC affiliates, real estate LLC, 401(k) plan. GL policy lists only a single LLC, with a different entity type than the Auto NI ('LLC' vs 'Inc'). Issues: (1) Runbeck Election Services Inc (Auto NI) is NOT on the GL — meaning if Inc enters into a contract or has an exposure, it's uninsured under the GL. (2) The 401(k) plan, Investments LLC, Properties LLC, Graphics Inc, Lincoln Shields LLC, Black Mountain Investment LLC all carry Auto coverage but ZERO GL coverage. (3) Inc vs LLC mismatch on the GL Dec page is itself a red flag — entity-type errors on Dec pages are a common claims-denial vector. (4) No Broad Form Named Insured endorsement on GL means newly-formed/acquired entities not automatically extended.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy covers seven legal entities — Runbeck Election Services Inc, multiple LLCs, real estate LLCs, even the 401(k) plan. Your GL only covers ONE entity, and the entity type ('LLC') doesn't even match the operating company ('Inc') listed on the Auto policy. So: if a slip-and-fall happens at a real estate property owned by Runbeck Properties LLC, the GL doesn't respond. If Runbeck Graphics Inc is sued for a printing error, the GL doesn't respond. If a 401(k) participant sues the plan, the GL doesn't respond. This is a serious gap — the entire affiliated entity structure is uninsured for general liability.
findings.recommendation: (1) Reconcile Named Insured schedule across all program policies. Determine the correct legal-entity holding the operations contracts (Inc vs LLC) and ensure the operations-CGL (per finding-001) names the correct entity AND all affiliated entities scheduled on the Auto policy. (2) Add a Broad Form Named Insured endorsement to the operations-CGL (with explicit LLC inclusion language to avoid the 'partnerships and LLCs not automatically included' default in some forms). (3) Confirm the 401(k) plan carries appropriate Fiduciary Liability separately rather than relying on GL. (4) Investigate the Inc-vs-LLC mismatch on the Arch GL — likely an underwriter error worth documenting.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through the Runbeck legal-entity structure — which entity holds the Maricopa contract, which signs the Sacramento contract, which owns the Phoenix building, and which one employs the people doing election services work?
Did anyone notice that the GL policy is in the name of an LLC while the Auto policy is in the name of an Inc? Which one is correct for the operating company?
If Runbeck Properties LLC is sued for a slip-and-fall on the Phoenix premises tomorrow, which policy do you think responds? (Spoiler: not the GL, because Properties LLC isn't on it.)
Has the 401(k) plan ever had a Fiduciary Liability quote, or has it just been listed on the Auto policy as a named insured?

findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge — CGL Officer-Limited Endorsement Missing
findings.contract_quote: [RMF General §4 / CGL §25 — Notice & Knowledge: Is the policy wording endorsed so notice of an occurrence is only considered when an officer, the person responsible for insurance, and/or the risk manager is notified?]
findings.policy_quote: [NO 'NOTICE OF OCCURRENCE' OR 'KNOWLEDGE OF OCCURRENCE' OFFICER-LIMITED ENDORSEMENT IDENTIFIED IN GL FORM SCHEDULE]
findings.policy_page: N/A — not present in form schedule
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO CG 00 01 §IV.2 imputes 'knowledge of an occurrence' to the insured. Without an officer-limited endorsement (e.g., 'Notice Manager,' 'Knowledge of Occurrence' restricted to executive officer / risk manager / insurance manager), a low-level employee's awareness of an incident — that they fail to escalate — can be deemed knowledge by the entity, and any subsequent late-reporting to the carrier can be grounds for denial. For a 50–200 employee election services manufacturer with multi-shift operations, this is a real exposure. No such endorsement appears in the GL form schedule.
findings.plain_english: Right now, if a forklift driver sees a near-miss, doesn't tell anyone, and a related claim shows up nine months later, your carrier could argue the company 'knew' about the incident through that employee and wasn't reported in time — and deny the claim. The fix is a small endorsement that says only an officer, risk manager, or insurance manager's knowledge counts. Without it, every employee is a coverage-denial risk.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Notice/Knowledge of Occurrence officer-limited endorsement on the operations-CGL. Common form names: 'Knowledge of Occurrence,' 'Notice Manager,' or carrier-specific equivalents. Standard market carriers offer this at no additional premium. Apply the same to any replacement security-guard CGL.
discoveryQuestions: Who in your organization is officially responsible for reporting incidents to the insurance carrier — and does every employee know that's the chain?
If a guard saw a slip-and-fall at a customer site, didn't think it was serious, and didn't report it, would your management chain ever find out before the claim letter arrived nine months later?
Does your handbook or supervisor training spell out incident reporting up the chain, or do employees use their own judgment?

findings.requirement_type: Notice & Knowledge — Auto via 461-0155 Item 17
findings.contract_quote: [RMF General §4 / Auto §13]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Business Auto Coverage Broadening Endorsement, Item 17 — Knowledge of accident requires notice to executive officer/insurance manager.
findings.gap_description: Hanover Broadening Endorsement Item 17 limits 'knowledge of accident' to executive officer or insurance manager — exactly the broker target. Strong compliance.
findings.plain_english: On the Auto side, only an executive officer's or the insurance manager's knowledge of an accident triggers reporting obligations. Nice protection, already in place.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Severability of Interest — Standard ISO Compliance
findings.contract_quote: SEVERABILITY OF INTEREST: The CONTRACTOR's insurance shall apply separately to each insured against whom claim is made or suit is brought, except with respect to the limits of the insurer's liability.
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §IV.7 Separation of Insureds — standard.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO CG 00 01 includes Separation of Insureds at §IV.7 — satisfies Sacramento §VII.D without need for additional endorsement.
findings.plain_english: Built into the standard ISO form. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Care, Custody & Control Exclusion — Standard ISO; No CCC Coverage Bought Back
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §2 — Does your Insured have or could they have property of others in their care custody and/or control?]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 — standard CCC exclusions in §I.A.2.j (property loaned to insured, in insured's care, etc.). No CCC giveback or bailee endorsement on the policy.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test handles county property: ballots provided by counties, customer mail-list data, election equipment delivered to customer sites, ballot packages held in transit. The standard ISO CCC exclusion strips coverage for damage to property of others in the insured's care, custody, or control. Without an Inland Marine policy (see finding-006) OR a CCC giveback endorsement OR a bailee endorsement, damage to a customer's ballots, equipment, or data while in Run-Test's possession is uncovered.
findings.plain_english: When you have a customer's ballots, equipment, or data sitting in your warehouse or your truck, and something happens to it (water damage, fire, theft, drop), the GL doesn't pay because it's 'in your care' — that's an exclusion. You'd need either an Inland Marine policy (the right answer) or a special endorsement to cover this. Right now, neither exists.
findings.recommendation: Place a proper Inland Marine policy with Bailee's Customer's Property coverage (per finding-006) at limits matching the maximum value of customer property held at any one time and in transit. Confirm scope to include ballots, ballot stock, customer equipment, and data media.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest dollar value of customer property — ballots, equipment, or data — that Run-Test has in its possession at any given time?
If a fire destroyed every ballot you were holding for a county the night before an election, who eats that cost — you, the county, or insurance?
Have any of your customers ever held you contractually responsible for damage to their equipment in your facility, and how did your team handle it?

findings.requirement_type: Contractual Liability — Insured Contract Standard Coverage with Sole Negligence Limitation
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §6 — Insured contract definition, additional insured/P&NC/WoS triggered automatically by written contract.]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §V.9 — 'insured contract' definition (standard ISO). Modified by 00 GL1058 Contractual Liability Limitation — 'insured contract' excludes that part of any contract that indemnifies any person for liability arising out of their SOLE negligence.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO contractual liability via 'insured contract' is in place. The 00 GL1058 sole-negligence carve-out aligns with California Civil Code §2782(b) and Sacramento §VII.B's Civil Code carve-out — actually consistent with the contract framework. Maricopa indemnity (§8.1.1) is comparative/proportional and does not extend to County's sole negligence either, so the carve-out matches that contract too. Good alignment.
findings.plain_english: Your policy covers contracts where you assume someone else's tort liability — but only to the extent the other party isn't 100% responsible for their own negligence. That actually matches what California law and both county contracts already require. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain on operations-CGL once placed.

findings.requirement_type: Contractual Liability for Personal & Advertising Injury — Not Endorsed Back
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §7 — Contractual liability for personal and advertising injury — has it been endorsed back on to the policy?]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §I.B.2.e — Coverage B excludes P&AI 'for which the insured has assumed liability in a contract or agreement.' No CG 22 74 or carrier-equivalent contractual liability for P&AI giveback endorsed.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO CGL excludes contractual liability under Coverage B (Personal & Advertising Injury). RMF best practice is to endorse coverage back via CG 22 74 (or carrier-equivalent) where contractual P&AI exposure exists. Run-Test's printing/election-services business has potential P&AI exposure (advertising/copyright/trademark on printed materials), and they assume contractual liability under MSAs. Whether this is material requires review of typical contract language.
findings.plain_english: If a contract makes you responsible for someone's libel, slander, copyright, or trademark exposure (Personal & Advertising Injury territory), the standard GL doesn't cover that contractual assumption. There's a giveback endorsement available — it's not on the policy. Worth flagging for the next renewal.
findings.recommendation: Review standard MSA language and customer contracts. If contractual P&AI assumption is common (typical for printers and SaaS companies), bind CG 22 74 or carrier-equivalent on operations-CGL.

findings.requirement_type: Coverage Territory — US/Canada Standard, Election Services Domestic-Only
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §8]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §V.4 — standard 'coverage territory' (US, Canada, Puerto Rico, international waters/airspace, products outside US/Canada with suit brought in US).
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO coverage territory. Run-Test serves U.S. election infrastructure exclusively (per client notes — 31 states + D.C.) — no foreign operations or product-export exposure flagged. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: Standard U.S. + Canada coverage territory. Run-Test is U.S.-only. Fine.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. If Run-Test ever bids on international election support (e.g., USAID democracy programs), revisit coverage territory.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Coverage Within CGL — Triple-Layered Exclusions
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §9 — Cyber Coverage first/third party. If endorsed on the CGL, get coalition help.]
findings.policy_quote: (1) CG 40 35 12 23 — Cyber Incident Exclusion (Pg 68); (2) CG 21 06 12 23 — Access or Disclosure of Confidential or Personal Material or Information (Pg 64); (3) CG 00 69 12 23 — Violation of Law Addressing Data Privacy, naming BIPA/CCPA/GDPR (Pg 56); (4) CG 00 01 §I.A.2.p — Electronic Data exclusion; (5) CG 00 01 §I.A.2.q — Recording/Distribution of Material in Violation of Law (TCPA/CAN-SPAM/FCRA).
findings.gap_description: Five overlapping cyber/privacy exclusions on the GL. Combined, they strip ZERO coverage from anything cyber- or privacy-related. CG 00 69 specifically names BIPA, CCPA, and GDPR. Run-Test handles voter PII for over 90 million voters — every active election cycle creates massive privacy exposure. Combined with the missing standalone Cyber policy (finding-003), this is the single largest coverage gap in the program after the missing operations-CGL.
findings.plain_english: Your GL has five different exclusions stacked on top of each other to make sure no privacy or cyber claim ever attaches to it. Standalone Cyber is the only fix. See finding-003.
findings.recommendation: See finding-003 — bind $5M standalone Cyber. The GL exclusions are not negotiable on this carrier.
discoveryQuestions: Do your IT and operations teams understand that ZERO cyber, privacy, or data-related claims attach to your GL — and that without standalone Cyber, the company is fully exposed?
If a CCPA action is filed against Run-Test by California voters whose data leaked, where does the defense bill go — and have you stress-tested that with counsel?

findings.requirement_type: Damage to Premises Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §10 — calculate prospect's exposure vs sublimit.] Sacramento §III.A: Fire Damage $100,000 minimum.
findings.contract_file: RMF best practices; Sacramento Appendix G
findings.policy_quote: Damage to Premises Rented to You: $1,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Damage to Premises sublimit of $1M comfortably exceeds Sacramento's $100,000 Fire Damage minimum and broker RMF expectations. Strong.
findings.plain_english: If you damage a rented premises, you have $1M of coverage. Sacramento only required $100k. Comfortable margin.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Duty to Defend — Standard ISO
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §13]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §I.A.1.a — 'We will have the right and duty to defend the insured against any "suit" seeking those damages.'
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO duty-to-defend on CGL. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: Carrier has the duty to defend any suit. Standard, compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: EBL — Employee Benefits Liability Not Present
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §14 — Does the insured have EBL coverage?]
findings.policy_quote: [NO EBL ENDORSEMENT IDENTIFIED. CG 04 35 NOT ON FORM SCHEDULE.]
findings.gap_description: Run-Test has 50–200 employees and a 401(k) profit-sharing plan (listed on Auto). Employee Benefits Liability covers errors in the administration of employee benefits — failure to enroll, misclassification, mishandled COBRA, miscommunication of plan terms. EBL is not on the GL and there's no standalone Fiduciary Liability identified in the program. ERISA fiduciary breach claims would also be uncovered.
findings.plain_english: When your HR team makes an honest mistake — fails to enroll someone in benefits, mishandles a COBRA notice, miscommunicates a plan rule — that's an Employee Benefits Liability claim. With 50–200 employees and a 401(k), this is a real exposure. There's no EBL endorsement on the GL and no standalone Fiduciary policy. Worth fixing.
findings.recommendation: (1) Add EBL endorsement (CG 04 35 or carrier-equivalent) to operations-CGL — typically $1k–$3k premium for $1M limit. (2) Separately consider standalone Fiduciary Liability policy for the 401(k) plan trustees — ERISA exposure is not covered by EBL.
discoveryQuestions: Who administers your 401(k) and benefits enrollment — internal HR or a third-party benefits administrator?
If an employee was missed in open enrollment and missed three months of health coverage, who would they sue and where would the defense come from?
Have you ever had a Fiduciary Liability quote for the 401(k) plan, or has the company's exposure to ERISA claims gone untested?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Employment Practices Liability Not Present
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §15 — EPLI included? Wage & Hour defense?]
findings.policy_quote: GL: CG 21 47 12 07 Employment-Related Practices Exclusion (Pg 65) — excludes BI and P&AI for refusal to employ, termination, employment-related practices, harassment, discrimination. [NO STANDALONE EPLI POLICY PROVIDED.]
findings.gap_description: GL excludes employment-related practices. No standalone EPLI policy in the program. With 50–200 employees, PE-backed ownership, and CA exposure under Sacramento contract, EPLI is essential. CA has the highest plaintiff-friendly employment-claim environment in the country (PAGA, FEHA, wage-and-hour class actions). Run-Test has high exposure and zero coverage.
findings.plain_english: If an employee sues for harassment, wrongful termination, discrimination, or wage-and-hour violations, you have NO insurance to defend you. With 50–200 employees and California exposure (the most plaintiff-friendly employment market in the country), this is one of the highest-frequency claims out there for a company your size. Defense alone runs $250k+ per case.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone EPLI policy at $1M-$3M with Wage & Hour defense sublimit. Carriers: Travelers, Chubb, AIG. Verify (1) Third-party harassment coverage (covers harassment by non-employees), (2) Wage & Hour defense sublimit minimum $250k, (3) Definition of 'Employee' includes temps and contractors, (4) Prior/Pending exclusion date precedes any known employment dispute. PE-backed status and CA operations argue for $3M minimum.
discoveryQuestions: How many employees have departed Run-Test in the past 24 months, and how many of those were involuntary?
If an employee filed a sexual harassment complaint with the EEOC tomorrow, where would the legal defense bill go — and have you stress-tested that with HR counsel?
Do you do business in California with employees, or only ship product? Because California PAGA wage-and-hour class actions are the #1 EPLI claim driver and Run-Test has zero coverage right now.
Has the PE sponsor ever asked about EPLI as part of portfolio insurance hygiene — and what did the answer look like?

findings.requirement_type: Faulty Work — Subcontractor Giveback Standard ISO
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §19 — Does the policy provide the giveback for subcontractors work?]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §I.A.2.l — Damage to your work in completed operations excluded UNLESS performed by a subcontractor.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO subcontracted-work giveback is in place. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: If a subcontractor's work caused damage, the policy responds. Built into standard ISO. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain on operations-CGL.

findings.requirement_type: Fellow Employee Exclusion — CGL Not Deleted
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §20 — Is the Fellow Employee Exclusion deleted?]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §I.A.2 (employment-related and 'employee' exclusions standard). [NO FELLOW EMPLOYEE COVERAGE GIVEBACK IDENTIFIED.]
findings.gap_description: Standard CGL excludes BI to fellow employees in the course of employment (covered by WC). Whether to delete the Fellow Employee Exclusion is a judgment call — preserves coverage for supervisor liability where one employee injures another. Most appropriate for management-heavy or high-supervision operations. Worth discussing for an election services manufacturer with 50–200 employees and supervisory chains.
findings.plain_english: If one of your employees hurts another employee through a wrongful or negligent act outside what WC covers (think: bullying, supervisor misconduct), the standard GL excludes that. There's an option to delete that exclusion. Whether to do so depends on your risk appetite and what your WC handles. Worth a conversation.
findings.recommendation: Discuss with client whether to add Fellow Employee Coverage on the operations-CGL. Often free or nominal cost from standard market.

findings.requirement_type: Fellow Employee Exclusion — Auto Amended via 461-0155 Item 6
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §9]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 6 — 'Amended Fellow Employee Exclusion (excess basis for owned/hired).'
findings.gap_description: Hanover Broadening Item 6 amends the Fellow Employee Exclusion to provide excess coverage for owned and hired autos, preserving Auto BI coverage for fellow-employee claims that exceed WC.
findings.plain_english: On the Auto side, the Fellow Employee Exclusion has been broadened so the policy provides excess Auto BI coverage if one employee is hurt by another in a covered auto. Built in.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Hired & Non-Owned Auto on CGL — Not Present (Auto Has It)
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §21 — HNOA on CGL when no Auto policy.]
findings.policy_quote: Auto Form 461-0168 (9-00) Item Four/Five — Hired auto liability rated on cost-of-hire basis (AZ, class 6611, 'if any' cost of hire); Employer's non-ownership liability rated on 55 employees (AZ class 6602).
findings.gap_description: HNOA is on the standalone Auto policy — Items 4 (Hired) and 5 (Non-Owned, 55 employees). No need for HNOA endorsement on CGL. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: Hired and Non-Owned Auto coverage is in place on your Auto policy. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Verify employee count is updated annually — currently rated for 55, but client profile indicates 50–200 employees, so audit at next renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Mental Anguish in BI Definition — CGL Not Endorsed
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §23 — Mental Anguish: included in BI definition? Want it standalone, not connected to BI.]
findings.policy_quote: CG 00 01 04 13 §V.3 — '"Bodily injury" means bodily injury, sickness or disease sustained by a person ...' — does NOT include mental anguish, mental injury, shock, or emotional distress as standalone triggers.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO BI definition is narrow — it does not include 'mental anguish, mental injury, shock, fright, humiliation, or emotional distress' as standalone triggers. RMF best practice for security operations and consumer-facing businesses is to endorse mental anguish into the BI definition (often via CG 00 01 amendatory or carrier-specific endorsement). For Run-Test's security guard operations specifically, this matters — security guard altercations often produce mental-anguish-only claims.
findings.plain_english: The standard policy says 'bodily injury' means physical injury or sickness — not just mental distress. So if someone sues claiming mental anguish without a physical injury (think: a customer or visitor traumatized by a security incident), the GL may not respond. There's an endorsement option to broaden the BI definition. Worth adding.
findings.recommendation: Bind Mental Anguish/Emotional Distress amendment to BI definition on operations-CGL — typically nominal premium.
discoveryQuestions: If a guard restrained someone at a customer site and that person sued for emotional distress without physical injury, would your team think the GL covers it?
Has any prior claim against Run-Test alleged mental anguish or emotional distress as the only damage element?

findings.requirement_type: Mental Anguish in BI Definition — Auto via 461-0155 Item 21
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §2]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 21 — 'Mental anguish included in BI.'
findings.gap_description: Hanover Broadening Item 21 expressly includes mental anguish in the BI definition. Strong compliance.
findings.plain_english: On Auto, mental anguish is built into the BI definition. Covered.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Per Project / Per Location Aggregate — CGL Not Endorsed
findings.contract_quote: Per-Project Aggregate: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503 ... (Sacramento §III.A); [CGL RMF §26].
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Appendix G; RMF best practices
findings.policy_quote: [NO CG 25 03 OR CG 25 04 OR CARRIER-EQUIVALENT PER-PROJECT/PER-LOCATION AGGREGATE ENDORSEMENT IDENTIFIED.]
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §III.A only triggers per-project aggregate IF the contractor is engaged in 'projects of construction.' Run-Test is an election services manufacturer — typically not implicated. However, RMF best practice is to bind per-project / per-location aggregate where the insured services multiple counties simultaneously, because a single bad election cycle could exhaust an aggregate across all clients. With Run-Test serving 31 states + D.C. and high-frequency election cycles, per-location/per-customer aggregate language is a meaningful protection.
findings.plain_english: Right now your $3M general aggregate is shared across every customer and every project. If Maricopa has a bad year and burns through $2M of your aggregate, Sacramento and your other 30+ states get whatever's left. A per-project or per-location aggregate endorsement gives each customer their own $3M tower. For a company serving 31 states, this is a meaningful upgrade. Sacramento technically only requires it for construction work (likely not Run-Test) but it's still smart to have.
findings.recommendation: Bind CG 25 03 (Per-Project Aggregate) or CG 25 04 (Per-Location Aggregate) on operations-CGL. For an election services company serving many counties, this is a sensible upgrade. Modest premium.
discoveryQuestions: How many county and state contracts is Run-Test running concurrently in any given election cycle?

If one bad ballot misprint in Maricopa exhausted $2M of your $3M aggregate, would you have enough capacity left for Sacramento, Pinal, San Luis Obispo, and the other 30 states for the rest of the year?
Has Patriot ever priced out a per-project or per-location aggregate endorsement for this program?

findings.requirement_type: Product Recall — Not Present
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §28]
findings.policy_quote: [NO PRODUCT RECALL ENDORSEMENT OR STANDALONE POLICY PROVIDED.]
findings.gap_description: Run-Test prints and ships ballots. If a printing error requires recall and reprint of millions of ballots — a real exposure in election services — the cost (printing, shipping, mail, county compensation, expedited turnaround) is uncovered without product recall coverage. Standard GL excludes 'Recall of Your Products' (CG 00 01 §I.A.2.n).
findings.plain_english: If you have to recall and reprint millions of ballots because of an error, that's potentially a multi-million-dollar event. The GL specifically excludes recall costs. There's a Product Recall endorsement (or standalone Recall policy) that covers it — not on the program.
findings.recommendation: Scope a Product Recall endorsement or standalone Product Recall policy. Sublimits typically $250k–$1M on endorsement; standalone can be higher. For election services manufacturer, $1M+ standalone is appropriate given catastrophic visibility of a ballot error.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest recall or reprint event Run-Test has ever absorbed — and what did it cost the P&L?
If Maricopa County ordered a full ballot reprint 14 days before an election due to a printing defect, do you know what your reprint and expedite cost would be?

findings.requirement_type: Stop Gap — N/A (No Monopolistic State Operations)
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §30]
findings.policy_quote: Per client profile: AZ-only operations; no monopolistic-state (OH, ND, WA, WY) employees identified.
findings.gap_description: Stop Gap Employers' Liability is needed when employees work in monopolistic-fund states (OH, ND, WA, WY). Client profile indicates AZ-only with operations potentially in CA — none of these are monopolistic-fund states. N/A.
findings.plain_english: Stop Gap is for states that don't allow private workers' comp carriers. Doesn't apply to your geography. Skipped.
findings.recommendation: Reassess if Run-Test ever expands employee operations into Ohio, North Dakota, Washington, or Wyoming.

findings.requirement_type: Total Pollution Exclusion — CGL with Limited Carve-Outs
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §31]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1047 00 01 25 — Total Pollution Exclusion with Hostile Fire and Self-Defense Spray Exception. 'Replaces ISO Exclusion f. Pollution. Exception only for hostile fire heat/smoke/fumes and use of mace/pepper spray normal to security operations.'
findings.gap_description: Total Pollution Exclusion is endorsed on the GL with only two narrow exceptions (hostile fire byproducts and mace/pepper spray for security ops). Run-Test operates a printing facility — printing inks, solvents, and toner are pollutants under this exclusion. Any pollution claim arising from facility operations (chemical spill, ink release, HVAC issue, fume exposure) is excluded. No CPL (Contractors Pollution Liability) or PLL (Premises Pollution Liability) policy in the program.
findings.plain_english: Standard CGL pollution exclusions. Even ink and toner can count as 'pollutants' under broad pollution exclusions. If a chemical spill or fume incident happens at the Phoenix facility, it's excluded. There's no Pollution Liability policy in the program. For a printing manufacturer, this is a real but moderate exposure.
findings.recommendation: Scope a Premises Pollution Liability (PLL) policy at $1M-$2M for the Phoenix facility, OR add a 'limited pollution buyback' endorsement on the operations-CGL. Standard market PLL premium is usually $2k–$8k.
discoveryQuestions: What inks, toners, solvents, and chemicals does the Phoenix printing facility use, and what's your largest single-day chemical inventory?
Has the building ever had a HVAC, fume, or chemical incident that required cleanup or third-party complaints?
Does the printing facility have an underground storage tank or any environmental compliance reporting obligations?

findings.requirement_type: TRIA / Terrorism — CGL Excluded; Auto NBC-Only Excluded
findings.contract_quote: [CGL RMF §32]
findings.policy_quote: GL: CG 21 73 01 15 Exclusion of Certified Acts of Terrorism (Pg 66). Auto: CA 23 85 01 06 Exclusion of NBC Terrorism only (does not exclude conventional terrorism) (Pg 59).
findings.gap_description: GL has a full Certified Acts of Terrorism Exclusion — TRIA-buyback was rejected or never offered. Auto has NBC-only exclusion (conventional terrorism remains covered on Auto). Run-Test is a high-profile target: election services for over 90 million voters, government contracts with 31 states + D.C., explicitly named in election-integrity controversy. Election infrastructure has been formally designated as 'critical infrastructure' by DHS since 2017. Conventional terrorism (bombing, active shooter, vehicle ramming at facility) is a real and growing exposure. The GL exclusion of certified terrorism is a meaningful gap — and there's no standalone TRIA policy or Active Assailant policy in the program.
findings.plain_english: Election services companies are now classified as 'critical infrastructure' by Homeland Security. The threat environment around elections has changed dramatically since 2020. Your GL specifically excludes certified terrorism. Your Auto policy excludes nuclear/biological/chemical terrorism but covers conventional terrorism. There is no standalone Active Assailant or TRIA-buyback policy. If a bombing, ramming, or active-shooter event happens at the Phoenix facility or a customer site, the GL doesn't respond. This is a real and growing risk for the industry.
findings.recommendation: (1) Buy back TRIA on the GL at next renewal — typically modest premium for the GL. (2) Strongly recommend a standalone Active Assailant / Workplace Violence policy ($1M-$5M) — covers conventional terrorism, active shooter, ramming, threat events, including business interruption and victim counseling. Carriers: Beazley, McGowan, Hiscox. (3) Confirm Auto conventional-terrorism coverage is preserved (currently appears to be).
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test ever been the subject of threats or social-media-driven targeting around election cycles, and what's your security posture for those events?
Does your Phoenix facility have Active Assailant training, response protocols, and physical security commensurate with a critical-infrastructure designation?
If a vehicle-ramming attack happened at your loading dock during a peak election week, do you understand that the GL would deny the claim under the certified-terrorism exclusion?
Have you priced standalone Active Assailant / Workplace Violence coverage — usually $5k–$15k for $1M-$2M of limit, but most companies don't even know it exists?

findings.requirement_type: Canine Liability Exclusion — Verify K-9 Use
findings.contract_quote: [CGL endorsement review.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1048 00 01 25 — Canine Liability Exclusion: 'Absolute exclusion for any BI/PD arising out of ownership, rental, maintenance or use of any dog or canine.'
findings.gap_description: Absolute K-9/canine exclusion on the security-guard CGL. Could matter only if Run-Test's security operation uses K-9 units. No information in client notes indicating K-9 use, but worth confirming.
findings.plain_english: If your security operation uses K-9 units (dogs), there's no coverage. Need to confirm whether you do.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with client whether security operations use K-9 units. If yes, push carrier for K-9 buyback or move security ops to a carrier without the absolute exclusion.

findings.requirement_type: Assault & Battery Coverage — Endorsed Back
findings.contract_quote: [CGL endorsement review for security operations.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1063 00 01 25 — Assault and Battery Coverage Endorsement: 'Modifies Expected/Intended exclusion to NOT exclude (1) BI from use of physical force to protect persons or property; or (2) claims arising out of assault/battery by an employee.'
findings.gap_description: Critical for security guard operations. Standard GL would exclude assault/battery as 'expected or intended.' Form 00 GL1063 endorses coverage back. Strong compliance for the security ops.
findings.plain_english: Your security guard policy specifically gives back coverage for assault and battery — both reasonable force to protect people/property and even employee misconduct. This is the right endorsement for a guard operation.
findings.recommendation: Maintain on security ops CGL.

findings.requirement_type: PFAS / Lead / Asbestos / Silica Exclusions
findings.contract_quote: [Endorsement review.]
findings.policy_quote: 00 MLL0008 PFAS Exclusion (Pg 3); 00 GL1061 Lead (Pg 35); 00 GL1062 Absolute Asbestos (Pg 36); CG 21 96 Silica (Pg 67).
findings.gap_description: Multiple absolute exclusions are standard in current market for these emerging-claim categories. Election services manufacturing is unlikely to have material PFAS, lead, asbestos, or silica exposure — minimal practical impact. Building ownership/leasing in older facilities could trigger asbestos issues.
findings.plain_english: Standard exclusions for emerging chemical/dust claims (PFAS, lead, asbestos, silica). Not unusual for current GL policies. Likely not material to a printing/election operation, but verify the Phoenix facility doesn't have asbestos.
findings.recommendation: Verify Phoenix facility (2800 S 36th St) does not have known asbestos-containing materials. If older building, consider Building Pollution survey.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Cyber §8.2.13 Specific Sub-Components — Cannot Verify Without Cyber Policy
findings.contract_quote: The policy shall include, but not be limited to; ... regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction.
findings.policy_quote: [NO CYBER POLICY PROVIDED]
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.13 is one of the most specifically-itemized cyber clauses in the audit. Sub-components include: regulatory FINES AND PENALTIES (not just defense — many forms exclude or sublimit fines), third-party fidelity (typically a Crime/Social Engineering coverage feature), computer fraud, funds transfer loss, no arrest/conviction requirement. Even when the $5M Cyber is bound (per finding-003), each of these sub-features must be verified line-by-line — many Cyber forms sublimit social engineering / funds transfer fraud at $250k or $1M, well below the $5M concurrent expectation Maricopa appears to demand.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wrote the most detailed Cyber clause we've ever seen. Even after you bind the Cyber policy, each sub-feature has to be checked — especially regulatory fines (often excluded), funds-transfer fraud (often sublimited), and social engineering (often a tiny sublimit). At binding, push for $5M concurrent across crime-style features.
findings.recommendation: When binding standalone Cyber, require itemized confirmation that each Maricopa-listed feature is in force at adequate sublimit: regulatory fines/penalties (where insurable), third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, social engineering, business interruption, dependent BI, cyber extortion, breach response, data restoration. Document carrier confirmation in writing.

findings.requirement_type: Carrier Rating — Sacramento A.M. Best A-VII
findings.contract_quote: ACCEPTABILITY OF INSURERS: Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII.
findings.policy_quote: GL: Arch Insurance Company (rated A+ XV per A.M. Best most recent affirmation). Auto: Allmerica Financial Benefit Insurance Company / The Hanover Insurance Group (rated A XV).
findings.policy_page: Carrier names on GL Pg 7 and Auto Pg 26
findings.gap_description: Both Arch and Hanover comfortably exceed Sacramento §VI.A.1's A-VII minimum and Maricopa §8.2.1's B++ minimum. Compliant on existing policies — same diligence required when binding new operations-CGL, Cyber, WC, E&O, Umbrella per recommendations above.
findings.plain_english: Both your current carriers are highly rated — well above either county's minimum. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Confirm A.M. Best A-VII or better on every new policy added per recommendations (operations-CGL, WC, Cyber, E&O, Umbrella, Pollution, EPLI). Sacramento's A-VII is the binding constraint — Maricopa's B++ is more lenient.

findings.requirement_type: California WC Compliance — AZ-Based Insured Performing CA Work
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance.
findings.policy_quote: [NO WC POLICY PROVIDED — CANNOT VERIFY ITEM 3.A STATES OR ALL-STATES 3.C COVERAGE]
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is AZ-based. If any employees physically perform work in California (delivery, on-site support, election event support), CA-statutory WC must apply. Either CA must be on Item 3.A of an existing WC policy, or a separate CA WC policy must be in force, or all CA work must be subcontracted. California is not an Other-States 3.C state — it generally requires admitted CA WC. This cannot be verified without seeing the WC policy (see finding-002).
findings.plain_english: Sacramento requires California-statutory Workers' Comp. AZ Workers' Comp doesn't satisfy California — California is one of those states where you can't rely on 'all states' coverage. If any of your employees ever work in California, you need actual California WC. Without seeing the WC policy, we can't confirm this.
findings.recommendation: Confirm WC policy includes California in Item 3.A. If not, do not allow any employees to perform any work in California until either (a) California is added to Item 3.A, (b) a standalone CA WC policy is bound, or (c) all CA work is performed by subcontractors with their own CA WC.

findings.requirement_type: Civil Code §2782(b) Carve-Out — Compliant by Standard ISO + 00 GL1058
findings.contract_quote: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1058 — 'Insured contract definition excludes that part of any contract that indemnifies any person/organization for liability arising out of their SOLE negligence.'
findings.gap_description: Sacramento's Civil Code §2782 carve-out is a contract-level acknowledgment, not requiring a special endorsement. The 00 GL1058 sole-negligence carve-out aligns with this requirement. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: California law says you can't agree to insure someone else's own active negligence on construction contracts. Your policy structure already aligns with that. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Pass-Through (Sacramento §VII.E)
findings.contract_quote: SUBCONTRACTORS: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: Independent Contractor Requirements Endorsement (00 GL1053): 'Insured must obtain COIs from independent contractors with limits ≥ insured's CGL limits. Failure does not eliminate coverage but converts contractor's costs to premium basis at contractor classifications.'
findings.gap_description: Form 00 GL1053 imposes a contractor-COI-collection regime on the insured. Sacramento §VII.E and Maricopa indemnity flow-down imply Run-Test must require subs to provide AI endorsements. Need to confirm Run-Test has a contract-management process for sub COIs and that flow-down language is in subcontracts.
findings.plain_english: Both contracts make Run-Test responsible for its subcontractors. Your policy has an endorsement requiring you to get COIs from your subs. Whether you actually do this in practice — and whether your sub agreements pass through the same insurance requirements — is an operational question that needs verification.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Run-Test's subcontract template includes flow-down insurance and indemnity requirements matching the upstream county requirements. Confirm operational discipline around collecting and retaining sub COIs.

findings.requirement_type: Deductibles / SIR Disclosure
findings.contract_quote: Any deductibles or self-insured retention that apply to any insurance required by this Agreement must be declared and approved by the COUNTY. (Sacramento §IV); ... contains deductibles or self-insured retentions. Such deductible and/or self-insured retentions shall not be applicable with respect to the coverage provided to County. (Maricopa §8.2.6)
findings.contract_file: Sacramento County Appendix G; Maricopa County contract
findings.policy_quote: GL: $1,000 BI/PD deductible per claim (CG 03 00, Pg 57). Auto: $1,000 Comp & Collision deductibles (Pg 26).
findings.gap_description: Deductibles are modest ($1k each) — easy to disclose to both counties. Sacramento's required pre-performance approval (and Maricopa's potential bond/LOC backing) are administrative steps. Compliant if disclosed on COI / contract documents.
findings.plain_english: Deductibles are small ($1k) and easy to disclose to either County. Just make sure the COI and any contract appendices reflect them.
findings.recommendation: Confirm deductibles are disclosed on COIs and any Required Endorsement Schedule submitted to either County. When Cyber, E&O, and Umbrella are bound, those will likely have larger SIRs/retentions ($25k–$250k typical) — those MUST be disclosed and approved per Sacramento §IV before performance.

findings.requirement_type: COI / Endorsement Copies — Operational Compliance
findings.contract_quote: Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. (Sacramento §I) ... Prior to contract award, Contractor shall furnish the County with valid and complete Certificates of Insurance, or formal endorsements as required by the contract in the form provided by the County, issued by Contractor's insurer(s). (Maricopa §8.2.14.1)
findings.policy_quote: [Operational — depends on broker process.]
findings.gap_description: Sacramento explicitly requires actual endorsement COPIES attached to COIs (not just references). Maricopa requires formal endorsements 'in the form provided by the County.' Operational compliance question — does the broker attach actual endorsement copies to the certificates issued to each County? Maricopa specifies certificate holder address: '301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003.'
findings.plain_english: Both counties want actual endorsement copies attached to the COI — not just a checkbox saying 'AI included.' Your broker process needs to deliver the actual CG 20 10 / CG 20 37 / WoS / P&NC endorsement copies to each county's risk management office every renewal.
findings.recommendation: Confirm Patriot's COI process attaches: (a) CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 (AI ongoing + completed ops), (b) CG 20 01 (P&NC), (c) Auto 461-0478 (blanket AI/P&NC), (d) Auto 461-0500 (WoS), (e) WC waiver of subrogation endorsement once WC is reviewed, (f) GL CG 24 04 (WoS) once added. Maricopa certificate holder: 'Maricopa County, c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003.'

findings.requirement_type: Notification of Claim / Lawsuit (Sacramento §X)
findings.contract_quote: Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.
findings.policy_quote: [Operational obligation on Contractor — independent of carrier notice obligations.]
findings.gap_description: Contractual obligation to notify Sacramento County of claims (30 days) and lawsuits (10 days). Independent of carrier notice obligations. Operational compliance only — confirm Run-Test's claims-handling protocol includes county notification timing.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento wants 30-day notice on any claim and 10-day notice on any lawsuit that could affect the County. Your in-house process needs to know about and meet those deadlines, separate from carrier reporting.
findings.recommendation: Document a claims notification protocol that triggers Sacramento County notification within the contractual deadlines, in addition to standard carrier notification.

findings.requirement_type: Right to Adjust Coverage (Sacramento §II.B)
findings.contract_quote: COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection for COUNTY ... COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount.
findings.policy_quote: [N/A — this is a contractual right reserved by the County, not a policy item.]
findings.gap_description: Sacramento reserves the right to demand additional coverage mid-term. Open-ended risk on lines and limits. Should be flagged at contract intake and in renewal planning so any County demand can be met without disrupting operations.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento can ask you for more coverage or higher limits anytime they want, mid-contract. Build that into your renewal planning so you have headroom.
findings.recommendation: Build 20–30% headroom into renewal limit selections to absorb potential mid-term increases without re-marketing. Document the §II.B clause in the contract intake file so Run-Test's CFO is aware of the open-ended risk.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Symbols 1/2 vs 7 Analysis
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §16 — Symbols 1 and 2 versus 7. Are mobile equipment items subject to motor vehicle law that need scheduling?]
findings.policy_quote: Auto policy schedules two specific vehicles (Auto 010 — 2013 Mercedes Sprinter; Auto 011 — 2018 Chevrolet Express). Symbol-driven coverage selection (1=Any Auto, 2=Owned Autos, 7=Specifically Described Autos) not visible in the chunked extract.
findings.gap_description: Only two specifically-described autos (Symbols likely 7 + 8 + 9). Symbol 1 (Any Auto) is broader and would automatically cover newly-acquired autos and any borrowed/temporary use. With only Symbols 7/8/9, coverage gaps may exist for newly-acquired autos beyond the initial 30 days, and for any auto used by employees in business that isn't 'hired or non-owned.' Best practice for active fleets is Symbol 1.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy specifically lists each vehicle. That's fine for known autos but creates gaps if you acquire a new van and it isn't reported in time, or if employees occasionally use other vehicles for business. Symbol 1 ('Any Auto') is broader and removes the schedule-management burden. Worth discussing at next renewal.
findings.recommendation: At next renewal, request quote for Symbol 1 (Any Auto) on Liability — usually modest premium difference for a 2-vehicle fleet. Confirms automatic coverage on newly-acquired and incidentally-used autos.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Lease Gap Coverage
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §4]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 15 — Auto Loan/Lease Gap.
findings.gap_description: Lease Gap coverage is built into the Hanover Broadening Endorsement Item 15. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: If a leased vehicle is totaled and the insurance payout doesn't cover the lease balance, this endorsement bridges the gap. Built in.
findings.recommendation: Maintain.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Drive Other Car (DOC)
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §5 — DOC, executive officers covered.]
findings.policy_quote: Run-Test Inc + LLC affiliates are entity Named Insureds, not individual executive officers. DOC endorsement is most relevant when an executive officer is named as an individual NI. With the entity-NI structure, DOC is generally N/A.
findings.gap_description: DOC trigger is exec officers as individual NIs. Not present here. N/A unless personal-vehicle exposure for executives.
findings.plain_english: Drive Other Car only matters if executives are named as individuals on the policy. Your structure is entity-only. N/A.
findings.recommendation: Confirm executives have personal auto policies of their own. If any executive lacks personal auto and uses company vehicles + occasionally non-company autos, consider adding DOC.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — No-Fault State Operations
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §11]
findings.policy_quote: Run-Test serves 31 states + D.C. — including potential no-fault states (NY, FL, MI, NJ, PA, KS, KY, ND, MN, MA, HI, UT). Vehicle schedule shows AZ-garaged. Drive-into-state exposure exists for some no-fault states.
findings.gap_description: Vehicles are AZ-garaged. Whether covered autos are driven into no-fault states for election support is unclear. AZ Auto policy does not typically include no-fault PIP for driving into no-fault states by default. Practical impact is generally low — most no-fault states require non-resident PIP only when garaged in-state.
findings.plain_english: If you ever drive your vans to a no-fault state to support an election, the no-fault rules of that state may apply. Generally not a problem for occasional drive-throughs. N/A for routine ops.
findings.recommendation: If Run-Test routinely drives vehicles into no-fault states (NY, FL, MI), discuss carrier's posture on PIP. For occasional travel, no action needed.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Mobile Equipment vs Auto Definition
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §12]
findings.policy_quote: Only two scheduled autos. No mobile equipment scheduled. Mobile equipment subject to motor vehicle law (forklifts, equipment over 1,000 lbs operated on public streets) would need to be scheduled or on a separate Inland Marine.
findings.gap_description: Election services manufacturing typically uses forklifts and material handling equipment. Whether any of that is subject to motor vehicle law (and thus needs to be on Auto vs CGL/IM) requires verification.
findings.plain_english: Forklifts and similar gear are usually 'mobile equipment' (covered by GL or IM, not Auto) — but if they're driven on public streets or registered, they become 'autos' that need to be on the Auto policy. Worth confirming what equipment Run-Test owns and how it's classified.
findings.recommendation: Inventory all powered equipment at the Phoenix facility. Confirm classification (mobile equipment under GL §V.12 vs auto). Schedule any equipment subject to motor vehicle law on the Auto policy.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Employee as Insured / Employee Hired Autos
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §6 — CA 9933 Employee as Insured + CA 2054 Employee Hired Autos.]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 4 — 'Employees as Insureds when using non-owned/non-hired autos in business.' Item 2 — 'Employee Hired Autos under Symbol 8.' [Hanover-proprietary equivalents to CA 99 33 and CA 20 54.]
findings.gap_description: Hanover Broadening Items 2 and 4 provide proprietary equivalents to CA 20 54 and CA 99 33 — Employee Hired Autos and Employees as Insureds. Coverage is in place but verify the actual scope of Hanover's Items 2 and 4 against the ISO equivalents — Hanover broadening forms can be narrower than the ISO endorsements.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy gives employees insured status when using their own cars on company business, and treats employee-rented cars as hired autos. Built in via the Hanover Broadening Endorsement. Verify the Hanover language is as broad as the ISO version.
findings.recommendation: Pull full text of 461-0155 Items 2 and 4 and compare to CA 99 33 and CA 20 54. If narrower, request true ISO endorsements at next renewal.
discoveryQuestions: How often do employees use their own personal vehicles for Run-Test business — particularly during election cycles or for customer-site visits?
Do employees ever rent vehicles in their own name for Run-Test work, and have they been told their personal credit card insurance might not be primary?

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Limited Pollution / CA 99 48
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §8 — Environmental: limited pollution endorsement at minimum.]
findings.policy_quote: Standard CA 00 01 pollution exclusion (Pg 33) — carve-back for fuels/lubricants/exhaust gases needed for normal functioning, and accidents away from premises caused by upset/overturn. [NO CA 99 48 BROADENED POLLUTION ENDORSEMENT IDENTIFIED.]
findings.gap_description: Auto policy has only the standard ISO pollution carve-back (auto fluids in normal operation, upset/overturn). CA 99 48 (Pollution Liability — Broadened Coverage for Covered Autos) extends coverage to broader pollution scenarios including loading/unloading. For an election services manufacturer transporting ballots, ink supplies, or cleaning chemicals, a broader pollution endorsement would address loading/unloading exposures.
findings.plain_english: If a chemical or ink shipment leaks during loading or unloading from one of your vans, the standard Auto pollution carve-back may not respond. There's a broader Auto pollution endorsement (CA 99 48) that covers more scenarios. Worth adding.
findings.recommendation: Add CA 99 48 Pollution Liability — Broadened Coverage for Covered Autos at next renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Excluded Driver (Malina Trujillo)
findings.contract_quote: [Operational risk — driver exclusion.]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0425 (9/10) Arizona Exclusion of Named Driver: 'Excludes coverage for any "accident" or "loss" resulting from operation/use of any covered auto by Malina Trujillo (with exception of UM/UIM).'
findings.gap_description: A specific driver is excluded from coverage on covered autos (UM/UIM excepted). If Malina Trujillo ever drives a company vehicle, any resulting accident is uninsured. This is an operational-control issue — HR and fleet management must enforce the exclusion.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy specifically excludes Malina Trujillo from driving any company vehicle. If she ever gets behind the wheel of one of your vans for any reason, an accident becomes a personal exposure to her and a corporate exposure to you, with zero insurance. Your fleet/HR policy needs to keep this enforced.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with HR/fleet manager that Malina Trujillo's name is on a no-drive list. If she is no longer with the company or if her driving record has improved (likely the reason for the exclusion is a poor MVR), discuss with Hanover whether the exclusion can be removed.
discoveryQuestions: Who is Malina Trujillo, is she still employed at Run-Test, and does the fleet team enforce a no-drive policy for her?
Why was she excluded — driving record, prior at-fault accident, license issue — and has the underlying issue been resolved?
Are there other employees Run-Test should consider excluding to keep the program premium reasonable, or do we have other employees with bad MVRs who should be excluded for the same reason?

findings.requirement_type: Auto — UM/UIM Selection Confirmation
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §18]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0368 07 20 — Arizona UM/UIM Coverage Offer and Selection/Rejection: 'Selection initials/signature appear blank/redacted in available chunks — confirm actual elections.' UM and UIM each $1,000,000 per Item Three.
findings.gap_description: Although UM/UIM are at $1M each per the schedule, the AZ-mandated UM/UIM Selection/Rejection form was redacted/blank in the audit packet. Confirm that the form was properly executed at policy inception. AZ requires UM/UIM offer be presented and either accepted or rejected in writing.
findings.plain_english: Your UM/UIM limits look right ($1M each). But the Arizona-required form where you elect or reject UM/UIM was blank or redacted in the file. Need to confirm it was signed at policy issue. If not, the policy may be deemed to have whatever UM/UIM the carrier defaults to.
findings.recommendation: Request the executed Form 461-0368 from the carrier. Retain in the renewal file annually.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Temporary & Leased Workers Definition
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §17 — Definition of 'employee' modified to exclude leased workers?]
findings.policy_quote: [NO TEMP/LEASED WORKER MODIFICATION TO 'EMPLOYEE' DEFINITION IDENTIFIED IN AUTO ENDORSEMENTS.]
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO Auto 'employee' definition does NOT specifically include leased workers (per CA 00 01). If Run-Test uses leased/temp workers during election peaks, ISO BAP definition is consistent — leased workers are not 'employees' for coverage triggers and exclusions. Confirm whether Run-Test uses temporary or staffed labor and whether their coverage flows correctly.
findings.plain_english: If you use temp or leased workers (likely during election peaks), the Auto policy's exclusions and coverage rules treat them differently than full-time employees. Need to confirm whether you use staffing agencies and what their auto-use looks like.
findings.recommendation: Document whether Run-Test uses temp/leased labor. If yes, confirm staffing agency provides Alternate Employer endorsement on their WC, and that any auto use by leased workers is contemplated by Run-Test's Auto coverage — typically Hanover Broadening Item 4 (Employees as Insureds when using non-owned/non-hired autos) will respond, but verify.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Parked Vehicles Aggregate Deductible
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §15]
findings.policy_quote: Only two covered autos. No fleet-parking aggregate exposure.
findings.gap_description: Aggregate deductible on parked vehicles relevant when many autos are stored in close proximity (catastrophic windstorm/hail/fire could exceed per-vehicle deductibles). With only 2 vehicles, aggregate deductible structure is not relevant. N/A.
findings.plain_english: Aggregate deductible only matters with bigger fleets parked together. You have two vehicles. N/A.
findings.recommendation: Reassess if fleet grows beyond ~10 vehicles parked at one location.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Bodily Injury Mental Anguish (Auto-Specific)
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §2]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 21 — Mental anguish included in BI definition.
findings.gap_description: Confirmed. (Same as finding-040, emitted separately per always-emit instruction.)
findings.plain_english: Auto policy expressly includes mental anguish in BI definition. Compliant.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Broad Named Insured + All Affiliates Listed
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §3]

LLC. 461-0155 Item 3 — Broadened Named Insured for newly acquired/formed entities.
findings.gap_description: Auto policy has comprehensive Named Insured schedule + Broadened Named Insured for newly-acquired/formed entities (Hanover Broadening Item 3). Strong on the Auto side. Significant CONTRAST with the GL (only one NI). See finding-022 for the asymmetry issue.
findings.plain_english: Auto NI schedule is very thorough — all your entities are listed including the 401(k) plan, plus new entities are picked up automatically. The GL doesn't match this scope, which is the asymmetry flagged separately.
findings.recommendation: Maintain Auto NI structure; mirror it on the operations-CGL when bound (finding-022).

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Ownership of Vehicles Confirmation
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §14]
findings.policy_quote: Form 461-0167 schedules two corporately-owned vehicles (2013 Mercedes Sprinter + 2018 Chevrolet Express). No personally-owned or leased vehicles identified.
findings.gap_description: Both scheduled autos appear corporately owned. CA 99 16 (Auto Lease/Loan Coverage) and CA 99 47 (Employee as Lessor) are not applicable absent personally-owned/leased vehicles. Compliant.
findings.plain_english: Both vans are owned by the company. No leased or employee-owned vehicles to worry about. Compliant.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. If new vehicles are leased or any employee starts using a personally-owned vehicle as a primary work vehicle, revisit.

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Hired Auto Physical Damage
findings.contract_quote: [CA RMF §10 — HNOA + physical damage on hired autos.]
findings.policy_quote: 461-0155 Item 11 — Hired Auto Physical Damage up to $50,000 per accident plus $1,000/day lessor loss of use up to 7 days.
findings.gap_description: Built into Broadening Endorsement. $50k limit is moderate — likely sufficient for typical car-rental use, but verify if any larger-vehicle rentals occur (cargo trucks, sprinter vans for election logistics).
findings.plain_english: If an employee rents a vehicle for company business and damages it, the policy responds up to $50k of damage. Standard limit, built in. If you ever rent more expensive vehicles, this limit may need to go up.
findings.recommendation: Confirm $50k Hired Auto Physical Damage limit is adequate for actual rental practices. If renting cargo trucks or sprinters for election cycles, consider increasing to $100k.

findings.requirement_type: Crime / Fidelity / Social Engineering — No Standalone Policy
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.13 implies third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer loss within Cyber, but standalone Crime is broker best practice.]
findings.policy_quote: [NO STANDALONE CRIME / FIDELITY / SOCIAL ENGINEERING POLICY PROVIDED]
findings.gap_description: Run-Test (50–200 employees, PE-backed, government contracts) has classic employee theft, funds transfer fraud, and social engineering exposure. Counties make wire payments. Vendors send invoices. AP teams process payments. Without a standalone Crime policy, employee theft, forgery, computer/funds transfer fraud, and social engineering / impersonation fraud are uncovered. Cyber will pick up some of this when bound, but Cyber social engineering sublimits are typically $100k–$250k — well below the standalone Crime market norm of $1M-$5M.
findings.plain_english: Two of the most common loss types for companies your size are employee theft and 'social engineering' — someone impersonates a vendor or executive and tricks your AP team into wiring money. Neither is covered today. Cyber policies cover some of this when they're added, but usually with low sublimits. A real Crime policy is the right answer at $1M-$5M.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Commercial Crime policy at $1M-$5M with explicit coverage for: (1) Employee Theft, (2) Forgery or Alteration, (3) Computer Fraud, (4) Funds Transfer Fraud, (5) Social Engineering / Impersonation Fraud (often a separate insuring agreement, push for full limit not sublimit), (6) Client property coverage, (7) Third-party coverage if customer funds are handled. Carriers: Travelers, Chubb, AIG, Federal/Chubb.
discoveryQuestions: How many AP/finance employees handle wire transfers, and what dollar threshold requires multi-person approval?
Has Run-Test ever experienced or near-missed a vendor impersonation or executive impersonation wire fraud?
If an employee embezzled $250k over six months, who would discover it, and where would the recovery come from?
Does the PE sponsor's portfolio insurance schedule require standalone Crime coverage, and at what limit?

findings.requirement_type: Directors & Officers Liability — No Policy in Program
findings.contract_quote: [Not directly required by either contract — but PE-backed, government-contract, election-industry exposure makes D&O essential standard practice.]
findings.policy_quote: [NO D&O / MANAGEMENT LIABILITY POLICY PROVIDED]
findings.gap_description: Run-Test is PE-backed, holds government contracts in 31 states + D.C., and operates in one of the most politically scrutinized industries in the U.S. economy (election services). D&O exposures are real and elevated: Side A protection for individual directors/officers from non-indemnifiable claims (regulatory, securities-style, election-integrity litigation, derivative actions); Side B reimbursement for entity indemnification of officers; Side C entity coverage for securities-style claims. PE portfolio companies almost universally carry D&O. With no D&O on the program, individual board members and the C-suite have personal exposure for: regulatory investigations (DOJ, state AGs, election regulators), election-integrity-related litigation, antitrust, ERISA fiduciary, and customer/contract disputes naming individuals.
findings.plain_english: There is no Directors & Officers Liability policy. For a PE-backed company in the election services space, this is unusual and exposes the C-suite, the board, and the PE sponsor's appointees personally. D&O is the policy that defends individual officers when they're sued for decisions they made in their corporate role. Without it, every regulatory investigation, election-integrity lawsuit, derivative claim, and securities-adjacent dispute lands directly on personal assets. The PE sponsor almost certainly requires D&O on portfolio companies — confirm with the deal team.
findings.recommendation: Bind a Management Liability / D&O package at minimum $5M with: (1) Side A DIC tower for non-indemnifiable claims; (2) broad definition of 'Claim' (formal investigations, regulatory subpoenas, derivative demands); (3) entity investigation cost coverage; (4) prior/pending litigation date acceptable to client knowledge; (5) regulatory defense — important for election regulators and state AGs; (6) bump-up exclusion negotiated narrowly; (7) Insured-vs-Insured exception for whistleblowers. Carriers: Chubb, AIG, Travelers Bond & Specialty, Beazley. Given PE ownership and election-industry visibility, $10M is more appropriate.
discoveryQuestions: Does the PE sponsor's portfolio insurance schedule mandate D&O at a minimum limit, and is Run-Test currently compliant?
If a state AG opened an investigation into election services accuracy, who would defend the CEO and board members personally — and from what funds?
Has any Run-Test officer or director been individually named in election-related litigation in the past three election cycles?
What's the indemnification provision in the corporate bylaws and operating agreement, and is the company financially capable of honoring it without insurance backing?

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Per-Project Aggregate Construction Trigger — Likely N/A
findings.contract_quote: Contractors and Contractors engaged in other projects of construction shall have their general liability Aggregate Limit of Insurance endorsed to apply separately to each job site or project, as provided for by Insurance Services Office form CG-2503.
findings.policy_quote: [Trigger only if Run-Test performs construction work for Sacramento. Per client profile, scope is election services / printing / mail / SaaS — not construction.]
findings.gap_description: The Sacramento per-project aggregate requirement is conditional on construction-project work. Run-Test is an election services manufacturer — not a construction contractor. Scope confirmation needed but very likely N/A for the contractual trigger. (Separate per-location aggregate recommendation made under finding-041 for general best-practice reasons.)
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's per-project aggregate language only kicks in if you're doing construction. You're not. Per-project aggregate is best practice anyway (covered in finding-041), but you don't have to add it just for Sacramento.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Sacramento contract scope that no construction services are contemplated. If at any point a Sacramento contract includes construction (facility build-out, equipment installation), bind CG 25 03.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Course of Construction (COC) — N/A
findings.contract_quote: Course of Construction (COC) Waiver of Subrogation: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR ... 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: [Conditional on Builders Risk / COC policy. None applicable to election services scope.]
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §IX is conditional — only triggers if a COC/Builders Risk policy is maintained. Not applicable to Run-Test's election services scope. N/A.
findings.plain_english: Builders Risk / Course of Construction only matters if you're doing construction. You're not. N/A.
findings.recommendation: If Run-Test ever undertakes construction at the Phoenix facility or for a county under contract, bind COC with County as loss payee and WoS endorsed.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Insurance Survival / Material Breach
findings.contract_quote: All insurance required herein shall be maintained in full force and effect until all work or service required to be performed under the terms of the contract is satisfactorily completed and formally accepted. Failure to do so may, at the sole discretion of County, constitute a material breach of this contract.
findings.policy_quote: Both GL and Auto are in force with current 2025–2026 terms. Operationally compliant.
findings.gap_description: Both current policies are in force. Operationally compliant on this clause TODAY. The risk is renewal discipline — Sacramento §VI.A.2 requires 10-day pre-anniversary evidence; Maricopa requires uninterrupted maintenance. Lapses would convert to material breach. Calendar discipline is the protection.
findings.plain_english: Both policies are currently in force. The contract says letting them lapse is a material breach. Make sure renewals don't slip.
findings.recommendation: Calendar all policy renewals 60+ days in advance. Ensure 10-day pre-anniversary evidence to Sacramento and uninterrupted COIs to Maricopa.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Indemnity — Uncapped by Policy Limits
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: [Standard non-limitation clause — Contractor's indemnification obligations are not capped at insurance limits.]
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.1.3 is a standard non-limitation clause. The indemnification obligation under §8.1.1 is uncapped by insurance limits — meaning if a covered loss exceeds policy limits, Run-Test still owes indemnity from balance sheet. With current $1M GL / $1M Auto / no umbrella, the uninsured exposure above policy limits is enormous. This is the structural argument for higher umbrella limits (finding-005).
findings.plain_english: If you owe Maricopa $5M of indemnity and you only have $1M of insurance, the other $4M comes out of your bank account. The contract specifically says insurance limits don't cap your obligation. This is exactly why a meaningful umbrella matters.
findings.recommendation: Address via the umbrella binding recommendation in finding-005. Target $10M-$25M umbrella to align Run-Test's insurance posture with its uncapped indemnity obligations.
discoveryQuestions: Does your CFO have a balance-sheet view of the gap between policy limits and your contractual indemnity obligations across all customer contracts?
If a $5M loss happened tomorrow under the Maricopa contract, what's your plan for the $4M shortfall above the $1M GL?
Has anyone modeled a worst-case-scenario insurance gap analysis for the PE sponsor or board?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Indemnity — AZ Comparative Negligence Aligned
findings.contract_quote: [Indemnity] but only to the extent caused by the negligent acts or omissions of the contractor, a subcontractor, anyone directly or indirectly employed by them ... The scope of this indemnification does not extend to the sole negligence of County.
findings.policy_quote: Standard ISO contractual liability via 'insured contract' definition, modified by 00 GL1058 (sole-negligence carve-out aligned with both Maricopa and Sacramento).
findings.gap_description: Maricopa indemnity is comparative-negligence-based with a sole-negligence carve-out for the County. This aligns with Arizona's comparative negligence regime and with the GL's 00 GL1058 sole-negligence carve-out. Compliant in structural terms — limited only by the upstream Classification Limitation issue (finding-001).
findings.plain_english: The Maricopa indemnity language is reasonable — it tracks Arizona's comparative negligence rules and excludes the County's own sole negligence. Your policy structure aligns. Compliant on this point (assuming the operations-CGL is placed).
findings.recommendation: Maintain alignment when binding operations-CGL.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Deductible Bond/LOC Backing Reservation
findings.contract_quote: County, at its option, may require Contractor to secure payment of such deductibles or self-insured retentions by a surety bond or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit.
findings.policy_quote: Current deductibles: GL $1k / Auto $1k. Cyber, E&O, and Umbrella SIRs (when bound) likely $10k–$250k.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa reserves the right to demand bond or LOC backing for deductibles/SIRs. Currently low risk given $1k deductibles, but as Cyber, E&O, and Umbrella are added with larger SIRs, Maricopa could demand collateral. Plan for it.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa can require you to post a bond or letter of credit to back any deductible or SIR. Right now your deductibles are tiny ($1k). When you add Cyber and E&O with bigger retentions, Maricopa could ask for collateral. Worth knowing in advance so the CFO isn't surprised.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate Cyber, E&O, and Umbrella retentions to a level Run-Test can demonstrably self-fund without LOC backing — typically retentions under $25k avoid most LOC/bond demands.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Claims-Made Retro Date — 2-Year ERP
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: Maricopa contract effective date: 11/01/21. Cyber and E&O (when bound) must have retro date on or before 11/01/21 OR continuous coverage from such retro date.
findings.policy_page: N/A — no claims-made policy currently in program
findings.gap_description: Once Cyber (finding-003) and E&O (finding-004) are bound, the retro date on each must precede 11/01/21 (Maricopa contract effective date) or continuous coverage must be evidenced from such retro date. Sacramento §V.A also requires retro to precede the Sacramento contract effective date. With no current claims-made policies, ERP language is forward-looking only — but binding instructions for new claims-made policies must specify a retro date acceptable to both Counties.
findings.plain_english: When you add Cyber and E&O, those are 'claims-made' policies — they only cover claims reported during the policy period for events that happened after a 'retro date.' Maricopa wants that retro date to be before 11/01/21. Sacramento wants it before their contract date. If you can't get a retro that early on a brand-new policy, you'll need ERP/tail coverage on top.
findings.recommendation: Bind new claims-made policies with retro date as early as possible. If carriers won't go back to 11/01/21 (likely on a fresh placement), document the retro and price an ERP for any prior period the County requires backstop on. Negotiate with each County's Risk Manager — Maricopa may accept inception-date retro plus 2-year ERP commitment in writing.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento Claims-Made E&O — 1-Year Tail
