[§8.2.9] If available, the insurance policies required by this contract may be combined with Commercial Umbrella Insurance policies to meet the minimum limit requirements.
findings.policy_quote: Schedule of Underlying: Auto — Allmerica AW4 H221414 05, $1M each accident. Umbrella: $10M each occurrence (Coverage A follows form over Auto).
findings.policy_file: Hanover Commercial Umbrella UH4 H221416 05 + underlying Allmerica Auto
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.11 requires $2M Auto CSL. Underlying Auto is $1M CSL. §8.2.9 (program-level umbrella permission) allows umbrella stacking to meet limits. §8.2.11 (Auto specifically) does NOT inline-mention umbrella attachment — creating interpretive ambiguity. Strict reading: $1M Auto + $10M Umbrella does NOT satisfy $2M Auto minimum because §8.2.11 didn't say umbrella OK. Permissive reading: $1M + $10M = $11M, satisfies $2M because §8.2.9 grants program-level umbrella permission. Per audit methodology guidance on ambiguous umbrella attachment, this is a Needs Review, with a separate Bad finding for the underlying shortfall against the $2M Auto floor IF strict reading applies.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M on Auto. Your primary Auto is $1M. Your $10M umbrella sits on top of Auto, so combined you have $11M of Auto limits. The question is whether Maricopa interprets their own contract permissively or strictly. Their general umbrella-stacking rule (§8.2.9) says yes-stack-OK. The auto-specific clause (§8.2.11) doesn't repeat that permission. Most county risk managers read it permissively and accept stacking. But this is a Needs-Review item — get it in writing from Maricopa before treating as fully compliant.
findings.recommendation: Email Maricopa Risk Management (the address listed at §8.2.14: 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 910, Phoenix, AZ 85003) to confirm in writing that umbrella stacking is acceptable for the $2M Auto CSL minimum under §8.2.9. Store the response. As a fallback, increase primary Auto to $2M CSL (typically modest premium increase on an Auto schedule with limited fleet) — this eliminates the interpretive question entirely. Recommend the increase: cleaner, removes ambiguity, and matches the broker default of leading with primary limits matching the highest contract requirement.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella $10M (subject to Maricopa accepting Auto-line stacking)

findings.requirement_type: Underlying Auto CSL Shortfall vs Maricopa $2M (Strict Reading)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services or use or maintenance of the premises under this contract.
findings.policy_quote: Schedule of Underlying Policies: Auto — Allmerica AW4 H221414 05, $1M each accident.
findings.gap_description: Underlying primary Commercial Auto is $1M CSL. Maricopa §8.2.11 requires $2M CSL. Even setting aside the umbrella interpretation question, the primary alone does NOT meet the $2M Maricopa floor. If Maricopa rejects umbrella stacking (or even questions it during a COI review), Run-Test is non-compliant on primary Auto. Sacramento §III.B is satisfied at $1M CSL — so the $2M issue is Maricopa-specific.
findings.plain_english: Forget the stacking question for a moment. On primary Auto alone, your $1M CSL is half what Maricopa wants. Sacramento is fine at $1M. But Maricopa is $2M. If Maricopa's certificate review process is strict — as some county procurement teams are — the COI for $1M primary Auto could get rejected outright, regardless of how big your umbrella is. Cleanest fix: bump primary to $2M.
findings.recommendation: Increase primary Auto CSL from $1M to $2M. This eliminates the §8.2.9 vs §8.2.11 stacking ambiguity AND meets every county auto requirement on primary alone. Premium impact for a small fleet (an election mail printing/processing operation likely runs a small fleet of vans, sprinters, and possibly box trucks) should be modest — quote at renewal (4/1/26) or earlier mid-term endorsement.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella $10M provides excess auto coverage (subject to Maricopa accepting stacking — see Needs-Review companion finding)
discoveryQuestions: How many vehicles are on your auto schedule today, and what's the rough split between owned, leased, and personally-owned-by-employee?
Has Maricopa or any other Arizona county ever pushed back on a $1M Auto CSL? Your primary is $1M and Maricopa wants $2M — that's a known gap that depends on stacking interpretation.
What's your tolerance for bumping primary Auto to $2M to remove the ambiguity entirely? Premium increase on a small fleet is usually a few hundred dollars.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Comp / Employers Liability Limits ($1M/$1M/$1M Match)
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.12] Workers' compensation insurance to cover obligations imposed by Federal and State statutes... Employer's Liability insurance of not less than $1,000,000 for each accident, $1,000,000 disease for each employee, and $1,000,000 disease policy limit. [Sacramento §III.C-D] EMPLOYER'S LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per accident for bodily injury or disease.
findings.contract_file: Maricopa County and Sacramento County Contracts
findings.policy_quote: Schedule of Underlying: WC/EL — Mass Bay WD4 H218283 06, $1M each accident / $1M disease each employee / $1M disease policy limit.
findings.gap_description: Underlying WC/EL provides $1M/$1M/$1M, matching both Maricopa §8.2.12 and Sacramento §III.D. Umbrella Coverage A follows form over EL (Coverage B excludes EL — §VII.3.e — but Coverage A is the relevant follow-form path for excess EL). Stacked with $10M umbrella, total EL is $11M/$11M/$11M, which is more than enough to support the umbrella attachment. RMF WC-6 (EL adequate to support umbrella) is satisfied.
findings.plain_english: Your Employers Liability matches both contracts at $1M/$1M/$1M, and the umbrella sits on top of EL through Coverage A — so total is $11M. That's plenty to support an umbrella attachment.
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal. Confirm at every WC renewal that the EL limits don't drop below $1M/$1M/$1M. The umbrella's Coverage A will follow form over the underlying EL — verify in Schedule of Underlying.

findings.requirement_type: WC California Statutory Coverage (Sacramento Contract)
findings.contract_quote: WORKERS' COMPENSATION: Statutory requirements of the State of California and Employer's Liability Insurance.
findings.policy_quote: Schedule of Underlying: WC/EL — Mass Bay WD4 H218283 06. The All States Endorsement / Item 3.A vs 3.C state schedule is NOT visible in the umbrella's per-policy analysis JSON. Run-Test is AZ-based.
findings.policy_page: 475-0003, Page 14 (umbrella schedule); underlying WC dec page not in this audit
findings.policy_file: Mass Bay WC/EL underlying — analysis NOT provided
findings.gap_description: Sacramento contract requires California statutory WC. Run-Test is Arizona-based per client notes. Per audit methodology, California is a non-monopolistic state — coverage typically provided either by: (a) primary WC policy with CA listed in Item 3.A, OR (b) a California-state-specific WC policy if Mass Bay is not licensed in CA. The umbrella's per-policy analysis JSON does not provide visibility into Item 3.A states or whether the underlying Mass Bay policy includes California. RMF WC-3 (All States Endorsement / 3.A vs 3.C) cannot be evaluated from the umbrella alone. CRITICAL: if Run-Test sends ANY employees to California to perform under the Sacramento contract without CA in 3.A, there is a potential uninsured WC exposure — California's WC system does not honor 'Other States' (3.C) coverage as adequate for in-state employment.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County wants California-statutory workers comp. You're an Arizona company. The question is: does your Mass Bay WC policy explicitly list California in its Item 3.A schedule (the states where coverage applies on a true statutory basis), or is California only picked up by 'Other States' (Item 3.C)? Item 3.C is NOT enough for California — California requires the policy to be issued by a CA-admitted carrier or to have CA explicitly scheduled. If you ever send a Run-Test employee to a California polling site or county facility to do contract work, and you only have California in 3.C, you have an uninsured exposure. We need to pull the WC dec page to confirm.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: Pull Mass Bay WC/EL dec page (Information Page Item 3.A states schedule). If California is NOT listed in 3.A, either (a) add CA to 3.A (carrier-dependent — Mass Bay may not be CA-admitted), OR (b) procure a separate CA WC policy from a CA-admitted carrier (e.g., State Compensation Insurance Fund of California). DO NOT perform any work in California under the Sacramento contract until this is confirmed. Same review needed for any other state Run-Test enters under any of its 31-state election services footprint.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation — Multi-State Footprint (31 States)
findings.contract_quote: [RMF WC-3] All States Endorsement on WC / Additionally are any states omitted from 3.A that were picked up under 3.C in the previous year? If so, this can be very problematic.
findings.policy_quote: Client notes: Run-Test serves 'local, county, and state election officials across 31 states and the District of Columbia.' Underlying WC: Mass Bay WD4 H218283 06 — Item 3.A states not visible.
findings.policy_page: Underlying WC not analyzed in this audit
findings.gap_description: Run-Test operates across 31 states + DC. Workers' Comp must be statutorily compliant in every state where Run-Test has any employee presence — even temporary travel to deliver/install equipment, train election staff, or service ballot processing systems. Monopolistic states (ND, OH, WA, WY) require coverage purchased through state fund — a private carrier policy cannot include them. For non-monopolistic states, employees performing in-state work require either Item 3.A coverage or a state-specific policy. Item 3.C (Other States) is NOT statutorily adequate in California, New York, or several other states with strict in-state coverage rules.
findings.plain_english: You serve 31 states. Workers comp law is state-by-state. If you send an employee to install equipment in Ohio, you need Ohio coverage from the Ohio state fund — your Mass Bay policy literally cannot cover it. If you send someone to California, the policy needs California explicitly listed. The 'Other States' coverage on most policies (3.C) is a backstop — it picks up incidental travel, but most states do not consider it adequate for actual work. We need a state-by-state map: where do you send employees, and is each one covered correctly?
findings.recommendation: Build a state-by-state workforce footprint matrix: list every state where Run-Test has any employee presence (even one-day site visits for equipment install/training) and verify WC coverage per state. Specific concerns: (a) Monopolistic states — ND, OH, WA, WY — separate state-fund policies needed if any employees travel there; (b) High-coverage states — CA, NY, NJ — must be in Item 3.A or have separate state policies; (c) Voluntary Comp endorsement may be needed in non-required-WC states if Run-Test contractors/independents travel. Annual reconciliation between 31-state contract footprint and Item 3.A schedule is mandatory.

findings.requirement_type: WC Waiver of Subrogation (Maricopa & Sacramento)
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento §VIII] The workers' compensation policy required hereunder shall be endorsed to state that the workers' compensation carrier waives its right of subrogation against the COUNTY... [Maricopa §8.2.8 + §8.2.12] The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation)... [§8.2.12] Contractor, its subcontractors, and sub-subcontractors waive all rights against this contract...
findings.policy_quote: Underlying WC (Mass Bay WD4 H218283 06) endorsement schedule not provided in this audit. Standard WC requires WC 04 03 06 (Waiver of Our Right to Recover from Others — California specifically requires the CA-state form).
findings.gap_description: Both contracts require WC waiver of subrogation. California specifically requires WC 04 03 06 (state-specific Waiver of Our Right to Recover from Others) — and the waiver must be either blanket (any party where required by written contract) or scheduled (Sacramento County and Maricopa County named). Premium charge typically applies (1-3% of WC premium). Underlying WC analysis not provided. The umbrella is irrelevant for WC waiver — the waiver must be on the underlying WC policy, not the umbrella.
findings.plain_english: Both Sacramento and Maricopa contracts say your WC carrier must agree not to come after the County to recover money it pays out on a Run-Test employee's claim. This is the 'Waiver of Subrogation' on WC. California has a specific form for this. The waiver must be on your primary WC policy. The umbrella has nothing to do with WC waiver. We need to pull the WC dec page and verify (a) waiver is endorsed, (b) waiver is blanket, OR (c) Sacramento and Maricopa Counties are scheduled by name.
findings.recommendation: Pull Mass Bay WC dec/forms list and confirm: (a) Blanket WC Waiver of Subrogation (preferred) or scheduled WoS naming Sacramento and Maricopa Counties; (b) If California work is performed, the California-specific WC 04 03 06 endorsement is in place. If neither blanket nor scheduled, request endorsement before performing under either contract. WC waiver typically has separate premium charge — disclose to CFO.

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Coverage — Standalone Policy Status (Maricopa $5M Broad Spec)
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence... [enumerated components: regulatory defense + fines and penalties, cyber extortion, business interruption, computer fraud, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, etc.]
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Cyber policy is included in this audit's POLICY ANALYSES array. Schedule of Underlying on the Hanover umbrella does NOT list a cyber policy.
findings.gap_description: The Maricopa contract requires extremely broad $5M cyber including: (a) regulatory defense AND fines and penalties (not just defense), (b) cyber extortion, (c) network business interruption, (d) computer fraud / funds transfer loss, (e) third-party fidelity, (f) breach notification / credit monitoring, (g) loss outside premises (no premises restriction). The umbrella explicitly EXCLUDES all cyber loss (475-0654, 475-0655, 475-0661 — see finding-002). This audit's policy analyses do NOT include a standalone Cyber/Tech E&O policy. Run-Test handles voter PII for 90M+ registered voters across 31 states — cyber is the SINGLE highest-stakes line. If a standalone Cyber policy exists it must independently meet ALL §8.2.13 components — pull and audit. If no Cyber policy exists, this is an URGENT, IMMEDIATE Ugly placement gap separate from the umbrella exclusion finding.
findings.plain_english: Your audit folder didn't include a standalone Cyber policy. The Maricopa contract demands $5M of very broad cyber. The umbrella excludes cyber entirely. So the standalone Cyber policy — if it exists — has to do ALL the work to meet that spec. We need to pull whatever cyber policy is in place (or confirm whether one exists) and audit it line-by-line against §8.2.13. If there's no cyber in the program at all, this is an immediate placement priority.
findings.recommendation: STEP 1: Confirm whether a standalone Cyber/Tech E&O policy exists. STEP 2: If yes, pull dec page, full forms list, and provide for audit. STEP 3: If no, place immediately — for an election services company handling voter PII this is malpractice-level uninsured exposure. Recommended structure: $5M+ standalone Cyber covering all §8.2.13 enumerated components, with retro date on/before 11/01/21 (Maricopa contract effective). Carriers to consider for election technology: Coalition, Beazley, At-Bay, Tokio Marine HCC. Note: this is a SEPARATE finding from finding-002 (umbrella exclusion), which was tagged Ugly because of the umbrella drop-down strip; this finding focuses on the raw question of whether the underlying Cyber exists.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / Tech E&O — Policy Status
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento §II.D, §III.E] PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. [§II.E] Umbrella expressly cannot be used to satisfy this minimum.
findings.policy_quote: No Professional Liability/Tech E&O policy is included in this audit's POLICY ANALYSES array. Schedule of Underlying on the Hanover umbrella does NOT list a professional liability policy. Umbrella expressly excludes Professional Liability via 475-0031 (Coverage A) and §VII.3.k (Coverage B).
findings.gap_description: Sacramento contract REQUIRES $1M/$1M Professional Liability with retro on or before contract effective AND ERP of at least 1 year if claims-made cancelled/non-renewed. The umbrella excludes professional services entirely — and the Sacramento contract expressly excludes umbrella from satisfying the PL minimum. So the underlying PL/E&O must independently hit $1M/$1M. Audit policy analyses do not include a standalone PL/E&O. Run-Test's professional services exposure is significant: ballot printing accuracy, mail sortation correctness, election software/hardware reliability, voter data processing accuracy. A processing error that misallocates ballots, mis-sorts election mail, or causes incorrect tabulation could trigger massive professional liability exposure under several theories.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County requires you to carry $1M/$1M Professional Liability — and they specifically say you can't use your umbrella to make that limit. The umbrella also has its own Professional Liability exclusion. So the only thing standing between you and a professional liability claim is your standalone E&O / Tech E&O policy. That policy is not in this audit's folder. We need to confirm: (a) does it exist, (b) is it $1M/$1M minimum, (c) does it cover election services as a defined professional service, (d) what's the retro date.
findings.recommendation: STEP 1: Confirm whether a standalone Professional Liability / Tech E&O policy exists. STEP 2: If yes, pull the dec page, professional services definition, retro date, and full audit. The 'professional services' definition MUST cover ballot printing, election mail processing, software/hardware integration for elections, voter data handling, and any consulting/training services. STEP 3: Verify retro on/before original Sacramento contract effective date (and ideally on/before original Run-Test inception). STEP 4: If no PL exists, immediate placement is required for Sacramento compliance — likely $2M-$5M minimum given the breadth of Run-Test's election services and cross-state voter PII handling.

findings.requirement_type: Additional Insured on Umbrella (Follow-Form vs Express Endorsement)
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.7] The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds. [Sacramento §VII.A] The COUNTY... are to be endorsed as additional insureds...
findings.policy_quote: checklist.additional_insured_blanket = false; additional_insured_scheduled = false; additional_insured_completed_ops = false. additional_insureds[] is empty. Coverage A follows form over the underlying CGL/Auto, so any AI status on underlying flows up.
findings.policy_page: Per-policy analysis JSON — no AI endorsement located on umbrella
findings.gap_description: The umbrella analysis shows NO Additional Insured endorsement on the umbrella itself, no scheduled AIs, and no completed operations AI. For a true follow-form umbrella (Coverage A), this is typical and acceptable — the umbrella follows the underlying CGL's blanket AI / scheduled AI treatment. For Coverage B (true umbrella claims with no underlying), the absence of an AI endorsement on the umbrella means counties named as AI on the underlying CGL may NOT be AI on a Coverage B umbrella claim. Most counties accept Coverage A follow-form AI. But strict county risk managers sometimes require an express AI endorsement on the umbrella itself. Cannot determine compliance from umbrella analysis alone — depends on (a) what underlying CGL provides, and (b) Maricopa/Sacramento risk manager interpretation.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella doesn't have its own Additional Insured endorsement listing the counties. That's not unusual — most umbrellas just follow whatever the primary GL says. So if your primary CGL has a blanket AI for any party where required by contract, the umbrella picks up the same parties. The question is twofold: (1) does your primary GL have a blanket AI, and (2) will Maricopa and Sacramento accept a follow-form AI on the umbrella, or do they want an express umbrella AI endorsement? Most counties accept follow-form. But it's worth confirming.
findings.recommendation: Pull underlying CGL (Citizens ZB4 H221415 05) and confirm: (a) blanket AI endorsement (CG 20 33, CG 20 38, or carrier proprietary) covering any party where required by written contract; (b) ongoing operations CG 20 10; (c) completed operations CG 20 37 — Sacramento §VII.A specifically requires both ongoing AND completed operations AI; (d) primary and noncontributory CG 20 01. If all present on primary, umbrella's Coverage A follow-form will inherit. For Coverage B, request a Hanover umbrella AI endorsement scheduling 'any party where required by written contract' — typically free or low-cost. This closes the Coverage B gap.

findings.requirement_type: Waiver of Subrogation on Umbrella (Follow-Form)
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.8] The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees for any claims arising out of Contractor's work or service.
findings.policy_quote: checklist.waiver_of_subrogation = false. 475-0001 §VIII Conditions includes a Transfer of Rights of Recovery clause (standard) but NO blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement was located on the umbrella per the analysis.
findings.policy_page: 475-0001 §VIII (Transfer of Rights), Page 36+; no blanket WoS endorsement located
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.8 requires Waiver of Subrogation on all policies except WC and E&O — including the umbrella. The umbrella analysis shows checklist.waiver_of_subrogation = false. Standard Hanover umbrella has a Transfer of Rights condition but NOT a blanket waiver. Coverage A (Follow Form Excess) will follow form over the underlying CGL/Auto WoS — so if underlying has blanket WoS, umbrella inherits via follow form. Coverage B (true umbrella) needs an express WoS or the Maricopa requirement is not met for umbrella-only claims. Cannot determine compliance from umbrella alone.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants every policy except WC and E&O to have a Waiver of Subrogation — meaning your insurance carriers can't sue the County to recover what they paid on a claim. Your umbrella does NOT have its own blanket waiver. If your primary GL and Auto have blanket waivers, the umbrella inherits via follow-form for Coverage A. But for Coverage B (true umbrella claims), without an express umbrella waiver, you may not meet the Maricopa requirement. We need to confirm the underlying policies have blanket WoS, and request an express umbrella WoS endorsement to close any Coverage B gap.
findings.recommendation: Two-step: (1) Pull underlying CGL and Auto and confirm blanket Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (best practice: 'any party where required by written contract'). (2) Request Hanover endorse umbrella with express blanket WoS — typically minor or no cost. The follow-form treatment for Coverage A is acceptable but Coverage B without an express waiver may not satisfy a strict Maricopa risk manager review.

findings.requirement_type: Primary & Noncontributory on Umbrella (Follow-Form)
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.4] Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it. [Sacramento §VII.C] For any claims related to this Agreement, the CONTRACTOR's insurance coverage shall be endorsed to be primary insurance...
findings.policy_quote: checklist.primary_noncontributory = false. 475-0001 §VIII Other Insurance — 'this insurance is excess over any other insurance' (standard umbrella position).
findings.gap_description: Standard umbrella forms position the umbrella as 'excess over any other insurance' — which is appropriate for the umbrella's role but creates an interpretive question with primary-and-noncontributory contract requirements. RMF UMB-3 specifically calls out: 'Does the other insurance clause within the condition section of the policy create a primary/non-contributory issue for an Additional Insured named under the primary and umbrella?' If County is AI on Coverage A (via follow-form), County's own self-insurance is likely subordinate to Coverage A through follow-form mechanics. But Coverage B's 'excess over any other insurance' could be interpreted to make Coverage B contributory with County's own insurance/self-insurance. Cannot fully determine from analysis JSON alone.
findings.plain_english: Your contract says your insurance must be primary — Maricopa or Sacramento should not have to contribute their own coverage before yours pays. Most umbrellas have language saying 'we're excess over any other insurance,' which is normally fine because the umbrella is supposed to be excess to YOUR primary. But the question is: when a county is named as Additional Insured on your umbrella, does that 'excess over any other insurance' clause kick in to make your umbrella treat the county's own insurance as a primary they have to use first? That's the 'horizontal limit exhaustion' issue. The fix is usually an endorsement that says when an AI is on your umbrella, your umbrella is primary as respects them.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with Hanover: does 475-0001 §VIII Other Insurance condition treat AI parties differently from Named Insureds? Standard Hanover language typically does — the 'excess over any other insurance' applies between Hanover umbrella and Named Insured's other insurance, not between Hanover umbrella and an AI's separate insurance/self-insurance. If language is ambiguous, request a Primary & Noncontributory endorsement scheduled for 'any party where required by written contract.' For Coverage A, follow-form from the underlying CGL/Auto P&NC endorsement is sufficient — verify underlying has CG 20 01 or equivalent.

findings.requirement_type: Carrier Rating — Hanover Umbrella vs A.M. Best A-VII (Sacramento) and B++ (Maricopa)
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento §VI.A.1] Insurance is to be placed with insurers with a current A.M. Best's rating of no less than A-VII. [Maricopa §8.2.1] AM Best, Inc. category rating of B++.
findings.policy_quote: Carrier: Hanover Insurance Company.
findings.gap_description: Hanover Insurance Company carries a current A.M. Best rating of A (Excellent) with size category XV (currently — confirm at COI issuance). Both Sacramento (A-VII minimum) and Maricopa (B++ minimum) requirements are easily exceeded by Hanover's A XV rating. Same rating check needed for underlying carriers Citizens (CGL/EBL), Allmerica (Auto), Mass Bay (WC) — all are Hanover-family carriers and should similarly exceed the rating thresholds.
findings.plain_english: Hanover Insurance Company is rated A (Excellent) by A.M. Best, with the largest size category. That's well above what either Sacramento or Maricopa requires. Same goes for Citizens, Allmerica, and Mass Bay — all part of the Hanover Insurance Group. No carrier rating concerns on this program.
findings.recommendation: At every COI issuance, verify current A.M. Best rating is still A-VII or better for all carriers in the program. Hanover Insurance Group has been stable for years; no immediate concern. If Run-Test ever moves any line to a carrier with weaker rating (e.g., E&S placement on cyber or professional liability), document the placement justification — Sacramento contract permits Risk Manager waiver but it must be requested in advance.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Underlying Claims-Made ERP (475-0618)
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento §V.A-C] If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown... B. Insurance must be maintained and evidence of insurance must be provided for at least one (1) year after completion of the Agreement. C. If coverage is cancelled or non-renewed... CONTRACTOR must purchase 'extended reporting' coverage for a minimum of one (1) year after completion.
findings.policy_quote: [475-0618] Provides 60-day Automatic ERP if cancelled/non-renewed (not for nonpayment). Optional ERP available with additional premium: 1 year = 100% of annual premium; 2 years = 150%; 3 years = 200%.
findings.gap_description: 475-0618 governs Underlying Claims-Made Coverage ERP for the umbrella itself — provides 60-day automatic ERP plus optional 1/2/3-year extended reporting at 100%/150%/200% of annual premium. The Sacramento §V requirement for 1-year ERP applies to the underlying claims-made Professional Liability, NOT to the umbrella. The umbrella's 1-year optional ERP at 100% of annual premium aligns favorably with the Sacramento requirement IF the umbrella ever became the policy needing ERP — but practically, Sacramento §V's ERP requirement targets the standalone PL/E&O, which is not provided in this audit.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella has a built-in Extended Reporting Period option: 60 days automatic if cancelled, plus 1/2/3-year optional ERP at standard rates. This is good. But Sacramento's 1-year ERP requirement is really about your standalone Professional Liability policy — it's claims-made and they want a tail. The umbrella is only the secondary concern here. Once we have the standalone E&O in hand, we'll audit it against Sacramento §V.
findings.recommendation: Maintain existing ERP availability. Sacramento §V applicability — and the meaningful ERP audit — turns on the standalone PL/E&O, which is not provided in this audit (see finding-026). Ensure that policy has matching or better ERP terms.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Limits ($10M) vs Higher County Stacking Needs
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.10 GL] $2,000,000 each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, $4,000,000 General Aggregate. [Maricopa §8.2.11 Auto] $2,000,000 CSL. [Maricopa §8.2.12 EL] $1M/$1M/$1M.
findings.policy_quote: Each Occurrence: $10,000,000; Products/Completed Operations Aggregate: $10,000,000; General Aggregate: $10,000,000; Retained Limit: $0.
findings.gap_description: $10M umbrella limits provide ample stacking capacity over $1M underlying CGL ($11M total each occurrence), $1M underlying Auto ($11M total), and $1M underlying EL ($11M total). Even on the largest county contracts in Run-Test's 31-state footprint, $11M-$14M in total liability capacity is appropriate for a $5M-$25M revenue election services manufacturer with PE backing. PE backing typically demands $10M+ umbrella as a baseline. $0 retained limit (Self-Insured Retention) means the umbrella attaches at the underlying limit with no gap.
findings.plain_english: Your $10M umbrella stacked on $1M primary gives you $11M of each-occurrence liability capacity. That's appropriate for your size (PE-backed $5M-$25M revenue manufacturer) and easily exceeds every county requirement. The umbrella also has zero retention/SIR, meaning there's no gap between when your primary maxes out and when your umbrella picks up — clean attachment.
findings.recommendation: Maintain $10M as the floor. As Run-Test grows or takes on larger county contracts, consider increasing to $15M or $25M — particularly relevant given (a) PE-backed company with regulatory exposure, (b) 31-state footprint amplifies aggregation risk, (c) cyber/election infrastructure exposure profile, (d) defense costs in election-related litigation can be heavy. Get quotes for $15M/$25M umbrella at next renewal (4/1/26) for benchmarking.

findings.requirement_type: Indemnity Uncapped by Insurance Limits (Maricopa §8.1.3)
findings.contract_quote: The amount and type of insurance coverage requirements set forth herein will in no way be construed as limiting the scope of the indemnity in this section.
findings.policy_quote: Umbrella limits $10M aggregate. Combined with primary $1M, total program liability capacity is $11M each occurrence / $14M aggregate (subject to umbrella stacking acceptance).
findings.policy_file: Hanover Commercial Umbrella UH4 H221416 05 + underlying
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.1.3 expressly provides that contractor's indemnity obligations to County are NOT capped at insurance limits. So if a covered loss exceeds $11M each occurrence (or $14M aggregate), Run-Test is contractually obligated to indemnify Maricopa for the excess — directly from balance sheet. For a $5M-$25M revenue manufacturer with PE backing, a $25M+ election-related liability could materially impair or exceed the entity's capacity. This isn't a coverage gap to fix with insurance — it's a contractual term to (a) recognize, (b) communicate to PE board and CFO, and (c) potentially negotiate at next contract renewal.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa's contract has a quiet but important sentence: insurance limits don't cap your indemnity. Translation — if a $25M judgment lands and your insurance pays $11M, you owe Maricopa the $14M difference out of company funds. For a PE-backed company your size, that's potentially business-threatening. There's no insurance policy you can buy that fully fixes this; the only solutions are (1) negotiate a cap into the contract at renewal (rarely accepted by counties), (2) increase umbrella limits to make the gap less likely, or (3) make sure your PE board and CFO know this exists.
findings.recommendation: (1) Brief CFO and PE board sponsor on the uncapped indemnity exposure under Maricopa and similar county contracts. (2) Increase umbrella limits to $25M at renewal to reduce probability of breach (incremental premium typically modest at higher tiers). (3) At Maricopa contract renewal, propose mutual cap on contractual indemnity at policy limits — most counties reject, but the ask costs nothing. (4) Confirm Sacramento and other county contracts have similar uncapped indemnity language — likely yes, treat as portfolio-wide.
discoveryQuestions: Maricopa's contract explicitly says insurance limits don't cap your indemnity obligation. Has this been raised with your PE sponsors? They may want this disclosure on the risk register.
If a single election-related judgment came in at $20M and your program paid $11M, where would the $9M difference come from?
How many of your other 30+ county contracts have similar 'insurance does not limit indemnity' language? This may be portfolio-wide and worth quantifying.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Subcontractor Pass-Through (Sacramento §VII.E)
findings.contract_quote: SUBCONTRACTORS: CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella has no subcontractor-specific scope limitation; follows form over underlying CGL.
findings.policy_page: N/A — flow-down obligation is contractual on Run-Test, not insurance
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.E imposes a contractor-level obligation to be responsible for subcontractor acts/omissions and to obtain AI endorsements from subs. This is a flow-down requirement — not directly addressable by Run-Test's own umbrella. Run-Test must (a) include matching insurance requirements in subcontractor agreements, (b) require subs to add Run-Test AND Sacramento County as Additional Insureds on sub policies, (c) require subs to provide AI endorsement copies, (d) require subs to maintain matching limits and waiver of subrogation. Audit cannot determine compliance from Run-Test's own policies — depends on sub agreements.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento says you're responsible for what your subcontractors do, and you have to pass insurance requirements down to them. This isn't something we can verify from your insurance policies — it's about what's in your subcontractor agreements. The question is: do you have a standard subcontractor agreement that requires subs to (a) carry matching insurance, (b) name Run-Test AND the County as additional insureds, (c) provide certificates and endorsement copies before starting work?
findings.recommendation: Audit Run-Test's standard subcontractor template against Sacramento §VII.E flow-down requirements. Required terms in sub agreements: (1) sub carries GL, Auto, WC matching county minimums; (2) sub names Run-Test AND county as AI on GL and Auto; (3) sub provides waiver of subrogation; (4) sub provides COI + endorsement copies before starting work; (5) sub maintains coverage through completion + applicable tail. Same review needed for Maricopa subcontractor flow-down (typically same requirements). Recommend a subcontractor risk transfer review as a separate engagement.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine — Equipment / Election Technology Coverage
findings.contract_quote: [Sacramento §IX] Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: No Inland Marine policy is included in this audit's POLICY ANALYSES array. Schedule of Underlying on the Hanover umbrella does NOT list Inland Marine.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §IX is conditional — only triggers if Run-Test maintains Inland Marine. RELEVANT to Run-Test given client notes flag 'High-value equipment.' Election technology vendors typically have material Inland Marine exposure: ballot processing equipment, mobile printing presses, mail sorting machinery, computers/servers in transit between counties, ballot drop-box hardware. Whether Run-Test has an IM policy and whether it has WoS for County is unverified from this audit.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento says: if you carry Inland Marine insurance, the county wants a waiver of subrogation on it. You probably DO have Inland Marine, given Run-Test's client profile mentions 'high-value equipment' and you ship/store election technology. We need to pull whatever IM policy is in place to (a) verify it covers your high-value election equipment, (b) verify limits match the equipment values, (c) confirm WoS endorsement is in place per Sacramento §IX.
findings.recommendation: STEP 1: Confirm whether Run-Test has Inland Marine. STEP 2: If yes, audit against: (a) total insured value vs current equipment schedule (election technology often appreciates rapidly with software updates), (b) coverage in transit vs at premises vs at customer locations (counties), (c) blanket WoS or scheduled WoS for any party where required by contract, (d) ordinary wear/tear, mechanical breakdown, electronic data exclusions. STEP 3: If no IM exists, assess exposure — given high-value election equipment in transit between 31 states, IM is likely indicated.

findings.requirement_type: Crime / Fidelity Coverage — Implied by Maricopa Cyber Spec
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa §8.2.13] ...computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: No standalone Crime/Fidelity policy is included in this audit's POLICY ANALYSES array.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.13 includes 'third-party fidelity' (employee dishonesty extending to client property — i.e., County's funds/data) and 'computer fraud / funds transfer loss' inside its Cyber spec. Many cyber policies sublimit these substantially or exclude them. A standalone Crime/Fidelity policy is the proper home for: employee theft of County property, forgery/alteration, social engineering fraud, computer fraud, funds transfer fraud. Whether Run-Test has Crime/Fidelity is unverified.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants 'third-party fidelity' and 'computer fraud / funds transfer loss' inside the cyber spec. These are typically Crime/Fidelity coverages, not pure cyber. Many cyber policies will sublimit these heavily — meaning you might have $5M cyber but only $250K of social engineering or computer fraud. The cleanest fix is a standalone Crime/Fidelity policy at meaningful limits (typically $1M-$2M for a manufacturer your size). Given Run-Test handles voter PII and county election funds may be processed through your operations, this is real exposure.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether a standalone Crime/Fidelity policy exists. If yes, audit limits against: (a) Employee Theft — at least $1M, (b) Forgery/Alteration — at least $1M, (c) Computer Fraud — at least $1M, (d) Funds Transfer Fraud — at least $1M, (e) Social Engineering — at least $250K-$1M, (f) Third-Party (Client Property) coverage — required by Maricopa, must extend to County funds/property. If no Crime exists, place at $1M-$2M minimum given client profile (PE-backed manufacturer, voter data + county facility access). Coordinate with Cyber to avoid overlap and confirm sublimits in cyber are not relied upon for Crime exposure.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Per-Policy RMF Walk Item Coverage Summary
findings.contract_quote: [RMF Umbrella Items 1, 2, 13, 14] Endorsements list / Non-follow-form exclusions / Underlying policies listed / Specific follow form concerns.
findings.gap_description: Comprehensive endorsement review confirms standard Hanover commercial umbrella structure: Coverage A (Follow Form Excess) + Coverage B (Umbrella). Schedule of Underlying lists all four primary policies (CGL, Auto, WC/EL, EBL). Twelve material exclusions reviewed (pollution, professional liability, abuse, lead, fungi/bacteria, silica, discrimination, EBL, terrorism, phthalates, three cyber). Multiple Named Insured endorsement properly schedules LLCs. Arizona Changes endorsement applies state-specific cancellation/non-renewal terms.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella has been comprehensively reviewed against the broker's umbrella checklist. The structure is standard: dual-coverage form (follow-form excess plus true umbrella), four underlying policies properly scheduled, your LLC affiliates correctly listed, Arizona-specific terms applied. The exclusion landscape is the typical Hanover stack with two notable additions in 2023-2025: phthalates (manufacturing-relevant) and cyber-incident (election-PII relevant). All material findings are documented separately above.
findings.recommendation: At every renewal: (1) re-audit against this same checklist, (2) flag any new endorsements added year-over-year (the cyber incident exclusion 475-0661 was new on this 4/1/25 renewal), (3) reconcile Schedule of Underlying with actual primary policy numbers/limits, (4) verify Multiple Named Insured endorsement still lists current entities post any M&A or restructuring.

findings.requirement_type: Civil Code §2782(b) Carve-Out (Sacramento §VII.B)
findings.contract_quote: CIVIL CODE PROVISION: Coverage shall not extend to any indemnity coverage for the active negligence of the additional insured in any case where an agreement to indemnify the additional insured would be invalid under Subdivision (b) of Section 2782 of the Civil Code.
findings.policy_quote: [475-0001 §III Insureds] Standard separation of insureds and AI scope rules apply; no special endorsement is required for §2782(b) carve-back.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.B is a contract-level acknowledgement that California Civil Code §2782(b) prohibits indemnity for the AI's active negligence. This does NOT require a special policy endorsement — it's a contract recital ensuring the parties acknowledge California public policy limits. Standard ISO and Hanover proprietary AI endorsements are written to be consistent with §2782(b) and do not need modification.
findings.plain_english: California has a public policy rule (Civil Code §2782(b)) that prevents you from indemnifying the County for the County's own active negligence — even if your contract said you would. Sacramento's contract just acknowledges that. No insurance endorsement is needed. Your policies as written are already consistent with this rule. Compliance is automatic.
findings.recommendation: No action needed. Document the §2782(b) acknowledgement in the contract compliance file for Sacramento. If/when other California county or municipal contracts come up, expect similar §2782(b) carve-back language — same automatic compliance.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Coverage B Personal & Advertising Injury Limited
findings.contract_quote: [RMF UMB-2] Exclusions and Non follow form exclusions or endorsements that are different, unique to the umbrella and/or broader than the underlying. You must note these.
findings.policy_quote: [§VII.3.i] Coverage B PI/AI exclusions including IP infringement, breach of contract, internet content, chat rooms, etc.
findings.gap_description: Coverage B (true umbrella) limits Personal & Advertising Injury coverage by excluding IP infringement, internet content disputes, chat rooms, and breach of contract. Coverage A (Follow Form Excess) follows the underlying CGL's PI/AI treatment — but if a PI/AI claim is umbrella-only (Coverage B), these exclusions apply. Combined with 475-0661 cyber-content exclusion (already strips cyber-delivered PI/AI), Run-Test's Coverage B PI/AI is significantly narrower than underlying.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella's true umbrella side (Coverage B) is narrower than your primary GL on Personal & Advertising Injury — it excludes IP infringement, internet content, chat rooms, and breach of contract claims. Combined with the new cyber content exclusion (475-0661), if someone sues you for, say, copyright infringement on your election software code or website content, the umbrella might not contribute on Coverage B. Coverage A (which follows your primary) might still pick it up if your primary covers it.
findings.recommendation: Confirm primary CGL's PI/AI form. If primary CGL provides PI/AI without these Coverage-B exclusions, follow-form on Coverage A picks up the gap. If primary also excludes (most do for IP/internet/chat), this is a known gap — manage through professional liability / tech E&O / cyber. For an election technology vendor, IP infringement claims (someone alleging copied election software, defamation through election communications) are real exposures that need a clear coverage home — typically Tech E&O or Cyber.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Possibly Coverage A if primary CGL covers; otherwise Tech E&O / Cyber (separately)
discoveryQuestions: Has Run-Test ever been involved in an IP dispute over election software, website content, or marketing material?
If a competitor alleged your election processing software or workflow infringed their patent or trade secret, what policy would you turn to first?
Do you have content for your website, social media, or proposals that's been reviewed for IP clearance? Many election technology vendors get pulled into vendor-on-vendor IP fights.

findings.requirement_type: Notification of Claim — Contractual Duty (Sacramento §X)
findings.contract_quote: If any claim for damages is filed with CONTRACTOR or if any lawsuit is instituted against CONTRACTOR... CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit.
findings.policy_quote: [475-0001 §VIII Conditions] Notice condition requires Insured to provide prompt notice to Hanover of an Occurrence. Sacramento §X is a separate contractual duty owed by Contractor to County, not a carrier-notice issue.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §X imposes contractor-level claim/lawsuit notification duties to County (30 days from claim, 10 days from service of process). This is independent of carrier notice obligations and does NOT need an insurance endorsement. Operationally, Run-Test must have an internal protocol that ensures (a) any claim received is reported both to Hanover/carriers AND to Sacramento County within 30 days, (b) any lawsuit served is reported to County within 10 days. Same operational protocol applies for any other county contract with similar reporting requirements.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has a contract-level rule: tell us within 30 days of getting a claim and within 10 days of getting served with a lawsuit. This is separate from telling Hanover. You need an internal claim-handling process that hits both targets — your insurance carrier AND Sacramento County. This isn't an insurance fix; it's an operational fix. Most companies handle this via the General Counsel or risk manager.
findings.recommendation: Establish an internal claim notification matrix that maps each county contract's notification window. Sacramento: 30/10. Maricopa: §8.2.15 requires 2 business days for carrier notices. Brief operations and legal teams. Embed into incident response playbook (which should also exist for cyber events given Maricopa §8.2.13's broad cyber spec).

findings.requirement_type: Right to Adjust Coverage — County Unilateral Modification (Sacramento §II.B)
findings.contract_quote: COUNTY shall retain the right at any time to review the coverage, form, and amount of the insurance required hereby. If in the opinion of the County Risk Manager, insurance provisions in these requirements do not provide adequate protection for COUNTY and for members of the public, COUNTY may require CONTRACTOR to obtain insurance sufficient in coverage, form and amount to provide adequate protection.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — open-ended contract right, not addressable by current insurance language.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento reserves a unilateral right to require ADDITIONAL coverage mid-term if their Risk Manager deems current insurance inadequate. Open-ended risk — limits and lines could grow without warning. For a multi-year county contract this is a meaningful exposure: an increase in cyber from $5M to $10M, or addition of a new line (e.g., environmental, fiduciary), is the County's unilateral call. Run-Test bears the premium and placement risk.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has a clause that lets their Risk Manager say at any time, 'we want more insurance.' They can change limits, add new policies, modify forms — and you have to comply or be in breach. This is a typical county contract clause but worth knowing. It means your insurance budget for a county contract isn't fixed; it can rise mid-term. Most counties don't actually invoke this, but it exists.
findings.recommendation: (1) Brief CFO on the open-ended adjustment right; (2) Maintain a line-of-credit or insurance budget cushion to absorb mid-term coverage changes; (3) Build relationship with Sacramento Risk Manager so any concerns are raised collaboratively before becoming a unilateral mandate; (4) Track which other county contracts have similar unilateral adjustment rights — many will. Same review for Maricopa contract.
discoveryQuestions: Has Sacramento or any other county ever invoked their right to ask you for more insurance mid-contract? If yes, what triggered it?
Is there a budget line item for mid-term coverage modifications that counties might require? An election cycle event (security incident anywhere in industry) could trigger sudden requirements.
Have you mapped which of your county contracts have similar unilateral adjustment rights? This is portfolio-wide risk worth quantifying.
